papers.title: Co--dsorption of terrylene and tetrapentacontane on hexagonal boron nitride - towards a two-dimensional Shpolskii matrix
papers.abstract: Organic molecular emitters are promising building blocks for quantum technologies, but their use at two-dimensional interfaces is limited by diffusion, aggregation, and photobleaching. We present work towards constructing an ultrathin two-dimensional Shpolskii-like host-guest matrix on hexagonal boron nitride (hBN) by co-depositing terrylene fluorophores with the long-chain tetrapentacontane in a solution-phase process. We demonstrate that this approach disperses terrylene in a roughly one-nanometer-thin alkane layer without detectable phase separation and allows tuning the emitter density from ensembles to isolated emitters showing characteristic blinking behavior consistent with single-molecule fluorescence. Time-lapse confocal microscopy, autocorrelation analysis, and fluorescence recovery after photobleaching show that suppressed diffusion and stable emitter positions can be achieved in several samples with a tetrapentacontane matrix. Encapsulation with hBN from the top side further improves photostability, with emitters demonstrating long lifetimes despite high photon doses. Successful co-adsorption of isolated emitters and alkane matrix is a milestone towards extending Shpolskii-type molecular isolation to hBN and provides a route towards stable, interface-integrated molecular qubits.

papers.title: Theory of Convective Diffusion
papers.abstract: We obtain a hydrodynamic theory of diffusive-scale dynamics in one-dimensional systems with interacting sound modes in the absence of self-interactions. Chaotic systems generically feature three distinct Gaussian relaxation processes: besides normal diffusion, driven by microscopic noise stemming from fast-decaying non-hydrodynamic modes, collisions between sound modes lead to two additional channels: convective diffusion manifesting as an effective multiplicative temporal noise, and an effective additive noise generated by the surrounding hydrodynamic modes. Our theory also includes, as a subclass, integrable systems described by generalized hydrodynamics, representing a pure realization of convective diffusion. Focusing on convective diffusion, we obtain an exact closed-form expression for the higher-point dynamical correlation functions and contrast their structure with those of normal diffusion. Additionally, we show that in convective diffusion each sound mode features a universal non-Gaussian distribution of charge transfer in its comoving frame, thereby establishing anomalous fluctuations as a characteristic feature of diffusive-scale dynamics in integrable systems.

papers.title: VariaFlow: Uncertainty-Aware Flow Matching for Unsupervised Anomaly Detection
papers.abstract: Reconstruction-based anomaly detection no longer fails at reconstruction. Generative models produce high-quality pseudo-healthy reconstructions, and the remaining difficulty is the step of scoring residuals. The residual between a scan and its reconstruction has two indistinguishable sources, genuine pathology and the anatomical variation that separates one healthy brain from another. Scoring against a single reconstruction treats both as anomalous, inflating false positives where healthy anatomy varies most while small or subtle lesions are lost in the surrounding reconstruction error. We identify the missing quantity as the predictive variance, how much a healthy reconstruction can vary at each location. We introduce VariaFlow, which estimates this variance from an ensemble of mask-guided restorations under an unconditional flow matching prior, each started from a different noise initialization, and which normalizes the residual by the resulting standard deviation. Few-step flow matching keeps the ensemble computationally affordable, and restoring at two spatial scales captures lesions of different size. Across three brain MRI datasets spanning stroke and tumor, VariaFlow is trained once on healthy anatomy and generalizes across all three, attaining the highest AUROC (0.94, 0.80, 0.78) on each and the highest AUPRC on both cross-domain datasets, exceeding the strongest baseline by 37% and 50%. Under domain shift, the same baseline drops by up to 52% in AUPRC, whereas VariaFlow stays more stable and achieves the best small-lesion Dice on all three datasets.

papers.intro:
Brain anomaly detection localizes pathology in medical scans, such as tumors and stroke lesions. Supervised segmentation methods are effective [23, 20, 22, 40] but require pixel-wise lesion annotations and segment only the pathologies they were trained on. Unsupervised methods instead learn the distribution of healthy anatomy and flag deviations from it, reconstructing an input as a pseudo-healthy image with a deep generative model and scoring the residual between the input and that reconstruction. Alternatively, feature-based methods detect anomalies by projecting images into a feature space via networks usually pre-trained on natural images [36, 17]. Recent advancements extend this by extracting representations directly from large foundation models [14, 18, 39]. However, the reliance on natural priors introduces a semantic gap, reducing their reliability in the medical domain. In contrast, reconstruction-based methods remain the dominant paradigm for brain MRI anomaly detection, as they yield intuitive pixel-level anomaly maps that are more suitable for segmentation tasks [6].

Among these reconstruction-based methods, autoencoders [33, 44, 43] learn the distribution of healthy anatomy but output blurry reconstructions, which misses small or subtle pathology and inflates residuals from normal anatomical variation [10]. While Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) sharpen the reconstructions, they are unstable to train and prone to mode collapse [38, 37]. Diffusion models offer superior training stability and deliver high-fidelity reconstructions, but do so at a high cost of many iterative sampling steps [42, 9, 7]. Flow matching models have gained in prominence to address this computational cost by learning straighter generative trajectories [26, 27]. The REFLECT method has recently adapted flow matching to generate pseudo-healthy reconstructions of anomalous scans [8], but it does so in a compressed latent space which again leads to smoothing or even missing of subtle anatomical details or lesions.

We hypothesize that a flow matching prior for efficient reconstruction-based anomaly detection requires the uncompressed input representation, as provided by recent flow priors for image restoration and inpainting [31, 19]. Moreover, we argue that the standard practice of aforementioned reconstruction-based methods, i.e., to score residuals against a single reconstruction, is insufficient. Healthy reconstruction is an ill-posed inverse problem. Once pathology is removed, many healthy anatomies can map to the same observation because individuating structure, such as cortical folding, is underdetermined by the input. The conditional distribution over healthy reconstructions is therefore diffuse, and a point estimate, the conditional mean or a single sample, discards its spread. False positive detections therefore concentrate exactly where anatomy is most variable. Previous works have attempted to suppress false positives using restoration-based Maximum-A-Posteriori (MAP) estimation [15] or by modeling predictive uncertainty to calibrate anomaly scores [30, 16]. However, such uncertainty-aware methods typically rely on heavily modified training pipelines and explicitly force ensemble disagreement [16], assuming that ensembles will primarily disagree on anomalous regions. We argue that for high-fidelity generative models, this assumption is reversed: ambiguous healthy regions inherently exhibit high variance across an ensemble, whereas anomalous inputs are consistently mapped to similar pseudo-healthy reconstructions.

Based on these insights, we propose VariaFlow, an uncertainty-aware anomaly detector that generates an ensemble of mask-guided restorations with an efficient flow matching prior. While pathologies and healthy anatomical variations both deviate from a single reconstruction, only the latter falls within the variation expected across the ensemble. Penalizing the median residual with the per-pixel variance effectively suppresses false positives in healthy regions. We extract these components at both a coarse and a fine masking scale, and fuse them via geometric mean before computing the final anomaly score, thus flagging a pixel only where both scales agree. We evaluate VariaFlow on multiple brain MRI datasets spanning two pathologies, stroke and tumor, and three acquisition sources, BraTS, UCSF, and ATLAS. papers.title: Secure Deterministic Identification with Feedback and Sensing over State-Dependent Wiretap Channels
papers.abstract:
Identification differs from classical transmission in that the receiver determines whether a particular identity was sent rather than recovering a message. We study secure deterministic identification over state-dependent discrete memoryless wiretap channels with private noiseless feedback and a sensing distortion constraint. The encoder has no local randomness and uses only the identity and past feedback. A symbol-wise input restriction guarantees the sensing constraint.
  We show that the secure deterministic identification capacity equals its non-secure feedback counterpart when the admissible main channel has positive ordinary transmission capacity and H(Y|Z,X=x)>0 for some fixed admissible input x. This equality does not require positive classical wiretap secrecy capacity. For achievability, noiseless feedback generates common randomness for identification and enables secret-key extraction by privacy amplification. The extracted key one-time-pad encrypts a short identification tag, whose reliable transmission requires only a sublinear number of additional channel uses. We also present an alternative construction in which feedback-generated randomness replaces the local randomization of a stochastic wiretap encoder.
  We further prove that secure identification capacity vanishes whenever non-secure identification capacity is zero. We also identify a class of channels with input-independent wiretapper observations that achieves full non-secure identification capacity even when the private conditional feedback entropy is zero, illustrated by a binary state-dependent wiretap channel. Thus, feedback can support both identification and secrecy without local encoder randomization while satisfying sensing constraints.

papers.intro:
Identification (ID) via discrete memoryless channels (DMCs), introduced by Ahlswede and Dueck [AhlswedeDueck1989], provides a fundamentally different communication paradigm compared to classical message transmission over DMCs [6773024]. Instead of requiring the receiver to reconstruct the transmitted message, the receiver performs a binary hypothesis test for each candidate identity. When local randomness is available at the encoder, the number of identifiable messages can grow double-exponentially with the blocklength. Hence, the ID rate is measured as 1n​log⁡log​N\frac{1}{n}\log\log N, rather than the classical transmission rate 1n​log⁡N\frac{1}{n}\log N. This setting is commonly referred to as randomized ID. In contrast, without local encoder randomness, deterministic ID supports only exponentially many identifiable messages, and its rate behaves similarly to the classical transmission rate [salariseddigh2021deterministic].

When local randomness is available at the encoder, the number of identifiable messages can grow double-exponentially with the blocklength. Hence, the ID rate is measured as 1n​log⁡log​N\frac{1}{n}\log\log N, rather than the classical transmission rate 1n​log⁡N\frac{1}{n}\log N. This setting is commonly referred to as randomized ID. In contrast, without local encoder randomness, deterministic ID supports only exponentially many identifiable messages, and its rate behaves similarly to the classical transmission rate [salariseddigh2021deterministic].

The central feature of ID is that randomization is so important that feedback can enable double exponential rate even in the absence of local randomness [wiese2022identification, labidi2024joint, zhao2025identification], by making the randomness of the stochastic channel output available to both the transmitter and the legitimate receiver. This common randomness determines the ID capacity and forms the basis of achievability schemes [ahlswedeCai1999, verdu2008information, shemuel2022feedback]. This suggests that the randomness required not only for ID but also for secrecy need not be produced at the encoder itself, but can instead be extracted from the communication process. The main insight of this work is that feedback-induced randomness is sufficient to achieve full ID performance, making encoder randomization unnecessary even in the presence of a wiretapper.

This observation is particularly relevant for practical resource-constrained systems, such as IoT sensors, implantable medical devices, backscatter nodes, and molecular or nanoscale communication systems, where generating reliable local randomness may be costly, infeasible, or insecure. Insufficient entropy can lead to weak cryptographic keys and serious security vulnerabilities [heninger2012mining], while randomness sources are often limited by hardware and environmental constraints [capkun2025security]. In extreme molecular or nanoscale scenarios, transmitters may even lack mechanisms for controlled randomization [nakano2013molecular, sabu2020analysis]. This limitation makes the considered framework particularly relevant to molecular communication, where the combination of post-Shannon communication and security has been identified as an interesting open problem and a promising direction for future research [haselmayr2019integration]. The scenario considered is motivated by integrated sensing and communication (ISAC), where sensing and data transmission share the same physical resources [fettweis20216g]. In such systems, nodes must observe a dynamically changing environment while simultaneously exchanging information, which calls for a joint design rather than a separation-based approach. Existing ISAC studies focus mainly on waveform design and signal processing aspects [sturm2011waveform, bliss2014cooperative, bica2015opportunistic, huang2015radar].

Although information-theoretic studies have characterized sensing and communication-tradeoffs for conventional message transmission [2025exploring, ahmadipour2022information, chang2023rate], secure sensing-constrained ID with feedback in the absence of local encoder randomness remains unexplored. The inclusion of a wiretapper is motivated by the broadcast nature of wireless systems. In particular, identifying transmitted messages may reveal sensitive information about the system state or operational behavior. This issue is especially critical in sensing-integrated systems, where communication signals are closely coupled to the environment. Incorporating a wiretapper therefore captures fundamental security constraints and enables the characterization of reliable and confidential ID under sensing constraints.

papers.title: WorkIng: A Real-World and Synthetic Highway Work-Zone Benchmark Dataset for Autonomous Navigation
papers.abstract: Highway work zones are critical edge cases for autonomous vehicles (AVs), combining atypical geometries and jurisdiction-specific regulations that existing benchmarks fail to capture: real-world datasets lack 360{\deg} multi-modal, full-scene 3D work zone annotation, and no single recorded site can span the layouts and regulatory variants needed for generalizable models. We present WorkIng, a dual-domain benchmark and training resource. WorkIng-Highway provides a 360{\deg} multi-modal work zone benchmark with synchronized 128-channel LiDAR, six RGB cameras, and RTK-GPS across 32 km, yielding 12,000+ annotated frames and 227,399 tracked 3D bounding boxes. WorkIng-CARLA complements this with procedural simulation spanning 24 regulation-aware scenarios across six canonical topologies and six international traffic standards, populated by 100+ custom 3D assets. Benchmarking representative 3D detection and end-to-end planning architectures shows that real-world data remains the primary performance driver, and that scenario-stratified synthetic augmentation improves architectures across 2D recognition, 3D detection, and trajectory planning. Resources: https://github.com/cvims/WorkIng

papers.title: DIFFNAS: Predictor-Free Neural Architecture Search via Diffusion Model and Zero-Cost Evaluation
papers.abstract: Neural Architecture Search (NAS) has advanced the automated design of deep networks, but remains computationally expensive due to reliance on model training or performance predictors. We introduce DIFFNAS, a predictor-free NAS framework that leverages a discrete graph diffusion model guided by zero-cost performance proxies. Unlike prior diffusion-based NAS methods that require learned performance predictors, DIFFNAS conditions the generative process on training-free metrics such as MeCo and SWAP, enabling efficient architecture search with minimal computational overhead. Experiments on NAS-Bench-201 show that DIFFNAS finds the optimal architectures for CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100 (94.37% and 73.51%) without a pretrained predictor, while reducing search cost by up to 17.5x compared to DiffusionNAG. On the MobileNetV3 search space, its accuracy is lower than that of DiffusionNAG. These results highlight the promise of diffusion models combined with zero-cost proxies for scalable and effective architecture search.

Designing efficient neural network architectures plays an important role in modern deep learning, but it remains a compute-intensive task (Peng et al., 2022). Neural Architecture Search (NAS) can automate the process but also typically has high computational cost, with numerous methods needing either thousands of candidate architectures trained or tested (Elsken et al., 2019). Even predictor-based methods attempt to save this cost by learning performance predictors, with those methods also requiring significant amounts of training and adding new sources of bias and error. The fundamental problem is in the search for performing architectures in a resource-efficient way, independent of costly evaluations or surrogate model training.

Existing methods for NAS are broadly classified into predictor-based (Wen et al., 2020; Wei et al., 2022), training-free zero-shot methods (Mellor et al., 2021; Jiang et al., 2023; Peng et al., 2024), and diffusion process-based generative models (An et al., 2024). Predictor-based methods learn a proxy model that approximates the performance of potential architectures, but this lowers search cost in exchange for an increased burden of training and labeled data. Training-free methods employ handcrafted metrics, such as gradient magnitudes or feature correlation statistics, to estimate architecture quality without requiring training, but their performance is task- and search space-dependent. More recently, diffusion-based methods have demonstrated potential in representing the distribution of top-scoring architectures (An et al., 2024; Asthana et al., 2024). Nonetheless, those methods usually need to train complicated dataset-informed predictors for conducting the generative process, rendering scalability and generalizability challenging.

papers.title: Two-loop matter power spectrum from FFTLog and kite integrals
papers.abstract: We present a fast and accurate method for computing the two-loop matter power spectrum in the Effective Field Theory of Large-Scale Structure (EFTofLSS). Using FFTLog, we decompose the linear power spectrum into complex power laws, reducing the two-loop corrections to cosmology-independent massless Feynman integrals of kite topology. A central numerical challenge is the evaluation of these integrals for complex powers with large imaginary parts, where the highly oscillatory integrands make accurate numerical evaluation particularly challenging. We overcome this difficulty using a Mellin--Barnes representation summed over a uniform lattice, achieving approximately ten digit precision even for large imaginary powers, with an error estimate for each integral. The resulting precomputed matrices allow the two-loop power spectrum to be evaluated for a new cosmology in a few milliseconds. Comparing with direct numerical integration, we find agreement at the $10^{-4}$ level relative to the power spectrum up to $k=0.2$ $h$Mpc$^{-1}$ after accounting for EFTofLSS counterterm contributions and FFTLog decomposition errors. The same framework extends to biased tracers and redshift-space distortions, providing the building blocks for general two-loop calculations in EFTofLSS. We make the code for evaluating the kite integrals publicly available, together with precomputed matrices and an implementation for the two-loop matter power spectrum as a concrete application. Our results can be directly incorporated into existing FFTLog-based codes for large-scale structure, extending their current one-loop capabilities to two loops within the same computational framework.

(2011). In a cosmological analysis these integrals have to be repeated at every point in parameter space Cataneo et al. (2017). The most direct way integrates over the loop momenta numerically, with the integrand arranged so that large infrared contributions cancel point by point Carrasco et al. (2014a); Blas et al. (2014); the two-loop power spectrum has been computed in this way with full time dependence, in redshift space and with local subtraction of singularities Garny and Taule (2021); Garny and Taule (2022); Taule and Garny (2023); Anastasiou et al. (2025), and the three-loop spectrum has been obtained Blas et al. (2014); Konstandin et al. (2019). Fast methods instead expand PlinP_{\rm lin} in a fixed set of functions, so that each loop correction becomes a sum of cosmology-independent integrals, computed once, with coefficients that carry all the dependence on cosmology: complex power laws (FFTLog) Hamilton (2000); McEwen et al. (2016); Schmittfull et al. (2016); Schmittfull and Vlah (2016); Fang et al. (2017); Simonović et al. (2018), massive propagators Anastasiou et al. (2024), or a basis optimized for a range of cosmologies Bakx et al. (2025); Bakx et al. (2026c), recently applied to the two-loop power spectrum Bakx et al. (2026d). Bases fitted to the spectra of interest need few functions and therefore few integrals. Complex power laws need more, typically several tens, but they are not tied to any cosmology: the same precomputed integrals apply to any linear spectrum that the power laws resolve, and they also evaluate the integrals of an optimized basis Bakx et al. (2026c).

In the FFTLog approach to loop integrals of large-scale structure Simonović et al. (2018), each power law acts as a massless propagator raised to a complex power, so every loop integral becomes a cosmology-independent massless Feynman integral in three dimensions. At one loop these integrals are ratios of Gamma functions, and the method is in production use Chudaykin et al. (2020). At two loops they reduce to the massless kite integral with complex powers; this reduction, series representations of the kite integral and the full set of two-loop formulas were given in ref. Simonović et al. (2018). The remaining difficulty is the evaluation of the kite integrals at the powers that FFTLog requires. We evaluate the MB representation on straight contours by summing the integrand over a lattice of equally spaced points, and continue it analytically to all powers Czakon (2006). The comparison has to account for what FFTLog computes. The sum of power laws represents the linear spectrum on a finite interval of wavenumbers and continues it periodically outside, and the loop integrals are defined by analytic continuation in the powers, which sets power-law divergences at large loop momenta to zero Simonović et al. (2018); Pajer and Zaldarriaga (2013). FFTLog thus evaluates the loop integrals in analytic regularization. (1986); Jain and Bertschinger (1996); Scoccimarro and Frieman (1996b); Carrasco et al. (2014b); Baldauf et al. papers.title: Resolving the spinon hierarchy of the Heisenberg antiferromagnet
papers.abstract: A local spin fluctuation in the spin-$\tfrac12$ Heisenberg antiferromagnet creates an even number of fractional spinon excitations. We resolve its zero-temperature dynamical structure factor through six spinons directly in the thermodynamic limit. Beyond the established two-spinon contribution of $72.89\%$, the four-spinon response gives approximately $21.90\%$ of the integrated intensity and six spinons contribute a further $4.3\%$, bringing the response to about $99\%$ of both the intensity and first-frequency-moment sum rules. We derive momentum-independent first-moment fractions in the calculated sectors and a general upper-edge law $S_n\sim A_n(k)(\omega_{n,u}-\omega)^{(n^2-3)/2}$ for every even $n$ at nonzero momentum. The rapid growth of the edge exponent explains why the expanding multiparticle bandwidth carries very little high-energy weight, while higher sectors remain appreciable within the lower-sector continua.

papers.title: The Geometry of Multitask Learning: Sharp Rates for Shared Subspace Estimation
papers.abstract: Learning a shared subspace in multitask learning is an important statistical problem, yet exact rates remain poorly understood in many of the formal settings considered in the literature. To address this gap, which arises from limitations of existing upper-bound techniques, we propose a general multitask lemma. The lemma provides sufficient conditions for fast subspace estimation in generic multitask settings, in the form of geometric conditions on the task regression functions and their estimators. We subsequently show that the multitask lemma yields sharp minimax rates---previously unknown---for linear regression and classification in the regimes considered, and rates matching up to logarithmic factors for additive-noise regression.

papers.intro:
Multitask representation learning exploits common structure across a collection of related prediction problems. Rather than learning each task separately in the ambient covariate space, one first estimates a shared low-dimensional representation and then carries out task-specific prediction within that representation. This principle, often referred to as pretraining or feature learning, is now the prevalent approach in modern machine learning: e.g., various downstream tasks such as classification, image segmentation, depth perception across evolving categories of objects all rely on pretrained image features (Radford et al., 2021; Oquab et al., 2024; Bolya et al., 2025; Zhuang et al., 2025); this is the same with modern text analysis and completion (question answering) with LLMs which all rely on pretrained features of natural language (McCann et al., 2018; Raffel et al., 2020; Sanh et al., 2022; Chung et al., 2024). Multitask representation learning also arises in scientific applications in which the shared representation is itself the inferential target. Examples include identifying common functional patterns across neuroimaging studies (Marquand et al., 2014; Mensch et al., 2021; Wang et al., 2026), recovering biological pathways shared across treatment-response problems (Yuan et al., 2016; Wu et al., 2025), and estimating latent risk factors across different financial assets (Lettau and Pelger, 2020; Wan et al., 2024).

These modern applications motivate understanding how accurately a shared representation can be learned from data across tasks. We study this question in settings where each task’s regression function ft​(x),t∈[T]f_{t}(x),t\in[T], depends on the covariates only through their projection onto a common low-dimensional subspace 𝒱\mathcal{V}. In other words, learning the shared representation amounts to estimating 𝒱\mathcal{V} by somehow aggregating data from the collection of tasks. The accuracy of this estimation depends not only on the number of tasks and sample sizes per task, but also on how strongly different directions in 𝒱\mathcal{V} are represented across the task collection. A weakly represented direction can become a statistical bottleneck, even when other directions are well represented. The central question of this paper is therefore How does the geometry of the task collection determine the statistical rate for estimating the shared representation subspace 𝒱\mathcal{V}?

papers.title: PrivacyFlow: Privacy in AI Agents through Information Flow Analysis and Consequence-Aware Risk Management
papers.abstract: Autonomous LLM agents executing multi-step workflows over personal data often misalign with user privacy expectations and leak sensitive, out-of-context information. Although Contextual Integrity (CI) formalizes this problem, existing benchmarks and defenses rarely operationalize CI for realistic multi-step task sequences in evolving environments. In this work, we first introduce agentic PrivacyBench, a benchmark of 5873 tasks in 986 task sequences with dynamic environment updates and CI-grounded allow-sets for sensitive information. We also introduce PrivacyFlow, a defense that separates deliberative privacy planning (System 2) from task execution (System 1), treating each sharing decision as a structured risk-management problem. Before execution, PrivacyFlow traces the provenance and purpose of each planned data flow, models recipient background knowledge, and simulates what external actors could infer. This allows us to model the downstream consequences of disclosure, including inference attacks and context-dependent harms. It then weighs the remaining disclosure risk against task utility and executes a minimized plan, blocks it, or consults the user. Across six models, PrivacyFlow significantly reduces step-level privacy failures and raises the share of completed task sequences without a detected privacy violation by 22--55 percentage points. We further highlight a new privacy--utility--autonomy tradeoff: allowing PrivacyFlow to proactively prompt the user in case of uncertainty can increase authorized task completion at the cost of shifting decision effort back to the user. Our results suggest that proactive CI reasoning can substantially improve agentic privacy and motivate further study of this tradeoff.

Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed as autonomous agents that access user environments and communicate with external services on the user’s behalf. Unlike single-turn interactions, agents act over multiple steps, accumulate context from emails and calendars, and take actions like sending messages or calling APIs. This raises the risk of forwarding legitimately accessed information to inappropriate recipients, as at each step the agent must decide not only what to do but also what information to share, in what form, and with whom (Mireshghallah et al., 2024; Bagdasarian et al., 2026).

We also design PrivacyFlow, which separates privacy-aware planning (System 2) from execution (System 1), to enable agents to reason about contextual privacy and decide on the exact information to share in each case. The main challenge is that no pre-defined rule, norm, or policy can be generic enough to apply to all combinations of complicated contexts and scenarios. Consequently, the agent must dynamically follow a decision-making process that guides it through fetching the right information for the case at hand without oversharing, while balancing utility and privacy with minimal confirmation requests to the user. We solve this problem by framing it as a risk-management task: the agent performs a comprehensive information flow analysis to identify the source, ownership, purpose, and creation context of the data. It then predicts the risks of sharing this data with the recipient, evaluating what can be contextually inferred and the potential downstream consequences. By mapping these consequences through context analysis, the agent translates the privacy challenge into a structured decision-making process to determine precisely what information can be shared, and in what form, to avoid causing harm. This structured reasoning allows us to make privacy-preserving decisions in highly complex scenarios, closing the gap between current models’ strong privacy-reasoning capabilities and weak privacy-preserving behavior. Only when uncertainty remains, PrivacyFlow may also ask for user clarification and confirmation before execution.

papers.title: Cavity-engineered ferroelectricity in SrTiO$_3$
papers.abstract: Interfacing quantum materials with photonic cavity architectures is at the vanguard of materials engineering. The structured electromagnetic fluctuations of a dark cavity environment can renormalize fundamental thermodynamical material properties and energy scales, holding promise to create a rich ecosystem of cavity-induced ground states and functionalities absent in the bare material. However, direct experimental demonstrations that cavity coupling can stabilize or enhance genuinely new phases of matter have remained scarce. In this work, we establish the presence of cavity-induced and cavity-enhanced ferroelectric phases in free-standing SrTiO$_3$ membranes coupled to dark THz-frequency photonic crystal cavities. Using THz spectroscopy, we observe ultrastrong coupling (USC) between the ferroelectric soft mode in SrTiO$_3$ and the cavity resonance. The structural response of SrTiO$_3$ to this USC is measured via second harmonic generation imaging, which reveals a substantial (greater than 400%) enhancement of signal in the cavity environment and a distinct modification of the crystalline symmetry, indicating the onset and enhancement of ferroelectricity. We interpret these observations as resulting from renormalized piezoelectric and flexoelectric couplings, which in turn arise from the cavity-modified dielectric environment. This interpretation is supported with microscopic modeling via DFT-based multi-scale dynamics simulations and by macroscopic Ginzburg-Landau theory. Altogether, our experimental and theoretical results firmly confirm that cavity engineering can indeed be used to create new ground states in materials and enhance existing ones. This work establishes a new paradigm for materials engineering with direct applications for quantum transduction, quantum sensing, and nonlinear integrated photonics.

papers.title: Bridging Scales: Multi-Zone GRMHD-Informed Anisotropic AGN Feedback in Galaxies
papers.abstract: We present a galaxy-scale black hole (BH) accretion and feedback model incorporating results from multi-zone general relativistic magnetohydrodynamic (GRMHD) simulations spanning the event horizon to the Bondi radius. The model replaces a fixed suppression of the Bondi rate with a nuclear-environment-dependent factor, $\kappa^{\rm hot}_{\rm cho}$, set by the local ratio of Bondi to gravitational radius, and distributes outflow mass, kinetic energy, and thermal energy according to the angular structure measured in the large-dynamic-range GRMHD calculations. We apply it to idealized isolated simulations of an M87*-like massive elliptical and a Milky Way/Sgr A*-like galaxy, spanning over three orders of magnitude in BH mass without tuning accretion or feedback efficiencies to match observables. In the M87*-like system, the GRMHD-informed angle-dependent feedback model suppresses late-time stellar mass growth more effectively than the isotropic reference model, despite similar long-term BH accretion rates. Varying the uncertain mass loading of the collimated polar component has a modest impact on BH growth and star formation, indicating that feedback anisotropy matters more than its detailed mass loading. We find that $\kappa^{\rm hot}_{\rm cho}$ varies with nuclear environment and time, yielding BH growth histories markedly different from fixed-suppression models. For Sgr A*, this variable factor yields an accretion rate more consistent with Event Horizon Telescope (EHT) constraints than a fixed, suppressed Bondi model. These results show that nuclear-environment-dependent accretion and feedback angular structure affect BH-galaxy evolution, requiring subgrid models to include more than a universal Bondi suppression factor and a scalar feedback efficiency.

papers.intro:
Understanding how supermassive black holes (SMBHs) are fueled, how much of the gas supplied to their sphere of influence ultimately reaches the event horizon, and how the energy released by accretion couples back to the host galaxy is an intrinsically multiscale problem. Gas is supplied on circumgalactic and galactic scales, transported through the nuclear region, and ultimately accreted on scales of the order of the gravitational radius, while the associated feedback can propagate back outward to affect the interstellar medium (ISM), circumgalactic medium (CGM), and, in sufficiently powerful systems, scales comparable to the virial radius. The feeding and feedback problem is therefore fundamentally bi-directional: the large-scale environment determines the boundary conditions of the accretion flow, while processes operating close to the black hole (BH) determine how much of that inflow is accreted and how much mass, momentum, and energy are returned to the host.

The enormous dynamic range involved has traditionally required a separation between simulations of BH accretion and simulations of galaxy evolution. General relativistic magnetohydrodynamic (GRMHD) calculations can resolve the dynamics of magnetized plasma close to the event horizon and power BH feedback self-consistently, but they cannot ordinarily follow the surrounding galactic atmosphere over their relevant spatial and temporal scales [16, 58, 41, 5, e.g.,]. Conversely, galaxy-scale and cosmological simulations can follow gas dynamics from the ISM to the CGM and beyond, but cannot resolve the gravitational-radius-scale accretion flow. They therefore require sub-resolution prescriptions to connect resolved gas properties to the BH accretion rate and to specify the energetics, mass loading, and geometry of the resulting feedback, with model parameters – often implicitly or explicitly dependent on BH mass – tuned to match observed scaling relations [30, 14, 2, 57, 61, e.g.,]. Prescriptions of this kind are used in major simulation suites [46, 45, 1, 60, 44, 35, 62, 4, 3, e.g.,]. While some simulations [25, 18, e.g.,] have adopted zoom-in methods to resolve the flow down to BH-relevant scales, the outward propagation of the BH feedback to galactic scales remains inaccessible. A central challenge is consequently to replace phenomenological assumptions in these prescriptions, wherever possible, with physically motivated relations derived from calculations that bi-directionally connect the relevant scales directly.

papers.title: Learning Galaxy Kinematics from Spatially Unresolved Spectra
papers.abstract: Galaxy kinematics encode information about the assembly histories of galaxies and the black holes at their centers, motivating the measurement of kinematic parameters for large galaxy populations. In particular, such parameters have been shown to help identify galaxies that host supermassive black hole binaries, a major outstanding question in multi-messenger astrophysics. Yet, inferring kinematic properties from spatially unresolved observations, where distant galaxies appear as point sources, remains a challenge. Spectroscopy can address this challenge because Doppler effects encode internal motions into spectral line profiles. Exploiting this encoding requires knowing how spatial structures map onto the line profiles but this cannot be derived from first principles for complex systems such as galaxies. We present a neural network trained on spatially resolved spectra that infers kinematic properties from spatially integrated spectra, offering two advantages over classical approaches: it learns the kinematic encoding directly from data without requiring spatial resolution and remains effective even when spectral resolution only marginally resolves the lines. This enables recovering the kinematic properties for millions of unresolved galaxies in existing and future surveys.

papers.intro:
Contrary to nearby systems that can be studied through spatially resolved methods, the vast majority of astronomical observations reduce complex, extended structures to point sources, collapsing spatial information into a limited set of integrated measurements. This creates a central inference problem: how to recover the underlying multi-dimensional structure, dynamics, and kinematics of a system from observations that lack direct spatial resolution. Historically, spectroscopy has provided one of the few avenues to address this challenge, using Doppler-induced distortions of spectral lines to encode information about internal motions and spatial structure.

This creates a central inference problem: how to recover the underlying multi-dimensional structure, dynamics, and kinematics of a system from observations that lack direct spatial resolution. Historically, spectroscopy has provided one of the few avenues to address this challenge, using Doppler-induced distortions of spectral lines to encode information about internal motions and spatial structure.

A widely used example of inferring internal structure and kinematics from unresolved observations is the analysis of stellar spectral line profiles [25]. Stellar rotation imparts a characteristic broadening to spectral lines that can be modeled to infer the projected rotational velocity [26, 27, 16, see, e.g.,]. Inhomogeneities on the stellar surface, such as starspots, produce localized dips in line profiles that encode their position and contrast [32, 30, see, e.g.,]. Stellar winds produce the characteristic P-Cygni line profile, where a redshifted emission component and blueshifted absorption component together encode the radial velocity structure of the outflow [8, 23, 19, see, e.g.,]. In each case, knowledge of the physical process allows for the spatial structure to be forward-modeled and compared to the observed line profile.

A widely used example of inferring internal structure and kinematics from unresolved observations is the analysis of stellar spectral line profiles [25]. Stellar rotation imparts a characteristic broadening to spectral lines that can be modeled to infer the projected rotational velocity [26, 27, 16, see, e.g.,]. Inhomogeneities on the stellar surface, such as starspots, produce localized dips in line profiles that encode their position and contrast [32, 30, see, e.g.,]. Stellar winds produce the characteristic P-Cygni line profile, where a redshifted emission component and blueshifted absorption component together encode the radial velocity structure of the outflow [8, 23, 19, see, e.g.,]. In each case, knowledge of the physical process allows for the spatial structure to be forward-modeled and compared to the observed line profile.

Exploiting spectral line profiles to infer internal structures and kinematics requires prior knowledge of the mapping between the physical properties of the source and the resulting line profile. For the stellar cases described above, this mapping is relatively tractable due to the spherical symmetry of stars and the geometrically simple nature of rotation and outflows. Such first-principles approaches become much harder to follow for more complex systems. For galaxies, the vast majority of sources in current spectroscopic surveys are spatially unresolved. However, using such observations to infer kinematic properties is challenging both because galaxies are three-dimensional, differentially rotating systems and because they have more complex and diverse internal structures than stars.

papers.title: CaPtain: A Pipeline for Post-Training Code-as-Policy Robot Agents
papers.abstract: Across coding, web, and tool-use tasks, language-model agents are now routinely trained with the same recipe: supervised fine-tuning (SFT) to learn the interface, then multi-turn reinforcement learning (RL) to master it. Code-as-policy (CaP) casts robot manipulation in the same form, as the policy writes code against robot APIs and reads back the results, so the same recipe should apply. Yet existing CaP agents sidestep training: they either prompt closed frontier models or delegate manipulation to pre-trained vision-language-action models (VLAs) and high-level skills, while small open vision-language models (VLMs) fail outright. We present CaPtain, an open post-training pipeline that turns a small open VLM into a capable CaP agent, with no VLA, frontier model, or privileged state at test time. CaPtain trains and deploys the policy inside CaPtain-Harness, which exposes low-level perception, geometry, and guarded-motion primitives across simulation and real hardware. We first align the base model via SFT on synthetic trajectories generated with GPT-6 Astra, then apply multi-turn RL. Multi-turn RL must credit tens of agent requests, whose physical effects often surface turns later, from a single end-of-episode outcome. We therefore introduce a physical critic that reads privileged simulator state, never seen by the policy, and credits each request by how much it changes the predicted chance of success. Starting from Qwen3.5-4B (0% zero-shot), CaPtain-4B reaches 55.4% held-out LIBERO success after SFT and 73.8% after RL. On LIBERO-PRO, it reaches 78.5%, surpassing several frontier-model agents, and its RL gains persist across three perturbation suites (+17.6 to +21.2 points). Without target-domain training, it attains 83.3% on SimplerEnv WidowX, exceeds frontier models on CaP-Bench, and runs on a real robot after simulation-only adaptation. We release all code, data, and model weights.

Language-model agents have improved rapidly in coding, web navigation, and tool use, and much of this progress follows a common recipe: the agent acts inside a fixed execution harness, supervised fine-tuning (SFT) teaches it the interface, and multi-turn reinforcement learning (RL) refines its behavior from the outcomes of its own interactions [26, 72, 25, 19]. Code-as-policy (CaP) agents [43, 27, 58] give robot manipulation the same form: the policy observes camera images, writes programs against perception and motion APIs, and reads back what happened. Since the program is composed at test time, a CaP agent inherits much of the generalization of the language model that writes it, and frontier models have made this approach strikingly capable. Used directly as a robot policy, GPT-6 Astra ranks above every public entry on the RoboDojo leaderboard [90], and with a coding harness it solves 94.0% of LIBERO-PRO episodes [67]. In practice, existing CaP agents sidestep training, and in doing so hand the manipulation itself to components the agent cannot learn to improve. One line of work prompts closed frontier models without weight updates [13, 39, 93, 50, 40]. These systems come with high finical cost of calling frontier models in each episode [13, 39, 93], cannot be fine-tuned for new robots or tasks, and cannot run on onboard compute. Another line delegates manipulation to pre-trained vision-language-action models (VLAs) or high-level skills. PyRUA trains a 4B coder over a frozen VLA and a motion planner [67], AgenticRoboRL trains a planner around a frozen LIBERO-trained VLA [48], SenseNova-RoboRSI builds a 27B agent around reusable skills and optional VLA calls [64], and Gemini 4 Argon exposes code-as-policies through skills such as grasp and place [22]. In these systems, the code decides which skill to call, but the skill decides how to grasp, approach, and place. Therefore, the agent stays bounded by the data on which the skill was trained, and RL can at best learn to sequence it. Small open vision-language models (VLMs), meanwhile, fail outright when asked to control a robot directly. Applying the recipe at this low level is harder than at the skill level, for a reason that does not arise for language agents. Without semantic skills such as grasp and place, the policy must itself decide where to grasp, from which direction to approach, and when to close the gripper, and these decisions are spread over tens of requests per episode, most of which only perceive or verify. Multi-turn RL must then credit these requests, whose physical effects often surface several turns later, with a single outcome observed only at the end of the episode. Outcome-only RL assigns the same credit to every request, while a language-model critic would have to infer physical progress indirectly from text and images. Robot learning, however, offers an asymmetry that language agents lack: training runs in simulation, where exact object poses, grasp states, and sub-goal progress are known, even though the deployed policy must act from its cameras alone. A critic can thus read the physical state that the policy cannot see, and credit each request by how much it moves the task toward success, while the policy itself still acts from its cameras at test time.

papers.title: Circumventing the Computational Hardness of Computational Arbitrage
papers.abstract: AI model marketplaces host providers with heterogeneous costs and capabilities. These differences create an opportunity for computational arbitrage (Olmedo et al., 2026), in which an intermediary purchases inference from a portfolio of models and resells it to users at a profit. Beyond creating profit opportunities for the arbitrageur, computational arbitrage offers financial value to both consumers and providers and could therefore significantly influence AI model markets. While prior work empirically demonstrates the feasibility of computational arbitrage for small model pools, scaling it to large marketplaces requires arbitrage strategies that are both computationally tractable and inexpensive to identify and deploy. In this work, we formalize computational arbitrage as an allocation problem and prove that it is generally NP-hard. However, we show that the optimal allocation can be computed efficiently under a natural diminishing-returns condition on how model performance scales with inference spending. We further develop a sample-efficient method for estimating model performance from limited data, reducing the upfront cost of identifying arbitrage strategies. Our analysis also yields several economic insights: at the optimum, every funded model delivers the same marginal utility per dollar; arbitrage directs revenue away from providers offering little utility relative to their prices; and it rewards complementary specialization.
papers.intro:
The proliferation of AI models with heterogeneous costs and capabilities makes it increasingly difficult for users to decide which service to choose. Even among models offering comparable performance, inference costs can differ substantially. For example, reaching a 40%40\% solve rate on Terminal-Bench can cost anywhere from less than a dollar to more than $60\$60; reaching 70%70\% can cost from roughly $10\$10 to over $180\$180 (see Figure 1). Such price dispersion creates the potential for computational arbitrage, where an intermediary allocates inference budget across model providers, achieves a given level of performance at a lower cost, and resells it to users at a profit. Computational arbitrage brings broad economic benefits, including lower consumer prices, reduced market segmentation, and easier market entry for smaller providers (Olmedo et al., 2026).

Despite these benefits, computational arbitrage is not yet deployed at scale in AI marketplaces, due to several challenges. First, given model prices and capabilities, an arbitrageur must determine how to allocate an inference budget across models to maximize utility. As the number of models grows, exhaustively searching over possible allocations becomes computationally infeasible. Second, even after the budget is allocated, the arbitrageur must determine the order in which to query models to avoid unnecessary spending. Third, computing an effective allocation requires knowing how each model’s success probability varies across queries and inference budgets, quantities that are generally unavailable and prohibitively expensive to estimate, as doing so requires many paid model calls.

In this work, we address these challenges and show that the optimal arbitrage strategy is both tractable to compute and inexpensive to identify and deploy in large model marketplaces. Our results yield several interesting economic implications. At the optimum, every funded model delivers the same marginal utility per dollar. Revenue therefore flows toward providers whose performance justifies their prices, while those offering little utility relative to their prices receive little or no revenue. This result contributes to the growing literature on LLM service pricing: regardless of the billing scheme used, a provider’s ability to attract revenue ultimately depends on the utility it delivers per dollar. Providers can therefore compete in two ways: by offering sufficiently low prices or by specializing in queries that other models are likely to fail; computational arbitrage hence creates an incentive for complementary specialization.

We then show that whenever inference spending has diminishing returns in log-failure reduction, the objective is jointly concave and its global optimum is computable efficiently even in large model markets. Across four agentic and coding benchmarks, our arbitrage strategy achieves a better cost–performance trade-off than any individual model (see Figure 2). • Deployment order. An arbitrageur can reduce their realized costs by querying funded models sequentially and stopping once an acceptable solution is found. Across benchmarks, our greedy ordering closely tracks the best order found by exhaustive search (see Figure 4). • Sample-efficient utility estimation. papers.title: Construction and Commissioning of a Compact Xenon Gas Recycling System for a High-Harmonic Generation VUV Frequency Comb
papers.abstract: A compact, closed-loop xenon recycling system for application in a High-Harmonic Generation (HHG) Vacuum-UV (VUV) frequency comb laser systems is designed, constructed and commissioned. It consists of three main sections, a low-pressure section (LPS) pre-filtering the gas of particulates, water and hydrocarbons, then a compression station (CS), allowing for a variable pressure of up to 60 bar, and a high-pressure section (HPS) with more filtering, pressure control and monitoring. The system proves to meet all design criteria in gas quality (the sum off all hydrocarbon contaminations up to 120 amu and CO$_{2}$ being below 10$^{-8}$ mbar) and recovery efficiency (>99.8$\%$ for all expected operational cases, neglecting possible geometric gas catcher losses in the HHG laser itself). The operation and results are presented and discussed. Furthermore, the system is compared to the performance of a similar system from which it is derived.

papers.intro:
High-harmonic generation (HHG) is a non-linear optical process that generates odd-order harmonic frequencies of a high-intensity infrared laser that impinges on a centrosymmetric jet of gas or non-linear solid-state media. The laser light generated by this process ranges from the Deep-Ultraviolet (DUV) and Vacuum-UV (VUV) into the soft-X-ray section of the spectrum [6]. Molecular or noble gases may be used, but for most applications, noble gases are more suitable as they are chemically inert and pose no direct threat to mirrors or other optical components. Furthermore, krypton and xenon offer the highest harmonic yield in the longer-wavelength UV range due to their low ionization potential [11].

High-harmonic generation (HHG) is a non-linear optical process that generates odd-order harmonic frequencies of a high-intensity infrared laser that impinges on a centrosymmetric jet of gas or non-linear solid-state media. The laser light generated by this process ranges from the Deep-Ultraviolet (DUV) and Vacuum-UV (VUV) into the soft-X-ray section of the spectrum [6]. Molecular or noble gases may be used, but for most applications, noble gases are more suitable as they are chemically inert and pose no direct threat to mirrors or other optical components. Furthermore, krypton and xenon offer the highest harmonic yield in the longer-wavelength UV range due to their low ionization potential [11].

The xenon-gas recycling system presented in this work was constructed for a VUV-frequency comb to be used for the direct laser excitation of Thorium-229 nuclei to their isomeric state, Thorium-229m. The project aims to excite the transition in a single 229Th3+ ion trapped in a Paul trap and sympathetically cooled with 88Sr+. When successfully excited, this transition provides a possible frequency standard for a so-called "nuclear-clock" with potential relative uncertainties of 10−1910^{-19} or below [4]. An in depth overview over the experiment is given in Ref. 12. The VUV light starts out as an ultra stable IR-frequency comb centered at ≈\approx1040 nm. This comb light is then amplified and injected into an enhancement resonator, where the 7th harmonic output light at ≈\approx148 nm is generated through HHG [18]. The resonator is treated in Ref. 17. Operating HHG-laser systems with krypton or especially xenon is very costly: These gases are scarce on earth and only few companies worldwide extract them; prices are high and volatile. Under typical operational conditions for the laser used in the group, six-digit yearly operating costs just for gas consumption can therefore be expected without gas recovery. A more economical solution is recycling, which must fulfill two essential criteria: Firstly, the enclosed noble gas must remain highly purified, as contaminants like hydrocarbons can lead to mirror degradation and thus a decrease in laser power [5, 3]. Secondly, the system must be as leak-tight as possible to avoid any loss of the valuable xenon gas. Since the freezing point of xenon lies at −-118 ∘C, which is lower than most hydrocarbons, cryoextraction, i.e. freezing-out of other components or contaminants, may be an accessible solution [9]. To return to operating pressure this then either necessitates a compression stage, or liquefaction of the xenon at lower temperatures to generate bottle pressure after the gas evaporates again. Furthermore, HHG is often performed using a helium/xenon mixture to enhance gas flow speed and prevent steady state plasma formation [15]. This is the case for the laser the system is designed for. papers.title: Calibration of Large Model Quantization based on HiFloat4 Format
papers.abstract: Quantization of Large Language Models (LLMs) has be- coming increasingly important for reducing the computa- tional costs and resource requirements for practical deploy- ment.Growinginterestinthisareahasmotivatedthecommu- nity to move beyond 8-bit quantization towards 4-bit preci- sion, leading to the development of customized 4-bit formats such as MXFP4 and NVFP4. Recently, HiFloat4 (HiF4) has emerged as a competitive alternative which adopts a Block Floating-Point(BFP)formatwithathree-levelscalinghierar- chy, thereby achieving a significantly larger dynamic range. While quantization can substantially reduce memory usage and accelerate inference, it frequently introduces accuracy degradation. Calibration is therefore essential for narrowing theperformancegapbetweenlow-precisionquantizedmodels and their full-precision counterparts. Nevertheless, existing calibration methods are mainly designed and validated us- ing integer-precision formats, such as INT4, lacking support for HiF4 due to its hierarchical BFP structure. In this paper, weinvestigatethreecalibrationapproaches,namelyHiGPTQ, HiAutoRound, and HiFlatQuant, to further enhance model quantizationbasedontheHiF4format.Extensiveexperiments demonstratethatallthreeproposedapproachesimproveinfer- ence accuracy compared with direct HiF4 conversion, reduc- ing the gap between HiF4 and BF16 to less than 1% and out- performing the state-of-the-art NVFP4 format across various models and downstream tasks.
papers.intro:
Recent years have witnessed a surge in Large Language Models (LLMs) with increasing model sizes and widespread deployment across diverse applications (Naveed et al. 2025). Consequently, the trade-offs among model performance, memory usage, and deployment cost have received substantial attention, particularly for resource-constrained deployment scenarios (Zhou et al. 2024). As a result, model quantization has emerged as a critical approach for reducing memory consumption and improving computational throughput by converting high-precision model parameters into low-bit numerical formats (Lang et al. 2024). Research on model quantization is mainly advanced through two complementary directions: designing low-bit data formats to improve numerical expressiveness (Rouhani et al. 2023b) and developing calibration algorithms to reduce accuracy degradation caused by low-precision representation (Yang et al. 2025).

Recent years have witnessed a surge in Large Language Models (LLMs) with increasing model sizes and widespread deployment across diverse applications (Naveed et al. 2025). Consequently, the trade-offs among model performance, memory usage, and deployment cost have received substantial attention, particularly for resource-constrained deployment scenarios (Zhou et al. 2024). As a result, model quantization has emerged as a critical approach for reducing memory consumption and improving computational throughput by converting high-precision model parameters into low-bit numerical formats (Lang et al. 2024). Research on model quantization is mainly advanced through two complementary directions: designing low-bit data formats to improve numerical expressiveness (Rouhani et al. 2023b) and developing calibration algorithms to reduce accuracy degradation caused by low-precision representation (Yang et al. 2025).

Recently, 8-bit formats such as FP8 (NVIDIA 2022), MXFP8 (AMD 2025; Rouhani et al. 2023b) and HiF8 (Eric 2025; Luo et al. 2024) have been deployed in commercial products, motivating further investigation into even higher compression rates. As a result, 4-bit formats have emerged as a promising direction for further reducing model sizes. For example, MXFP4 (Rouhani et al. 2023b) uses a block size of 32, representing each element with a 4-bit E2M1 format and assigning an E8M0 scaling factor to each block. Here, in the EXXMYY notation, XX denotes the number of exponent bits, while YY represents the number of mantissa bits. Similarly, NVFP4 (Abecassis et al. 2025) adopts the same E2M1 format for each element, but uses an E4M3 floating-point scale and reduces the block size to 16, enabling a more fine-grained representation. More recently, HiFloat4 (HiF4) (Luo et al. 2026) has emerged as a competitive alternative, which introduces a three-level hierarchical scaling mechanism with a block size of 64, capturing both inter- and intra-group dynamic ranges within the limited 4-bit representational space. As a result, HiF4 achieves a broader dynamic range and higher accuracy while also reducing hardware cost.

While low-bit data formats define the underlying representation schemes, model quantization refers to the process of converting high-precision model parameters, such as FP32, FP16 or BF16, into low-precision formats (Yang et al. 2025). Model quantization can be classified into two categories: Quantization-Aware Training (QAT) and Post-Training Quantization (PTQ) (Zhu et al. 2024). QAT refers to training models with quantization in mind, enabling the models to adapt to the effect of quantization during training. In contrast, PTQ directly quantizes a full-precision model without the requirement for retraining. While QAT frequently achieves better results, its dependence on model retraining requires substantial training data and computational resources, making PTQ a more practical choice for large-scale deployment (Zhou et al. 2024).

Despite its benefits in reducing memory usage and accelerating inference, quantization inevitably introduces quantization error, which reflects the discrepancy between the quantized model and the high-precision counterpart (Sun et al. 2024). To mitigate this error, various calibration techniques have been proposed within the PTQ framework, including GPTQ (Frantar et al. 2022), AutoRound (Cheng et al. 2024) and FlatQuant (Sun et al. 2024). papers.title: HAWC, Fermi-LAT and Chandra Detections of High Energy Particles in the S106 Star Forming Region
papers.abstract: Local star-forming regions have recently been the subject of scrutiny as cosmic-ray accelerators and sources of ultra-high-energy gamma-ray emissions. The Cygnus-X region is one of the richest star forming regions in the galaxy and over the last few decades has been extensively studied. Here we report the detection of a star-forming region located in the southern part of Cygnus-X, Sharpless 106 (S106), using the HAWC Observatory. The S106 region is spatially located near the cataloged gamma-ray source 1LHAASO J2027+3657. In this work, we perform a multi-wavelength analysis of S106, by combining HAWC data with re-analysis of Fermi-LAT and archival Chandra data. We construct a fully leptonic model for the multi-wavelength emission from S106 from a single population of high-energy leptons, with the gamma-rays greater than 1 TeV being produced by inverse Compton scattering of the locally-produced IR photon field from S106 itself. Our models show that hadronic mechanisms are not always required to explain the observed flux from gamma-ray star-forming regions and that understanding the specific details of local photon fields is crucial to modeling the multi-wavelength emission from star-forming regions.

papers.intro:
Recent surveys by Very High Energy (VHE; 100 GeV–100 TeV) and Ultra High Energy (UHE; >100>100 TeV) instruments like the High-Altitude Water Cherenkov Observatory (HAWC) [11] and the Large High Altitude Air Shower Observatory (LHAASO) [24] have discovered a substantial population of TeV and PeV sources concentrated in the galactic plane, but the nature of these objects is still uncertain. Given that these gamma-ray sources emit particles and photons at energies far exceeding those in human-made particle accelerators, modeling the processes that produce their gamma-ray emission can contribute to the identification of new astrophysical laboratories to test the limits of our fundamental theories.

Several ongoing surveys are conducting low-energy investigations of promising galactic gamma-ray sources that lack confident association with known counterparts. Studies over the past decade have revealed that galactic gamma-ray sources can be attributed to a wide range of astronomical phenomena, including pulsars, pulsar wind nebulae (PWN), and supernova remnants (SNR). Despite wide-ranging interest, many gamma-ray sources remain “unassociated”, lacking confident low-energy counterparts. Identifying the low-energy counterparts of unassociated gamma-ray sources is a vital step towards completing the census of extreme systems within our own galaxy.

Whether high-energy systems produce observed gamma rays via leptonic – synchrotron, inverse Compton (IC), Bremsstrahlung – or hadronic – pion decay, proton synchrotron – processes is a particularly timely question, given the recent discovery of high-energy neutrino fluxes from flaring blazars [34], the galactic plane [25], and the nearby Seyfert galaxy NGC 1068 [35]. High-energy neutrino emission requires hadronic processes that produce or destroy leptons, creating neutrinos to conserve lepton number. The identification of galactic gamma-ray emitters as hadronic can help explain the observed galactic neutrino flux.

papers.title: EMT Assessment of SCR and X/R Effects on Current-Priority-Dependent LVRT Response of a Grid-Following BESS
papers.abstract: Low-voltage ride-through (LVRT) forces a grid-following inverter to allocate finite converter current between active- and reactive-current objectives. This paper uses a PSCAD electromagnetic-transient (EMT) representation of an aggregated battery energy storage system (BESS) to quantify how short-circuit ratio (SCR) and grid impedance X/R ratio alter that tradeoff. Active-current priority and reactive-current priority are compared for five paired grid conditions under the same 150-ms balanced three-phase fault, with pre-fault active power approximately 0.84 pu, POI reactive-power exchange near 0 pu, and a 1.0-pu dq-current limit. Fundamental positive-sequence voltage and power are reconstructed from 100-$\mu$s three-phase EMT outputs. Across the fixed-fault SCR sweep, the Q-priority late-fault voltage advantage increases from 0.046 pu in the strongest tested grid to 0.129 pu in the weakest; the weakest P-priority case also shows active-power reversal and a pronounced controller-frequency excursion. At fixed SCR, changing X/R produces a smaller increase from 0.092 to 0.112 pu, mainly through reduced P-priority voltage support. Because the common physical fault also deepens the passive retained-voltage condition as SCR decreases, the SCR result is interpreted as a fixed-fault grid-strength sensitivity rather than a constant-sag comparison. Grid strength is the larger sensitivity in the tested matrix, while X/R remains an additional modifier under the studied fault conditions.

papers.intro:
Transmission-connected inverter-based resources (IBRs) are expected to remain connected through specified abnormal-voltage conditions and provide controlled current response during ride-through events [1]. Once the converter current limit is reached, the controller must divide finite current capability between active- and reactive-current objectives. IEEE Std 2800 uses reactive-current priority as the default balanced-fault ride-through mode unless active-current priority is specified by the transmission-system owner [1]; the P-priority cases considered here therefore represent the permitted alternative operating mode rather than a recommended default.

Prior phasor-domain studies have shown that active- and reactive-current priority can materially change disturbance behavior of grid-following IBRs [2, 3]. Utility-scale BESS work has likewise demonstrated strong coupling among active power, reactive power, converter limits, and weak-grid voltage response [4]. Current-limit design has received renewed attention in the context of IEEE Std 2800 ride-through requirements [5]. Although developed for grid-forming control, related fault-control work has implemented a Q-priority AC current-limiting structure under fault conditions [6]; the present study instead evaluates priority selection in a grid-following BESS. In parallel, NERC guidance emphasizes EMT studies for IBR interconnections, while WECC generic BESS specifications provide a complementary planning-model framework [7, 8].

In parallel, NERC guidance emphasizes EMT studies for IBR interconnections, while WECC generic BESS specifications provide a complementary planning-model framework [7, 8].

EMT studies retain fast voltage, current, synchronization, and current-limiting interactions during fault inception and clearing. Existing EMT investigations have examined current-priority behavior from protection and generic fault-contribution perspectives [9, 10], while phasor-versus-EMT comparisons show that model choice can affect converter fault behavior [11]. Separately, grid-following converter behavior depends on grid strength and network impedance angle [12, 13, 14, 15]. Severe voltage depressions can also challenge synchronization of PLL-based grid-following converters when substantial current is maintained during a fault [16, 17].

papers.title: Control-Layer Interpretation of Reactive Power Recovery Limits in EMT-RMS Model Benchmarking of Inverter-Based Resources
papers.abstract: EMT--RMS benchmarking is widely used to verify cross-platform consistency of inverter-based resource (IBR) dynamic models. This paper examines a 200 MW anonymized IBR represented in PSCAD and PSS/E. The EMT model separates inverter electrical capability from a plant-level power plant controller (PPC) recovery target, whereas the RMS model represents these functions through REECC and REPCA parameters. Directly assigning the PPC target of $\pm 0.2764$ pu to REPCA hard reactive limits is initialization-inconsistent at the original lagging operating point because the initial reactive command is 0.396273 pu. A second, near-unity-power-factor operating point initializes successfully with the same diagnostic limit, demonstrating that the conflict is operating-point dependent. Using the non-conflicting capability mapping removes the original hard-limit conflict, but the benchmark still shows 18.5--30.2 MVAr post-event POI reactive-power differences from PSCAD. A one-at-a-time REPCA $K_c$ sensitivity under matched benchmark initial conditions further shows that RMS recovery is parameter- and limit-dependent: at $K_c=0.05$ and 0.10 the aggregate machine reactive output reaches the configured capability bounds, while $K_c=0.15$ moves VDOWN, VUP, and HVRT off those bounds and changes their settled POI reactive power by 8.94, 18.00, and 3.17 MVAr, respectively. Machine-to-POI accounting further shows why machine-side saturation need not reproduce the POI-level PPC recovery magnitude. The results distinguish initialization feasibility from recovery equivalence and provide a control-layer diagnostic workflow beyond waveform comparison.

Electromagnetic transient (EMT) and positive-sequence root-mean-square (RMS) models are widely used in IBR interconnection studies, including grid-edge distributed energy resources, battery energy storage systems, renewable generation, and large flexible-load interconnections. Recent verification and co-simulation workflows emphasize EMT–RMS consistency because generic positive-sequence models reduce detailed converter, protection, and plant-controller behavior [1, 2, 3, 4]. Related studies have also examined model adequacy and aggregation effects under transient conditions [5, 6]. Complementary work has examined fault-resilient grid-forming converter control and auxiliary battery-energy-storage control for LVRT and load-smoothing applications, providing related examples of converter- and plant-level control behavior in modern IBR applications [7, 8].

Waveform overlay is an important first benchmarking check, but agreement or disagreement alone does not identify whether the underlying control quantities have equivalent physical meaning. A reactive quantity in an EMT model may represent converter electrical capability, whereas a numerically similar quantity in an RMS plant controller may act as an operational constraint. WECC guidance distinguishes plant-controller quantities from converter-level controls and emphasizes that generic positive-sequence models remain reduced-order representations whose applicability requires engineering judgment [2, 9].

Building on verification and model-quality workflows that use prescribed disturbance-response checks [1, 18], the methodological contribution of this paper is a compact three-stage diagnostic workflow that extends waveform comparison by: (i) identifying the control-layer meaning and common per-unit base of reactive parameters; (ii) testing hard-limit initialization feasibility across operating points; and (iii) separating hard-limit effects from plant-controller parameter effects using controlled sensitivity. The distinction is that parameter meaning, initialization feasibility, and recovery sensitivity are evaluated as separate checks rather than treating waveform agreement as the sole diagnostic. The study uses one anonymized 200 MW plant and therefore does not claim statistical generality across vendors, grid strengths, or control structures. Instead, the numerical results illustrate a repeatable diagnostic sequence for EMT models that separate electrical capability from PPC recovery logic and RMS models that represent these functions through generic control blocks.

papers.title: Physically Constrained Kinematic Calibration for High-Precision Robotic Needle Guidance
papers.abstract: Percutaneous needle insertion is a common practice in minimally invasive procedures whose clinical success depends on accurate needle placement. However, achieving the necessary precision is a challenge for manual operators. Robotic assistance can improve targeting accuracy and reduce operator dependence, but residual millimeter-scale errors persist because nominal kinematic models do not fully represent the physical manipulator. This paper presents a robust bound-constrained kinematic calibration method designed to improve positional accuracy for a 6-Degree-of-Freedom (6-DoF) robotic needle-guidance manipulator. The approach uses physically plausible parameter ranges to regularize a compact 19-parameter geometric identification model. By treating these bounds as active optimization constraints rather than mere numerical safeguards, the framework effectively mitigates parameter coupling and overfitting, ensuring highly stable parameter identification. In simulation, the proposed method reduced end-effector Root Mean Square Error (RMSE) from 3.422 mm to 0.690 mm (a 79.8% improvement). In benchtop hardware experiments, the calibrated model achieved sub-millimeter validation accuracy, including 0.865 mm RMSE in experimental trajectory validation and 0.610 mm RMSE in a coordinate-lattice verification task. These results demonstrate that physically constrained kinematic calibration can enhance robotic needle-targeting accuracy, establishing a high-precision foundation for future clinical applications.

papers.intro:
Accurate percutaneous needle insertion is a critical component of various minimally invasive interventions, including biopsies, localized drug delivery, and thermal ablation. Among these, percutaneous thermal ablation for liver tumors represents a particularly demanding application. While ablation serves as a primary therapeutic alternative for patients ineligible for surgical resection [1, 2, 3], its clinical efficacy relies heavily on precise targeting. Achieving complete tumor necrosis requires a strict 5–10 mm safety margin while carefully avoiding collateral damage to adjacent vasculature and bile ducts [4, 5, 6, 7]. Even small targeting deviations can lead to incomplete ablation or severe complications. Consequently, robotic assistance has emerged as a promising solution for reducing operator variability and enabling consistent, high-precision workflows [3, 7, 8].
