papers.title: VoxLution: Evolving Voxels for High-Fidelity 3D Scene Generation
papers.abstract: High-resolution 3D indoor scene generation is crucial for immersive applications such as virtual reality, spatial computing, and robotics simulation. We introduce VoxLution, a coarse-to-fine transformer-based approach that generates high-fidelity indoor scenes with rich details, overcoming the overly smooth geometry typical of existing generative models. First, we generate a low-resolution spatial layout; then, based on this structural information, we progressively refine the scene geometry locally in chunks. Key to our approach is formulating 3D super-resolution as a sequence modeling problem over multi-resolution sparse voxel grids. To achieve this, we introduce a training-free, resolution-invariant tokenization scheme that compactly encodes the geometric information of eight octants into a single decimal number. We formulate the transformer sequence to include multiple resolutions, allowing the coarse layout to guide the generation of fine local details. To ensure coherence across local chunks, we incorporate adjacent chunk boundary information directly into the transformer sequencing. VoxLution achieves scene generation at a finer voxel resolution than existing baselines, demonstrating state-of-the-art performance on standard benchmarks with 59.6% lower FPD and 51.1% lower FID on 3D-FRONT, and 70.5% lower FPD and 73.8% lower FID on Scannet++.

papers.intro:
Generating 3D indoor scenes that reflect the geometric complexity of the real world is a fundamental problem in computer graphics and vision. Many applications in virtual reality, spatial computing, and robotics simulation require 3D environments that match the dense clutter, irregular layouts, and wide variation of object type and scale found in the real world. For instance, immersive VR or spatial computing experiences feel sterile when populated with only tidy, sparsely furnished rooms such as those in synthetic 3D scene datasets, and robotics policies trained in clean synthetic apartments transfer poorly to homes with cluttered shelves or irregularly stacked objects. Real 3D scans [65] capture these properties directly, yet the noise and incompleteness from sensor limits and view occlusions leave them largely untapped for generative learning.

Generating realistic 3D scenes is intrinsically challenging. Scenes vary enormously in spatial extent, with no standard canonicalization analogous to the single-object setting. A good generator must not only capture coherent global structure in scene layouts, but also produce fine-scale detail across furniture and object clutter. Faithfully representing such detail requires high spatial resolution, which can impose significant demands due to the high dimensionality of 3D space, particularly for fine-grained resolutions where the surface represents a small percentage of a full 3D volume.

In contrast, we introduce VoxLution11 1 Project page: daoyig.github.io/VoxLution/, an autoregressive generative model over discrete scene geometry tokens designed to match the irregular structure of scene geometry in 3D space. VoxLution operates over a sparse scene hierarchy, built on a shared, resolution-invariant voxel codebook. Central to our approach is a training-free tokenization that generalizes across spatial resolutions: each voxel’s eight child octants are encoded as a single byte, yielding a fixed 256-entry codebook shared across all resolution levels. We then serialize the multi-resolution scene hierarchy into a single token sequence ordered from coarsest to finest, with coarser levels directly conditioning the generation of finer details, casting scene synthesis as a coarse-to-fine super-resolution task. Our approach natively supports the inherent sparsity and incompleteness of real 3D scene scans, generating tokens only where geometry exists, adaptively omitting empty or unobserved regions, and thus enabling scalable modeling of fine-grained geometry details.

Each new chunk generation is conditioned on boundary voxels of already-generated neighbors, ensuring coherent chunk transitions. papers.title: From Anoxic to Oxic Earth: Detectability of Atmospheric Biosignatures across Stellar Hosts with ELT/ANDES
papers.abstract: Earth's atmosphere evolved from an anoxic, methane-bearing Archean state through Proterozoic oxygenation to the O$_2$-rich modern atmosphere. However, most biosignature detectability studies focus on modern Earth, leaving earlier atmospheric states comparatively unexplored. We investigate how atmospheric evolution and stellar environments influence the detectability of O$_2$, CH$_4$, H$_2$O, and CO$_2$, and their potential to distinguish anoxic from oxygenated atmospheres. We construct two complementary photochemical grids: representative Archean, Proterozoic, and modern-Earth scenarios around the Sun, and four geological epochs (3.9, 2.0, 0.8 Ga, and modern Earth) across FGKM hosts. Combining one-dimensional photochemical modeling, high-resolution transmission spectral simulations, and instrument-noise modeling, we assess molecular detectability with ELT/ANDES under optimistic photon-noise-limited conditions. For solar-host Archean and Proterozoic models, CH$_4$ requires approximately 33 and 42 transits, respectively, to reach the adopted 5$\sigma$ criterion, whereas O$_2$ remains below 3$\sigma$ within the observing limits. Modern-Earth O$_2$ reaches 3$\sigma$ after approximately 38 transits. Across the FGKM grid, O$_2$ does not reach 5$\sigma$ for the 3.9 Ga models. However, For the M3V, K2V, and M8V proxies, modern-Earth O$_2$ reaches 5$\sigma$ in 9, 15, and 20 transits, respectively, whereas CH$_4$ requires 11, 12, and 28 transits at 3.9 Ga and only 2--4 transits across the oxygenated epochs. These results reveal a strong O$_2$ detectability contrast around M and K-dwarfs, but not Sun-like hosts in the YJH bands. Robust biosignature interpretation requires complementary molecular constraints, including informative non-detections, within the context of atmospheric evolution and stellar environment.

papers.intro:
The remote search for life beyond the Solar System is necessarily an exercise in comparative planetology with Earth. Observations of our own planet, from spacecraft flybys to disk-integrated spectra and Earthshine, have demonstrated that atmospheric composition and surface-atmosphere interactions can encode information about habitability and biological activity [67, 71, 38, 59, 65, 64]. However, the modern atmosphere represents only the most recent state in a long evolutionary sequence. Over the past ∼4\sim 4 Gyr, Earth evolved from a largely anoxic world through prolonged partial oxygenation to the O2-rich atmosphere observed today [34, 45, 10, 53]. Evidence for life on Earth extends back to at least ∼3.8\sim 3.8 Ga based on isotopic and geological signatures from some of the oldest terrestrial rocks [48, 18], implying that inhabited conditions existed long before modern oxygen levels were established. In the future, temperate rocky exoplanets in habitable zones will be observed at unknown stages of geological and biological evolution, with some of these exoplanets following evolutionary trajectories that only partly resemble Earth’s. Thus, interpreting every potentially habitable planet through a modern-Earth lens could cause us to miss inhabited worlds with little or no oxygen. It could also lead to false positives if abiotic gases are interpreted as signs of life without considering the broader planetary context [47, 69, 76].

The simultaneous presence of an oxidized species such as O2 or O3 and a reduced species such as CH4 is a long-standing example of atmospheric chemical disequilibrium as a possible biosignature [43, 44, 70, 47, 69]. Its interpretation, however, depends strongly on atmospheric redox state and geochemical boundary conditions [40, 41]. Abiotic processes can generate O2 and O3 under some stellar and atmospheric conditions, CH4 can have both biological and geological sources, and inhabited planets need not sustain remotely detectable modern-Earth O2 abundances [47, 76]. Individual molecules are therefore insufficient in isolation; O2 and CH4 are most informative when considered together and with environmental tracers such as CO2 and H2O.

Earth’s own atmospheric history illustrates this problem directly. The Archean atmosphere was predominantly anoxic, with CO2 and CH4 being the important greenhouse gases and with organic haze expected under sufficiently methane-rich conditions [77, 1, 10]. Atmospheric O2 began to rise during the Great Oxidation Event near ∼2.4\sim 2.4–2.3 Ga, but much of the Proterozoic remained weakly oxygenated with atmospheric redox chemistry influenced by CH4, volcanic gases, and the sulfur cycle [34, 45, 86, 10]. A later rise in oxygen toward the Neoproterozoic preceded the modern high-O2 atmosphere [45, 53]. These stages span methane-rich anoxic atmospheres, intermediate states containing both reduced and oxygen-bearing species, and the strongly oxidized modern atmosphere. They provide useful evolutionary analogues for inhabited terrestrial planets without implying that all such planets must follow Earth’s specific trajectory.

Atmospheric O2 began to rise during the Great Oxidation Event near ∼2.4\sim 2.4–2.3 Ga, but much of the Proterozoic remained weakly oxygenated with atmospheric redox chemistry influenced by CH4, volcanic gases, and the sulfur cycle [34, 45, 86, 10]. A later rise in oxygen toward the Neoproterozoic preceded the modern high-O2 atmosphere [45, 53]. These stages span methane-rich anoxic atmospheres, intermediate states containing both reduced and oxygen-bearing species, and the strongly oxidized modern atmosphere. They provide useful evolutionary analogues for inhabited terrestrial planets without implying that all such planets must follow Earth’s specific trajectory.

The observable consequences of these states also depend on the host star. Stellar ultraviolet radiation controls photolysis and therefore the steady-state abundances of species such as O3 and CH4 [71, 64], while stellar evolution changes the incident radiation field with time [12]. Consequently, similar atmospheric boundary conditions can produce different chemical structures around different stellar hosts. Earth-through-time calculations have explored this dependence from both geological and stellar perspectives. Kaltenegger et al. [38] modeled the spectral evolution of Earth across geological epochs, while subsequent studies extended these calculations across FGKM stars [65, 64]. In particular, Rugheimer and Kaltenegger [66] considered 3.9, 2.0, and 0.8 Ga atmospheres together with modern Earth around an F0V–M8V grid, showing that molecular features depend jointly on geological state and host spectral type. Later high-resolution studies likewise demonstrated that combinations such as O2+CH4 and O3+CH4 can remain informative before modern oxygen abundances are reached [36, 37, 55].

High-resolution spectroscopy provides a route for testing such atmospheric states observationally. At resolving powers of R∼105R\sim 10^{5}, molecular bands are resolved into dense forests of spectral lines whose combined Doppler-shifted signal (at a few km s-1) can be recovered from quasi-stationary stellar and telluric features through high-resolution cross-correlation spectroscopy (HRCCS) [74, 75, 85, 7, 8, 6, 9, 68, 24, 21, 14, 20, 16]. papers.title: Biomechanics do not predict perceptual and cognitive consequences of force augmentation
papers.abstract: Wearable force-augmentation technologies, including exoskeletons and soft exosuits, are being developed for occupational and rehabilitation settings to enhance performance by reducing the muscular demands of movements. Yet enhanced performance also requires users to perceive the environment accurately, adapt to changing conditions, and decide whether actions are worth their physical cost. We used an elbow-assisting exosuit to investigate the physiological, perceptual and cognitive consequences of force augmentation during lifting. We assessed weight perception, adaptation in a volatile environment, and effort-based decision-making with and without assistance. While assistance reduced muscle activity, its behavioural outcomes did not simply reflect this biomechanical change. Assistance reduced perceived weight, but this effect was strongly shaped by participants' initial experience. Assistance also selectively reduced adaptation to changing environmental contingencies. Finally, reducing the muscular demands of lifting did not translate straightforwardly into how demanding the action felt or whether participants chose to perform it: differences in effort-based decisions were shaped by initial experience rather than simply tracking reductions in muscle activity or perceived fatigue. Together, we show that the perceptual and cognitive consequences of force augmentation cannot be inferred from its biomechanical benefits alone. Effective augmentation therefore requires perceptual and cognitive outcomes to be evaluated alongside physical performance.

papers.title: The Evolution of the Circumgalactic Medium after a starburst in DESI Post-Starburst Galaxies
papers.abstract: We present a statistical study of the cool circumgalactic medium (CGM) around massive post-starburst galaxies, traced by Mg II $\lambda\lambda2796,2803$ absorption in background quasar spectra from the Dark Energy Spectroscopic Instrument (DESI) Data Release 2. Cross-matching ~1.98 million quasar sightlines with luminous red galaxies at $0.4 < z < 0.76$ with stellar masses between $10.6 < \log_{10}(M_*/\mathrm{M}_\odot) < 12$ yields ~143 million galaxy-quasar pairs, 50-60 times more per impact-parameter bin than our previous SDSS-based analysis. We stack the Mg II absorption as a function of projected separation and classify the foreground galaxies using mean-field independent component analysis (MFICA), further subdividing the post-starburst population into sub-samples ordered by time since the starburst. The mean Mg II equivalent width declines with impact parameter for every class. Post-starburst galaxies show the strongest absorption of any spectral class, reaching $W_{\rm MgII} = 1.58 \pm 0.32$ {\AA} within 71 kpc, well above star-forming ($0.69 \pm 0.15$ {\AA}) and quiescent ($0.22 \pm 0.05$ {\AA}) galaxies of comparable stellar mass at the same projected separation. Within the post-starburst phase the absorption profile evolves systematically: the youngest systems show the highest, most centrally concentrated absorption and the steepest radial decline, whereas progressively older systems show weaker inner absorption and enhanced absorption at intermediate radii (~300-1000 kpc). Independent Bagpipes star-formation-history fitting confirms that this ordering corresponds to an ageing sequence. We interpret this evolution as the outward redistribution of cool gas expelled by feedback-driven winds, consistent with characteristic outflow velocities of a few hundred km s$^{-1}$, with a residual inner cool-gas reservoir persisting throughout the post-starburst phase.

papers.intro:
Understanding how galaxies regulate and ultimately cease their star formation remains one of the central challenges of galaxy evolution. Since the peak of cosmic star formation activity at 1<z<31<z<3 (Madau and Dickinson, 2014), an increasing fraction of galaxies have transitioned from actively star-forming systems to the quiescent population observed in the local Universe. Explaining this transformation requires understanding not only the processes occurring within galaxies themselves, but also the evolution of the gas reservoirs surrounding them.

Since the peak of cosmic star formation activity at 1<z<31<z<3 (Madau and Dickinson, 2014), an increasing fraction of galaxies have transitioned from actively star-forming systems to the quiescent population observed in the local Universe. Explaining this transformation requires understanding not only the processes occurring within galaxies themselves, but also the evolution of the gas reservoirs surrounding them.

The circumgalactic medium (CGM) forms the interface between galaxies and the larger-scale environment. It acts both as a reservoir of gas available for future star formation and as the destination of material expelled through stellar and active galactic nucleus feedback (Tumlinson et al., 2017; Péroux and Howk, 2020, see review by). The exchange of mass, metals and energy between galaxies and their CGM is now recognised as a fundamental component of the baryon cycle, linking gas accretion, star formation, feedback and quenching.

The exchange of mass, metals and energy between galaxies and their CGM is now recognised as a fundamental component of the baryon cycle, linking gas accretion, star formation, feedback and quenching.

Direct observations of cool gas beyond galaxy disks remain challenging. While neutral hydrogen can be detected through 21 cm emission in nearby systems, the low surface brightness of this emission limits studies to relatively local and gas-rich galaxies (Maddox et al., 2021; Dutta et al., 2022, e.g.). Deep integral-field spectroscopy has recently extended emission-line mapping to higher redshift, revealing extended Mg 2 and [O 2] emission around individual galaxies and in stacked samples out to a few tens of kpc (Dutta et al., 2023; Pessa et al., 2024, e.g.). These measurements provide spatially resolved views of the cool circumgalactic medium that single sightlines cannot, but the steep cosmological dimming of surface brightness restricts them to modest samples and to the brighter, inner regions of haloes. Absorption-line spectroscopy of bright background sources provides a more sensitive probe of diffuse gas extending throughout galaxy haloes. In particular, quasar absorption lines allow the detection of cool circumgalactic material over a broad range of redshifts and environments.

Among the available absorption tracers, the Mg II λ​2796,2803\lambda 2796,2803 doublet is one of the most extensively studied. Owing to its strength and favourable wavelength range, Mg II can be observed over a substantial fraction of cosmic history using large optical spectroscopic surveys. With an ionisation potential similar to that of neutral hydrogen, Mg II traces cool (∼104\sim 10^{4} K), relatively dense gas that is often associated with Lyman limit systems and self-shielded structures within the CGM (Bergeron and Stasińska, 1986; Churchill et al., 2000; Rigby et al., 2002; Churchill, 2025, e.g.). Although Mg II equivalent width is not a direct measure of gas mass because the transition is typically saturated, it provides a sensitive probe of the covering fraction, kinematic complexity and spatial distribution of cool circumgalactic gas.

Large observational studies have established that Mg II absorption depends strongly on galaxy properties. Both targeted and blind absorber–galaxy studies and statistical stacking analyses show that stronger absorption is associated with higher stellar masses, smaller impact parameters and increased star formation activity (Chen et al., 2010; Nielsen et al., 2013; Lan and Mo, 2018; Huang et al., 2021; Anand et al., 2021; Chen et al., 2025, e.g.). These trends suggest a close connection between the cool CGM and the processes that regulate galaxy growth.

A natural interpretation is that stellar feedback plays an important role in shaping the distribution of circumgalactic gas. Simulations predict that episodes of intense star formation drive metal-enriched outflows into galaxy haloes, transporting cool gas to large distances and contributing to a multiphase CGM (Muratov et al., 2015; Nelson et al., 2020; Faucher-Giguère and Oh, 2023, e.g.). However, substantial uncertainties remain regarding how long this gas survives, how far it propagates, and whether it subsequently returns to the galaxy through recycling flows. Observational constraints on these timescales are particularly limited.

Observational evidence for such feedback-driven outflows is now well established. Blueshifted absorption lines and emission-line kinematics reveal large-scale winds in both local and high-redshift starburst galaxies, with outflow velocities ranging from a few hundred to over 1000​km​s−11000\,{\rm km\,s^{-1}} in the most extreme systems (Heckman et al., 2000; Rubin et al., 2014, e.g.). Post-starburst galaxies also exhibit evidence for powerful outflows. Tremonti et al. (2007) identified Mg II absorption signatures indicating cool gas moving at velocities up to ∼1000​km​s−1\sim 1000\,{\rm km\,s^{-1}}, demonstrating that substantial quantities of material can be accelerated during or shortly after the starburst phase. Such winds are capable of transporting metals and cool gas far beyond the stellar body of the galaxy, potentially altering the structure of the circumgalactic medium on timescales of hundreds of Myr. However, the ultimate fate of this material remains uncertain. Outflowing gas may escape the halo entirely, remain suspended in the CGM, fragment into smaller clouds, mix with the ambient medium, or eventually return to the galaxy through galactic fountain flows. Determining which of these processes dominates is crucial for understanding how feedback regulates galaxy evolution and the long-term evolution of circumgalactic gas reservoirs.

These systems have experienced a significant burst of star formation within the past ∼1\sim 1 Gyr followed by rapid quenching, leaving distinctive stellar population signatures that preserve information about the timing and strength of the burst (Wild et al., 2009; Pawlik et al., 2018, e.g.). papers.title: Does Reasoning Make Language Models Agree?
papers.abstract: Language models face two opposing concerns: monoculture, in which models err in correlated ways, and multiplicity, in which equally accurate models make conflicting decisions. The rise of reasoning models has complicated this debate: On the one hand, reasoning may increase model agreement if models anchor on the same salient features or follow similar reasoning paths. On the other hand, stochastic reasoning traces may introduce additional branch points leading to more diverse predictions. We resolve this tension by distinguishing reasoning as an intervention from reasoning as an observed behavior. We compare agreement under controlled changes in reasoning effort with agreement across observed reasoning lengths, measuring both against the agreement expected from model accuracy. Across nine models from two developers and three classification tasks, enabling reasoning increases agreement between models evaluated on the same individuals. Yet the individuals who elicit longer reasoning traces receive less consistent predictions across models. Both patterns persist after accounting for differences in accuracy. Asking models to reason more thus promotes agreement, while observing them reason longer signals disagreement.

papers.intro:
When different models assess the same individual in consequential settings, two seemingly opposing concerns arise. Under algorithmic monoculture, decision makers rely on the same or similar models, potentially leaving individuals unable to escape erroneous assessments by switching models (Kleinberg and Raghavan, 2021; Creel and Hellman, 2021; Bommasani et al., 2022a). Under model multiplicity, similarly accurate models make conflicting predictions, so model choice can determine an individual’s outcome (Marx et al., 2020; Black et al., 2022).

Under algorithmic monoculture, decision makers rely on the same or similar models, potentially leaving individuals unable to escape erroneous assessments by switching models (Kleinberg and Raghavan, 2021; Creel and Hellman, 2021; Bommasani et al., 2022a). Under model multiplicity, similarly accurate models make conflicting predictions, so model choice can determine an individual’s outcome (Marx et al., 2020; Black et al., 2022).

Prior work on language models finds correlated errors across models (Goel et al., 2025; Kim et al., 2025). On predictions about individuals, similarly accurate language models agree more often than an independent-error baseline would suggest, but remain well below complete agreement, an extreme form of monoculture (Gorecki and Hardt, 2025). That study examines base and instruction-tuned models, leaving open how reasoning changes this picture. Does more reasoning push predictions towards greater monoculture or greater multiplicity?

That study examines base and instruction-tuned models, leaving open how reasoning changes this picture. Does more reasoning push predictions towards greater monoculture or greater multiplicity?

Reasoning introduces additional computation before a model commits to an answer, with demonstrated gains on tasks such as mathematics and code (OpenAI et al., 2024; DeepSeek-AI et al., 2025). Its implications for agreement are less clear. Models could converge by attending to similar features or following similar reasoning patterns, consistent with evidence of correlated errors across increasingly capable models (Goel et al., 2025; Kim et al., 2025). Alternatively, stochastic intermediate generations could introduce variability. Questions eliciting longer traces have been found to receive less consistent answers from a single model (Hägele et al., 2026). These findings make both greater agreement and greater disagreement plausible, but concern different forms of consistency and do not settle what reasoning does to agreement between models.

Under reasoning as an intervention, we vary reasoning settings while holding the model and prompt fixed. Under reasoning as behavior, we compare individuals who elicit different trace lengths within a fixed setting. The first analysis measures the effect of enabling reasoning; the second identifies where models disagree. This distinction yields a clear empirical picture (Figure 1): asking models to reason longer promotes agreement, while observing them reason longer about an individual signals less consistent predictions across models. Both patterns persist after accounting for accuracy.

In this work, we examine how reasoning shapes inter-model agreement and individuals’ access to a correct prediction through model switching. Our analysis distinguishes intervention effects from observed associations by comparing the same models with reasoning enabled and disabled, and separately examining how agreement varies with realized trace length within fixed reasoning settings. In both analyses, we measure pairwise agreement and the number of models predicting each individual correctly, comparing both with what independent errors at the models’ observed accuracies would imply. This distinguishes agreement on correct predictions from shared errors that persist across model choices and shows which individuals receive a correct prediction from some, all, or none of the evaluated models.

Enabling reasoning also concentrates individual outcomes at both unanimous correctness and unanimous error (Figure 3), raising the share of individuals misclassified by all nine models by 2.02.0-2.42.4 percentage points. Work on algorithmic monoculture examines shared errors and exclusion when decision makers rely on the same or similar models (Bommasani et al., 2022a; Bommasani et al., 2022b), as well as aggregate welfare losses (Kleinberg and Raghavan, 2021; Kleinberg et al., 2026). Empirical studies find shared failures across commercial models (Chen et al., 2022; Toups et al., 2024) and repeated rejection of applicants when assessed by a shared hiring vendor (Bommasani et al., 2026). Work on model multiplicity studies how conflicting individual predictions, explanations, or other outcomes can arise among models with similar predictive performance (Breiman, 2001; Marx et al., 2020; Black et al., 2022; D’Amour et al., 2020; Ganesh et al., 2025). The normative implications of consistency and divergence across model outputs depend on the decision context (Creel and Hellman, 2021; Jain et al., 2024; Hedden and Raghavan, 2026; Gur-Arieh and Lee, 2025; Gur-Arieh et al., 2026; Jain et al., 2026). Our contribution is empirical: We study how reasoning affects agreement and shared errors.

papers.title: SAR-TS-BERT: Physics-Guided Self-Supervised Pre-Training With Polarimetric Features for SAR Time-Series Crop Classification
papers.abstract: Multitemporal synthetic aperture radar (SAR) imagery provides continuous, cloud-free observations of crop phenology for agricultural monitoring in cloudy and rainy regions, yet high-accuracy classification typically requires extensive labeled samples. Although self-supervised pre-training mitigates label dependency in remote sensing, existing frameworks primarily target optical imagery or generic spatial SAR scenes, underutilizing temporal backscatter dynamics and polarimetric scattering mechanisms. We propose SAR-TS-BERT, a physics-guided BERT-style self-supervised pre-training framework for SAR time-series crop classification. SAR-TS-BERT integrates backscatter intensities and polarimetric ratio features (VV, VH, and VV/VH) with dual-polarimetric Cloude-Pottier decomposition parameters ($H/\alpha/A$) into a six-band input representation through two core designs: 1) a physics-guided span masking strategy (SpanPhysics) that adaptively selects contiguous masked spans based on temporal backscatter change rates to prioritize key phenological transitions; and 2) a dual-branch cross-modal fusion encoder that models backscatter and polarimetric decomposition features through separate Transformer branches followed by bidirectional cross-attention fusion. On independent test sets in Estonia (EuroCropsML) and the USA (California CDL), SAR-TS-BERT achieves overall accuracies (OAs) of 96.78% and 87.29%, respectively, and attains a mean monthly OA of 99.37% on Chongming Island, Shanghai. On the Estonia benchmark, pre-training improves OA and Macro F1 by 1.17 and 1.59 percentage points over training from scratch under full supervision, and by 2.58 and 5.19 percentage points using only 1% labeled data. Incorporating SAR scattering physics into temporal self-supervised pre-training effectively enhances crop classification accuracy, parcel-level mapping consistency, and few-shot transferability.
papers.intro:
Accurate and timely crop-type mapping is fundamental to agricultural monitoring, planting structure inventory, yield estimation, and food security assessment [1, 2]. With the continuous advancement of Earth observation capabilities, satellite image time series (SITS) have become a primary data modality for large-scale crop identification, as sequential acquisitions capture distinct phenological trajectories across growth stages [3, 4, 5]. Among multi-source remote sensing modalities, synthetic aperture radar (SAR) provides all-weather, day-and-night imaging that bridges observation gaps caused by persistent cloud cover in optical time series [6, 7]. In particular, the Sentinel-1 mission delivers open-access C-band dual-polarimetric SAR imagery with high revisit frequency, establishing a reliable data source for operational multitemporal crop monitoring [1, 8].

In particular, the Sentinel-1 mission delivers open-access C-band dual-polarimetric SAR imagery with high revisit frequency, establishing a reliable data source for operational multitemporal crop monitoring [1, 8].

Effective representation learning for SAR time-series crop classification relies on both temporal dynamics and physical scattering properties. While deep learning models extract temporal crop signatures in an end-to-end manner, achieving high accuracy typically demands extensive labeled samples. Because field surveys and visual interpretation are costly and labor-intensive, ground-truth labels remain scarce across many geographical regions and minor crop types [5, 9]. Self-supervised learning (SSL) mitigates this annotation bottleneck by formulating pretext tasks on unlabeled data, demonstrating strong transferability in optical SITS and multimodal remote sensing [5, 10, 11]. Concurrently, multitemporal SAR observations encode rich physical scattering information beyond raw amplitude. Co-polarized (VV) and cross-polarized (VH) channels record backscatter responses across orthogonal polarization states, whereas polarimetric decomposition parameters characterize the underlying scattering mechanisms of vegetation canopies and soil surfaces. In the dual-polarimetric Cloude–Pottier H/α/AH/\alpha/A decomposition, polarimetric entropy (HH), mean scattering angle (α\alpha), and anisotropy (AA) quantify scattering randomness, the transition between co- and cross-polarized dominant scattering mechanisms, and the relative contrast between secondary and primary scattering components, respectively. These polarimetric descriptors complement backscatter intensity and separate crop types that exhibit similar amplitude trajectories but distinct structural scattering mechanisms [12, 6, 13, 14].

Existing studies on SAR and SITS crop classification have explored diverse modeling paradigms. Supervised machine learning and deep sequence models typically ingest multitemporal VV, VH, and VV/VH series using Random Forests (RF), recurrent neural networks (RNNs), temporal convolutional networks (TCNs), or self-attention mechanisms to model crop growth dynamics [1, 7, 15]. Several works further incorporate polarimetric covariance matrices or decomposition features to enhance sensitivity to canopy scattering structures [13, 14]. In self-supervised pre-training, SITS-BERT introduced BERT-style masked reconstruction to optical satellite time series, SatMAE extended masked autoencoders (MAE) to multispectral and temporal dimensions, and Presto and CROMA investigated multi-sensor and radar–optical representation learning [5, 10, 9, 11]. Meanwhile, SAR-oriented foundation models such as SARATR-X, SAR-W-MixMAE, and SARMAE have advanced self-supervised learning for SAR imagery [16, 17, 18]. papers.title: Locality-Controlled Out-of-Distribution Guidance for Robust Regulatory DNA Sequence Design
papers.abstract: Designing regulatory DNA sequences for targeted gene-expression control is an important challenge. Recent approaches frame this task as property-conditioned generation, where diffusion models trained on natural sequences are guided toward high predicted activity through reward-based fine-tuning or sampling-time guidance. We show that single-reward evaluation can obscure reward-hacking behavior. By decomposing evaluation into property, novelty, and plausibility, we identify an empirically underexplored region of the evaluation space in which all three objectives are satisfied, but no existing baseline succeeds. We postulate that this gap arises because prior methods treat guidance primarily as a matter of magnitude. In regulatory DNA, however, sequence grammar is spatially nonuniform: motif positions are sensitive to perturbation, while background regions allow more exploration. We therefore propose LOCOGEN by reformulating guidance as a problem of locality. LOCOGEN learns an invariant motif mask through sequence-level invariance learning to protect motif positions, while applying OOD damping only to background positions. It operates at sampling time on a frozen diffusion backbone, without retraining the backbone. Across HepG2, K562, and SK-N-SH, LOCOGEN reaches this previously underexplored region of the property-novelty-plausibility space. Code is available at https://github.com/Lotfollahi-lab/LocoGen.

Diffusion models are powerful generative models used in many domains, including images, language, molecules, and biological sequences. Beyond unconditional generation, recent work increasingly focuses on property-conditioned generation, such as generating regulatory DNA sequences that optimize a target property (e.g. gene expression). These advances make diffusion models useful for de novo regulatory DNA design, where candidate sequences can be generated and tested in a lab-in-the-loop setting.

We argue that the generated candidates must satisfy three axes simultaneously: (i) high target property, (ii) novelty, and (iii) plausibility —preservation of the natural grammar of regulatory DNA (e.g. motif usage diversity/density). No single axis suffices. High property without plausibility fails to reproduce in the wet lab; high novelty without plausibility drifts off the functional manifold; high property without novelty merely reproduces the training distribution. Only when all three axes are jointly satisfied is a candidate worth its wet-lab budget.

Moreover, their apparent property gains often arise not from targeted regulatory improvement, but from distortions of regulatory motif structure, exposing a common limitation of existing guidance methods (§5.3).

This is problematic because regulatory DNA grammar is positional: motif sites are highly constrained, whereas intervening background regions are more permissive. Thus, in the property–novelty–plausibility design space, current baselines fall short of the desired regime: high activity on both readouts, high novelty, and low compositional deviation. We call this unoccupied region the empty corner, and ask whether guidance can shift the empirical trade-off landscape toward it.

papers.title: Existence and uniqueness of the dual solution for obstacle problems in the space BV
papers.abstract: We consider the variational problem of minimizing the multiple integral $\int_\Omega f(\nabla u) \, dx$ with a convex density $f$ being of linear growth among functions $u$: $\Omega \to \mathbb{R}$ satisfying the Dirichlet boundary condition $u = u_0$ on $\partial\Omega$ and for which $u \ge \Psi$ holds throughout the domain $\Omega$. We prove that the dual problem has a unique solution. This result is extended to the case of interior obstacle problems, where the validity of $u \ge \Psi$ is only required on a subset $E$ of $\Omega$. Moreover, we discuss the vectorial setting, i.e. the case of functions $u$: $\Omega \to \mathbb{R}^N$, $N > 1$, combined with the additional condition $u(\Omega) \subset A$ for a closed convex set $A \subset \mathbb{R}^N$, again showing the existence and the uniqueness of the associated dual solution.

papers.title: Type classifiers
papers.abstract:
We extend dependent type theory by type classifiers and construct an interpretation in the category of contextual categories with families. Type classifiers extend contexts by type variables, complementing the usual context extensions by term variables of specified types. This allows statements with arbitrary type parameters to be formulated without assuming a universe.
  We show that substituting isomorphic types induces isomorphisms between the resulting types even in extensional type theory, giving an analogue of the invariance supplied by the univalence axiom in homotopy type theory. Omitting function types from the theory, so that all type formers are covariant, extends this naturality to arbitrary, possibly noninvertible maps.
papers.intro:
Many mathematical assertions involve a free type parameter. A theorem about all groups, for example, must quantify over all possible carrier types. In dependent type theory, such quantification is usually expressed using universe types, whose elements encode types. This approach works well in practice, but it has limitations.

Girard’s paradox rules out a universe that contains itself. We can thus either restrict the theorem to small types, those classified by a chosen universe, or introduce an infinite hierarchy U0∈U1∈⋯∈Uℓ∈⋯U_{0}\in U_{1}\in\cdots\in U_{\ell}\in\cdots and use universe polymorphism to quantify over its levels ℓ\ell. But universe polymorphism only shifts the quantification problem, since types quantifying over the whole indexed hierarchy need not belong to any of its universes. Such types can be interpreted in a larger universe U∞U_{\infty}, but this universe then lies outside the hierarchy over which we quantified. The quantification still fails to cover all types of the enlarged theory.

It can be specialized by substitution to any particular group. The theorem is formulated in this extended context, rather than as a dependent product over a universe in the empty context.

In particular, sections correspond to objects of the base topos. This similarly permits reasoning about arbitrary objects without requiring an internal universe object classifying them.

papers.title: Turbulence on Hybrid Lattices: regular grids meet self similar cascade models
papers.abstract: Turbulent cascades in high Reynolds number regimes span many decades in scale, which can be challenging for numerical simulations. Cascade models that use logarithmic discretization can help, but these have limited capabilities to describe spatial structures or real space details. Hybrid Lattices (HLs) are proposed in order to provide a novel framework to investigate turbulent cascades in Fourier space, combining regular grids and cascade models based on logarithmic discretisations. The approach consists of a regular spectral region, capable of resolving large scale coherent structures, that is extended in a recurrent, asymptotically self similar fashion, spanning many decades in scale. The idea comes from shell models and their extensions, namely the logarithmic lattices, the nested polyhedra models or the spiral chain models. The logarithmic spacing factor of those models, such as the golden ratio, typically prevents interactions between a regular grid and a self similar model. HLs are constructed by expanding a regular region in Fourier space through recurrence relations (e.g. the Fibonacci recurrence relation), generating an asymptotically logarithmic lattice where Cartesian components remain integer multiples of the regular Fourier space grid spacing. This way, the resulting grid preserves triadic interactions linking regular and recurrent regions, allowing energy transfer across these different regions. However, the sharp reduction in triads connecting the two regions creates a bottleneck effect, and in order to address this issue, a region of ghost points at the boundary had to be introduced, efficiently allowing the flux to leak into the recurrent part. The HL framework is then tested for the one dimensional Burgers equation, and for two dimensional incompressible Navier Stokes turbulence.

papers.title: Chronos-2: A foundation model for multivariate time series forecasting
papers.abstract: Accurate forecasting with uncertainty quantification is critical in a variety of scientific applications ranging from epidemiology and economics to energy systems and earth sciences. Yet most forecasting models still need to be developed and trained separately for each domain-specific dataset. Time series foundation models (TSFMs) aim to remove this limitation and enable the application of the same model across domains through large-scale pretraining. However, most existing TSFMs treat each time series independently and therefore cannot model interactions among time series and external drivers. Here, we introduce Chronos-2, a foundation model for zero-shot forecasting that models the interactions between multivariate time series and heterogeneous covariates, which commonly arise in scientific applications. The model infers relationships among time series directly from historical context and generates probabilistic forecasts without task-specific treatment. Across various benchmarks, Chronos-2 achieves state-of-the-art accuracy on average by improving skill scores by 5.2 percentage points relative to the strongest baselines and increasing win rates by 10 percentage points. Chronos-2 is also computationally efficient, generating forecasts for 100 time series in under one second on a single mid-range GPU, 50x and 1000x faster end-to-end than the best task-specific point and probabilistic forecasters, respectively. In addition, we demonstrate its effectiveness in diverse scientific settings -- including infectious-disease forecasting, macroeconomic modeling, carbon-flux prediction, and runoff simulation -- where the model matches or surpasses specialized methods developed for each domain. These results show that a single pretrained model can capture structure shared across temporal systems.

Many natural and human-centric systems evolve as coupled processes. For example, epidemics spread across interconnected populations (Vespignani et al., 2020), economic indicators co-evolve through complex causal relationships (Sims, 1980), ecosystems exchange energy and carbon through linked feedback systems (Reichstein et al., 2019), and weather events drive river runoff across hydrological basins (Beven, 2012). These phenomena are typically observed as collections of time series, whose joint evolution encodes the underlying dynamics of the system. Accurate forecasting of this temporal data is central to decision-making across disciplines ranging from public health to macroeconomics to energy systems to earth sciences.

For example, epidemics spread across interconnected populations (Vespignani et al., 2020), economic indicators co-evolve through complex causal relationships (Sims, 1980), ecosystems exchange energy and carbon through linked feedback systems (Reichstein et al., 2019), and weather events drive river runoff across hydrological basins (Beven, 2012). These phenomena are typically observed as collections of time series, whose joint evolution encodes the underlying dynamics of the system. Accurate forecasting of this temporal data is central to decision-making across disciplines ranging from public health to macroeconomics to energy systems to earth sciences.

Despite decades of progress, forecasting approaches remain largely application-specific due to the heterogeneity of temporal patterns and task characteristics — including varying granularities, context lengths, missing values, and diverse multivariate interactions, both among targets (the primary variables to be forecast) and with external covariates (auxiliary variables that provide predictive context). Classical statistical models (Hyndman & Athanasopoulos, 2018) effectively capture simple temporal structure, but struggle to leverage large-scale datasets or jointly model many related variables. Modern machine learning methods (Salinas et al., 2020; Lim et al., 2021; Nie et al., 2023) can represent more complex dynamics, yet typically require task-specific training and careful tuning for each dataset. In contrast, recent time series foundation models (TSFMs) enable zero-shot forecasting on unseen datasets through large-scale pretraining (Ansari et al., 2024a; Das et al., 2024; Woo et al., 2024; Cohen et al., 2025). However, most TSFMs still treat each time series in isolation (Ansari et al., 2024a; Das et al., 2024), which prevents them from capturing the multivariate interactions that characterize real-world systems. While some recent TSFMs have attempted multivariate pretraining (Woo et al., 2024; Ekambaram et al., 2024; Taga et al., 2025), none have demonstrated effective zero-shot multivariate forecasting with covariates.

To address the aforementioned limitations, we introduce Chronos-2, a multivariate foundation model that forecasts collections of time series in a zero-shot manner. Central to our approach is in-context learning (ICL): rather than fitting parameters separately for each task, Chronos-2 infers multivariate dependencies directly from historical context at inference time. This capability is enabled by two key design choices: a novel group-attention mechanism and a diverse synthetic multivariate pretraining corpus. The group-attention mechanism enables information aggregation across arbitrary sets of target time series and heterogeneous covariates, which supports their joint forecasting. The synthetic pretraining corpus exposes the model to diverse instantaneous and lagged multivariate dependencies, encouraging generalization across domains.

papers.title: Near-Optimal Second-Order Convex Finite-Sum Optimization under Individual Smoothness
papers.abstract: We study the stochastic second-order oracle complexity of solving smooth convex finite-sum optimization with $n$ components. Very recently, Tsedenov \& Kovalev (2026) showed that the minimax optimal complexity under averaged smoothness and convexity is $\tilde{\Theta}(n + n^{6/7} \epsilon^{-2/7})$ by establishing nearly matching upper and lower bounds. In this paper, we show that individual smoothness and convexity provably enable further acceleration, where the lower complexity bound is $\Omega(n+ n^{5/7} \epsilon^{-2/7})$ under this stronger assumption. Then, by establishing a novel second-order self-bounding inequality, we design a new Taylor-corrected lazy Newton method, which can lead to a better complexity of $\tilde{\mathcal{O}}(n + n^{5/7} \epsilon^{-2/7})$ by applying the optimal Monteiro-Svaiter acceleration, matching our lower bound up to only logarithmic factors.

papers.title: Stochastic Rayleigh-Ritz Ascent: Global Linear Convergence under a Spectral Gap
papers.abstract: We consider the adjoint-free random-plane iteration algorithm for finding the top eigenvector of a matrix proposed in (SIAM J. Matrix Anal. Appl. 47 (2026), 1349-1374). Unlike standard methods such as the power method or gradient descent, the above algorithm lacked linear convergence guarantees in the presence of a spectral gap. In this paper, we establish explicit spectral-gap-dependent global linear convergence rates in expectation, providing quantitative guarantees for the empirically observed convergence.

papers.title: Observation of light-induced Haldane gap in graphene
papers.abstract: Symmetry and topology, encoded in electronic wavefunctions, play a central role in the electronic properties and emergent phenomena of quantum materials. While these properties are conventionally determined by the equilibrium Hamiltonian, strong optical fields offer a fundamentally different route by reshaping the Hamiltonian on ultrafast timescales, turning symmetry and topology into dynamically controllable degrees of freedom. Graphene provides a paradigmatic platform for realizing this concept, where circularly polarized light has long been predicted to dynamically break time-reversal symmetry (TRS) and open a topologically nontrivial gap at the Dirac point. Despite extensive experimental efforts, direct observation of this Dirac gap-the defining spectroscopic signature of the dynamical TRS-breaking induced topological phase-has remained missing. Here we directly observe this light-induced Dirac gap in monolayer graphene. Time- and angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy reveals that the gap emerges simultaneously with the optical field and exclusively under circularly polarized driving, directly linking its opening to dynamical TRS breaking. Together with Floquet theory, we identify the gap with a light-induced Haldane mass and reveal the associated nontrivial Floquet Berry curvature and Chern topology. By demonstrating dynamical TRS breaking in a prototypical non-magnetic material, our results establish optical driving as a route to ultrafast engineering of symmetry and topology, opening opportunities for dynamically tunable quantum matter beyond equilibrium.

papers.title: 6G-Enabled Cooperative Connected and Automated Mobility: Are We There Yet?
papers.abstract: Connected, cooperative, and automated mobility (CCAM) is a key enabler of future intelligent transportation systems, requiring seamless integration of communication, sensing, computing, and automation technologies. This paper surveys the state of the art in CCAM, focusing on key use cases and performance indicators, enabling technologies, system architectures, and standardization and regulatory developments relevant to large-scale deployment. Particular attention is given to cooperative perception, collective awareness, artificial intelligence and machine learning as fundamental building blocks of future CCAM ecosystems. The paper further identifies major research challenges related to scalability, interoperability, and real-time operation in highly dynamic mobile environments. Finally, it outlines future research directions toward achieving large-scale, safe, and resilient CCAM systems supported by next-generation communication networks.

Although CCAM is a cornerstone of further urban digital development, in accordance with sustainable development goals,22 2 https://sdgs.un.org/goals current systems struggle with fragmented sensing, limited field of view, and lack of coordination across agents, hindering the scalability and reliability of safety-critical functions. A possible game changer at the heart of CCAM is represented by CP [2], which refers to the ability of vehicles and infrastructure to share sensor data and contextual information in real time. This enables a collective awareness of the traffic environment far beyond what individual entities can achieve alone, and also incorporating the non-connected actors in the network, at least from the perspective of sensing/detecting them. Recent work has further demonstrated the benefits of infrastructure-assisted cooperative perception. For example, Meng and Zhao [3] proposed VI-BEV, a vehicle–infrastructure collaborative perception framework that fuses sensing information from vehicles and RSU to improve 3D object detection in bird’s-eye-view representations. By leveraging complementary sensing perspectives, the framework extends perception coverage and mitigates occlusions, thereby enhancing environmental awareness beyond the capabilities of standalone perception systems.

Thanks to the addition of CP, CCAM can address today’s most pressing transportation challenges while unlocking a future of safer, greener, and more integrated and efficient mobility ecosystems. The potential impact of CCAM and CP is revolutionary, particularly when applied to the following key use case groups: (i) Vulnerable road user (VRU) protection, based on CP-enabled detection and localization of non-connected users such as pedestrians and cyclists [4, 5]. Shared perception data from vehicles or infrastructure allows for early warning and proactive collision avoidance, even in occluded or low-visibility conditions; (ii) Platooning and chauffeuring, meaning tightly coupled vehicle groups acting as an unique convoy. This implies reduced inter-vehicle gaps, improved aerodynamics, and fuel savings, thus enhancing efficiency together with safety [6]; (iii) Intersection Management, which benefits from real-time communications-enabled exchange of positions, intentions, and priorities between vehicles and infrastructure. CCAM enables in this scenario smoother merging, conflict-free crossing, and reduced delay, which in turn leads to improved traffic flow capacity, energy efficiency, and safety [7]; (iv) Tele-operated driving (ToD), which refers to the remote operation of vehicles by remote (human or otherwise) drivers located outside the vehicle itself [8]. This scenario is particularly relevant in situations where full autonomy is not feasible, and enables human oversight and intervention in real time, bridging the gap between the current driver-centric and the future fully automated mobility; and (v) Multimodal transportation, where road traffic interacts with public transport, micro-mobility, and logistics services. In this use case, CCAM can facilitate safe and efficient coordination, thus supporting smoother integration of various transport modes and optimized infrastructure usage.

Current wireless technologies may not be sufficient to fully enable CCAM, with CP at its heart and with a requirement to enable the listed challenging use cases. Therefore, work is being done to improve the enabling technologies. This in part refers to the communication techniques improvements, for example including FD (FD), NOMA, or RIS (RIS) solutions, and utilizing additional frequency bands (e.g., sub-THz bands). Furthermore, enabling CCAM will necessitate going beyond pure communications to include aspects such as ISAC (ISAC), AI (AI) and ML (ML), DT, and network virtualization, which might need to be considered from the beginning of the system design if the promise of CCAM is to be fulfilled.

papers.title: The assembly of dusty galaxies at $z \geq 4$: grain growth and the evolutionary origin of the dust-to-stellar-mass scatter
papers.abstract: Understanding dust evolution is essential for interpreting the properties of galaxies across cosmic time. Nearby galaxies have revealed a detailed picture of dust enrichment, but whether the same picture applies in the early Universe remains unclear. Here we explore the origin of interstellar dust in simulated galaxies at $z \sim 5$. Starting from the dust-to-stellar mass relation, we select five simulated star-forming galaxies with $SFR> 1 M_\odot yr^{-1}$ and $ log(M_\star/M_\odot) > 8$. We focus on three low-mass systems with comparable stellar masses ($log(M_\star/M_\odot) \sim 8.7$) but significantly different dust masses ($log(M_{\rm dust}/M_\odot) \sim 5.1-6.2$), to investigate the origin of the scatter in the relation. Our analysis combines outputs from the cosmological hydrodynamical simulation dustyGadget, a semi-analytical model for stellar dust production, and radiative-transfer post-processing with SKIRT. We confirm that stellar dust production alone reproduces only the low-dust branch of the relation. Grain growth is required to recover both its S-shape and the observed scatter, as established for nearby galaxies. The transition to efficient grain growth occurs at lower metallicity than locally, consistent with the denser interstellar medium of high-redshift systems. Differences in dust content reflect different stages of galaxy assembly. Progressively longer star formation histories lead to greater chemical enrichment and denser ISM, promoting increasingly efficient grain growth. We therefore identify the assembly stage as the key regulator of dust growth at high redshift. Mock observations show that JWST multi-band imaging can reveal the structural diversity of galaxies within the scatter, although the reconstruction of clumpy morphologies may remain incomplete. Their dust continuum emission remains below the sensitivity of current ALMA continuum surveys.

A detailed exploration of the first low-mass galaxies has long remained challenging, primarily due to their intrinsic faintness. The advent of high-sensitivity facilities has opened a new observational window, allowing the interstellar medium (ISM) to be probed with unprecedented detail even at high redshift. In particular, multi-wavelength observations with the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) and Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimiter Array (ALMA) are rapidly reshaping our view of early galaxy evolution (see e.g. Herrera-Camus et al. 2026 and Curti 2026 for recent reviews). JWST observations have revealed that the mass–metallicity relation was already established within the first billion years (Nakajima et al., 2023; Curti et al., 2024; Chemerynska et al., 2024), implying rapid metal production, while the large scatter around the fundamental metallicity relation suggests that many high-redshift galaxies are still far from equilibrium, undergoing stochastic gas accretion and enrichment processes (“chemical chaos”, see e.g. Heintz et al. 2023; Curti et al. 2024).

papers.title: OASIS I: Spectroscopy of Mini-Quenched and Lulling Galaxies Constrains the Quiet Side of Bursty Star Formation at z > 4
papers.abstract: JWST has revealed that star formation in early galaxies is bursty, including episodes of violent suppression, so-called mini-quenching. But these were largely serendipitous discoveries in samples of UV-bright, emission-line-dominated galaxies, so that the quiet side of the burst cycle has remained poorly explored. With the JWST Cycle 3 program OASIS (GO 5997), we searched for such galaxies deliberately, using deep 28-hour NIRSpec/PRISM spectroscopy across the full burst cycle at z>4. We identify three mini-quenched galaxies with log(M*/Msun) = 8.3-8.9 and no detectable Balmer emission, at least 1.2-1.7 dex below the star-forming main sequence (SFMS), five lulling galaxies with weak Balmer emission above the quenching threshold, and 17 nearly-main-sequence galaxies just below the SFMS. Finding them required spectroscopy: seven of our ten photometric candidates for suppressed (mini-quenched and lulling) galaxies turned out to be nearly-MS or above the SFMS, and photometric fits overestimate their current star-formation rates and cannot distinguish lulling from mini-quenched ones. The suppressed galaxies are common: five of the eight come from tiers not selected on star-formation state, where they make up 29% of the galaxies at z = 4-5.5 and log(M*/Msun) = 8-9.5, a number density of ~1.6x10^-3 Mpc^-3 dex^-1. Simulations predict them to be an order of magnitude rarer at these masses and to occur mainly at lower masses. The suppressed galaxies are also old: Balmer-break strength and stellar age both increase as galaxies fall further below the SFMS, with light-weighted ages of 5 Myr for galaxies above it, ~30 Myr for the lulling galaxies and above 100 Myr for the mini-quenched ones. They show little stellar reddening (E(B-V) < 0.2), consistent with depleted gas reservoirs. Suppressed phases at z>4 are therefore neither rare nor brief, but a common and lasting part of early galaxy growth.

The first years of JWST operations (Gardner et al., 2023; Rigby et al., 2023) have transformed our view of galaxy formation in the early Universe (redshift z>4z>4). Before JWST, the stellar mass assembly of galaxies was largely observed as a steady, secular growth process. However, JWST has revealed that early galaxies instead evolve through short, feedback-regulated episodes of intense, bursty star formation driven by rapid, stochastic processes. Multiple observational lines of evidence now support this emerging picture: (i) large scatter around the star-forming main sequence in the star-formation rate–stellar mass (SFR–M⋆\text{M}_{\star}) plane (Clarke et al., 2025; Cole et al., 2025; Simmonds et al., 2025; Rinaldi et al., 2025a, e.g.,) and in the rest-frame ultraviolet magnitude–stellar mass MUVM_{\mathrm{UV}}-M⋆M_{\star} relation (Muñoz et al., 2026); (ii) signatures of stochasticity in reconstructed star-formation histories (SFHs) (Tacchella et al., 2023; Looser et al., 2025; Dressler et al., 2024; Ciesla et al., 2024; Carvajal-Bohorquez et al., 2025; Navarro-Carrera et al., 2026); (iii) deviations from the gas-phase fundamental metallicity relation (Curti et al., 2024; Langeroodi & Hjorth, 2023; Faisst et al., 2026, e.g.,); (iv) unexpectedly bright systems relative to pre-JWST UV luminosity function predictions at the highest redshifts11 1 We note, however, that multiple mechanisms likely contribute simultaneously, and bursty star formation alone appears insufficient to account for the excess (Gelli et al., 2023). (Harikane et al., 2023; Finkelstein et al., 2023; Robertson et al., 2024; Donnan et al., 2024; Whitler et al., 2025; Mitsuhashi et al., 2026; Stiavelli & Ricotti, 2026, e.g.,); (v) galaxies observed during phases of suppressed star formation (Looser et al., 2024a; Strait et al., 2023; Looser et al., 2025; Baker et al., 2025a; Witten et al., 2026; Chen et al., 2026; Harikane et al., 2026, e.g.,); and (vi) evidence for recent rejuvenation, i.e., strong upturns of star formation following quenched phases, in individual galaxies (Witten et al., 2025). Together, these findings suggest that burstiness – rather than continuous growth – dominates stellar-mass assembly at early times. However, we have only scratched the surface of this stochastic behavior, and much remains to be understood.

papers.title: OASIS II: The Ionized Gas Traces Feedback-Driven Declines into the Quiet Side of Bursty Star Formation at z > 4
papers.abstract: Models of bursty star formation in low-mass (10^8-10^9.5 Msun) galaxies at z>4 differ most in the suppressed phases: what drives the decline, how fast star formation falls, and how long it stays low. OASIS Paper I showed that such quiet galaxies are common and old; here we measure how they got there and how their ionized gas responds. We compare Balmer-line star-formation rates (SFRs) with 100-Myr averages from the stellar continuum, in NIRSpec/PRISM spectra of 54 OASIS galaxies at z>4, including three mini-quenched galaxies below the quenching threshold and five lulling galaxies at least 0.6 dex below the star-forming main sequence (SFMS) but still star-forming. Galaxies above the SFMS rise and fade equally often, whereas those below it are mostly fading: the lulling galaxies formed little more than a tenth of their mass in the last 100 Myr, and their decline began tens to ~100 Myr before observation. Suppressed phases thus last of order 100 Myr, as long as or longer than in most simulations, whereas recovery is much faster: few galaxies below the SFMS are rising. The ionized gas tracks these changes in star formation. [OIII]/[OII] falls from galaxies above the SFMS to the lulling ones, even at fixed mass and after dust correction, and follows the recent change in SFR (SFR_10/SFR_100) more closely than the position relative to the SFMS: two rising galaxies below the SFMS are highly ionized. This is expected if fewer and softer ionizing photons than in strongly star-forming galaxies meet gas depleted by earlier star formation. Lulling galaxies show ISM conditions distinct from those of strongly star-forming galaxies. The declines are faster than passive gas exhaustion predicts, favoring feedback that expels the gas or keeps it from forming stars. Quiet phases are thus long, feedback-driven episodes, and the ionized gas traces where a galaxy is in its burst cycle.

These are the most direct tests of feedback models, but they are hard to answer from a single snapshot, because the instantaneous SFR alone does not reveal whether a galaxy is forming stars at a steady rate or whether its star formation is rising or fading, and photometric SED fits recover the recent change only loosely (OASIS Paper I).

Several mechanisms could drive the decline. Low-mass halos at these redshifts are fed by cold streams at inflow rates per unit halo mass far higher than today (Sect. 5), so that suppression requires the gas to be removed or heated, or its supply interrupted. Stellar feedback can expel gas in outflows with mass-loading factors of order unity to tens (Muratov et al., 2015; Pandya et al., 2021), although supernova feedback alone may act too slowly to truncate star formation abruptly (Gelli et al., 2023b); radiation pressure may clear the star-forming regions of the most intensely star-forming galaxies (Ferrara, 2024); and accreting black holes, now found in substantial numbers at z>4z>4 (Kocevski et al., 2023; Harikane et al., 2023; Maiolino et al., 2024; Juodžbalis et al., 2026, e.g.,), can eject or heat the gas even in dwarf galaxies (Koudmani et al., 2022; Arjona-Gálvez et al., 2024). Ionized outflows are common in low-mass galaxies at z>3z>3 (Carniani et al., 2024), and neutral-gas outflows capable of quenching have been observed in quiescent galaxies (Belli et al., 2024; D’Eugenio et al., 2024; Wu, 2025; Valentino et al., 2025; Oh et al., 2026; Sapori et al., 2026; Zhu et al., 2026, e.g.,), but so far only in massive ones. These samples are, however, dominated by star-forming galaxies, so that the suppressed side of the cycle, where the nebular lines are weakest, remains poorly sampled.

Diagnostics of this kind have been applied to simulations (Sparre et al., 2017, e.g.,), to photometric samples (Ciesla et al., 2024; Atek et al., 2022; Asada et al., 2024; Navarro-Carrera et al., 2024; Endsley et al., 2025; Carvajal-Bohorquez et al., 2025, e.g.,), and to spectroscopic ones (Broussard et al., 2019; Endsley et al., 2024; Clarke et al., 2025; Looser et al., 2025; Perry et al., 2025; Ulivi et al., 2026, e.g.,). These samples are, however, dominated by star-forming galaxies, so that the suppressed side of the cycle, where the nebular lines are weakest, remains poorly sampled.

papers.title: OASIS III: Bursty star formation drives observed galaxy sizes at $z\geq4$
papers.abstract: We employ JWST/NIRSpec MSA PRISM spectroscopy together with NIRCam imaging to investigate the impact of star-formation variability on galaxy sizes for a representative sample of 51 galaxies at $z\geq4$. The OASIS survey enables us to probe low-star-formation-rate (SFR) lulling and mini-quenched galaxies down to $\log_{10}(M_\star/M_\odot)=8.3$ and $\log_{10}(\mathrm{SFR}/M_\odot\,\mathrm{yr}^{-1})<-1.6$, i.e. more than one order of magnitude below the star-forming main sequence (MS). This enables us to probe objects that are often missed by shallower spectroscopic surveys, in addition to the MS and starburst systems, yielding an SFR- and mass-representative sample at high redshift. We derive galaxy half-light sizes using ForcePho, enabling us to resolve the highly compact nature of these sources, and we analyse their star-formation histories and interstellar medium (ISM) properties with the full-spectral-fitting code ppxf. We find a clear anti-correlation between burstiness, as traced by the ratio of the SFR from H$\alpha$ compared to that from non-parametric spectral fitting averaged over 100 Myr, and galaxy UV/optical half-light radii as measured with ForcePho from a combination of well-sampled NIRCam photometry. Using partial correlation coefficients we show that the anti-correlation between burstiness (as traced by the SFR ratio) and size cannot simply be explained by secondary dependencies on stellar mass or redshift. We interpret this relation as the effect of central starbursts in SFR-rising (bursting) systems, where intense central star formation reduces measured galaxy half-light sizes. This burstiness then regulates galaxy sizes at high redshift. Should the same mechanism be present at $z>10$, this could explain the size bimodality seen in the UV luminous galaxies as simply stemming from a more fundamental relationship between burstiness and size.

These stochastic processes, and their interplay, cause oscillations around the ‘Star-forming Main Sequence’ (hereafter MS), a relation between a galaxy’s stellar mass and its associated star-formation rate (SFR) (Brinchmann et al., 2004; Noeske et al., 2007; Speagle et al., 2014; Tacchella et al., 2016b; Simmonds et al., 2025; Rinaldi et al., 2025; Clarke et al., 2025; Cole et al., 2025), itself a by-product of the connection between SFR, stellar mass, and gas mass (Baker et al., 2023a, at least up to z∼3z\sim 3,). Hence, these stochastic modulations are associated with the duty cycle of these high-redshift galaxies, their feedback, and gas-accretion processes (Tacchella et al., 2016b; Gelli et al., 2025). Stochasticity is predicted by cosmological simulations and semi-analytic models to become more pronounced at higher redshifts and lower masses, due to effects such as shallower gravitational potentials, shorter dynamical timescales, and highly fluctuating gas accretion rates (Tacchella et al., 2016a; Dome et al., 2024; Gelli et al., 2023; Sun et al., 2023b; Gelli et al., 2025; Kravtsov and Belokurov, 2024; Muñoz et al., 2026). These faint, low-mass galaxies show clear Balmer breaks, relatively steep UV slopes, and a lack of strong emission lines, all of which is consistent with a picture in which these galaxies have very recently (either completely or nearly completely) ceased forming new stars, likely within the previous 10-100 Myr. This neatly explains the observed properties of these galaxies: no strong line emission, due to a lack of star formation within the previous ≈\approx10 Myr (Looser et al., 2024; Baker et al., 2025a), a visible Balmer break, due to an absence of the hottest and youngest stars (Sawicki and Yee, 1998; Looser et al., 2025; Witten et al., 2025), and an often blue UV slope due to a young stellar population of 50-150 Myr (Wilkins et al., 2011) (Looser and others, 2026b, hereafter OASIS Paper I). 11 1 It can be most convenient to think of the ‘mini-quenched’ galaxies as a separate population compared to the more traditional definition of a ‘massive quiescent’ galaxy. papers.title: Gapless and Non-Equilibrium Topology in Blockaded Ladders
papers.abstract: We propose a multi-leg PXYP model as a minimal setting to explore constraint-induced intertwinement between itinerant and internal degrees of freedom. We argue that the Rydberg-like blockade induces correlations in squeezed space, providing a unified mechanism for nontrivial string order both in and out of equilibrium. In a two-leg geometry, this leads to an intrinsically gapless topological ground state, which can terminate at a supersymmetric multicritical point. This mechanism also leads to the preservation of string order for parametrically long times after a quench, which we verify using tensor network simulations and a classical stochastic approximation to the dynamics. In a three-leg geometry, the blockade leads to an additional emergent $U(1)$ symmetry, resulting in a multicomponent Luttinger liquid where both itinerant and internal degrees of freedom are critical. This family of models arises naturally in a range of quantum simulator platforms such as Rydberg tweezer arrays and dipolar atoms in optical lattices.

papers.title: Magnetic scattering experiments with an ultrashort pulsed soft X-ray source using iLGADs
papers.abstract:
Inverse Low Gain Avalanche Diode (iLGAD) sensors developed at the Paul Scherrer Institute (PSI) in collaboration with the Fondazione Bruno Kessler (FBK) have demonstrated an excellent Signal-to-Noise Ratio (SNR) and Quantum Efficiency (QE) in the soft X-ray range. In the current batch, single-photon detection is achievable at 400 eV with an SNR > 5, while the QE surpasses 85 % at 250 eV. Combined with the high frame rates of CMOS readout ASIC, iLGAD sensors make the hybrid pixel detectors excellent candidates for time-resolved magnetic Small Angle X-ray Scattering (mSAXS) experiments in the soft X-ray energy range.
  In this contribution, we evaluated ILGAD sensors bump-bonded to 25 {\mu}m pitch charge-integrating M\"ONCH chips at a laser-driven soft X-ray source. During the experiments, we measured energy-dispersed radiation between 600 eV and 1500 eV. These measurements were performed for the iLGAD sensor, as well as for the standard silicon sensor. Using the high-precision electronic trigger of the X-ray source, we were able to synchronise the detector with the X-ray source delivering few-picosecond pulses and optimise the timing parameters for the acquisition.
  Finally, we successfully performed the mSAXS experiment probing the magnetic domain pattern of a FeGd heterostructure, demonstrating better performance than a M\"ONCH detector with a standard silicon sensor. ILGAD sensors achieved a significantly higher photon detection efficiency and, consequently, a higher sensitivity compared to standard silicon sensors under the same conditions, particularly for the lower-energy Fe L3 edge.

papers.intro:
Soft X-ray experiments, especially those dealing with a weak observable photon signal, are limited by the capabilities of the state-of-art X-ray detectors. This applies both to the experiments yielding weak measurable signal including both at high flux radiation facilities as well as the lab based experiments with sources emitting orders of magnitude lower photon flux. In such experimental environments, high Quantum Efficiency (QE), single-photon detection capabilities, high acquisition rates, and high duty cycles are essential for efficient data collection.

papers.title: Quantifying Linepack Storage Potential of Hydrogen Networks
papers.abstract: Future hydrogen systems depend on large-scale storage to balance supply and demand. Hydrogen networks can store energy in the pipelines themselves, but the potential of this linepack storage has not been quantified comparably to dedicated storage facilities. We transfer metrics established for conventional storage, such as volume capacity and full-cycle equivalents, to hydrogen networks. To evaluate them, we formulate an optimization problem maximizing linepack storage utilization, subject to non-convex PDE-based constraints describing transient gas flow. We solve the optimization problem over a full-year horizon to capture seasonal variations and to assess the interaction with cavern storage. For computational tractability, we propose a simulation-informed sequential convex programming approach with adaptive time stepping that reduces problem size by up to 98% at accuracy comparable to fixed-resolution methods. For the GasLib-40 topology with German scenario data, the network provides a volume capacity of 24 million normal cubic meters at 28 full-cycle equivalents per year.

papers.intro:
Future hydrogen systems will require significant storage capacity to bridge temporal imbalances between supply and demand across time scales from hours to seasons [1, 2, 3, 4]. On a seasonal scale, storage demand arises primarily from hydrogen-fired power generation during periods of low renewable availability. On shorter, intraday time scales, storage is required to buffer the volatile output of renewable-powered electrolyzers. In most energy system models, the entire hydrogen storage demand is assigned to underground storage facilities such as salt caverns, which represent the most cost-effective solution for large-scale storage [5, 6]. However, these facilities are limited in their operational flexibility: frequent and intensive charging and discharging cycles can significantly reduce their service lifetime [7, 8]. Complementary short-term storage options are therefore likely to be required in real-world systems, yet such alternatives are either not represented or only very simplistically modeled in most energy system frameworks [1, 2, 3, 4].

Potential short-term hydrogen storage options include dedicated underground pipe storage and the inherent linepack storage capacity of the hydrogen transport network itself. Pipe storage, well established in the natural gas sector, is incorporated into some energy system models but is rarely selected in optimization due to its relatively high cost [6]. An alternative that has received little attention so far is linepack storage, i.e., the temporary storage of hydrogen within the transport pipelines by varying the network pressure level [4]. Unlike dedicated storage facilities, linepack requires no additional infrastructure and is inherently available in any pipeline network.
