Pipe storage, well established in the natural gas sector, is incorporated into some energy system models but is rarely selected in optimization due to its relatively high cost [6]. An alternative that has received little attention so far is linepack storage, i.e., the temporary storage of hydrogen within the transport pipelines by varying the network pressure level [4]. Unlike dedicated storage facilities, linepack requires no additional infrastructure and is inherently available in any pipeline network.

However, energy system models are fundamentally unsuited to quantify linepack storage potential. These models typically represent gas networks using steady-state or linear flow balances that assume an instantaneous equilibrium between supply and demand at each time step [1, 2, 3, 4]. Under such assumptions, no mass can accumulate within the network, and the concept of linepack — which arises precisely from transient pressure and mass flow variations — cannot be captured. A physically consistent assessment of linepack storage therefore requires a transient fluid-mechanical network model that resolves the temporal evolution of pressure and flow throughout the pipeline system.

No detailed analysis of the technical potential of linepack storage in hydrogen networks has been conducted to date. We therefore address the following research question: How can the maximum technically feasible potential of linepack storage in a hydrogen network be quantified? In answering this question, we focus exclusively on the technical storage potential as determined by network topology, operational constraints, and transport scenarios. Economic viability and regulatory considerations are beyond the scope of this work.

The existing literature addressing linepack storage can broadly be divided into three strands: (i) studies quantifying the storage potential of individual pipelines, (ii) research on the transient operational optimization of gas networks, in which linepack storage is exploited implicitly, and (iii) a few works that explicitly maximize the linepack storage potential of gas networks.

The first strand includes [9], which compares the linepack storage potential of natural gas and hydrogen for a single pipeline. However, the assessment is limited to operation at the design point of the pipeline. Its applicability to entire networks under varying load conditions is therefore limited. Moreover, the proposed storage metric does not allow for a direct comparison with other types of storage. In [10], a single pipeline is used as a buffer for the mismatch between supply and demand in a simulation with full-year horizon. The annual supply–demand mismatch is scaled down until the operational limits of the pipeline are satisfied, and the remaining imbalance is absorbed by unspecified buffer storage. Neither the size of this external buffer storage nor a metric for the pipeline storage potential are reported.

papers.title: The Importance of Curium-250 to the $\gamma$-Ray Signature of $r$-Process Remnants
papers.abstract: Identifying the astrophysical sites of the heavy rapid neutron-capture process ($r$-process) remains one of the most prominent unsolved problems in nuclear astrophysics. Emitted $\gamma$-rays from the decay of unstable nuclei have been identified as a potential observable marker on both prompt and delayed timescales which could provide conclusive evidence of the presence of $r$-process activity. In this work, we identify and discuss the importance of $^{250}$Cm to the $\gamma$-ray spectra of remnants, showing that the decay spectrum of $^{250}$Cm dominates the $\gamma$-ray spectra of $r$-process ejecta across a broad timescale ($\sim$ 2,000 - 20,000 years). We highlight the uncertain nature of this spectra: $^{250}$Cm may decay via $\alpha$-decay, $\beta$-decay, and spontaneous fission, but the decay branchings are not experimentally known, and each decay channel produces unique spectral lines which may be observable. We examine the potential for observation of the most prominent spectral signatures, finding that for conventional neutron star merger remnants, $\gamma$-ray lines will be detectable in current and future detectors only in the very near galaxy ($\sim$ 1 kpc), but other sites which could produce a larger ejecta mass may have greater observable distances. Our findings highlight the potential of actinide decay chains to indicate r-process nucleosynthesis and further underscore the necessity of measuring the nuclear properties that define their characteristic spectral signatures.

The most studied sites of the rr-process include Core-Collapse Supernovae ( Woosley et al. 87, Qian and Woosley 61, Wanajo et al. 82, Fryer et al. 24), and compact object mergers (see Lattimer and Schramm 41, Eichler et al. 18, Rosswog et al. 67, Freiburghaus et al. 21, Goriely et al. 25, Korobkin et al. 37, Hotokezaka et al. 28, Bauswein et al. 8, Wanajo et al. 83); however, there are many proposed secondary sites, including magneto-rotational supernovae (Winteler et al. 86, Nishimura et al. 56, Yong et al. 88), collapsars/hypernovae (Banerjee and Mukhopadhyay 6, Siegel et al. 70, An et al. 4, Anand et al. 5, Mumpower et al. 53), and magnetars (Cehula et al. 13, Patel et al. 58). In particular, the site of the heavy rr-process remains particularly uncertain, as the conditions necessary for a heavy rr-process have not fully manifested in simulations of CCSNe [12, 30], magneto-rotational supernovae [63, 62, 64], or magnetars [59].

The landmark multi-messenger observations of GW170817 (see [1]) have provided evidence that NSMs are a site of the rr-process; in particular, the observed kilonova, a radioactive transient thought to be powered by the decay of the synthesized, unstable rr-process nuclei. The observed peak in the near-infrared and optical bands has been widely interpreted as evidence that NSMs undergo a strong rr-process (Drout et al. 17, Kasen et al. 32, Kasliwal et al. 33, Murguia-Berthier et al. 55, Tanaka et al. 75, Waxman et al. 85, Brethauer et al. 9) due to the high opacities of ionized lanthanides (see e.g., Domoto et al. 16, Flörs et al. 20), which when present, have been shown to result in a kilonova that peaks in the infrared ([31, 74]). While we do not wish to understate the importance of kilonova observations and their significance in indicating the presence of an rr-process at these sites, the multiphysics required in kilonova modeling presently make it challenging to make definitive conclusions about the nature of the rr-process. While the widely argued interpretation that a red kilonova provides evidence of lanthanide production has merit, there are also alternative interpretations. For example, the observations of GRB211211A and GRB230307 have also been shown to be consistent with a collapsar scenario which produces only a weak rr-process component, despite an observed peak in the infrared [65]. There are additionally numerous poorly constrained model parameters which have been shown to have significant impact on the resultant light curve (see e.g., Barnes et al. 7, Zhu et al. 89, Korobkin et al. 39, Fryer et al. 22, Lund et al. 43), which may change the interpretation of observable results. In particular, we highlight [73] and [23], which showed that different ejecta velocity assumptions may lead to late-time features which mimic the presence of lanthanides. As a consequence of the uncertainties present, it may be challenging to conclusively identify the site of the heavy rr-process from kilonova observations alone.

In particular, as the ejecta becomes transparent in the days and weeks after the event, specific strong γ\gamma-ray lines from the decay of unstable nuclei may be directly observable (e.g. [60, 27, 84, 38, 76, 81, 26]). The observation and identification of a known γ\gamma-ray decay line of an actinide would provide conclusive, direct evidence of heavy rr-process activity, bypassing the difficult multiphysics required to understand kilonova light curves. This approach has its own challenges – at prompt timescales, the ejecta is expanding rapidly, which leads to Doppler broadening of the spectral emission lines. This, combined with the large number of potential γ\gamma-ray lines at early timescales, makes it challenging to tie observed lines to a specific source nucleus [26]. It has also been suggested that γ\gamma-rays might be observable in remnant objects when the ejecta has slowed and the number of nuclei decaying are minimized, which decreases the challenges of the identification of spectral lines, although, in this case, the incident flux is smaller and the observational range reduced [38, 3].

Although 250Cm has been identified as a potential source of γ\gamma-ray lines in other studies of remnants (Korobkin et al. 38, Amend et al. 3), the uncertainty of its spectral emission profile and its importance to the spectral emission has not been elucidated. In addition, one of the most prominent γ\gamma-ray lines has been incorrectly identified in past work, as the α\alpha-decay chain of 250Cm populates the nuclear isomer 246mAm rather than the ground state, which dominantly emits a 1079 keV line instead of the reported 679 keV line. The observation of a γ\gamma-ray line resultant from 250Cm decay would be consequential, as it would represent direct detection of a heavy rr-process.

papers.title: Optimization Techniques for Solving the Minimum Red--Blue Separating Set Problem with an Application to Human--AI Text Separation
papers.abstract: We study the so-called Minimum Red''Blue Separating Set Problem (MRBSSP) which arises from computational geometry. In particular, we propose a compact Set-Cover ILP formulation, safe preprocessing rules, a Greedy Randomized Adaptive Search Procedure (GRASP), and two exact approaches: one is based on Logic-Based Benders Decomposition (LBBD) approach, and the second represents a novel Branch-and-Benders-Cut (BBC) approach. These two exact approaches are compared to ILP--alongside GRASP and the Variable Neighborhood Search (VNS) from literature. Experiments on 250 random graphs with up to 500 vertices reveal complementary strengths: ILP yields the best feasible solutions, LBBD provides the strongest lower bounds and smallest mean optimality gap, and BBC certifies optimality most frequently. We further introduce an NLP application distinguishing human- and AI-generated texts through vocabulary-based graph features. On 42 instances, BBC achieves the smallest mean optimality gap, certifying 16 optima, while GRASP outperforms VNS. Structural analysis of optimal vocabulary separators identifies 113 mandatory and 151 replaceable features across 272 tests, highlighting substantial variability among optimal solutions. Overall, our results demonstrate the effectiveness of complementary optimization strategies and the interpretability of optimal vocabulary-based discrimination.

papers.intro:
Separating objects of different types by a small number of selected features, tests, or sensors is a recurring theme in combinatorial optimization, data analysis, and network design [4, 1, 2, 25, 26]. In graph settings, this principle leads naturally to separation problems in which the goal is not merely to dominate or cover vertices, but to distinguish pairs of vertices belonging to different classes. The Minimum Red-Blue Separating Set Problem (MRBSSP) captures this requirement in a particularly compact form. Given a graph G=(V,E)G=(V,E) and two disjoint sets of terminals, red vertices RR and blue vertices BB, the task is to select a minimum-cardinality subset S⊆VS\subseteq V such that every red-blue pair (r,b)∈R×B(r,b)\in R\times B is separated by at least one selected vertex. A vertex v∈Vv\in V separates the pair (r,b)(r,b) if its closed neighborhood N⁡[v]N[v] contains exactly one of rr and bb. Thus, each selected vertex acts as a local test: it distinguishes precisely those terminal pairs for which one endpoint is inside its closed neighborhood and the other is outside.

MRBSSP can be viewed as a structured Set-Cover problem [7, 22, 10]. The universe of elements to be covered is the Cartesian product R×BR\times B, and each candidate vertex v∈Vv\in V covers the subset of red-blue pairs that it separates. The natural integer programming formulation therefore contains one binary variable for each vertex and one covering constraint for each red-blue terminal pair. This formulation is conceptually simple and results in a direct exact model, but it can become large even for moderate instances, since the number of constraints grows with |R|​|B||R||B|. Moreover, many of these constraints may be irrelevant for a large part of the search, because a candidate solution typically violates only a small subset of all red-blue pairs. This observation is the starting point for the decomposition and cut-generation methods [32, 33] studied in this paper.

The problem is closely related to several established lines of research. At the most general level, MRBSSP inherits the modeling structure and computational difficulty of Set Cover and Hitting Set [35, 17], classical NP-hard problems for which integer programming, greedy heuristics, and approximation algorithms form the standard methodological toolkit [14]. It is also related to Red-Blue Set Cover, introduced by Carr et al. [8], where the objective is to cover all blue elements while minimizing the number of red elements covered. Although MRBSSP has a different graph-based separation semantics, both problems share the same red-blue modeling philosophy: one must satisfy conditions involving one color class while controlling how the other color class is affected. More directly, MRBSSP is connected to the Red-Blue Separation problem on graphs studied by Dev et al. [13], where a small set of vertices is selected so that every red-blue pair is distinguished by the closed neighborhood of at least one selected vertex. That work establishes the graph-theoretic and complexity foundations of the problem, including hardness results and approximation guarantees for the general case. Complementing this theoretical line, Milojković [28] recently proposed a Variable Neighborhood Search (VNS) [30] heuristic for the MRBSSP, showcasing that neighborhood-based metaheuristics can provide competitive feasible solutions for graph instances. The present paper builds on this emerging computational perspective by focusing on exact and hybrid methods, using the VNS method from the literature [28] and the newly introduced GRASP as strong heuristic reference baselines while emphasizing certification and dual-bound progress.

From an algorithmic perspective, MRBSSP is particularly well suited to decomposition. Once a candidate set SS of selected vertices is fixed, assessing feasibility reduces to a simple set-intersection test: for every red-blue pair (r,b)(r,b), one verifies whether SS contains at least one vertex that separates the pair. If such a pair is not separated, the corresponding Set-Cover constraint is violated and can be added as a cut. This structure is a natural match for Logic-Based Benders Decomposition (LBBD) [23], where a master problem proposes a candidate solution and a logical subproblem either verifies feasibility or returns violated constraints. It is also a natural match for Branch-and-Benders-Cut (BBC), where the same feasibility oracle is embedded inside a single branch-and-bound tree through lazy constraint generation [31], in the spirit of the combinatorial Benders cuts of Codato and Fischetti [12]. The essential distinction is that iterative LBBD repeatedly solves a sequence of master problems, whereas BBC preserves the global search tree and injects cuts only when they are needed.

We investigate this question on two deliberately different benchmark families. The first is a broad Random benchmark composed of synthetically generated graphs with varying sizes and densities. Its role is to stress the algorithms under controlled structural variation and to permit a systematic comparison of primal performance, dual-bound progress, optimality gaps, certification rates, and heuristic stability. The second is an NLP-derived benchmark in which human- and AI-generated texts are represented through vocabulary-incidence graphs. In this family, the selected separator has a direct feature-selection interpretation: a minimum set of vocabulary features is sought that distinguishes every human–AI text pair. The NLP instances therefore complement the synthetic study with a real-data setting in which both computational performance and the structure of the resulting optimal separators can be interpreted. The two benchmark families serve different but complementary purposes.

papers.title: Effective threshold dynamics for the cubic nonlinear Klein-Gordon equation in three dimensions
papers.abstract: We consider the focussing cubic Klein-Gordon equation on $\mathbb{R}^{3+1}$ in the radial setting. Foundational work by Nakanishi-Schlag gives a complete qualitative characterisation of the dynamics near the ground state $Q$, in particular revealing a threshold phenomenon, whereby a co-dimension one Lipschitz manifold separates finite time blow up from scattering solutions in forward time. Our aim in this paper is to derive an effective bound for the scattering norm $\|u\|_{L_t^3([0,\infty);L_x^6(\mathbb{R}^3))}$, for scattering energy class solutions $u$ with data sufficiently near $Q$ and close to the threshold manifold. This requires the development of an induction on energy strategy in a setting where an alternative to the usual Morawetz approach appears necessary.

papers.title: KV-Cache Patching: Tracing How and Where Fine-Tuned Behaviors Arise
papers.abstract: Fine-tuning a language model changes how it responds, but where is this fine-tuned behavior instantiated? To better understand this, we evaluate whether the change in model behavior arises only during the generation of the answer tokens where the change manifests, or whether altered processing of previous tokens causes it via the attention mechanism. For this, we patch the KV cache from a LoRA fine-tuned model into the unmodified base model, and vice versa. Our results show that for some behaviors, like responding in German or emergent misalignment, patching the KV cache can indeed transfer them from the fine-tuned to the base model. Correspondingly, patching the KV cache from base to fine-tune can partially or fully remove fine-tuned behavior. Furthermore, we find that the effect of patching grows with how much of the KV cache is patched and concentrates at a few pivotal positions, with system-prompt and chat-template tokens having disproportionate influence.

Fine-tuning can substantially alter the behavior of language models, enabling them to acquire new task capabilities, behavioral dispositions, or desired response patterns. But how are these behavioral changes implemented during inference? They could arise either from altered computations only during generation, changing how the model selects its outputs, or from altered processing of preceding tokens, changing the representations on which subsequent generation depends.

Fine-tuning can substantially alter the behavior of language models, enabling them to acquire new task capabilities, behavioral dispositions, or desired response patterns. But how are these behavioral changes implemented during inference? They could arise either from altered computations only during generation, changing how the model selects its outputs, or from altered processing of preceding tokens, changing the representations on which subsequent generation depends.

Autoregressive generation reuses representations of previously processed tokens through the KV cache, which stores their keys and values to avoid recomputation at each generation step. These representations are subsequently accessed through attention, mediating how preceding tokens influence future computation and providing a direct handle for testing whether fine-tuning alters behavior through changes in the processing of the preceding context. Selectively altering the KV cache has been shown to modify model behavior (Belitsky et al., 2025; Li, 2026; Liu et al., 2026a): partial reuse of the KV cache across fine-tunes can preserve task performance while full reuse can degrade it (Liu et al., 2026b), and emergent misalignment can use the KV cache to “piggyback” onto out-of-domain queries (Zhao et al., 2026a).

papers.title: Mathematical foundations of second quantization: an introduction through spin-boson models
papers.abstract: These lecture notes originate from a one-semester course on the mathematical foundations of second quantization, first given at the Department of Physics of the Friedrich-Alexander-Universit\"at Erlangen-N\"urnberg in the Winter Semester 2025/26 to a mixed audience of physics and mathematics students. Their guiding thread is a class of physical models: spin-boson models, describing a two-level system coupled to a boson field. After summarizing the necessary background on unbounded operators, up to the Kato-Rellich and KLMN theorems, and developing direct sums and tensor products of Hilbert spaces and of unbounded operators, we treat single-mode boson fields, constructing the ladder and number operators and characterizing their domains, before moving to Fock spaces, second quantization, bosonic and fermionic annihilation and creation operators, and the canonical (anti)commutation relations. Throughout, spin-boson models provide both the motivation and the test bench for the formalism: we rigorously establish their self-adjointness, solve the pure dephasing and Jaynes-Cummings models explicitly, deriving their spectra and the qubit channels they induce, show how their multimode counterparts display irreversible decoherence and decay, and, in an appendix, prove the rotating-wave approximation for the quantum Rabi model with an explicit error bound. Finally, we use the KLMN theorem to construct spin-boson models with non-normalizable form factors, and briefly discuss stronger ultraviolet divergences and the need for renormalization. Exercises with full solutions are included.

Second quantization lies at the crossroads of two communities. Physics students typically meet it early, as a set of rules: one introduces annihilation and creation operators, imposes canonical (anti)commutation relations, and manipulates expressions such as H=∫ω⁡(k)​a†​(k)​a​(k)​𝑑kH=\int\omega(k)a^{\dagger}(k)a(k)\;\mathrm{d}k (1.1) but often with little idea of which mathematical objects are hiding behind such expressions: on which domain they are defined, whether a given Hamiltonian is self-adjoint (and thus generates a dynamics at all), or in which sense an approximation is justified. Mathematics students, on the other hand, are perfectly at ease with the formalism, but rarely get to see what physicists actually do with Fock spaces: which models they study, why, and which questions they care about. Both communities are served by excellent literature: second quantization is an everyday tool in textbooks on many-body physics and quantum optics [1, 2, 3, 4], and Fock spaces and quantum fields are treated with full mathematical rigor in several monographs [5, 6, 7, 8, 9].

These notes are an attempt to address a mixed audience of physicists and mathematicians, making each half of the story accessible to the readers who are more familiar with the other one. To this end, they are built around a single class of models: spin–boson models, describing a two-level system---a spin, or qubit---coupled to a boson field. Models of this kind are ubiquitous in physics, from quantum optics and cavity or circuit quantum electrodynamics to the theory of open quantum systems, where they are the standard models of decoherence and dissipation; already in their simplest instances---the pure dephasing, Jaynes--Cummings and quantum Rabi models---they display decoherence, Rabi oscillations, and the subtleties of the rotating-wave approximation. At the same time, they are arguably the clearest example of a class of models whose mathematics is largely under control; and yet, they are typically handled only formally in the physics literature, while rigorous treatments of field--matter interaction usually address physically complete but technically demanding models, such as the Pauli--Fierz model of non-relativistic quantum electrodynamics (see e.g. [7]), at research level. These notes aim to fill the gap in between. The rigorous treatment of spin–boson models requires the whole machinery of second quantization—Fock spaces, annihilation and creation operators, second quantized operators, and tensor products of unbounded operators—and, conversely, these models provide the motivation and the test bench for each piece of this machinery: everything in these notes is developed with them in mind.

papers.title: Stabilization of counter propagating currents by energy conservation in collisions
papers.abstract: Current filamentation generates magnetic fields and shapes electron transport in dense plasmas, where collisions can either suppress or enhance its growth. Here we show that conserving electron kinetic energy in a collisional model can change both the dominant instability and its characteristic wavelength. We develop a linear kinetic theory for drifting, anisotropic electron populations with a relaxation operator that conserves particle number and laboratory-frame kinetic energy while allowing momentum transfer to a stationary ion background. For counterstreaming currents, energy conservation maintains the stabilizing influence of charge separation over a broader range of collision frequencies than a model conserving particle number alone. At intermediate collision rates, the resulting suppression of transverse filamentation allows a nearly aperiodic oblique mode to dominate, reducing the maximum growth rate and shifting the wavelength of the fastest-growing perturbation. Two-dimensional particle-in-cell simulations support predicted growth rates of up to more than a magnitude lower than expected without energy conserving collision.

papers.title: ObjectGuidedMap: An Object-Aware Model for Robust Bird's Eye View Map Prediction in High-Occlusion Scenarios
papers.abstract: Accurate BEV map prediction is a critical component of autonomous driving systems, enabling downstream planning and control. Recent approaches such as Mask2Map achieve strong performance by predicting vectorized, instance-level map elements directly from multi-view images. However, existing BEV map prediction models operate largely independently of object-level scene understanding, despite the fact that traffic participants frequently occlude or implicitly encode information about road geometry. In this work, we propose a multitask architecture that jointly predicts BEV maps and 3D objects, explicitly enabling information exchange between the two tasks. Building upon Mask2Map, we introduce an object detection branch and incorporate cross-task feature fusion at both the BEV feature level and the instance-query level via deformable attention and cross-attention mechanisms. This design allows map instances to leverage object context while remaining robust to occlusions caused by traffic participants. Experimental results on the nuScenes and Argoverse 2 datasets demonstrate that our approach consistently improves BEV map prediction accuracy, with particularly significant gains of 21% mAP in scenes containing heavy object occlusion.

papers.intro:
The construction of Bird’s Eye View (BEV) maps of the static environment around the ego-vehicle is a crucial part of the perception pipeline involved in autonomous driving [40, 41]. While some early systems relied on pre-recorded High-Definition (HD) maps of their environment [4, 14, 16], this approach proved unreliable and difficult to scale. Modern systems rely on online BEV map construction [33, 34, 66, 6], performed alongside object detection (OD) and the downstream trajectory prediction and planning tasks. The prediction of these maps usually relies on image input from an array of surround cameras, sometimes augmented with Radar or LiDAR data. Current BEV map predictors primarily reason geometrically but lack explicit relational conditioning on dynamic scene elements. After some early works that modeled the task as a semantic segmentation problem [46, 31, 45], most modern methods replace the segmentation approach with vectorized map prediction. Here, the map is represented as a set of map instances which are individual elements making up the environment, such as lane lines or curbs. Each such map instance is represented by a sequence of points defining a polyline, alongside a class label. Existing methods for constructing vectorized BEV maps, such as BeMapNet [47], MapTRv2 [34], and Mask2Map [6], are already highly robust under ideal visibility conditions. However, poor weather, low lighting, and especially occlusions remain significant challenges that have not yet been resolved in the current literature. This is due to a key limitation in these existing approaches: They infer map geometry primarily from visible evidence in the image domain, without explicitly conditioning on the spatial configuration of surrounding traffic participants. In scenarios where map instances are occluded or their visibility is otherwise degraded, this lack of relational conditioning can hinder reliable reconstruction. To systematically address this gap in the existing research, we introduce our novel ObjectGuidedMap model. We hypothesize that enabling the model to take into account information about the objects present in the environment should make it more resilient against occlusions from these objects. Additionally, in poor-visibility scenarios, knowing the location of the surrounding objects should also provide a strong prior for the placement of certain map instances, e.g. the position of a car parked on the side of the street should provide useful information for the position of the curb or a lane line. Hence, instead of performing the map prediction task in isolation, our approach introduces attention modules utilizing information from a parallel object detection branch in both the model’s encoder and decoder. This enables our model to generate more robust BEV map predictions, as exemplified by the much improved prediction in Fig. 1: Here, due to the large occlusion from the van in front of the ego-vehicle, the baseline model fails to predict the occluded lane lines, while our model’s prediction is not impacted by the occlusion.

papers.title: No More Import Errors: Constrained Decoding for Guaranteed Valid Imports in LLM-Generated Tests
papers.abstract:
One of the most common failure reasons of LLM-based test generation pipelines is import errors. Grammar constrained decoding can modify the probabilities of the LLM's final layer during token generation to guarantee valid imports. However, we find that it can lead to degenerate solutions, i.e., repetitive valid imports (import streaks) that exhaust the token budget before a test is generated. We propose Constrained Beam Decoding with Lookup (CBDL), a novel method that guarantees import validity while addressing import streaks by avoiding premature commitment to tokens that lead to repetitive imports. Because it operates at the decoding stage, CBDL can be integrated into existing LLM-based test generation pipelines.
  We implement CBDL for Python and Java and evaluate it on two test generation tasks, showing that generated tests have 100% valid imports, outperforming both static (RAG and LIBRO) and dynamic (Agentic Repair) import-validity approaches that leave 45%, 10%, and 43% of import errors unresolved. CBDL converts on average 14% of initial import errors into functionally correct tests, increasing overall test correctness by 1-4 percentage points over unconstrained generation.
  Even when import validity does not directly lead to a correct test, it allows agentic repair pipelines to allocate the repair budget to remaining errors, increasing correct tests by 2-7 percentage points for Python and 1-6 for Java. Finally, we show that a hybrid pipeline, where a small local model equipped with CBDL generates imports while the frontier GPT-5.2 model generates the test body, outperforms generating both with GPT-5.2 alone by 1-3 percentage points.
  Overall, CBDL removes a major bottleneck in LLM-based test generation: by guaranteeing import validity with a small overhead (16-21 seconds per test), it improves test correctness and enables cost-effective hybrid generation.

papers.intro:
Large language model (LLM)-based test generation pipelines generate tests by feeding the code-under-test, related context, and a task-specific prompt to an LLM (or LLM-based agent), which generates a test consisting of import statements, a test prefix, and assertions. Then, the test is executed to check if it satisfies the target task, e.g., by failing in the buggy and passing in the patched code (F→\rightarrowP), in which case the test is returned as output, otherwise it is discarded or refined in an agentic repair loop.

Such pipelines are of increasing interest both in research and practice [1]. For example, Google generates issue-reproducing tests by feeding an issue description to an LLM pipeline and checking whether the generated test fails in the presence of the issue and passes in its absence, in which case the test is considered an issue-reproducing test, or an F→\rightarrowP test [2]. Similarly, Mozilla deployed a tool that is triggered on pull request (PR) creation and feeds the linked issue and patch to an LLM-based pipeline to generate an F→\rightarrowP test that guards against future regressions [3]. Finally, Meta uses an LLM pipeline to generate tests that pass in the current version of the code and improve the coverage of the existing test suite [4].

However, such pipelines often fail to generate an appropriate test. Literature [5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 10, 11] consistently ranks import errors as one of the most prominent causes for this failure. An import error occurs when the LLM-generated test imports an entity (e.g., class, module, package) that does not exist in the runtime environment. For example, running import com.tools.checkstyle.utils.CommonUtil yields an import error if the CommonUtil class does not exist or resides in a different package. Chen et al. [6] analyzed eight state-of-the-art LLM-based agents and found that import errors were the leading cause of failure, accounting for 15151515 (23%) errors across all agents and dataset instances, followed by type errors at 992992 (15%). Our results corroborate these findings: even the state-of-the-art GPT-5.2 produces an import error in 18/103 Java test generation tasks.

To guarantee import validity efficiently we formulate this problem as a constraining problem: generated import statements must belong to a set extracted from the execution environment. However, we find that enforcing this constraint through greedy grammar constrained decoding [14] leads to import streaks, i.e., degenerate solutions where the model repeatedly generates valid imports without proceeding to the test body, aligned with prior findings on low quality output of grammar constrained decoding [15, 16]. Our analysis suggests that import streaks are caused by prematurely committing to a locally optimal import, motivating Constrained Beam Decoding with Lookup (CBDL). By retaining alternative continuations, beam search avoids local optima, substantially reducing import streaks. A complementary lookup mechanism preserves generated class names when they exist under a different package and activates constrained decoding only when lookup cannot resolve the import. Together, these components address both import validity and the repetitive outputs introduced by enforcing it.

papers.title: Recommendation Feedback Loops Shape Urban Income Segregation and Venue Visitation
papers.abstract: Location-based recommender systems shape where people go in cities and learn from the visits they steer, forming a human-AI feedback loop. This feedback loop shapes whom people share places with across income groups and which venues keep attracting customers. Yet platforms judge these systems by their offline accuracy on past visits, a test in which the suggestions never change where people go and which therefore cannot capture long-term effects. Studying these effects in cities is challenging because, unlike online resources, travel constraints and limited venue capacity shape where people can go, while each recommended visit also changes whom other visitors encounter. To capture such features, we build a long-term simulation framework based on fine-grained human mobility data from four U.S. metropolitan areas, with distance and capacity constraints. Focusing on food venues, we study two urban consequences: how unevenly people's exposure is distributed across income groups (experienced income segregation) and the share of venues receiving no visits from simulated residents (venue disappearance). We find that, under every algorithm and in every metropolitan area, at least a fifth of venues stop receiving visits, and that more than half of this loss arises from retraining. More importantly, more accurate algorithms leave people more segregated, and the most accurate algorithm leaves people 15-21% more segregated than they actually are. We then test a re-ranking intervention that favours less popular venues and runs on top of a platform's existing algorithm. It lowers both venue disappearance and segregation across algorithms, largely without directing people to venues where they may feel less comfortable. Our results suggest that impact assessments of recommender systems should account for the feedback loop and report segregation and venue disappearance beyond accuracy.

papers.intro:
Online platforms shape which places people discover and visit in urban environments (Anderson and Magruder, 2012): maps and review platforms rank the restaurants nearby, food apps suggest where to eat next, and large language models (LLMs) answer open-ended questions about where to go (Banerjee et al., 2020; Pappalardo et al., 2025; Chen et al., 2026a; Cornacchia et al., 2026). Unlike a printed guide, the location-based recommender systems behind these online platforms learn from the visits they steer, forming a human–AI feedback loop that affects both people and places (Pedreschi et al., 2025). For people, a crucial outcome at stake is experienced income segregation: how unevenly an individual’s time at venues spreads across the income groups (Moro et al., 2021; Athey et al., 2021; Nilforoshan et al., 2023; Xu et al., 2025). Low experienced income segregation means a person’s daily places mix incomes, creating chances for cross-income ties, which predict upward income mobility (Chetty et al., 2022). For places, a key outcome at stake is venue disappearance: the share of venues that receive no visits from simulated residents. The feedback loop can concentrate visits on already popular venues (Mauro et al., 2026), and a venue without visits is then no longer recommended. Venue disappearance matters for small businesses that depend on online visibility to attract customers (Banerjee et al., 2020), as well as for the neighbourhoods they serve. As the feedback loop unfolds and the recommender system keeps retraining, both outcomes can build up over time, and their burden can fall unevenly across income groups and neighbourhoods. These effects of the feedback loop are distributional, long-term consequences of algorithmic deployment on the Web. They extend beyond the screen into residents’ lived experiences of the city and bear on the fairness of the urban environments that online platforms increasingly help to shape. Understanding and mitigating them is therefore integral to building a responsible Web (Milano et al., 2020).

Yet these algorithms are rarely evaluated for their long-term effects on communities, including how they shape segregation across income groups and the distribution of visits across local businesses. Standard offline accuracy measures assess how well an algorithm predicts past behaviour, leaving these collective outcomes largely unexamined. This out-of-loop test evaluates the recommender system once, using data describing visits that were not shaped by its recommendations. Therefore, it cannot capture experienced income segregation or venue disappearance that may emerge as the feedback loop unfolds (D’Amour et al., 2020; McNee et al., 2006). Although regulation has begun to require platforms to assess the systemic risks of their recommender systems (European Parliament and Council of the European Union, 2022), methods for assessing such long-term effects are still lacking.

Prior work has mainly studied human–AI feedback loops for online items such as songs, movies and products (Jiang et al., 2019; Chaney et al., 2018), which any number of users can consume without affecting one another. Urban venues, by contrast, differ from online items in at least three respects: (1) Spatio-temporal constraints. People choose venues near their current location and at times that fit their daily routines; recommendations therefore shape choices within a small set of locally accessible options. (2) Finite capacity. A restaurant can serve only a limited number of customers at a time; when recommendations send many people to the same venue, some must wait or go elsewhere. (3) Social coupling. Visitors to a venue share the same physical space; as a result, a recommendation to an individual also changes whom the other visitors meet.

People choose venues near their current location and at times that fit their daily routines; recommendations therefore shape choices within a small set of locally accessible options. (2) Finite capacity. A restaurant can serve only a limited number of customers at a time; when recommendations send many people to the same venue, some must wait or go elsewhere. (3) Social coupling. Visitors to a venue share the same physical space; as a result, a recommendation to an individual also changes whom the other visitors meet.

To the best of our knowledge, no existing study can capture these three factors together. Audits find that review sites and LLM assistants expose venues unevenly across neighbourhoods (Singhal et al., 2025; Chen et al., 2026a), but they do not measure how exposure changes as recommendations and user behaviour feed back on one another. Simulations can reproduce the feedback loop, but they simplify the setting: some use synthetic users (Chaney et al., 2018), others focus on online content or retail goods (Anwar et al., 2024; Barlacchi et al., 2026). The closest urban simulation study measures how venue concentration changes throughout the feedback loop but does not account for venue capacity nor measure experienced income segregation (Mauro et al., 2026). Taken together, these gaps leave three research questions unanswered: • RQ1: How does retraining within the feedback loop affect experienced income segregation and venue disappearance? • RQ2: How do different recommendation algorithms shape experienced income segregation and venue disappearance? • RQ3: Can an algorithmic intervention reduce venue disappearance and experienced income segregation within the feedback loop?

Simulations can reproduce the feedback loop, but they simplify the setting: some use synthetic users (Chaney et al., 2018), others focus on online content or retail goods (Anwar et al., 2024; Barlacchi et al., 2026). The closest urban simulation study measures how venue concentration changes throughout the feedback loop but does not account for venue capacity nor measure experienced income segregation (Mauro et al., 2026). Taken together, these gaps leave three research questions unanswered:

RQ1: How does retraining within the feedback loop affect experienced income segregation and venue disappearance?

RQ2: How do different recommendation algorithms shape experienced income segregation and venue disappearance?

RQ3: Can an algorithmic intervention reduce venue disappearance and experienced income segregation within the feedback loop?

To address these questions, we develop a realistic simulation of the human–AI feedback loop in four large U.S. metropolitan areas (Fig. 1). In each area, we simulate 4,000–8,000 residents on their GPS-recorded daily schedules, drawn in equal numbers from four income quartiles. We model recommendations only for food venues and exclude destinations for trips home or to work because they are largely determined by daily routines. We compare the outcomes of four representative recommendation algorithms: UR-POI (User Returner over Points Of Interest) recommends the venues a person visits most often, ItemKNN and UserKNN learn from co-visitation patterns through similar venues (Sarwar et al., 2001) and similar people (Resnick et al., 1994), respectively, and Markov uses population-wide transitions from the last venue (Gambs et al., 2012). To isolate the effect of retraining, we compare our results with those from an out-of-loop baseline, where each algorithm is trained just once on the observed visits.

papers.title: Prompt Less, Infer More: Static Analysis-Guided LLM Type Annotation for Python
papers.abstract: Type annotations improve the maintainability and reliability of Python programs, but many real-world projects remain under-annotated because manual annotation is time-consuming and error-prone. Recent neural and LLM-based type inference systems can recover missing annotations, yet they often trade accuracy for efficiency. Existing approaches often fail to exploit project-wide type evidence, or do so inefficiently through unnecessary model calls and noisy prompts. We present SALT, an LLM-based type inference system guided by static analysis. SALT integrates static analysis with LLM inference to resolve types statically, prioritize LLM queries, and construct concise type-aware context. To demonstrate the effectiveness of SALT, we evaluated it on 12 real-world Python projects. SALT achieves the best accuracy among the evaluated systems and reduces estimated LLM cost by up to 78.5% compared with a strong coding-assistant baseline. It also shows similar cost savings with the frontier model GPT-5.5, demonstrating that SALT remains effective with strong LLMs.

papers.title: A Self-Supervised Pose Estimation Approach for Construction Machines
papers.abstract: Pose estimation is a computer vision task used to estimate a skeleton of dynamic systems to predict future movements. Most of the research in this direction is based on a supervised learning approach which requires a massive amount of labeled datasets. In this paper, a self-supervised three-stage model based on a contrastive learning approach is introduced for estimating a skeleton of dynamic construction machines; such as excavators without using any labeled images for the first stage. The whole model structure is divided into three stages: the pre-train stage using the SimCLR contrastive approach, and two fine-tuning stages for the transfer learning and the downstream task. The model can leverage the features and learn from a huge unlabeled dataset called ACID to two small datasets generated from NVIDIA Isaac and MATLAB Simscape simulators as well as transfer the knowledge to a smaller dataset with a ratio of 3.5% from the original ACID dataset. The results show that the proposed approach can improve the accuracy of pose estimation for heavy construction machines in real images by 11% and 13% in comparison to the normal self-supervised approach with two backbones ResNet-50 and HRNet-W32, respectively.

papers.intro:
Pose estimation is a computer vision task that is used to estimate a skeleton of dynamic systems to predict future movements [6, 23]. Most of the research in this direction is based on a supervised learning approach which requires a massive amount of labeled data [20, 7]. To the best of the authors’ knowledge, there is no benchmark data for pose estimation for construction machines produced yet. The only benchmark dataset in this field is the ACID dataset [25], which consists of 10K images of 10 different classes of heavy construction vehicles, such as excavators, backhoes, and trucks. All of these are only labeled in the form of bounding boxes. This labeled format is only suitable to work with downstream tasks such as object detection and segmentation, which makes the task of pose estimation for such objects a challenging topic. In this paper, a self-supervised contrastive learning model is designed to estimate a skeleton of dynamic heavy machines without using any labeled images, as the model depends on data augmentation to learn the visual representations that distinguish objects from one another in different images. The model leverages the concept that images produced from the same source have similar visual representations and features, while the ones produced from different sources will have a variant representation. The model is trained on a huge dataset and then fine-tuned on smaller ones. By reusing the structure of the SimCLR model [5], the proposed model can detect the keypoints of heavy machines and produce a skeleton in different situations and positions. The model outperforms the supervised approach on two simulated datasets from MATLAB Simscape Multibody [17] and NVIDIA Omnivers environments by 1.7% and 0.8% AP, respectively. In addition, it is fine-tuned over a small amount of the dataset and gives an increase of 11% and 13% AP for two different backbone models.

papers.title: On k-nearest-neighbor regression in metric spaces
papers.abstract: We study mean squared consistency of k-nearest-neighbor regression for metric space valued features. For a fixed feature distribution mu with atomless distance distributions, we describe how neighbor selection redistributes probability through the density of a uniformly chosen neighbor of an independent query. This gives separate conditions for the approximation error and the conditional response variance, and weakens Stone's domination condition when stronger response moments are available. In particular, when k_n tends to infinity and k_n/n tends to zero, a uniform L2(mu) bound on the selection densities suffices under a finite fourth response moment. We give a corresponding condition in terms of neighborhoods of fixed population mass and recover the Euclidean density bound. Finite global Nagata dimension gives Stone's domination. While sigma-finite Nagata dimensionality is known to ensure universal consistency of k-NN classification in complete separable spaces, we show that this is not the case for mean squared consistency with unbounded responses: we construct a space in this class on which one fixed noiseless response with all finite moments has diverging mean squared error.

papers.title: DAPS: Dependency-Aware Premise Selection for LLM Theorem Proving
papers.abstract: LLM-based theorem proving in Lean 4 has advanced rapidly, but provers are difficult to leverage newly contributed lemmas, because retrieval skews toward popular foundational lemmas, leaving the right premises buried among hundreds of thousands of candidates. Existing neural selectors rank candidates by semantic similarity, with three intrinsic limitations: frequency-skewed retrieval, isolated pairwise ranking, and degradation on out-of-distribution queries such as competition problems and informal language. Given that mathematics is structured by dependencies rather than similarities, we restore this signal to both the training data and the model. We curate two underused dependency resources. We conduct the first systematic mining of 53 Lean Blueprint projects, a previously untapped corpus of 3,805 manually curated informal+formal nodes that capture rare, research-level premises absent from Mathlib4. We further pair it with the extraction of comprehensive, typed, multi-level Mathlib4 dependencies. We then introduce DAPS, a dependency-aware premise selector with a structural neighborhood encoder, a group-level contrastive objective, and a Mathlib-then-Blueprint adaptation procedure. DAPS reaches mean Recall@32 of 89.25 on Mathlib4-Heldout (+11.41 over the strong selector LeanHammer), and maintains this lead on two out-of-distribution benchmarks. Further experiments demonstrate that DAPS premises improve theorem proving on miniF2F and IMO-ProofBench. Project page: https://daps-eth.github.io/.

papers.title: GraphNIAH: A Benchmark for Long-Context Reasoning over Real-World Graphs
papers.abstract: The needle-in-a-haystack (NIAH) benchmark was introduced as a test for measuring a model's ability to find small relevant facts within a very large body of input text. However, existing NIAH benchmarks each suffer from one or more of the following limitations: (1) reliance on synthetic data, so their evaluations may not generalize to real-world settings; (2) reuse of previously published datasets, leading to the risk of benchmark contamination; (3) dependence on manual annotation, which requires human effort to create and update data and is prone to future benchmark contamination; and (4) unrealistic simplification of long-context multi-hop reasoning where each next step is trivial given previous steps, while real-world reasoning often requires planning over multiple possible proof paths. To address these limitations, we introduce \Benchmark, a dynamic benchmark built from real citation relationships among scientific papers published after the evaluated models' knowledge cutoff date, which utilizes real-world information while ensuring no benchmark contamination. The fully automated benchmark construction pipeline samples representative subgraphs of the citation graph formed by these papers and converts each subgraph into a long-context QA example with a verifiable answer. We use GraphNIAH to evaluate eight LLMs from the GPT-5.6, Gemini-3, and Qwen3.5 families. We find that accuracy falls as questions require longer reasoning paths: at question depths of 16 and 32, the GPT-5.6 and Qwen3.5 models answer YES/NO questions no better than random guessing, mostly by answering NO; four of the eight models answer no counting example correctly, and the others model get worse as the subgraph size increases. These findings suggest that current LLMs often stop searching the citation relationships in their context before they reach the answer, even though every fact they need is in the context.

With the rapid evolution of large language models (LLMs) in recent years, their native context length has also increased significantly from 2,048 tokens of GPT-3 (Brown et al., 2020) to 128k tokens of Llama-3.2 (Grattafiori et al., 2024), and now, to 1M tokens of DeepSeek-V4 (DeepSeek-AI, 2026). With context extension techniques, such as RoPE-based scaling (Liu et al., 2024b; Ding et al., 2024) and long-context training (Hu et al., 2025; Gao et al., 2025), context length can be extended to upwards of 4M tokens. With this ability to receive extremely long input text sequences, LLMs have been adopted for many complex long-context tasks, such as deep research (Du et al., 2026), long-context summarization (Laban et al., 2024; Wright et al., 2025), and long-horizon reasoning and planning (Chen et al., 2025a; Erdogan et al., 2025). Furthermore, as downstream tasks increase in complexity and input prompts increase in length, it is becoming increasingly important for LLMs to be able to process key information in very long contexts, and then combine it with other information to solve such tasks (Koh et al., 2022; Pal et al., 2025; Adams et al., 2025). The needle-in-a-haystack (NIAH) test (Kamradt, 2023) evaluates whether LLMs can retrieve a small relevant fact, called a needle, from a long context containing unrelated information. However, single-hop NIAH tests do not accurately reflect real-world scenarios where relevant facts are often derived from multiple parts of the context or conversation. Hence, several multi-hop NIAH benchmarks have been proposed, including RULER (Hsieh et al., 2024), Sequential-NIAH (Yu et al., 2025), and U-NIAH (Gao et al., 2026), which require models to connect multiple facts.

This process requires no manual annotation, so new examples can be generated automatically as new papers are published. Each sampled subgraph contains several connected components, so that some papers are reachable from the source paper while others are not. papers.title: Long-term variability of the 35-day cycle in Her X-1
papers.abstract:
Her X-1 is an eclipsing X-ray binary system consisting of an accreting neutron star and an optical component HZ Her. In addition to the 1.24-s X-ray pulsations and the 1.7-d orbital period, the system also shows a 35-day X-ray variability related to the precessional motion of a tilted and twisted accretion disk around the neutron star. The long-term persistence of the 35-day X-ray variability suggests the presence of a stable clock mechanism, most likely free precession of the magnetized neutron star.
  We have studied the long-term behavior of the 35-day cycle of Her X-1 using all available CGRO/BATSE, RXTE/ASM, Swift/BAT, Fermi/GBM, MAXI data and archival turn-on moments of the 35-day cycle spanning more than 50 years. We have used a sliding-window averaged X-ray phase light curve and the classical O-C (observed minus calculated) diagram for individual 35-day turn-ons to inspect the long-term trends of the O-C diagram. The O-C diagram demonstrates two similar parabolic trends separated by an anomalous low state (ALS) of the source suggesting a secular decrease in the 35-d precession period with $\dot P_\text{35} =(-1.3\pm0.2)\times10^{-5} \,\mathrm{~s\,s}^{-1}$ and $\dot P_\text{35} =(-4.7\pm0.1)\times10^{-5} \,\mathrm{~s\,s}^{-1}$ before and after the ALS, respectively.
  We conclude that the decay of the 35-day period as inferred from the O-C analysis can be interpreted in terms of the direct relationship between the change of the precessional period of the accretion disk to the long-term decrease of the period of the free precessional neutron star - due to continued accumulation of accreted matter.

The 35-day cycle in Her X-1 is thought to be due to counter-orbital precession of the accretion disk (Gerend and Boynton, 1976; Crosa and Boynton, 1980). There are different physical models of the precessing accretion disk in Her X-1 (see, e.g., Schandl and Meyer (1994); Wijers and Pringle (1999); Shakura et al. (1999); Scott et al. (2000)). The precessing tilted accretion disk should undergo tidal wobbling (nutation) twice the orbital period (Katz et al., 1982; Levine and Jernigan, 1982; Klochkov et al., 2006). Traces of the disk nutation were recently found in Her X-1 observations by Mikhail Pavlinsky ART-XC telescope onboard SRG X-ray observatory (Revnivtsev et al., 2025).

The long-term stability of 35-day cycle has been addressed by different authors (Staubert et al., 1983; Shakura et al., 1998; Leahy and Igna, 2010). A viable model to explain it involves a freely precessing NS as a clock mechanism (Bahcall and Bahcall, 1972; Truemper et al., 1986; Shakura et al., 1998; Staubert et al., 2009a). Observational signatures of the freely precessing NS in Her X-1 were obtained from the analysis of X-ray pulse variations (Truemper et al., 1986; Postnov et al., 2013), from the analysis of the optical UBV light curves of HZ Her (Kolesnikov et al., 2020) and recently from the Fermi/GBM NS spin period variability (Kolesnikov et al., 2022). In this model, a freely precessing magnetized NS produces variable illumination of the HZ Her hemisphere periodically changing the initial conditions of the gas stream forming a tilted accretion disk around the NS (Shakura et al., 1999). The variability of matter outflow through the vicinity of the inner Lagrangian point L1L_{1} in Her X-1 due to a changing reflection effect was confirmed by 3D hydrodynamical simulations in Lukin et al. (2024). The tilted accretion disk interacts with the rotating NS magnetosphere which forces the inner disk parts to align with the NS rotational equator (Lipunov and Shakura, 1980; Lai, 1999; Romanova et al., 2013). Thus, a twisted accretion disk is formed. Its outer parts precess under the joint action of tidal forces and dynamical interaction of gas streams forming the disk thus producing a variable shadow on the HZ Her hemisphere (Shakura et al., 1999). The changing shape of the shadow with 35-day phase during the precessional motion of the disk provides a feedback to keep the outer disk tilted to the orbital plane by the variable gas streams. papers.title: Creating functional nanostructures for vortex manipulation in superconducting Bi$_\text{2}$Sr$_\text{2}$CaCu$_\text{2}$O$_\text{8+x}$ thin films via focused He ion beam irradiation
papers.abstract: Bi$_2$Sr$_2$CaCu$_2$O$_{8+x}$ (Bi-2212) is a highly anisotropic high-temperature superconductor exhibiting unique vortex dynamics due to its layered structure. Precise nanoscale patterning of ultrathin Bi-2212 films remains challenging, limiting controlled studies of vortex pinning. Here, we employ 30 keV focused helium ion beam (He-FIB) irradiation to fabricate periodic arrays of columnar defects with 100 nm spacings in optimally-doped Bi-2212 thin films, thereby creating artificial vortex pinning centers. Magnetotransport measurements reveal pronounced vortex matching effects, evidenced by minima in magnetoresistance and peaks in critical current at commensurate magnetic fields. The angular dependence of magnetoresistance and critical current scale with an effective magnetic field, indicating strong confinement of pancake vortices along irradiation-induced tracks. These findings demonstrate the efficacy of He-FIB nanopatterning in modulating the superconducting properties in Bi-2212 thin films, providing a platform for fundamental studies of vortex matter and advancing prospects for device applications based on this highly anisotropic superconductor.

Here, ξa​b\xi_{ab} and ξc\xi_{c} denote the Ginzburg-Landau coherence lengths at temperature T=0 KT=$0\text{\,}\mathrm{K}$ parallel and perpendicular to the CuO2 layers of Bi-2212, respectively, and λa​b\lambda_{ab} and λc\lambda_{c} are the zero-temperature London penetration depths for magnetic fields oriented parallel to the crystallographic cc axis and along the a​bab planes, respectively.

papers.title: Proof-Carrying Evolution: Black-Box Search, White-Box Flight
papers.abstract: We study whether a language model can help design controllers whose behavior can be formally checked. In proof-carrying evolution (PCE), a search proposes controllers together with their certificates. Their mathematical forms are fixed; a proposer chooses their numerical parameters together. Certificate checks guide selection, and only a certified candidate can be returned. The deployed artifact is a control law and its certificate; the language model is used only during design. We compare four language models with classical search and synthesis on docking under a speed limit, pursuit of a maneuvering target, and attitude control on SO(3), using paired runs and shared proposal allowances. Certificates are checked in exact rational arithmetic during search on the linear problems. On SO(3), the search uses floating-point checks, followed by exact re-verification of every reported champion. The best run of each method also receives Lean 4 proofs of its stated control properties. On the linear problems, the strongest models beat the standard classical baselines on every run, but a classical optimizer that chooses certificates for the same objective closes most of that lead. Among the cited pursuit champions, the ranking does not survive a change from Euler to zero-order-hold dynamics. On SO(3), no model detectably outperforms CMA-ES when mixed with classical mutation. When models write every proposal, one tested model improves on CMA-ES and the other performs worse than its mixed variant. All search medians remain below the hand-tuned law. In a docking control with the objective and mutation operator held fixed, retaining certified candidates yields new certified designs in every run; removing this rule yields none.

papers.intro:
Spacecraft controllers need guarantees whose assumptions and scope can be reviewed. For many critical maneuvers, opportunities for recovery are limited, so a review board asks not only whether a design worked in simulation but why it must work. Mission requirements are therefore often requirements on the strength of a guarantee under a stated model: the time within which a docking maneuver is guaranteed to reach its tolerance, the largest measurement or initial-state uncertainty under which it still succeeds, or the size of the set of states from which a vehicle is guaranteed to capture, or to evade, another under stated assumptions about its actions. Meeting such a requirement means finding both a control law and a certificate that establishes the property over the relevant operating conditions. This paper optimizes three such objectives: a certified docking-time bound, a certified capture radius against a maneuvering target, and the size of a certified attitude region on SO(3).

Classical methods such as LQR, H∞H_{\infty} design, gain scheduling and Lyapunov-based nonlinear design produce explicit laws that engineers can inspect and analyze, although explicit mathematical form alone does not make a complex system easy to understand. Choosing an explicit controller family still leaves a design problem: an initial law may admit no certificate in the chosen family, or its certified bound may be too weak for the mission. The certificate itself is part of this problem. Changing its parameters can improve the bound for a fixed control law, while changing the law can improve performance but lose the certificate. Searching over both gives the optimizer a way to improve what can be guaranteed.

A language model can instead act at design time, proposing parameters for an explicit controller and its certificate; executing the deployed law requires no model inference. We ask whether a language model can serve as the proposer inside such a certifiable design space, rather than replace it with a black box.

We call this approach proof-carrying evolution, after proof-carrying code (Necula, 1997). In proof-carrying code, an untrusted producer supplies a program and a proof that it obeys a safety policy; a consumer checks the proof before accepting the program. PCE applies this separation to control design (Fig. ). A proposer modifies controller and certificate parameters, a verifier checks the certificate conditions, and selection favors candidates with better certified objective values. Retained designs provide starting points for further proposals. Only a certified candidate can become a run’s result, so acceptance depends on checking rather than on trust in the proposer. Inside the loop the search proposes and a checker decides: certificates are checked in exact rational arithmetic on the linear problems. A certificate compiler turns a checked certificate into a Lean proof. An independent audit rejects proofs that rely on unfinished obligations or unapproved axioms. 2. Comparative evidence (§). Four models (gpt-6-astra, gpt-5.6-sol, Claude Opus 5.5 and the open-weight gpt-oss-120b; Astra, Sol, Opus and gpt-oss below) share paired seeds and proposal allowances with classical baselines (Table ). On the linear problems, Astra and Sol beat the standard classical baselines on every run. Among the cited pursuit champions, this ranking does not survive zero-order-hold dynamics (§). These comparisons use one reasoning-effort setting per model; apart from a detected but unsized benefit for Sol on pursuit, they do not establish whether feedback improves model proposals. On SO(3), no model detectably beats CMA-ES when it writes about one proposal in five; Opus does when writing every proposal (§). 3. Verification during search (§). Under a thrust limit, a hand-designed law and the best docking run of every arm but one have decrease theorems for the clipped dynamics. The best attitude controller of every arm has a regional decrease certificate on SO(3). The cited docking and pursuit designs also have decrease and trajectory theorems under bounded measurement noise and rounding error, assuming a bound on floating-point error. 5. papers.title: On approximate support versions of Donoho--Stark uncertainty principles for $k$-Hadamard operators
papers.abstract: In this paper we present results related to Donoho--Stark type uncertainty principles that were proved in the article "The uncertainty principle: variations on a theme" by Wigderson and Wigderson for $k$-Hadamard operators in the finite-dimensional setting. Namely, the authors showed that Donoho-Stark principles can be generalized to versions for approximate supports with respect to norms $\ell^{p}$ for $p=1$ and $p=2$. In the second case they assumed the so-called speciality condition, namely that a suitable matrix satisfies $A^{*}A = kI$. First we show that such theorems cannot be generalized to $p>1$ if matrices are not special $k$-Hadamard. Next we prove Donoho-Stark type principle for special $k$-Hadamard operators for $\ell^{p}$ norms within the range $1\leq p\leq 2$. Finally, we show that such theorems are false for $p>2$ even in the presence of the speciality condition.

papers.title: Counting kinks and magnons with the lattice: magnetoelastic effects in Cs$_2$CoBr$_4$
papers.abstract: We report low-temperature dilatometry and ultrasound measurements on the frustrated quasi-one-dimensional antiferromagnet Cs$_2$CoBr$_4$ across the entire cascade of field-induced magnetic phase transitions. The whole phase diagram can be recovered from these lattice probes, with distinct anomalies observed at each phase boundary. Elongation along the principal chain axis is found to closely track magnetization throughout the phase diagram. This behavior is interpreted in terms of kinks in the N\'eel structure and magnons in the transverse-ordered magnetic-BEC phases, each carrying a fixed lattice distortion. A simultaneous analysis of ultrasound and striction data allows us to quantify the strength of magnetoelastic coupling.

papers.intro:
Magnetoelastic coupling often plays an important role in frustrated quantum magnetic materials. In some cases the appearance of lattice distortions partially relieves degeneracies caused by frustration [1], stabilizing particular ordered phases and sometimes even driving transitions between them [2]. Among the more famous examples are pyrochlore [3, 4, 5] and triangular-lattice compounds [6], as well as the Shastry–Sutherland system SrCu2(BO3)2 [7, 8, 9]. Even for phases and phase transitions of purely magnetic origin, magnetoelastic coupling can lead to exciting new physics. In particular, strain [10], optical-phonon [11], and sound-propagation [12] anomalies are a common occurrence at magnetic phase transitions [13]. In certain cases they have even been used to directly measure two-spin correlation functions, as, for example, in the S=1S=1 quantum paramagnet NiCl2⋅{}_{2}\cdot4SC(NH2)2 (DTN) [14], the spin ladder (C5H12N)2CuBr4 (BPCB) [15], or SrCu2(BO3)2 [16]. Magnetoelastic coupling caused by exchange striction is particularly relevant in materials undergoing a cascade of field-induced phase transitions, especially those involving collinear plateau phases, the “lattice staircase” in CuFeO2 being a particularly well-known example [17].

Cascades of field-induced plateau states and other phases are known in several frustrated quantum magnets. Particular diversity is found among orthorhombic (space group Pn​m​anma) A2MX4 materials, where M is a magnetic transition metal, A an alkali metal, and X either a halogen or oxygen [18]. The best-known species with complex field-induced phases are Cs2CuCl4 [19] and Cs2CuBr4 [20, 21]. The extent to which these transitions involve the crystal lattice remains poorly understood, but is expected to be significant. Indeed, high-pressure experiments on Cs2CuCl4 show that magnetic interactions are sensitive to pressure [22]. A direct observation of magnetoelastic effects has recently been reported for Cs2CoI4 [23]. The focus of the present work is Cs2CoBr4. It stands out in that it exhibits one of the most complex cascades of field-induced phases [24] and is simultaneously one of the best characterized and well-understood species. Moreover, there is initial experimental evidence of strong magnetoelastic coupling in this material [25].

Over time, our understanding of Cs2CoBr4 has been evolving [24, 26, 27], but by now its magnetic Hamiltonian has been solidly established through neutron scattering and THz spectroscopy experiments [25] and numerical modeling [28]. Magnetism is due to S=3/2S=3/2 Co2+ ions subject to dominant XYZ anisotropy with the crystallographic bb direction being the “easiest” axis. This anisotropy is of predominantly easy-plane character with an anisotropy constant D=0.70D=0.70 meV [25]. As a consequence, the single-ion ground state responsible for most of the low-energy physics is an effective pseudospin S=1/2S=1/2 doublet [24]. The easy-axis role of the bb axis is further enhanced by the fact that the structure contains two crystallographically equivalent sets of magnetic ions with almost orthogonal anisotropy planes that share this direction. Compared to single-ion anisotropy, inter-ion interactions are considerably weaker. The dominant Heisenberg exchange coupling is antiferromagnetic, with J4=0.135​(5)J_{4}=0.135(5) meV. It involves the fourth-shortest Co–Co distance and builds antiferromagnetic chains that also run along bb. Next in the hierarchy is the nearest-neighbor Heisenberg coupling J1=0.06​(1)J_{1}=0.06(1) meV that binds pairs of adjacent chains with parallel anisotropy planes into frustrated zigzag ladders. This geometry is illustrated in Fig. 1. The most spectacular manifestation of its predominantly one-dimensional character is the zero-field excitation spectrum, a Zeeman ladder of spinon bound states observed by neutron spectroscopy and studied in detail numerically [27, 28]. Indeed, other magnetic interactions have also been identified but are weaker still. The strongest among them is J5=0.020​(5)J_{5}=0.020(5) meV, which diagonally connects adjacent chains in the (b,c)(b,c) plane. A more detailed discussion can be found in Ref. [25].

papers.title: Zero Crossings on the Accuracy-Smoothness Frontier: Maximal Monotone and Minimal Inflection Non Stationary Predictors
papers.abstract: The Smooth Sign Accuracy (SSA) framework resolves the smoothness--accuracy dilemma for stationary predictors by balancing mean squared error (MSE) against the frequency of sign changes. We generalize it to non-stationary integrated processes (I-SSA), deriving MSE-optimal predictors constrained by the expected duration between turning points (I(1)) or inflection points (I(2)). The resulting maximal-monotone and minimal-inflection predictors, filters, and smoothers customize classic benchmarks along a new efficient Accuracy--Smoothness (AS) frontier. Tracking the identity (the original data) along this frontier defines the \emph{I-SSA trend}, a novel smoothing concept that, unlike classical filters, imposes no artificial structure on the data-generating process and is directly interpretable through explicit control of turning- or inflection-point frequency. The optimization is a quadratically constrained quadratic program (QCQP) that reduces to a Generalized Trust Region Subproblem (GTRS) with hidden convexity. On its feasible, invertible region the problem is convex with a well-defined global optimum, and an exact closed-form expression delivers the efficient AS frontier. Under fairly general assumptions, finite-sample solutions converge to an asymptotic I-SSA predictor, devoid of integration boundary perturbations. The framework unifies mean squared error on non-stationary levels, and sign accuracy, zero-crossing frequency, and target correlation on stationary differences.

papers.intro:
Forecasting requires balancing conflicting objectives. The SSA framework (Wildi, 2024, 2026a) targets accuracy (estimating future levels) and smoothness (suppressing spurious noise). We propose I-SSA, extending SSA to non-stationary integrated series and letting users balance accuracy (A) and smoothness (S) along a novel, efficient AS-frontier. We focus on univariate, homoscedastic series (the multivariate stationary case is treated in Wildi, 2026b). I-SSA overcomes the limitations of the frequency-domain forecast trilemma (McElroy and Wildi, 2019), offering better interpretability, numerical efficiency, and robustness against overfitting.

We propose I-SSA, extending SSA to non-stationary integrated series and letting users balance accuracy (A) and smoothness (S) along a novel, efficient AS-frontier. We focus on univariate, homoscedastic series (the multivariate stationary case is treated in Wildi, 2026b). I-SSA overcomes the limitations of the frequency-domain forecast trilemma (McElroy and Wildi, 2019), offering better interpretability, numerical efficiency, and robustness against overfitting.

Traditional smoothing methods include curvature-penalized approaches (Whittaker, 1923; Henderson, 1924; Hodrick and Prescott, 1997)—despite recent critiques (Hamilton, 2018; Phillips and Shi, 2021)—splines (Eilers, Marx, and Durban, 2015; Wood, 2017), trend extraction (Harvey, 1989; Durbin and Koopman, 2012), and spectral filtering (Baxter and King, 1999; Pollock, 2000; Percival and Walden, 2000). Since our approach emphasizes turning and inflection points (TP/IP), a natural benchmark is the HP filter, a special case of Whittaker–Henderson smoothing, still widely used in business-cycle analysis and crisis prediction (Drehmann and Yetman, 2021); we complement the analysis with the boosted HP filter (Phillips and Shi, 2021, 2024). Broader comparisons are available in our R package.

While the HP filter minimizes curvature, SSA defines smoothness via the expected duration between sign changes (zero crossings, ZC) of a stationary, zero-mean predictor, building on Rice (1944). I-SSA extends this to integrated processes by targeting ZCs in stationary differences while minimizing MSE at the non-stationary levels. Economically, sign changes in growth rates mark transitions between expansions and contractions, so capturing business cycles requires sufficiently long intervals between crossings. This mean duration, the holding time (HT) (Wildi, 2024), is explicitly regulated in I-SSA for the growth (I(1)) or acceleration (I(2)) of the predictor via the rate of TPs or IPs.

I-SSA defines a novel Accuracy-Smoothness (AS) frontier: no other linear predictor of the same, or shorter length can improve both MSE on non-stationary levels (accuracy) and ZC rate in stationary differences (smoothness). Within this family, I-SSA is characterized by the fewest growth sign-changes, which justifies the terms maximal monotone (I(1)) and minimal inflection (I(2)).11 1 The method also yields minimal monotone and maximal inflection predictors for a given MSE, though such extreme ‘un-smoothing’ is typically irrelevant in prediction; see Wildi (2026a,b). The classic MSE predictor is one point on this frontier, whereas I-SSA covers it in full. We also give a closed-form link between HT and MSE along the frontier, extending the stationary AS dilemma (Wildi, 2024, 2026a,b) to integrated processes.
