Extending SSA to the non-stationary setting raises technical caveats. The cointegration constraint between the acausal target and the causal predictor, which ensures finite MSE on levels, introduces asymmetries in the Toeplitz structure of the system matrices. Permanent ‘unit-root’ memory prevents convergence to circulants, so the system matrices do not commute and a fixed Fourier eigenbasis is unavailable. We therefore use a generalized eigenvalue decomposition of a matrix pencil, as in cointegration (Johansen, 1988, 1991) and canonical correlation analysis (Box and Tiao, 1977), but with a structure originating in the optimization literature on the generalized trust-region subproblem (GTRS; Moré, 1993; Adachi et al., 2017) because the Hessian is generally indefinite. The pencil separately encodes the non-stationary level and stationary autocorrelation operators, which the generalized decomposition diagonalizes simultaneously. This yields a closed-form, MSE-optimal predictor constrained by the expected duration between turning points, to our knowledge not previously explored for integrated processes. Although the formulation matches the stationary case, the geometry differs fundamentally: the generalized eigenvectors are non-orthogonal and depend on the HT, and the acausal target and causal predictor rely on different spectral bases, leading to a counterfactual spectral decomposition (details below).

Formally, the optimization is a generalized trust-region subproblem (GTRS) with hidden convexity. If the classic MSE predictor is known, I-SSA reduces to a convolution with it that modifies its ZC rate while preserving MSE optimality; we call this transformation customization. For this problem, the region of invertibility and strict monotonicity reduce prediction to a one-dimensional search with certification of the global optimum. Under fairly general assumptions, finite-length solutions converge to a well-structured infinite-length I-SSA problem, free of finite-length boundary perturbations.

I-SSA customization means the projection of existing benchmark predictors onto the non-stationary AS frontier. In the applications, we customize the HP filter and its boosted variant, introducing the maximal monotone HP trend nowcast, obtained by targeting the acausal two-sided (boosted) HP filter in I-SSA. This reconciles growth sign analysis, in differences, with optimal level tracking. With the cursor on the frontier set to replicate the benchmark’s TP rate, the I-SSA trend achieves lower MSE, notably at TPs, with faster response (smaller retardation) and no over- or undershooting. All examples are replicable with our open-source R package (https://github.com/wiaidp/R-package-SSA-Predictor), which also extends customization to Hamilton’s regression filter (Hamilton, 2018), the Baxter–King filter (Baxter and King, 1999), and a refined Beveridge–Nelson decomposition (Kamber, Morley, and Wong, 2024).

papers.title: A Finite-Range, Translation-Invariant Counterexample to Weak Gibbsianity
papers.abstract: We construct a finite-range, translation-invariant counterexample to the Weak Gibbsianity property for quantum spin systems on $\mathbb{Z}^2$. The proof relies on showing how a local potential can induce macroscopically large deviations from an equilibrium configuration after a perturbation is introduced at the boundary of the lattice.

papers.title: Soft X-Ray Detection Down to the Nitrogen K-Edge Using a Pixelated iLGAD Sensor
papers.abstract: Hybrid pixel detectors represent the state-of-the-art technology for hard X-ray experiments at synchrotron light sources and free-electron lasers, owing to their high frame rates, extended dynamic range, and scalable detection areas. However, their application in the soft X-ray regime remains bottlenecked by the challenge of developing a sensor that can achieve high quantum efficiency and an sufficient signal-to-noise ratio at low photon energies. Here, we present inverse low-gain avalanche diode (iLGAD) sensors integrated with a thin entrance window, demonstrating single-photon resolution down to 390 eV (below the Nitrogen K-edge) with a signal-to-noise ratio of 5. Two gain layer designs, standard gain layer and shallow gain layer, were systematically investigated to evaluate their spectral response as a function of photon energy and operating temperature. A double-peak feature is observed in the energy spectrum, arising from the dependence of charge multiplication on photon absorption depth. Furthermore, a phenomenological spectral fitting model was established, enabling the quantitative extraction of the effective $\mathrm{n}^+$ layer thickness and gain layer depth. Beyond providing a fundamental understanding of iLGAD charge multiplication mechanisms and characterization results in the soft X-ray regime, these findings lay the foundation for developing large-area, high-frame-rate hybrid pixel detectors for soft X-ray. This advancement directly benefits soft X-ray photon science applications, including high-resolution ptychography, spectroscopy, and resonant scattering at synchrotron and FEL beamlines.

papers.intro:
Soft X-ray radiation (250 eV–2 keV) provides a unique probe for accessing the K-edges of low-ZZ elements for structural and chemical analysis; in particular, the “water window” (284–543 eV) between the carbon and oxygen K-edges offers high intrinsic contrast for biological imaging. Furthermore, this energy regime covers the L-edges of 3​d3d transition metals for probing magnetic and electronic states, as well as the M-edges of rare-earth elements. To achieve these scientific goals, a wide range of techniques operate in this energy regime, ranging from spectroscopic and scattering probes, including resonant X-ray diffraction [20] and resonant inelastic X-ray scattering [17], to high-resolution lensless imaging, most notably ptychography [13]. The successful implementation of these techniques relies heavily on 2D pixelated detectors. Driven by recent advances in accelerator-based light sources, particularly free-electron lasers like SwissFEL and EuXFEL alongside diffraction-limited storage rings like MAX IV and SLS 2.0, light sources are reaching unprecedented levels of brilliance and spatial coherence. Concurrently, the emergence of high-harmonic generation (HHG) technology has made tabletop soft X-ray sources viable. Together, these developments across large-scale facilities and laboratory platforms offer more opportunities across science and industry, while posing significant challenges to current detector technologies in the soft X-ray regimes.

Hybrid pixel detectors (HPDs), consisting of a sensor and a readout chip interconnected via bump-bonding, are widely used in the tender and hard X-ray regimes (> 2 keV). At the Paul Scherrer Institut (PSI), we have developed high-performance HPDs—such as JUNGFRAU [18, 14, 15], MÖNCH [9, 4, 19], and EIGER [21, 22, 2]—which are deployed at facilities worldwide. Their widespread adoption originates from their high dynamic range (up to 10410^{4} photons/pixel at 12 keV), fast frame rates (>2>2 kHz), and modular scalability for large-area coverage. However, their application below 2 keV2\text{\,}\mathrm{k}\mathrm{e}\mathrm{V} is fundamentally challenged by the low quantum efficiency (QE) and poor signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) of the silicon sensors in HPDs. In contrast, conventional detectors commonly used in the soft X-ray regime, such as charge-coupled devices (CCDs) and complementary metal-oxide-semiconductor (CMOS) imagers, often suffer from restricted active areas, low frame rates, and limited dynamic range. As a result, they increasingly struggle to meet the high readout speed and wide dynamic range demanded by next-generation soft X-ray experiments. Therefore, extending the application of HPDs to the soft X-ray regime offers a promising route to overcome these limitations.

Their widespread adoption originates from their high dynamic range (up to 10410^{4} photons/pixel at 12 keV), fast frame rates (>2>2 kHz), and modular scalability for large-area coverage. However, their application below 2 keV2\text{\,}\mathrm{k}\mathrm{e}\mathrm{V} is fundamentally challenged by the low quantum efficiency (QE) and poor signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) of the silicon sensors in HPDs. In contrast, conventional detectors commonly used in the soft X-ray regime, such as charge-coupled devices (CCDs) and complementary metal-oxide-semiconductor (CMOS) imagers, often suffer from restricted active areas, low frame rates, and limited dynamic range. As a result, they increasingly struggle to meet the high readout speed and wide dynamic range demanded by next-generation soft X-ray experiments. Therefore, extending the application of HPDs to the soft X-ray regime offers a promising route to overcome these limitations.

In the soft X-ray regime, shallow photon absorption near the sensor surface reduces the QE, while the small charge generated by soft X-rays is comparable to electronic noise, leading to a poor SNR. Crucial to mitigating these limitations in HPDs below 2 keV2\text{\,}\mathrm{k}\mathrm{e}\mathrm{V} is the optimization of the sensor, which absorbs incoming X-ray photons and transfers the generated signal to the readout chip. Therefore, to enable HPDs to operate in the soft X-ray regime, PSI has collaborated with Fondazione Bruno Kessler (FBK) to develop an optimized sensor: inverse low-gain avalanche diode (iLGAD) sensors incorporating a thin entrance window (TEW) [24]. LGAD technology introduces a doping-engineered gain layer that amplifies the photo-generated signal via impact ionization, with an internal gain typically ranging from 5 to 20. This signal amplification effectively raises the signal well above the noise floor and improves the overall SNR, thereby enabling single-photon discrimination with Poisson-limited statistics, provided that the detector system is not dominated by shot noise in the sensor. Crucially, this internal gain does not compromise the advantages of HPDs [24, 12]. Simultaneously, the integration of TEW technology minimizes shallow surface absorption, allowing low-energy photons down to the EUV regime to penetrate into the active silicon volume.

papers.title: On-device Detection of Wearer-induced NLOS on Chest-worn UWB Tags: Machine Learning, Link Indicators, or Both?
papers.abstract: Ultra-wideband (UWB) enables high-accuracy distance estimation (ranging), but performance degrades in non-line-of-sight (NLOS) conditions. When UWB tags are worn, the human body inevitably causes a wearer-induced NLOS (WNLOS), yielding significant errors; still, despite its relevance, WNLOS remains understudied. Moreover, WNLOS detection typically must occur on-device at the tag, requiring classification accuracy to be balanced against tight runtime and energy constraints often hard to meet with machine learning (ML) -- the dominating NLOS classification approach. Meanwhile, UWB radio link indicators (LI) offer a faster and lightweight alternative that has rarely been explored. We study existing on-device ML and LI classifiers when applied to WNLOS, and propose novel hybrid ones exploiting their complementarity. We focus on chest-worn tags and analyze 21 classifiers on a dataset of 1.5 million samples across channels, PHY settings, environments, subjects, and orientations. Results show that while all of them achieve good classification accuracy, relative performance, including ranging errors due to misclassification, depends heavily on channel and PHY configuration. Runtime and energy efficiency also vary dramatically; some techniques offer marginal accuracy gains while consuming up to 39.6x more energy. Therefore, we also introduce a recommender tool to identify optimal classifiers under user-defined constraints, publicly released with our dataset.

papers.intro:
Ultra-wideband (UWB) has become a reference technology for location-aware Internet of Things applications in indoor and GNSS-denied environments. Its integration into consumer devices, such as smartphones and smartwatches, has recently driven wider adoption and significant market growth (Markets & Markets Research Private Ltd., 2025), enabling disruptive UWB-based applications including keyless entry systems (Kalyanaraman et al., 2020), secure payments (UWB Alliance, 2026), robot navigation (Ledergerber et al., 2015; Xianjia et al., 2021), industrial process optimization (FiRa Consortium, 2026), and social interaction tracking (Biri et al., 2020). By transmitting signals over a wide bandwidth, UWB enables to estimate with high-resolution the signal’s time of arrival and corresponding time of flight, enabling decimeter-level distance measurements (ranging) and localization—a performance that narrowband wireless technologies such as ZigBee, Bluetooth, and Wi-Fi cannot match (Leitch et al., 2023).

papers.title: TheseusSyn: Unified Medical Image Synthesis via Context-Conditioned Masked Autoregression
papers.abstract: High-fidelity medical image synthesis is promising for data-efficient learning and privacy-preserving model development. However, most existing approaches rely on symbolic or label-based conditioning, which constrains generative diversity and limits case-specific contextual fidelity. Inspired by the Ship of Theseus paradox, we propose TheseusSyn, a novel context-conditioned synthesis paradigm that generates images through iterative content replacement. Our framework employs a multi-codebook discrete tokenizer to convert medical images into sequences of token indices, extracted with a global representation token that serves as a contextual constraint. A masked autoregressive generative model then iteratively masks and predicts tokens conditioned on both local neighborhoods and the global context. By progressively replacing image content until the entire token sequence is renewed, TheseusSyn produces synthetic samples that preserve anatomical coherence and semantic consistency while introducing controlled diversity. We evaluate the proposed framework on multiple datasets from MedMNIST by constructing synthetic datasets with varying masking strategies and training ResNet-18 classifiers exclusively on either real or synthetic data. Experimental results demonstrate that classifiers trained on TheseusSyn-generated images achieve competitive performance on official test sets, indicating that the synthesized data preserve diagnostically relevant features and semantic consistency. Systematic analysis of masking strategies reveals their impact on structural fidelity and downstream classification accuracy. These results suggest that context-conditioned masked autoregression provides an effective and generalizable solution for label-free medical image synthesis, offering a scalable alternative to conventional data augmentation and class-conditioned generative models in medical imaging applications.

The demand for high-fidelity synthetic medical data has surged, driven by the scarcity of large-scale, high-quality datasets required to train robust medical models Babu et al. (2025). Beyond data augmentation, synthetic generation is an important method to address data imbalance, ensuring generalisability across demographic groups and clinical representation for rare diseases Mendes et al. (2025). It also provides a robust response to the tightening constraints of patient privacy and data governance Giouroukou et al. (2025).

The rapid evolution of generative frameworks, including Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) Armanious et al. (2020), Diffusion Models (DMs) Graikos et al. (2024); Yellapragada et al. (2025), and Autoregressive (AR) Li et al. (2023); Yuan et al. (2024) models, has led to significant progress in medical image synthesis. Current state-of-the-art methods predominantly rely on conditional generation, typically utilizing class labels or text prompts as guidance. However, these paradigms face inherent limitations. Label- Yuan et al. (2024) or text-conditioned Xu et al. (2024); Kim et al. (2024) synthesis relies on discrete, artificial symbols to navigate the complex manifold of medical imaging. These methods often target distribution-level characteristics rather than case-specific nuances. Furthermore, class-conditioned methods frequently oversimplify clinical reality by using single-label conditioning, which ignores comorbidities and intersecting pathological factors present in real-world cases. Such models are also rigid, extending them to new labels or additional modalities usually necessitates retraining the entire architecture. For text-to-image synthesis, the challenge lies in the complex alignment between clinical narratives and radiological features, where the final quality is highly sensitive to the structure of the text prompt.

To overcome the constraints of symbolic conditioning, we propose a new paradigm for high-fidelity medical image synthesis that operates independently of human-defined labels. Our goal is to develop a generalizable synthesis framework capable of capturing the complex context of a medical image at a case-specific level. The inspiration for this approach is drawn from the “Ship of Theseus” paradox, a classic thought experiment regarding the nature of identity. The myth describes a ship restored part by part until no original components remain. If every part of the ship is replaced, is it still the same ship? This creates a state of duality: although its physical constituents change, its essential structure and identity are preserved. We adapt this logic to medical imaging: by treating an existing image as the “ship” and selectively replacing its components through masked autoregression, we can generate a novel sample, while preserving its clinical essence and semantics.

In this paper, we introduce TheseusSyn: a unified medical image synthesis framework based on context-conditioned masked autoregression. TheseusSyn consists of three core components: a unified multi-codebook discrete image tokenizer, a context-conditioned masked autoregressive generative model, and a high-fidelity decoder. Given a reference image, the framework discretizes it into token indices—analogous to the wooden planks of Theseus’ ship—and extracts a global context representation. By masking and then predicting these tokens conditioned on the global context, TheseusSyn reconstructs the “ship” with new components. This approach offers several distinct advantages: (1) Modality unification: by utilizing a context-based representation rather than explicit labels, a single model can generalize across diverse modalities and anatomical regions; (2) Case-Specific context conditioning: being label- and prompt-free, the model uses the image itself as the primary descriptor. This allows for the generation of high-fidelity synthetic images, even in presence of scarce data, such as for rare diseases; (3) Fine-Grained controllability: the masking mechanism allows precise control of the synthetic regions, providing a tunable balance between image fidelity and diversity. We evaluate TheseusSyn framework across 11 distinct image modalities representing 8 different organs, using MedMNIST 2D. Our results demonstrate that the proposed unified paradigm is highly effective to generate high-fidelity synthetic images, consistently improving downstream task performance across varied medical imaging domains.

papers.title: A Hybrid Message-Passing and Electric-Field Representation for Electrostatic QM/MM Embedding with Machine Learning Interatomic Potentials
papers.abstract: Within a hybrid quantum mechanics/molecular mechanics approach a small region of a large atomistic system is described quantum mechanically, while the rest of the system is represented by a classical force field. Despite this, the computational cost of the quantum calculation severely limits the accessible simulation and sampling time. Replacing the quantum calculation with a machine learning interatomic potential (MLIP) trained on quantum reference data can greatly increase the accessible simulation time. However, the accuracy and efficiency strongly depend on the specific way in which the MLIP incorporates information about the classical (electrostatic) environment. Here, we demonstrate that existing strategies based purely on features derived from an external electric field fail to distinguish certain environments, ultimately limiting their accuracy. As a solution, we propose an extension to the equivariant TensorNet architecture that mitigates this shortcoming by incorporating classical atoms close to the quantum region into the message-passing scheme, combined with features derived from the electric field for describing the environment farther away. We show that this combination achieves higher accuracy than either approach alone.

papers.intro:
While the fundamental physical laws governing essentially all of chemistry and material science are generally viewed as known1, (approximately) solving these equations turns out to incur costs that scale steeply with the system size (i.e., the number of atoms). There are many approaches that make the study of large systems tractable. They range from molecular mechanics (MM)2, which treats the system under study classically, through semi-empirical methods3, 4, 5, which introduce approximations to the quantum mechanical equations, to, more recently, machine learning interatomic potentials (MLIPs)6, 7, 8, which reproduce the quantum mechanical reference data they have been trained on at a reduced computational cost.

Due to the still comparatively large computational cost of semi-empirical methods and MLIPs for configurational sampling, the default approach for modeling large biomolecular systems comprising tens of thousands of atoms or more remains classical force-field-based molecular mechanics (MM). However, in cases where the process of interest is local (i.e., restricted to a rather small region of a larger system) and/or potentially complex in terms of the interactions involved, such as the active site of a protein, embedding techniques combining quantum-mechanical (QM) methods with classical force fields, usually denoted QM/MM, can be used. The small region is then described quantum mechanically, whereas the remainder of the system is treated classically9, 10. If high quantum accuracy is key, but sampling cannot be ignored, the advent of MLIPs has opened up the way to replace the QM method by an MLIP leading to machine learning/molecular mechanics (ML/MM) schemes11.

There exist different options for performing QM/MM calculations. In the simplest case, the so-called mechanical embedding, the QM calculation is performed in the absence of the MM region and the interaction is treated at the MM level. As a consequence, the polarization of the QM region by the MM region is neglected. By contrast, in electrostatic embedding, the MM point charges are included in the QM Hamiltonian and thereby allow the MM region to polarize the QM region. In biomolecular simulations, electrostatic embedding is the most widely used scheme9.

Various approaches for constructing MLIPs for ML/MM embeddings have been published in the literature and they use different techniques for integrating information about the MM environment into the model. In what is arguably the simplest case, the model never directly sees the environment. Instead, the model predicts the gas-phase energy of the QM region, which is then coupled classically to the MM region. In order to address these shortcomings, we developed a new approach, combining two different strategies. Next, in Section 3, we demonstrate that describing the MM environment using only local electric field features leads to degeneracies. We then evaluate the performance of our new approach, which circumvents this issue, using several model systems, before giving a conclusion in Section 4.

papers.title: Input-dependent Neuromodulation Enhances Mixed-Signal Neuromorphic Hardware
papers.abstract: Gating mechanisms allow a fixed neural network to adapt its computation to the current input by dynamically modulating its effective parameters. In the brain, neuromodulation uses this principle to move neural circuits between dynamical regimes, and deep learning exploits input-dependent gating, e.g., in gated recurrent networks and self-attention. Input-dependent modulation has also recently been shown to improve spiking neural networks, with particularly strong benefits in small, parameter-limited ones. This makes neuromodulation especially promising for neuromorphic processors at the edge, where area, memory and energy budgets constrain network size, while circuit physics limits parameter precision. Here we demonstrate input-dependent, within-trial neuromodulation of a spiking recurrent neural network on a mixed-signal neuromorphic processor. An off-chip modulator reads the on-chip network's input and activity and adjusts its population-level gains while the chip's analog circuits compute with the physics of the silicon. Neuromodulation raises binary spoken-digit classification accuracy by $+17.3 \pm 10.4$ percentage points, tested across five hardware network instantiations.

papers.intro:
Neuromodulation is a mechanism by which neural circuits change their computation without altering their wiring. Concretely, neuromodulators act on existing synapses and neurons to rescale and adapt synaptic weights and neuronal gains. For example, a single modulatory signal can multiply the strength of many synapses simultaneously, effectively reweighting the circuit’s connectivity on a timescale of milliseconds to seconds, far faster than any structural change [12, 13]. This is critically important because it allows a fixed anatomical circuit to express multiple, distinct dynamical regimes in response to context, arousal, or input statistics, rather than requiring separate dedicated hardware for each behavioral state [15, 8]. As neuromodulation decouples the structure of a network (which is slow to change) from its effective parameters (which can be rapidly reconfigured), it greatly expands the repertoire of computations accessible to a given set of connections [10]. Machine learning exploits a similar principle, where slowly learned parameters define a base network, while faster, input-dependent variables rescale its effective weights or gate its state updates on the timescale of a single input. For example, in GRU [5, 9] and slow–fast weight systems [16], slowly learned parameters generate fast, context-dependent rescalings of the network’s effective synaptic weights.

We implement the recurrent network as a fixed physical reservoir, while a separate modulator adjusts a small number of shared population-level gains, thereby reconfiguring the network’s computation without changing its underlying connectivity. Because gradients cannot be propagated through the analog circuits, the modulator is trained from the reservoir’s measured response to controlled changes in these gain parameters. papers.title: Efficient Simulation of Gate Leakage Currents in Ultra-scaled Transistors from First Principles
papers.abstract: To ensure high electrostatic integrity in ultra-scaled field-effect transistors (FETs), thin gate dielectric layers are typically needed, potentially giving rise to (strong) leakage currents. Being able to model this effect is therefore crucial. Here, we show how gate leakage currents can be computed at the ab initio level in WS$_2$-hBN FETs by extending the well-established quantum transmitting boundary method (QTBM). Two main challenges are tackled: (i) the calculation of the open boundary conditions (OBCs) for the gate contacts and (ii) the solution of the resulting sparse linear system of equations A x = b where the matrix A possesses an unstructured sparsity pattern. We demonstrate that the proposed method outperforms the state of the art and can be readily applied to simulate transistors with gate lengths exceeding 25 nm.

papers.intro:
As a consequence of the continuous miniaturization of the transistor dimensions and of their equivalent oxide thickness (EOT), gate leakage currents could become a major limiting factor in future technology nodes. This issue might specifically affect logic switches with channels made of two-dimensional transition metal dichalcogenides (TMDCs), e.g., WS2\text{WS}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}, for which no intrinsic oxides exist. To shed light on the importance of gate leakage in ultra-scaled devices, an ab initio quantum transport (QT) approach is crucial. Although such QT solvers have been used to investigate semiconductor-dielectric interfaces [1, 2], to the best of our knowledge, they have not yet been used to study gate leakage. While conventional ab initio QT tools typically support carrier injections at two contacts (source and drain) only, accounting for gate leakage currents requires introducing a third injection path at the gate location, which is placed on top of the oxide and extends across the entire channel region. In standard QT approaches, the presence of such a large spatial extent significantly degrades the computational performance because of (i) the calculation of the required open boundary conditions (OBCs) for the gate contact and (ii) the change in sparsity pattern of the resulting linear system of equations. In this work, we address these shortcomings by extending the quantum transmitting boundary method (QTBM) [3]. The developed approach is applied to the computation of the source-to-gate and drain-to-gate transmission functions of a monolayer WS2 field-effect transistor (FET) with a 1.8 nm thick hBN dielectric layer and a Pt gate metal contact as a representative example (Fig. 1(a)). The Hamiltonian and overlap matrices of the three different material regions defining this geometry, namely, the contacts consisting only of WS2\text{WS}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}, the buffer area including both WS2\text{WS}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\smash[t]{\text{2}}} and hBN, and the central area consisting of WS2\text{WS}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}, hBN, and Pt, are determined separately at the density functional theory (DFT) level with CP2K [4], whose basis relies on a linear combination of atomic orbitals (LCAO). Subsequently, the three regions are combined to form the complete device Hamiltonian, 𝐇\mathbf{H}, and the corresponding orbital overlap matrix, 𝐒\mathbf{S}, following the procedure outlined in Ref. [1]. These device matrices are passed to our open-source QT solver, quatrex [5], which implements the QTBM to compute the transport properties of multi-terminal nanoelectronic devices.

papers.title: Learning Stabilizing Latent Feedback Controllers via Multi-Step Backward Losses
papers.abstract: Can learned latent dynamics models support the design of feedback controllers that provably stabilize the original system? For linear time-invariant systems, we show that learning linear autoencoders and latent dynamics with multi-step prediction-reconstruction losses $\unicode{x2014}$ which we term "backward losses" as they encourage latent trajectories to reconstruct full state trajectories $\unicode{x2014}$ provably recovers the structure needed for stabilization. Specifically, a sufficiently long reconstruction horizon ensures that a minimum ${H}_\infty$-norm controller designed using the learned latent model stabilizes the original system through output-feedback via the corresponding encoder, provided the latent dimension is large enough to capture all non-stable modes of the underlying system. We also show why both reconstruction and a multi-step horizon are essential: forward prediction losses that require only low prediction error along latent trajectories admit global loss minimizers that discard unstable modes regardless of horizon length, while single-step reconstruction losses can yield latent models whose stabilizing controllers fail to stabilize the original system. Finally, experiments on a non-linear flexible-arm system illustrate the practical implications of our results for learning non-linear autoencoders and latent dynamics.

papers.intro:
Many control applications require stabilizing systems with high-dimensional, non-linear dynamics, including synchronizing large power grids after faults, suppressing aeroelastic flutter in flexible aircraft, stabilizing a pneumatically actuated silicone arm under external loads, and maintaining stable humanoid locomotion on uneven or slippery terrain. For such complex systems, where the complete state representation may be too high-dimensional to directly calculate an optimal state-feedback controller, a natural approach is to utilize a low-dimensional surrogate model of the system, e.g., a latent dynamics model, reduced-order model, or latent world model, which tracks the evolution of the original state xx under a (generally lossy) coordinate transformation z=E⁡(x)z=E(x), where the map EE is commonly referred to as an encoder. In an ideal setting, such a latent surrogate model simultaneously satisfies two key properties: (i) it is rich enough to capture the key dynamical behavior of the system, and (ii) it is sufficiently low-dimensional to enable the computation of an optimal—or at least stabilizing—feedback controller K⁡(z)K(z). Given properties (i) and (ii), an intuitive and computationally efficient feedback control strategy for the original high-dimensional system is to compose the latent state feedback controller K⁡(z)K(z) with encoder E⁡(x)E(x), yielding a form of output-feedback control.

The standard approach to designing such transformations from the full state to latent coordinates is to apply classical model reduction techniques, such as balanced truncation methods [1, 2], proper orthogonal decompositions [3, 4, 2], spectral submanifold theory [5, 6], or partial feedback linearization [7, 8]. In many cases, implementations of these techniques either strictly require, or are augmented by, knowledge of the true dynamics, an assumption that may not be practical in modern applications. More importantly, it is not always clear whether the application of these methods will yield stable zero dynamics; without such a guarantee, the behavior of the system on the zero manifold (i.e., kernel of the encoder EE) could be unstable, and not controllable from only observing the latent coordinates. This phenomenon is commonly encountered in partial feedback linearization, where the stability of zero dynamics, particularly for non-minimum phase systems, is not immediately apparent when choosing an output map. In proper orthogonal decomposition, the reduced coordinates are chosen by applying singular value decomposition to trajectory data, which can potentially lead to unstable zero dynamics via the truncation of weakly excited unstable modes that happen to contribute low energy over a finite observation window. Finally, balanced truncation requires more sophisticated extensions to handle unstable systems [2], as the infinite horizon Gramians become unbounded for unstable systems. While there exists techniques in the literature that address some of the aforementioned limitations [2, 9, 10, 11, 12, see e.g.,], we take a broader perspective in this work. Namely, we ask whether it is possible design a reduced-order modeling framework that is simultaneously (i) model-free, requiring only trajectory snippets from the underlying dynamics instead of a full description of the system dynamics, (ii) employs a unified algorithm that applies “out of the box” to both linear and non-linear systems, and (iii) provably enables stable feedback control design using the output-feedback design strategy described previously.

In this paper, we propose such a modeling framework by building on algorithms from the machine learning (ML) and reinforcement learning (RL) communities for learning latent dynamics models from data, where such methods fall under the general umbrella of world modeling [13, 14, 15, 16, 17, 18, 19]. The advantages of utilizing an ML/RL world modeling approach are evident, as they immediately satisfy the first two of our desiderata: (i) they operate directly on trajectory data (model-free), and (ii) they provide general algorithms that make little assumptions on the underlying dynamics (unified algorithms). However, the last desiderata—enabling stable feedback control design—remains an open question. Indeed, while the literature demonstrates impressive empirical results with planning algorithms that utilize learned world models in the loop [14, 18, 20, 19, see e.g.,], the theoretical foundations of such design procedures, including basic questions regarding closed-loop stability, safety, and performance, remain largely unaddressed in the literature. Our work initiates a study of these foundations, focusing on the following fundamental question: Can latent dynamics models and encoders learned with ML/RL approaches be used to design feedback controllers that are guaranteed to be closed-loop stable on the true underlying system?

papers.title: The psychophysics of affect in large language models
papers.abstract: Good decisions often require considering how outcomes will feel. Yet large language models (LLMs) increasingly enter decision workflows, despite little being known about how they map outcomes to feelings or use those mappings in choice. We tested how LLMs anticipated gambling or stock-trading outcomes would feel and whether they incorporated these ratings into choice. When outcomes were rated in isolation, ratings exhibited diminishing sensitivity to magnitude, resembling human value functions; but models rated gains more intensely than equivalent losses, an inversion of canonical loss aversion we call silicon gain amplification. When outcomes were rated together, enabling direct comparison, ratings linearised. In choice, the gain-loss asymmetry largely disappeared, and models' own ratings did not reliably explain their choices better than monetary utility did. These findings reveal malleable mappings from outcomes to affect, raising questions about whether and how agentic LLMs should incorporate anticipated feelings into decisions.

papers.title: CuPIQP: A Batched and Differentiable QP Solver on GPUs for Robot Learning and Control
papers.abstract: Quadratic programs (QPs) are fundamental building blocks of many robotic tasks such as inverse kinematics, whole-body control, and model predictive control. Extending these methods to large-scale robot learning and control requires solving many QPs concurrently and, for end-to-end learning, differentiating through their solutions. Efficient batched optimization is therefore essential to bringing established model-based methods into GPU-based robotics pipelines. We present \textsc{cuPIQP}, a batched and differentiable QP solver on GPUs based on a proximal interior-point method, with unified support for dense, sparse, and multistage problems. The solver exploits parallelism across independent QPs and their internal structure while preserving per-problem numerical updates and termination decisions. Benchmarks with up to 16384 QPs per batch demonstrate solve-time speedups of up to $18.8\times$ over \textsc{Moreau} and $4.26\times$ over eight-core \textsc{PIQP}. In an end-to-end learning task, \textsc{cuPIQP} accelerates training by $4.6\times$ over \textsc{QPAX} and $7.8\times$ over \textsc{Moreau}. By reducing the computational cost, \textsc{cuPIQP} provides efficient, reusable infrastructure for integrating model-based optimization into large-scale robot learning and control.

Quadratic programs lie on the critical path of many robot control tasks. QP solvers have traditionally been designed to minimize the online latency for solving one or a tiny batch of problems. Existing solvers such as qpOASES [1], OSQP [2], HPIPM [3], ProxQP [4] and PIQP [5] are highly effective under this execution model.

• Batch-native GPU execution. We design the solver around batches of independent QPs, exploiting problem-level parallelism for high throughput while retaining independent iterates, convergence decisions, solutions, and termination statuses for all problems in the batch. • Structure-specialized QP backends. cuPIQP supports dense, sparse, and multistage QPs through specialized data layouts and linear algebra backends under a unified solver interface, allowing users to exploit the structure of a variety of problem classes. • GPU-resident integration and differentiation. Problem data, solver iterates, per-problem statuses, and adjoint computations remain on the GPU. papers.title: ART of PIV: Agentic Real-Time Particle Image Velocimetry for Active Flow Control
papers.abstract: Particle image velocimetry (PIV) measures fluid motion from images of tracer particles, but its accuracy depends on choices throughout the estimation pipeline, including image preprocessing, flow estimation, and postprocessing. These choices are typically left to expert tuning, and a fixed configuration can become less accurate as conditions change. This matters especially when PIV supplies feedback for real-time control, where measurements must be both accurate and fast, and flow conditions vary. We introduce ART of PIV -- short for Agentic Real-Time and also a nod to the art of tuning a PIV pipeline -- which automates pipeline choice for each image pair. A learned agent selects a configuration according to a chosen measurement objective from a library assembled for a specified speed budget. Across cross-correlation, classical optical-flow, and learning-based estimators, ART of PIV reduces average end-point error (AEPE) by 12.2-22.4 % relative to the best single estimator at matched speed, with gains extending to 1000-4000 image pair/s. In a simulated local velocity regulation task, it reduces mean normalized closed-loop cost by 13.24-13.59 percentage points relative to a tuned fixed estimator, with the same classical controller in both cases. In a tabletop water channel, we illustrate two ways to tune ART of PIV for a fluidic pinball of three rotating cylinders: selecting between complementary optical-flow tunings for accuracy, and selecting regions of interest with coherent rotation or shear using a common flow estimator. For the first variant, we train a DreamerV3 reinforcement learning controller directly in the physical world and demonstrate tracking of a prescribed flow field in the wake of a fluidic pinball.

papers.intro:
Particle image velocimetry (PIV) (Adrian, 1991; Raffel et al., 2018; Westerweel et al., 2013; Scharnowski and Kähler, 2020) and related image-based flow-quantification methods (Horn and Schunck, 1981; Liu and Shen, 2008) are among the central tools for measuring flow fields, with applications spanning laboratory (Adrian, 1991), industrial (Raffel et al., 2018), microfluidic (Santiago et al., 1998), and environmental (Fujita et al., 2007) settings. Traditionally, their role has been observational: to reconstruct a velocity field for analysis, validation, and diagnostics. Performance has accordingly been measured almost exclusively through accuracy. For an image pair, the end-point error (EPE) is the ℓ2\ell_{2} distance between the estimated and ground-truth flow, averaged over pixels. Averaging these errors over the image pairs in a dataset gives the average end-point error (AEPE). Throughout, we use algorithm and estimator broadly to include the configured measurement pipeline: image preprocessing, flow estimation, and postprocessing, following the organization of FlowGym (Banelli et al., 2026). Two configurations may therefore differ in their crop, image conditioning, or output resolution while sharing the same underlying flow-estimation method.

Recent results in active flow control invite a broader perspective. Terpin and D’Andrea (in press) showed that, on a real-world flow-control task, an agent equipped with dense flow feedback discovers high-performance strategies within tens of minutes of real-world interaction, whereas an agent without that feedback fails to learn a policy that increases drag. Once flow quantification is embedded in a real-time learning or control loop, latency becomes as consequential as accuracy: a highly accurate but slow estimator simply cannot run online, while a fast but crude one risks yielding feedback too noisy to learn from. With accuracy as the measurement objective, this leads to the speed–accuracy trade-off: the best accuracy attainable at a given inference speed. Three estimator families span this trade-off: classical cross-correlation (Scarano, 2002; Liberzon et al., 2026), optical flow (Kroeger et al., 2016; Horn and Schunck, 1981; Farnebäck, 2003), and learning-based estimators (Cai et al., 2019; Huang et al., 2022; Luo et al., 2024). No single method dominates. For instance, using FlowGym (Banelli et al., 2026), we find that the accurate RAFT32-PIV (Lagemann et al., 2021) runs at only 1.7 image pair/s on an RTX 5090, while fast estimators such as DIS (Kroeger et al., 2016) and OpenPIV run from tens to thousands of image pairs per second at lower accuracy. In this work, we ask how a flow-measurement pipeline can adapt to changing conditions within a given inference-time budget. The preferred configuration can depend on both the flow and what the user wants to measure. Even when accuracy is the objective, the best-performing estimator or parameter setting can vary across flows and regions of a single image pair (Bonomi et al., in press). Tuning a PIV pipeline is therefore an art: as the 2014 PIV Challenge put it, “the largest uncertainties are introduced by the user who selects the evaluation parameters based on knowledge, experience and intuition” (Kähler et al., 2016). One line of work responds by adapting a single estimator’s parameters to the data: the interrogation window in cross-correlation (Scarano and Riethmuller, 1999; Theunissen et al., 2007; Theunissen et al., 2010), or the regularization in optical flow (Jassal et al., 2025). We build a library of configurations suited to different conditions and learn when to use each. The motivation is practical: tuning a pipeline for a particular regime can be easier than finding a common configuration for all regimes. Human expertise can guide library design and training labels. Alternatively, labels can follow a quantitative criterion, such as minimum estimation error when the true flow is known. The agent learns to predict the preferred configuration for new image pairs.

We introduce ART of PIV, an agent that learns to select a measurement pipeline for each image pair within a specified speed budget. A small convolutional neural network (CNN) predicts the preferred configuration from a supplied library and returns its flow; see Figure 1. The library and supervision encode the user’s measurement preferences, including choices of preprocessing, estimator tuning, and postprocessing. Selection can overlap with estimator execution to keep its additional latency small. Adapting the choice on every image pair is particularly relevant in active flow control, where the controller continually changes the flow conditions.

papers.title: ProSearch: Benchmarking Multi-Constraint Protocol Retrieval in Experimental Science
papers.abstract: In AI for Science scenarios, experimental design and method reproduction require retrieving protocols that satisfy multiple interdependent constraints, yet existing benchmarks lack systematic evaluation of this capability. To address this gap, we introduce ProSearch, a benchmark for multi-constraint protocol retrieval in experimental science. ProSearch has three key features: (1) realism, with queries grounded in real experimental records and expert-defined templates; (2) complexity, with 60 experimental fields and their dependencies; and (3) diagnosticity, with 3-5 explicit constraints per query, including numerical and negation constraints. We construct ProSearch through LLM-based extraction, data-driven constraint selection, controlled query generation, and evidence-based relevance validation. The resulting benchmark contains 1,515 queries across six experimental science domains. We conduct extensive experiments on ProSearch with 19 representative retrievers and complementary analyses. The best-performing retriever achieves an average nDCG@10 of only 0.290, which improves to 0.474 with reranking. Structured diagnostic analysis shows that explicit constraint matching provides a strong ranking signal, while manual error analysis identifies joint constraint binding as a key bottleneck. ProSearch provides a testbed for systematically evaluating scientific retrieval systems.

As AI for Science advances, artificial intelligence systems are increasingly being used for scientific tasks (Xie et al., 2025; Weng et al., 2026) such as experimental design (Ma et al., 2025; Wang et al., 2026) and protocol reproduction (Gridach et al., 2025; Chen et al., 2025b). In these settings, systems must not only understand the research question but also retrieve actionable methodological evidence from the scientific literature to identify protocols that meet specific experimental requirements (Kasmaee et al., 2025). In this context, protocol retrieval has become an important foundational capability for AI for Science (Kon et al., 2025; Eger et al., 2025; Gupta et al., 2022; Gu et al., 2021).

For example, a researcher may require a specific cell line to be cultured at 37∘37^{\circ}C while excluding the use of DMEM as the culture medium. Retrieval systems must not only identify these conditions but also verify that they hold within the same coherent experimental configuration. However, method paragraphs often describe multiple experimental configurations or variants within the same context (Sun et al., 2025). Therefore, even when all query conditions appear in the same paragraph, they may correspond to different experimental procedures, leading keyword-based retrieval methods to produce false matches.

To address these challenges, we develop an expert-guided construction pipeline. Domain experts define experimental fields, dependencies, and query templates. We instantiate these templates using values from extracted protocol records and select constraint combinations in the corpus. LLM-assisted filtering and query generation then produce meaningful natural-language queries. papers.title: Why delivered costs understate prices in an integrated global hydrogen market
papers.abstract: Delivered-cost estimates are often used as proxies for hydrogen import prices. Yet they measure average supply-chain costs, whereas marginal prices measure the system value of an additional unit. Market interactions can make the two diverge, potentially biasing long-term price assumptions. We quantify this gap using an 81-region global hydrogen-market model, comparing each region's costs and prices when only its demand is active and when all regions' demands are active. The 2045 price-cost gap is positive in 78 regions and averages 63 EUR/MWh (52% of the single-buyer cost) on a demand-weighted basis. Only 12 EUR/MWh reflects higher average sourcing costs due to competing demand. The remaining 51 EUR/MWh is the difference between the global-market price and the delivered portfolio's average cost. In several regions, wholesale prices rise while average delivered costs fall. Hydrogen strategies should distinguish delivered-cost benchmarks from market-price expectations, as low-cost supply does not guarantee low regional market prices.

Many governments see low-carbon hydrogen as an important option for defossilising hard-to-electrify sectors, and national hydrogen strategies often anticipate substantial imports from regions with low production costs [1, 2, 3, 4]. Progress has nevertheless fallen short of announced ambitions [5, 6, 7]. Uncertainty about future demand and prices remains an important barrier to long-term offtake agreements and investment [5, 8]. Because projected hydrogen demand responds strongly to assumed prices, expectations of future prices are central to these decisions [9, 10]. Yet few studies estimate future regional market prices [11, 12, 13, 14, 15]. Many published studies instead report production or delivered costs [16, 17, 18, 19], and these estimates vary widely. For Europe in 2050, they differ by approximately a factor of five [17]. The practical question is therefore not only where hydrogen can be produced and delivered at low cost, but also what price a region may face for the volumes it requires.

These delivered-cost estimates generally come from route-level supply-chain studies [16, 17, 18, 19]. They typically combine the levelised cost of producing hydrogen at a specified location with the costs of conversion, storage and transport along a particular route, at an assumed scale and utilisation rate. By themselves, however, these estimates do not show what price may emerge when several suppliers and buyers interact. Cost-derived assumptions are nevertheless used as regional import-price inputs in energy-system models that do not represent market prices endogenously [20, 21, 22, 23], and some national strategies use supply-cost targets as planning benchmarks [4].

Using delivered costs as price proxies may be reasonable when low-cost production and transport remain plentiful at the required volume, so that average delivered cost remains close to the marginal value of supplying the region. Global assessments suggest that low-cost production potential exceeds projected demand by a wide margin [24], although much of it lies away from demand centres and is constrained by water, land and renewable electricity availability [25]. Production potential available at a given cost is not the same as supply delivered to a region at that cost, once transport and demand elsewhere are taken into account. A region facing no competing demand from other regions uses the cheapest supply options first and turns to more expensive ones as demand increases. The average cost of its supply portfolio can therefore remain below the marginal value of supplying an additional unit, creating a price–cost gap even when the region is the only buyer. When other regions also demand hydrogen, they draw on the same finite production resources and transport routes. This can change both the average cost of the supply reaching a region and its marginal price. A region may even receive a cheaper average portfolio while facing a higher price.

Many report traded volumes, routes and delivered costs without calculating regional prices [27, 28, 29]. To our knowledge, these prices have not been compared against the delivered cost of the supply reaching each region. We address these questions using HyPriM [30], a global hydrogen-market optimisation model covering 81 regions from 2030 to 2050, building on [31]. For each focal region, we compare two matched configurations. In the single-buyer configuration, only the focal region’s prescribed demand is active, but all modelled production potentials and transport options remain available. This extends the cost logic of route studies to the region’s full demand, rather than replicating an individual study. In the global-market configuration, all regions have active demand and can produce and trade simultaneously. The focal region’s demand and techno-economic assumptions are unchanged, while investment, production and trade respond endogenously. In both configurations, we calculate the volume-weighted average delivered cost and the dual value of the regional hydrogen balance in the fixed-capacity pricing stage. We report the latter as a modelled long-run wholesale price conditional on the installed capacities and price-taking behaviour [32, 33]. The resulting four quantities allow two decompositions of the price–cost gap (Fig. 1). One separates the single-buyer price–cost difference from the price effect of competing demand. The other separates the sourcing effect, the change in average delivered cost, from the global-market price–cost difference. We examine supply changes for Germany and Japan in more detail. Germany has many pipeline options within Europe, whereas Japan has few pipeline options and can import from many potential suppliers only by ship. We find that modelled global-market prices exceed the matched cost benchmark in nearly all regions. On a demand-weighted basis, most of this difference reflects prices above average delivered costs rather than a more expensive supply portfolio. Delivered costs therefore remain useful for comparing supply options but should not be used directly as long-term price assumptions in hydrogen strategies and energy-system models.

papers.title: SAFARI: Semantic- And Frontier-driven Autonomous Risk Inspection
papers.abstract:
Robotic exploration can reduce human exposure to hazardous environments by autonomously searching unknown areas for objects of interest while constructing a complete, risk-aware map.
  However, existing autonomous exploration approaches typically prioritize geometric coverage or information gain, without explicitly coupling semantic object detection and the risk associated with operating near potentially hazardous objects.
  Moreover, many systems have been demonstrated primarily in simulation or controlled environments, leaving limited validation of risk-aware semantic exploration in complex, unstructured field settings.
  To address this gap, we propose SAFARI, a framework that treats object detection as a native channel of a unified probabilistic map, thereby jointly informing exploration and planning with both geometric and semantic evidence.
  We evaluated SAFARI in 11 missions across three field sites on a quadruped platform. The framework achieved an average coverage of 98.7% of the accessible mission area, without operator intervention for 97.6% of mission time, and detected objects with characteristic dimensions as small as 15cm.
  Lastly, through ablation studies and a detailed analysis of system behavior, we show that object-size awareness and safety-aware path planning are crucial for effective hazardous-object search.

A key challenge in these tasks is that the environments may contain unknown hazards. Such hazards can pose a threat not only to the robot but also to the environment or the robot operators. To make such tasks as safe as possible, reduction of human interaction through increased robot autonomy is a must [1].

Conducting reconnaissance autonomously can reduce human exposure to hazardous environments, while some tasks still require fine motor skills, precise judgment, and other capabilities that are not yet reliably reproducible by robots. Hence, a robot-led reconnaissance mission prior to human involvement directly addresses this problem: given an area to explore, the robot should detect objects of potential interest (OPIs) – hazardous items or any other mission-relevant class – and create a map that marks areas as dangerous, observed to be safe, or unobserved.

Hence, a robot-led reconnaissance mission prior to human involvement directly addresses this problem: given an area to explore, the robot should detect objects of potential interest (OPIs) – hazardous items or any other mission-relevant class – and create a map that marks areas as dangerous, observed to be safe, or unobserved.

Autonomous exploration around OPIs is challenging. To achieve complete coverage efficiently, the robot must continuously assess traversability, determine which regions are safe with sufficient confidence, and minimize mission duration while accounting for uncertainty in its observations. Depending on the task, a missed detection can range from inconvenient to catastrophic. Additionally, the range at which it is possible to detect visible OPIs decreases with object size: the robot must get closer to small objects to reliably detect them, whereas larger objects are discernible from farther away. Finally, traversability and OPI placement must be jointly reasoned over when deciding which region to explore next, since considering either in isolation omits critical information.

In this work, we present SAFARI, a detection, mapping, and path planning pipeline for autonomous exploration and reporting of OPIs in unstructured outdoor environments. SAFARI accumulates depth-supported positive detections and object-size-dependent negative evidence in a persistent risk field. The resulting observation demand guides frontier and viewpoint selection together with geometric traversability and risk. papers.title: Potentials of individual atoms by convergent beam electron diffraction
papers.abstract: In convergent beam electron diffraction (CBED) on two-dimensional (2D) materials, the intensity distributions within the individual CBED spots map the local atomic arrangements within the probed region. In this study we demonstrate that the average intensities within the CBED spots essentially depend on the scattering parameters by a single atom, thus, offering the possibility of the direct measurement of such parameters. Scattering potential of an individual atom can be approximated by the Gaussian function and its parameters, the standard deviation and the maximal phase shift, can be recovered from the ratio of the intensities in the zero- and higher orders spots in CBED pattern. In order to demonstrate this, we simulated CBED patterns and extracted the atomic scattering parameters from such patterns. In the simulated examples, no weak phase object approximation is applied and the proposed method provides accurate results even for materials with large phase shifts up to 1.5 rad, as for example tungsten. The scattering parameters recovered from the experimental CBED patterns of graphene and twisted graphene-hBN structure show good agreement with the theoretically obtained values.

papers.title: Contact-based optimization for collision-free motion planning for a million robots
papers.abstract: Multi-agent robotic systems have attracted growing interest in recent years, with applications ranging from coordinated drone shows to autonomous operations on land, in the air, and on water. At the planning level, robot motion is often modeled using double-integrator dynamics (with low-level controllers handling the physical dynamics during execution) with a minimum-energy objective subject to collision-avoidance constraints and limits on position, velocity, and acceleration. The complexity of the problem resides in the constraints, which couple the trajectories and make the optimization problem nonconvex. Existing numerical approaches typically discretize and optimize entire trajectories, which becomes expensive for large fleets. We exploit the structure of optimal trajectories by organizing optimization around contacts, at which robots reach the minimum allowed separation. We formulate a coupled algebraic system in contact variables and reconstruct trajectories analytically between contacts. Our algorithm, sequential contact insertion (SCI), starts from unconstrained trajectories, inserts contacts at separation violations, and jointly adjusts their times and states. Numerical experiments demonstrate planning for one million robots in minutes and thousands of robots in fractions of a second. On problems feasible for a fixed-grid sequential convex programming baseline, SCI achieves median speedups of several orders of magnitude at matching solution accuracy.

Multi-agent robotic systems have attracted growing interest in recent years, with applications ranging from coordinated drone shows to autonomous operations on land [26], in the air [1], and on water [17]. Planning collision-free motion for a robot fleet is difficult because each robot’s trajectory constrains the motion of the others. We consider transitions between prescribed initial and final states over a fixed time horizon with double-integrator dynamics, a squared-acceleration objective, collision-avoidance and box constraints on position, velocity, and acceleration. The complexity of the problem resides in the pairwise separation constraints that make the joint optimization problem nonconvex. The problem is therefore often solved numerically [21, 15, 25, 12, 24, 23], with sequential convex programming (SCP) as a popular choice [1, 20, 14, 27, 9].

papers.title: A complete analytical characterization of optimal collision-free motion for two robots
papers.abstract: Collision-free motion planning for multi-agent robotic systems remains an active research area because of the complexity of coordinating robot trajectories, with applications ranging from coordinated drone shows to autonomous operations on land, in the air, and on water. Importantly, the analytical difficulty of nonconvex collision-avoidance constraints has so far driven the development of exclusively numerical methods. We derive a complete analytical characterization of the optimal trajectories for two robots that start and end at rest, under double-integrator dynamics and a squared-acceleration objective. We prove that these trajectories belong to eight distinct contact families and determine which family applies for each configuration of initial and final positions. We analyze the geometrical properties of the optimal trajectories, provide a numerical algorithm for computing them, and discuss how these insights may improve the performance of existing numerical trajectory optimizers.

Collision-free motion planning for multi-agent robotic systems remains an active research area because of the complexity of coordinating robot trajectories, with applications ranging from coordinated drone shows to autonomous operations on land [40], in the air [2], and on water [21]. A variety of numerical methods exist to solve this problem, from sampling and graph search [22, 31, 30, 38] to joint assignment and planning [35] and hybrid search and trajectory optimization [18]. Trajectory optimizers use mixed-integer formulations [13], spline parameterizations [36, 39], sequential convex programming (SCP) [2, 29, 7, 15], learning-based methods [9, 17], distributed optimization [37, 32], and separation principles [33, 27].

Collision-free motion planning for multi-agent robotic systems remains an active research area because of the complexity of coordinating robot trajectories, with applications ranging from coordinated drone shows to autonomous operations on land [40], in the air [2], and on water [21]. A variety of numerical methods exist to solve this problem, from sampling and graph search [22, 31, 30, 38] to joint assignment and planning [35] and hybrid search and trajectory optimization [18]. Trajectory optimizers use mixed-integer formulations [13], spline parameterizations [36, 39], sequential convex programming (SCP) [2, 29, 7, 15], learning-based methods [9, 17], distributed optimization [37, 32], and separation principles [33, 27].

We consider collision-free motion planning under double-integrator dynamics, with fixed duration and endpoint data. The squared-acceleration objective measures control effort and is equivalent to squared-thrust minimization [2]. This objective is used for multi-agent assignment and collision avoidance [5, 4], navigation among polygonal obstacles [6], and, alongside other cost terms, distributed quadrotor planning [25]. In drone and floating-robot experiments, simplified planning models generate reference trajectories while low-level controllers handle the physical dynamics during execution [2, 25, 21]. However, these approaches compute trajectories numerically because nonconvex collision-avoidance constraints make an analytical solution difficult. Even for two robots, existing theory provides no complete analytical characterization of minimum-effort transitions between prescribed endpoint states over a fixed time horizon under double-integrator dynamics.

Even for two robots, existing theory provides no complete analytical characterization of minimum-effort transitions between prescribed endpoint states over a fixed time horizon under double-integrator dynamics.

Importantly, the two-robot case isolates the pairwise interaction that underlies fleet planning, and an analytical characterization would identify the fundamental properties of optimal collision-free motion, opening up new possibilities for efficient planning. Analytical characterizations exist in other settings. Hu et al. [19] construct exact optimal motions for two planar agents through a geometric analysis of the separation constraint. They minimize squared velocity and leave endpoint velocities free. Kirkpatrick and Liu [23] give a complete geometric characterization for two discs minimizing total path length, with paths consisting of straight segments and circular arcs. They extend this characterization to convex centrally symmetric robots [24]. The path-length objective does not distinguish different time parameterizations, whereas acceleration cost depends on them. For the squared-acceleration objective, Beaver and Malikopoulos [5] construct trajectories by successively inserting constrained arcs and solving for their joining times. Their method optimizes each agent against prescribed higher-priority trajectories and restricts sustained contact to constant relative speed. A complete characterization of the jointly optimal two-robot motion requires accounting for variable relative speed and determining which combinations of isolated contacts and sustained contact are globally optimal.

In this paper, we provide a complete analytical characterization for the optimal trajectories of two robots starting and ending at rest under double-integrator dynamics and a squared-acceleration objective. We prove that the contact set consists of finitely many isolated points and boundary arcs, with cubic motion between contacts. We derive an exact cost identity that gives a sufficient condition for global optimality (Sections 2.2.1 and 2.2.2). We prove planarity, classify selected minimizers into eight contact families, and show that their admissible construction images partition endpoint space (Section 2.2.3). We give a certified numerical procedure that recovers the selected trajectory and its cost to any prescribed positive accuracy for algebraic endpoint data (Section 2.2.4). Our two-robot characterization underlies the contact-based fleet planner in [20], which incorporates acceleration constraints and computes collision-free trajectories for one million robots in minutes.

papers.title: SCRBench: Beyond Equivalence Checking for Semantic Change Reasoning in Code
papers.abstract: Understanding how code changes affect program semantics is a core aspect of code reasoning in language models. It is commonly evaluated by asking whether two programs are semantically equivalent, but a yes/no answer does not reveal whether a model knows which code change caused a semantic difference, or which sequence of code changes produced the modified program. We study two tasks that ask these questions directly, diagnosing semantic change and reconstructing sequences of code changes, alongside detecting semantic equivalence. We build SCRBench, 67,658 Python program pairs generated by applying sequences of code changes that preserve or alter program semantics, and evaluate five language models on a stratified subset of 4,500 pairs. Detecting semantic equivalence exposes weaker models, whose accuracy declines as changes accumulate, but the strongest models remain near the ceiling. Diagnosing semantic change reveals weaknesses that equivalence accuracy hides: a model with 94.71% equivalence accuracy diagnoses only 54.44% of semantic changes. Reconstructing sequences of code changes is much harder: the best model reconstructs the exact sequence for only 39.27% of pairs, and no model exceeds 1.11% when five changes are applied. High equivalence accuracy therefore overestimates how well models reason about the semantic effects of code changes.

papers.intro:
Understanding how code changes affect program semantics is a core aspect of code reasoning in large language models (LLMs). Evaluating this understanding has received increasing attention (Wei et al., 2025). One common test asks a model whether two programs are semantically equivalent, that is, whether they produce the same output for every input (Oza et al., 2026). Existing benchmarks commonly construct such program pairs from seed programs by applying small automated code changes, called transformations, that either preserve or alter a program’s semantics (Wei et al., 2025; Maveli et al., 2025; Oza et al., 2026). In the simplest case, only a single transformation is applied (Maveli et al., 2025), so the evaluation does not test a model as transformations accumulate. CETBench addresses this by composing several transformations into one transformation sequence (Oza et al., 2026), but it still asks only whether the two programs are semantically equivalent. A yes/no answer, however, does not reveal how the model arrived at it. A model may correctly judge two programs as non-equivalent without knowing which transformation is responsible for the semantic difference or which sequence of transformations produced the modified program from the original. Equivalence accuracy alone therefore cannot measure this finer-grained reasoning. Measuring it requires asking the model these questions directly.

In this paper, we go a step further: beyond asking whether two programs are semantically equivalent, we ask which transformation changed their semantics and in which order the transformations were applied. To this end, we define three tasks on pairs of an original program and a modified program produced by a sequence of transformations. (T1) Detecting semantic equivalence: decide whether the two programs are semantically equivalent. (T2) Diagnosing semantic change: given a non-equivalent pair, identify which transformation altered the semantics. (T3) Reconstructing transformation sequences: recover the ordered sequence of transformations that produces the modified program from the original one. To investigate LLM performance on these tasks, we build SCRBench from 418 MBPP programs (Austin et al., 2021). We use each MBPP program as an original program and apply to it a sequence of one to five transformations from a catalog of nine semantics-preserving and semantics-altering transformations (Table 1). In every non-equivalent pair, exactly one of the applied transformations alters semantics, so T2 has a single correct answer. Every pair carries ground truth for all three tasks (Section 2). SCRBench contains 67,658 program pairs. From it we draw a stratified subset of 4,500 pairs to evaluate all three tasks as transformations accumulate: for each number of applied transformations from one to five, it contains 450 equivalent and 450 non-equivalent pairs. T1 and T3 use all 4,500 pairs, and T2, which applies only to non-equivalent pairs, uses the 2,250 non-equivalent ones.

We evaluate five language models on the stratified subset with a prompt that includes chain-of-thought reasoning and a one-shot example. Within each task, we analyze how accuracy changes as transformations accumulate (Sections 3.2–3.4). We also perform an ablation study on a single model to assess the impact of chain-of-thought reasoning and the one-shot example on accuracy (Sections 3.2–3.4). Detecting semantic equivalence (T1) and diagnosing semantic change (T2) show substantial variation across models, and T2 reveals differences that T1 hides. For example, Mistral-Small-24B is within five percentage points of the strongest models on T1 (94.71%) but about 40 points behind them on T2 (54.44%). Across all models, T1 accuracy ranges from 99.69% for Qwen3-235B to 55.49% for GPT-4.1-nano, and the strongest models remain accurate as transformations accumulate, while weaker models decline. T2 accuracy ranges from 97.07% for GPT-OSS-120B to 22.67% for Llama-3.1-8B. Reconstructing transformation sequences (T3) is more demanding, because it requires recovering the ordered sequence of transformations. Even models that are accurate on T1 and T2 show substantially lower accuracy on T3. GPT-OSS-120B, the strongest model on T3, reconstructs 39.27% of the sequences, and no model exceeds 1.11% when five transformations are applied. Qwen3-235B, the most accurate model on T1 (99.69%), reconstructs only 26.82% of the sequences.

papers.title: Real Computation or Merely Naming? A Pre-Registered Mechanism Audit of 25 Cognitive-Architecture Modules in an LLM-Based Agent System
papers.abstract: Agent systems built on local large language models are increasingly marketed through the vocabulary of cognitive architecture: modules named global workspace, theory of mind, causal reasoning, or active inference are listed as features, and the presence of the name is taken as the presence of the mechanism. We ask the prior question -- does the named computation actually happen -- and contribute a transferable verification method for the claim-implementation gap: a four-question static audit protocol with line-number evidence and call-chain tracing, demonstrated on two systems. We audit a system claiming 25 cognitive mechanisms, pre-register falsifiable predictions for 11 modules and execute the interventions, replicate the protocol on the IIT-phi core of a second, independent system with its own pre-committed falsification criteria, and run two repair experiments as positive controls. In 18 of 25 modules the computed value never reaches any production output; three idle-wiring shapes new to the dead-code and code-smell literatures emerge (connected-but-never-called, called-but-inert, called-but-content-blind). Of 61 frozen criteria across 12 interventions, 53 were confirmed, two partially adjudicated, five falsified, one adjudication-ambiguous. Repairs raised planner task success from 0.028 to 1.000 and cut state-controller error by 52%. Module names and module computations must be audited as independent claims; the protocol and the five-class failure taxonomy are reusable for the claim-implementation gap at two-system, case-level depth.

papers.intro:
Agent systems built on local large language models are increasingly described using the vocabulary of cognitive science. The substrate is real: code-generating models [1] plugged into tool-use, reflection, and role-playing loops [2, 3, 4, 5, 6] produce systems whose documented failure modes, including hallucination [7], are as well known as their capabilities. A repository announces a global workspace for consciousness, a theory-of-mind module, a dopamine system for reward prediction, a causal reasoning engine, and a least-action planner. The rhetorical force of these names is considerable: they suggest that decades of cognitive science have been operationalized in software. The engineering reality, however, is rarely examined. A name can be attached to a keyword counter, a constant, or to code that is never called; the claim and the computation are logically independent, and only the second can do work. Even self-correction machinery, one of the field’s standard answers to LLM unreliability, does not by itself repair reasoning errors [8].
