papers.title: Li$^{2}$SAO: Lifting Light Singl-Rollout Asynchronous RL Optimization via Group-Relative Actor-Critic Bootstrapping
papers.abstract: Asynchronous reinforcement learning (RL) is becoming a mainstream paradigm for post-training large language models (LLMs), as it improves training efficiency by updating the model as rollouts arrive. Recent work argues that group-wise sampling in GRPO does not naturally fit asynchronous RL training because rollout lengths follow a long-tailed distribution, and proposes Single-rollout Asynchronous Optimization (SAO) to improve stability and off-policy behavior, especially on agentic tasks. However, SAO relies on a closed-source value model obtained from scaling value pretraining. In this paper, we analyze GRPO and LiSAO, our lightweight reproduction of SAO without the pretrained value model, on single-turn reasoning and multi-turn agentic tasks. We find that GRPO outperforms LiSAO on reasoning tasks, while the reverse holds on agentic tasks. Since the value model of LiSAO is not yet well trained , LiSAO lags behind GRPO substantially in early training steps. To address this issue, we propose Li$^{2}$SAO, which Lifts Light Single-rollout Asynchronous Optimization with group-relative actor-critic bootstrapping: while the critic is cold, a group-relative advantage trains the actor and a group-centered return trains the critic, after which training switches to single-rollout GAE. Experiments show that Li$^{2}$SAO catches up with or surpasses GRPO in early training and further raises the later performance ceiling. Code is available at https://github.com/jd-cc-coder/Li2SAO.

Reinforcement learning (RL) has become a central approach for eliciting long chain of thought reasoning and multi-turn agentic behavior in large language models (LLMs), including tool use and environment interaction (Ouyang et al., 2022; Shao et al., 2024; DeepSeek-AI, 2025). Most existing RL systems couple generation and training by completing a full batch of trajectories under a fixed policy before each update, so variable lengths on long reasoning and tool use tasks force fast rollouts to wait for stragglers (Yao et al., 2023; Hu et al., 2024; Sheng et al., 2025). Asynchronous RL removes this coupling by running rollout generation and training concurrently, allowing trajectories to enter training as they become available without draining the rollout workers, which substantially improves training efficiency (Noukhovitch et al., 2025; Sheng et al., 2025; Zhong et al., 2025; Wu et al., 2025). A fully asynchronous extension is the in-flight weight-update scheme, in which rollout workers receive updated parameters and continue unfinished trajectories without discarding generated tokens (Fu et al., 2025; Piché et al., 2025).

GRPO must wait for all responses to the same prompt before computing group relative advantages, which recreates a synchronization barrier and increases the staleness of early responses. Its sequence level advantage also provides limited temporal credit assignment for long agentic trajectories with multiple decisions and environment interactions.

papers.title: Vector Valued Katok-Sarnak Formulas
papers.abstract: We introduce a version of the Katok-Sarnak formula linking twisted traces of scalar valued Maass cusp forms for $\Gamma_0(N)$ with $N$ square-free to Fourier coefficients of vector valued Maass cusp forms for the metaplectic group $\operatorname{Mp}_2(\mathbb{Z})$ and the Weil representation associated to a lattice of signature $(2,1)$. We prove this by computing the Fourier coefficients of the vector valued Siegel and Millson theta lift of a scalar valued newform by two different methods and comparing the results.

papers.title: Dynamic-Aware LC-DMA Beam Tracking for LEO Satellite Communications
papers.abstract: Liquid crystal (LC)-based dynamic metasurface antennas (DMAs) offer a power-efficient, low-cost, and scalable solution for low Earth orbit (LEO) satellite communications where large apertures are needed to compensate for large path loss in the Earth-satellite link. However, beam tracking with LC-DMAs is governed by two coupled dynamics: the required time-varying beam direction caused by user and satellite mobility, and the finite response time of the LC phase shifters. This raises the question of whether LC-DMAs can reconfigure sufficiently fast to support high-mobility LEO satellite links. To address this problem, we develop a dynamic-aware beam-tracking framework that explicitly accounts for both dynamics. In particular, we formulate an optimization problem to maximize the cumulative received signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) over a predictive tracking horizon subject to the physical dynamics of the LC unit cells as well as transmit power constraints. To solve this non-convex problem efficiently, we develop an alternating optimization framework combining a closed-form maximum ratio transmission (MRT) digital precoder and maximum ratio combining (MRC) with a parallel, closed-form dynamic-aware phase-shift update. Simulation results show that when the time response of LC-DMAs is properly accounted for, it can support practical mobility scenarios. Moreover, the proposed dynamic-aware algorithm maintains stable SNR and outperforms conventional designs, particularly at high vehicle velocities and low orbital azimuth angles.

papers.intro:
Non-terrestrial networks (NTNs) utilizing low Earth orbit (LEO) satellites have emerged as a key component for 6G wireless connectivity and providing continuous global coverage to remote areas and mobile devices [1, 2]. Nevertheless, establishing reliable uplink communication between LEO satellites and high-speed vehicles presents several challenges. Nevertheless, beam tracking with LC-DMAs is governed by two coupled dynamics: the mobility-induced dynamics of the vehicle-to-satellite link and the internal dynamics of the LC phase shifters. The former continuously changes the required beam direction due to vehicle and satellite mobility, while the latter limits how fast the beam can be reconfigured. In particular, the molecular reorientation speed of LC mixtures is fundamentally governed by rotational viscosity and elastic restoration forces, which results in switching response times on the order of milliseconds [11]. This mismatch between the required and achievable beam dynamics may become a performance bottleneck in LEO satellite systems. Conventional beam-tracking algorithms assume instantaneous phase transitions and aim to maximize the instantaneous signal-to-noise ratio (SNR). These algorithms may demand large phase changes across consecutive tracking steps that cannot be realized instantaneously with LC-DMAs, and hence result in transition periods during which the received SNR can severely degrade. This interplay between mobility and hardware dynamics raises the question of whether LC-DMAs can reconfigure sufficiently fast to support high-mobility LEO satellite links.

The main contributions of this work are summarized as follows: • We establish an analytical framework for LC-based DMA transmitters (Txs) in satellite uplink channels that jointly models guided-wave propagation and the physical rise/decay transition dynamics of the LC phase shifters in Section II. • We formulate a joint digital beamforming and dynamic-aware LC phase-reconfiguration problem to maximize the cumulative received SNR over a predictive tracking horizon, subject to the physical dynamics and phase limits of the LC unit cells and the transmit power constraint in Section III. • We propose an alternative optimization (AO) algorithm that alternates between a parallelized, closed-form dynamic-aware phase-shift optimization with linear complexity in the number of DMA radiating elements in Section III-A, and a closed-form digital precoder and combiner in Section III-B. • In Section IV, numerical simulations show that, when the time response of LC-DMAs is properly accounted for, they can support practical mobility scenarios. papers.title: Hard Sample-Conditioned Decorrelated Attention for Robust Face Recognition
papers.abstract: Multi-head attention in Vision Transformers (ViTs) allows independent attention patterns across heads, but without explicit regularization, heads may learn redundant patterns rather than complementary roles. Correlation-based penalties encourage head disentanglement, yet apply uniform regularization across all training samples. In face recognition (FR), hard samples whose embeddings lie close to competing identities are critical for optimization and generalization. Motivated by this, we propose ViT-HarDis, which conditions attention head disentanglement on sample difficulty: samples with high cosine similarity to negative class centers receive stronger head decorrelation, enforcing specialization where identity ambiguity is highest. Experiments show improvements over both the baseline and uniform disentanglement on most benchmarks. Our analysis shows that ViT-HarDis reduces the similarity of hard samples to competing class centers while decreasing inter-head attention similarity, and that applying disentanglement only to the final transformer layers outperforms regularizing the entire network. Trained on WebFace4M, ViT-HarDis achieves SOTA results among ViT-based methods on IJB-B, IJB-C, and TinyFace Rank-1, while achieving the best IJB-B and TinyFace results when trained on MS1MV3, improving FR without architectural modifications or additional inference cost. ViT-based FR systems have demonstrated competitive performance on evaluation benchmarks, establishing themselves as a promising direction for FR [4, 5, 20, 31, 8, 6].

Recent years have witnessed a shift from convolutional neural networks (CNNs) [15] to Vision Transformers (ViTs) [13], which leverage multi-head attention to capture complex spatial relationships and identity-discriminative patterns. ViT-based FR systems have demonstrated competitive performance on evaluation benchmarks, establishing themselves as a promising direction for FR [4, 5, 20, 31, 8, 6].

Although multi-head attention enables ViT to capture diverse representations, prior works [33, 26, 21] in general computer vision have shown that many attention heads become highly correlated or redundant, thus limiting the effective utilization of model capacity. An existing attention head disentanglement method [1], primarily developed for general vision tasks, addresses this issue by uniformly penalizing correlations between attention heads. However, this approach treats all samples equally and does not account for differences in sample difficulty. In practice, hard samples that lie near decision boundaries are more critical for learning and generalization [17, 25, 19]. We argue that attention head specialization should be adaptive, applying stronger disentanglement to these challenging cases, better exploiting model capacity while preserving complementary attention patterns where they are most needed.

Motivated by these observations, we propose ViT-HarDis, a hard sample-conditioned attention head disentanglement framework for ViT-based FR. Instead of uniformly encouraging attention head diversity, our method adaptively strengthens decorrelation according to sample difficulty, promoting specialization for identity-ambiguous samples while preserving the original architecture. Beyond this adaptive regularization strategy, we analyze attention head redundancy in ViT-based FR, revealing that increasing the number of attention heads leads to higher redundancy without improving recognition accuracy. Our experiments demonstrate that ViT-HarDis outperforms both the baseline ViT and uniform disentanglement (ViT-Dis) on most considered benchmarks, including IJB-B [35], IJB-C [24], and TinyFace [3], while reducing the similarity of hard samples to competing identity centers and decreasing inter-head attention similarity. papers.title: ElTab: Elastically Looped Tabular Transformers
papers.abstract: Tabular transformer models such as TabPFN achieve strong predictive performance but incur substantial inference costs, making them difficult to deploy in resource-constrained settings. While looped transformers reduce parameter count through weight sharing, they can lose significant predictive power when stopped early. To address this challenge, we introduce the Elastically Looped Tabular Transformer (ElTab), a single model trained to operate across different computational budgets through supervision at randomly sampled early exits. Across 30 OpenML classification datasets, a single ElTab model matches six depth-specific looped models while cutting training cost by more than half, and matches a 12-layer TabPFN-style baseline with 25% fewer inference FLOPs. These results show that elastic-depth training yields a single model that adapts to the deployment budget at hand, offering a favorable trade-off among predictive performance, storage, and computational cost.

papers.title: SimXAI: A Simple Drop-in Layer Increases Interaction Quality and Understanding in Conversational XAI
papers.abstract: Conversational explainable AI (ConvXAI) agents often use GUS-style architectures with separate modules for intent recognition, dialogue management, and template-based response generation. While faithful to the underlying XAI methods, these pipelines are hard to adapt and often struggle with context-dependent follow-up questions. We present SimXAI, a lightweight LLM-centric conversational layer that replaces these modules with a single tool-calling LLM that bridges access to existing XAI resources. Rather than a standalone agent, SimXAI serves as a modular interface that enables conversational access to external XAI resources. We further introduce an evaluation suite for single- and multi-turn parsing, faithfulness, and contextualization. Across existing and new datasets, SimXAI achieves strong function-selection accuracy and high faithfulness while better handling context-dependent requests. In a user study replacing only the conversational layer of TalkToModel, a representative GUS-based agent, users completed tasks more accurately and in fewer turn. Overall, SimXAI improves GUS-based design while preserving faithfulness and improving conversational quality.

papers.intro:
The XAI community has reached a consensus that explanations should take a conversational form Miller (2019); Lakkaraju et al. (2022); Zhang et al. (2025). Conversational explainable AI (ConvXAI) agents therefore move beyond one-off explanations and embrace conversational approaches to provide explanations. These conversational explanations have been demonstrated to be more effective for users’ model understanding Shen et al. (2023); Mindlin et al. (2024); He et al. (2025). Conceptually, a ConvXAI agent can be decomposed into two parts: (i) a conversational layer (ConvXAI layer), responsible for managing the interaction with the user, and (ii) the underlying XAI resources, which store or generate the explanatory information (e.g., model/data cards Mitchell et al. (2019); Pushkarna et al. (2022), or feature-attribution methods like SHAP Lundberg and Lee (2017) or counterfactual explanations Mothilal et al. (2020); Ross et al. (2021)). Most current ConvXAI agents (i.a., Nguyen et al. 2023; Slack et al. 2023; Feldhus et al. 2023; Wang et al. 2024a) adopt the traditional GUS (Genial Understanding System) architecture Bobrow et al. (1977) for the ConvXAI layer, which comprises three distinct components: natural language understanding (NLU) for intent recognition, dialogue management for context maintenance and rule application, and natural language generation (NLG) for response production. Although such GUS-based ConvXAI layers present explanations through interactive dialogue, they rely on multiple models separately fine-tuned on handcrafted data for intent recognition in NLU, rule-based dialogue management, and template-based response generation in NLG (Figure 1). As a result, they remain limited in contextualization, scalability, and generalization Rastogi et al. (2020). These limitations highlight the need for lightweight, adaptive, and flexible ConvXAI layers. Recent developments suggest that LLMs can fulfill this role and replace traditional ConvXAI layers in such systems Li et al. (2024).

Unlike rule- or template-based systems, SimXAI uses an LLM to support natural, context-aware dialogue without requiring handcrafted intent datasets or conversational fine-tuning. papers.title: Penetration of a sphere in a pool: Secondary pinch-off
papers.abstract:
The water entry of solid bodies, in particular spheres, has been the subject of numerous studies due to its relevance in multiple applications, especially focusing on cavity dynamics and the resulting forces and subsequent trajectories. The role of wettability in cavity formation and sustainability has been experimentally and theoretically addressed in the past; however, typically only up to the occurrence of a primary air cavity pinch-off. What is less explored is how wettability can influence higher-order pinch-offs. In the following study, especially secondary pinch-offs are shown to determine whether a sphere trajectory is terminally ascending, i.e., the sphere returns to the surface, or terminally descending: wettability is shown to be a strong influencing factor.
  This study begins with a series of systematic experiments, comparing the entry and trajectory of spheres over a range of impact Reynolds and Froude numbers, but also with varying surface wettability. From time resolved trajectories, a force balance is computed, illustrating the role of buoyancy, arising from the volume of any sustained air cavity in the wake of the sphere. Secondary pinch-offs alter this volume; hence, the terminal trajectory. A force-scale comparison and local radial balance at the cavity neck are then presented, suggesting how wettability influences the secondary pinch-off.

papers.intro:
The entry of a solid object into a liquid pool, commonly referred to as the water-entry problem, is a fundamental phenomenon in fluid mechanics with broad relevance across industrial, athletic, and biological contexts. These problems involve air entrainment, cavity formation, and transient hydrodynamic forces, which collectively govern the subsequent motion and trajectory of the impacting body. Understanding these interactions is crucial for a wide range of applications, including marine engineering and seaplane landings Seddon and Moatamedi [2006], vertical missile water entry May [1952], projectile-water impact analysis Truscott et al. [2014] and underwater robotics Yuh [2000], Neira et al. [2021]. A recent review by Jung [2025] highlighted the shared strategies governing water-entry and exit phenomena in both biological and engineering systems, demonstrating how insights into impact forces, body morphology, and dynamics can inspire advanced marine and aerial–aquatic designs.

The entry and penetration of a sphere into a deep liquid pool serves as a simplified yet generic representation of these practical applications. The foundational work in this area was conducted by Worthington [1883], who used high-speed photography to pioneer the study of a solid sphere impacting on the liquid. Subsequent research extended these insights, examining the influence of air pressure on splash and cavity formation Gilbarg and Anderson [1948], potential flow based models of cavity geometry Richardson [1948], the effects of surface roughness and impact angle on cavity dynamics May and Hoover [1965], Laverty [2005]. Later studies further explored the influence of surface grooves and impact velocity on cavity behavior Mehri and Akbarzadeh [2021], as well as the effects of sphere heating and the formation of Leidenfrost vapor layers on sphere dynamics Mehri and Akbarzadeh [2020], Vakarelski et al. [2014], Mansoor et al. [2017], Vakarelski et al. [2019a]. Further experimental and numerical investigations have examined the unsteady motion of hydrophilic and hydrophobic spheres, including pinch-off dynamics, vortex formation, and the resulting hydrodynamic forces Duclaux et al. [2007], Aristoff and Bush [2009], Aristoff et al. [2008], Truscott et al. [2012], Vakarelski et al. [2011], Speirs et al. [2019], Li et al. [2019]. In addition, the effects of stratified liquids Tan [2016], as well as capillary and viscous forces Marston et al. [2011], have been extensively investigated. The reduction of drag during underwater motion has also been the subject of recent studies Zhu et al. [2022], Zhao et al. [2025]. These studies have substantially advanced our understanding of cavity formation, sphere encapsulation, and deceleration processes. However, the influence of post-pinch-off air cavities on the subsequent dynamics of the sphere remains relatively underexplored.

However, the influence of post-pinch-off air cavities on the subsequent dynamics of the sphere remains relatively underexplored.

Surface wettability has emerged as a key factor governing water-entry dynamics. Hydrophobic and superhydrophobic surfaces can significantly alter wetting behavior, stabilize air layers, and influence cavity growth, entrained air volumes, and post-impact motion Truscott and Techet [2006], Duclaux et al. [2007], Mansoor et al. [2014], Vakarelski et al. [2019b], Guleria et al. [2021]. During the initial stages of impact, hydrophobic spheres typically generate an air cavity that undergoes pinch-off, leaving a residual bubble or air cavity in the wake of the sphere Aristoff and Bush [2009], Truscott et al. [2012], Vakarelski et al. [2017]. The size and persistence of this wake cavity depend on several factors, including the impact Reynolds number, density ratio, surface wettability, impact angle Asfar and Moore [1987], and possible rotation of the sphere Techet and Truscott [2011]. Truscott [2009] and Truscott et al. [2014], Truscott et al. [2012] further demonstrated that variations in contact angle, sphere density, and impact velocity significantly affect vortex formation and the resulting unsteady hydrodynamic forces during penetration, as revealed through Particle Image Velocimetry (PIV) measurements.

[1971], Galeano-Rios et al. [2017], Wang et al. [2015], Chen et al. [2018]. The water entry of SH cylinders was examined by Liu et al. [2007], employing potential flow and hydrodynamic theories to describe the sinking cylinder motion. Subsequently, capillary dominated impacts were investigated by Vella et al. papers.title: Consensus Within, Competition Between: Decentralized LLM Teams for Perimeter Defense
papers.abstract: The use of large language models (LLMs) to coordinate multi-agent teams raises a fundamental architectural question: whether task allocation should be centralized in a single LLM controller or distributed across autonomous LLM agents, particularly when communication is unreliable. In a deliberately simplified perimeter-defense simulation against LLM-controlled intruders, we compared a central commander, an auction-based consensus team and independent agents under five network conditions. Breach rates were 15% for the consensus team, 32% for the commander and 29% for independent agents, and of the different network conditions, only limited radio range changed a team's breach rate, raising the commander's. In consensus team, giving a low-cost LLM more authority over the bid computation raised breaches by 38 percentage points. With birds and civilian drones in airspace, we added a photograph for each to the input text state. Only the near-frontier model treated them apart from intruders. Intruders disguised as existing taxidermy bird drones were mistook as birds by both low-cost and near-frontier LLMs, going unpursued in 59-61% of near-frontier decisions (1-16% before). However, a one-sentence forewarning in the prompt lowered it to 0-25%. We find that LLM team with a dedicated external conflict resolution protocol results in fewest breaches. Code: https://github.com/the-kas-lab/consensus-within-competition-between.

papers.intro:
Large language models (LLMs) increasingly act as the decision-makers of multi-agent teams, from software agents that solve tasks together Guo et al. (2024); Shen et al. (2023); Zhan et al. (2026); Hong et al. (2024) to robot teams that divide work and plan joint actions Kannan et al. (2024); Mandi et al. (2024). In robotics, this division of work is studied as multi-robot task allocation, the question of which robot should execute which task Gerkey and Matarić (2004). Many LLM teams allocate tasks through a central component, such as an orchestrator that delegates work or a single LLM that assigns subtasks to the whole robot team Yang et al. (2025); Kannan et al. (2024). Central coordination brings scalability bottlenecks and a single point of failure, which leaves the team exposed when the coordinator fails or becomes overloaded Yang et al. (2025). Decentralized multi-agent LLM systems remove this component. Each agent decides from its own local information and communicates directly with its peers Tran et al. (2025). Without an orchestrator, the agents of AgentNet Yang et al. (2025) reached higher accuracy than centralized multi-agent baselines on mathematics, logical question-answering and function-calling benchmarks, and robot arms with one LLM agent each proposed sub-task plans and paths through dialogue Mandi et al. (2024). The evidence is not one-sided. In multi-robot planning tasks, Chen et al. Chen et al. (2024) compared four designs for coordinating the LLMs of a robot team. The robots in the study cooperated without opponents, and each LLM agent was assumed to know the full environment. In the decentralized architecture, agents relay messages through a peer-to-peer network and achieve consensus via sequential debate rounds—iterative challenge-response exchanges designed to verify reasoning steps and organically converge on consistent information. This setup had the lowest success rate, below a central planner, while hybrid designs did best and the central planner scaled worst as robots were added. In a separate study, Kim et al. Kim et al. (2025) evaluated 260 agent-system configurations and found that independent agents, which do not communicate, amplified errors more than centrally coordinated ones, and whether coordination helped depended on the task. Network degradation and agent attrition are unavoidable in distributed multi-agent systems, so we directly compare centralized and decentralized LLM coordination under these conditions. We study this problem in an adversarial game that serves as a simple abstraction of a cyber-physical system, aiming toward applications where an LLM in a hierarchical control setting decides and allocates tasks as an intruder approaches.

In perimeter defense, a team of defenders must intercept intruders before they reach a protected region Shishika and Kumar (2020), and the intruders score for each one that gets through Shishika et al. (2020). We call an intruder’s entry into the protected region a breach. Perimeter defense belongs to the broader family of pursuit-evasion and reach-avoid differential games Jaleel and Shamma (2020), in which a team of intruders attempts to reach a target region while defenders attempt to capture or neutralize them Chung et al. (2011); Weintraub et al. (2023); Weintraub et al. (2020); Zhou et al. (2025). Game-theoretic analyses build team strategies by decomposing the game into local games between small groups and assigning defenders to intruders Shishika et al. (2020), and learned policies imitate a maximum-matching assignment from each defender’s local perception Lee et al. (2023). In scenarios such as counter-drone defense, defenders must detect intruders with limited sensing Park et al. (2021), share observations over a communication network Maity and Pourghorban (2024), and cope with message loss over non-ideal channels Otte et al. (2020). Assigning defenders to intruders is therefore an allocation decision made under partial and evolving information, where the contextual reasoning of LLM planners can be beneficial. Acharya et al. Acharya et al. (2026) propose a hierarchical architecture in which a per-team LLM planner assigns tactical roles to robots under partial observability, with execution delegated to low-level model predictive controllers. Foundation models Bommasani et al. (2021), including large language models (LLMs) and vision-language-action models, have been applied across many aspects of robotics, from semantic perception to end-to-end control Firoozi et al. (2025); Hu et al. (2023). A common pattern is hierarchical: a language model plans at a high level while lower-level skills or controllers execute the plan Ichter et al. (2023); Jülg et al. (2025). One reason is speed as inference latency is a recognized obstacle to deploying foundation models on robots Firoozi et al. (2025). Our study follows a hierarchical control design (cf. Matni et al. (2024)): in our study a call to the LLM planner took a median of 2.0 s, while model predictive control (MPC) Morari et al. (2015); Mayne et al. (2000) converts each agent’s task into accelerations every 0.1 s, with a barrier constraint keeping agents collision-free except for when a defender is pursuing to neutralize an intruder. A second design choice is how much of each decision the LLM makes itself rather than leaving it to fixed rules, which we call its authority. At low authority the LLM chooses among options written in advance, as when SayCan Ichter et al. (2023) selects a robot’s next skill from a fixed set, which makes each step of the plan interpretable. At high authority it sets numbers that a solver then uses, as when an LLM writes the weights of a reward that MPC optimizes Yu et al. (2023). That design solved more robot tasks than an LLM that composed predefined skills, and its authors note that constraining what the LLM may set makes the system more stable at some cost in flexibility Yu et al. (2023). Our aim is to study how LLM-driven teams compete against each other in an adversarial game, and how centralized, and decentralized planners, with different levels of authority, compare under different communication conditions.

papers.title: Paraclassical Logics with Two Negations
papers.abstract: We study three paraclassical propositional logics with two negations, CLoaN, CLouN, and CLauN, obtained by pairwise combining the one-negation systems CLuN, CLaN, and CLoN.  CLuN's negation  is glut-tolerant and paraconsistent, CLaN's negationis gap-tolerant and paracomplete, and CLoN's negation is both paraconsistent and paracomplete. We provide sound and complete two-valued non-deterministic semantics for each of the two-negations systems. We then focus on CLauN, the system containing the primitive dual pair of CLaN and CLuN negations. In this setting, we show deductive relationships between different negations expressible in CLauN; we show two diferent ways to recapture classical logic by means of translations, locally and globally; and we show a duality results for the multiple conclusion consequence relation of the logic.

papers.title: Sparse Autoencoders for Expert-Assisted Interpretation of Histopathology Foundation Model Embeddings
papers.abstract: Histopathology foundation models learn rich embedding representations, but their internal structure remains difficult to inspect. Concept-level interpretability is particularly relevant in computational pathology because pathologists reason through recurring morphological and tissue-level patterns, including tissue architecture, cellular morphology, staining variation, and artifacts. In this work, we investigate whether sparse autoencoders (SAEs) can decompose embeddings from histopathology foundation models into sparse latent features suitable for expert-assisted interpretation. We train vanilla and Batch-TopK SAE variants on NCT-CRC embeddings, using CONCH as the primary foundation model and UNI2-h as an additional robustness evaluation, and characterize the resulting latent features through reconstruction fidelity, sparsity, coherence, label enrichment, and downstream class-signal preservation. The learned sparse representations preserve most downstream tissue-class information, and their latent features retrieve more coherent and label-concentrated patch groups than raw embedding dimensions or PCA components. Discussions with pathology experts further motivated a WSI-level latent visualization workflow that places feature activations into larger tissue context. Overall, the additional UNI2-h evaluation suggests that the observed behavior is not specific to CONCH, supporting the use of sparse autoencoders for expert-assisted analysis of histopathology foundation-model embeddings, while emphasizing that latent features should be treated as candidate concepts requiring pathological assessment rather than automatically validated histopathological concepts.

papers.intro:
Foundation models pretrained on large histopathology data collections are increasingly used as general-purpose backbones in computational pathology [20, 4, 31]. Instead of training task-specific representations from scratch, many modern pipelines first map tissue patches into dense embedding spaces using pretrained models such as CONCH [20], UNI [4], or Virchow [31], and then reuse these embeddings for downstream analysis tasks including classification, retrieval, clustering, slide-level aggregation, and multimodal alignment. These embeddings capture variation in morphology, spatial context, staining, and other tissue properties beyond a single task label. However, they are difficult to inspect directly: individual embedding dimensions are not designed to correspond to human-understandable histopathological concepts, and relevant information may be distributed across entangled directions. This makes it difficult to determine which histopathological structures are encoded in the representation space.

Existing interpretability methods in computational pathology often focus on localization, using saliency maps, attention visualization, or multiple-instance learning heatmaps to highlight image regions associated with a prediction [29, 10]. Such methods are useful for asking where the evidence may be located in the input, but they provide limited insight into what reusable histological structure is encoded in the representation space itself [24].

papers.title: Teacher-guided multi-task learning for integrated plasma monitoring on EAST
papers.abstract: This paper integrates tokamak plasma disruption prediction, Edge-Localized Mode (ELM) monitoring, Multifaceted Asymmetric Radiation From the Edge (MARFE) detection, and H/L-mode identification into a unified Multi-Task Learning (MTL) model. This integration aims to realize MTL's potential for improving task performance while reducing inference time. However, on datasets constructed from selected EAST discharges recorded between 2015 and 2020, this study found that the traditional MTL method underperformed the corresponding Single-Task Learning (STL) method on some tasks. This performance degradation is the well-known issue of negative transfer. To address this issue, this study proposes the teacher-guided MTL method, using task-specific STL ensembles (teachers) to guide the training of an MTL model (student). The ensemble teachers guide training through soft-target distillation losses for each task of the MTL student model, and increased weighting of each shot's peak-disruptivity window in the disruption prediction label-supervised loss. Test-set results showed that the teacher-guided MTL method outperformed the corresponding STL method in ROC-AUC for all four tasks, eliminating the negative transfer observed with the traditional MTL method. In addition, on the same single GPU or single physical CPU core, the MTL student model can substantially reduce the inference time required to generate all four task outputs compared with the four STL baseline models. This paper offers a promising route to plasma monitoring systems that cover a broader range of phenomena, improve per-task performance and reduce inference time with limited real-time computational resources, supporting future high-performance plasma operation.

papers.intro:
Automatic monitoring and prediction of plasma phenomena are important for high-performance plasma operation in tokamaks. This study focuses on four plasma monitoring tasks: Disruption Prediction (DP), Multifaceted Asymmetric Radiation from the Edge (MARFE) detection, Edge-Localized Mode (ELM) detection, and High/Low-Confinement-Mode (H/L) identification. The high stored energy and plasma current of high-performance plasmas can make disruptions particularly damaging to the device, requiring reliable DP to trigger protective measures in time [1, 2]. High-performance plasma operation typically relies on sustained H-mode confinement, motivating automatic H/L-mode identification to track the confinement state [3]. ELMs during H-mode operation impose transient heat and particle loads that can damage plasma-facing components, motivating ELM detection for control [4]. Higher plasma density is desirable for increasing fusion power, but the density limit must be avoided [5]. MARFE onset can indicate proximity to this limit [6], motivating automatic MARFE detection [7]. Together, these four tasks provide comprehensive information on plasma phenomena to support targeted intervention in future high-performance plasma operation.

MTL can reduce inference time by sharing feature extraction across tasks, so that shared features are computed once and reused for multiple task outputs.

However, MTL does not consistently improve task performance and may underperform the corresponding STL models on some tasks, an issue known as negative transfer [22]. Whether negative transfer occurs and how difficult it is to mitigate can depend on the task combination. The above H/L-mode identification [17] and MHD detection [18] studies did not report negative transfer with task-label losses alone. In contrast, previous studies on equilibrium reconstruction [23] and pedestal prediction [24] reported that some jointly learned outputs had lower R2R^{2} values than those obtained with the corresponding STL models. Ref. [25] integrated DP, ELM recognition, and regression of the energy-confinement enhancement factor H98 on EAST. To mitigate negative transfer, Ref. [25] used TaskAdapt modules, task-specific gates, and three-stage Progressive Multitask Optimization with uncertainty weighting and task-specific refinement. Despite these measures, DP AUC in Ref. [25] remained below that of the corresponding STL model. Negative transfer therefore remains a major obstacle to integrating more plasma monitoring tasks into MTL without degrading task performance.

This study integrates DP, MARFE detection, ELM detection, and H/L-mode identification into an MTL model, using datasets compiled from selected EAST discharges recorded during the 2015–2020 experimental campaigns. The traditional MTL method, which uses only task-label supervision, exhibits negative transfer for this task combination. To mitigate negative transfer, this paper introduces the teacher-guided MTL method. This method uses independently optimized task-specific STL ensembles as teachers to guide a unified MTL student model through soft-target distillation across all four tasks. The DP teacher also identifies each training shot’s peak-disruptivity window, which receives greater weight in the student’s DP label-supervised loss. After training, the MTL student model runs without the teachers, preserving the efficiency of shared computation.

To our knowledge, no previous study has used a distillation loss to mitigate negative transfer in tokamak plasma multi-task monitoring. Nor has any study proposed a teacher-guided strategy for identifying each shot’s peak-disruptivity window and increasing its weight in the label-supervised loss. Regarding distillation, Ref. [28] used it to compensate for accuracy loss in a lightweight plasma shape detection model, supporting faster inference, but did not evaluate its role in mitigating negative transfer. In other fields, such as natural language processing, soft-target distillation has been used to improve MTL performance [26, 39]. However, tokamak plasma monitoring has domain-specific characteristics: for example, different tasks may require different input signals, and the physical phenomena involved may have different characteristic time scales. Results from other fields therefore do not directly demonstrate that distillation is also effective in plasma monitoring. For teacher-guided disruption prediction, only Ref. [27] proposed a label-correction strategy based on the teacher’s classification results. In contrast, our DP peak-disruptivity window-weighting strategy does not correct labels but uses teacher guidance to make the student model focus more on peak-disruptivity windows during training.

papers.title: The role of symmetry in the performance of the Thresholding Greedy Algorithm
papers.abstract: This paper continues the study of conditional symmetric systems initiated in arXiv:2601.15784 and solves several problems posed there. While the interaction between unconditionality and symmetry is well known in the Banach setting following the work in arXiv:2304.05888 and arXiv:2601.15784, we broaden the scope and address similar questions for spreading systems in the more general setting of quasi-Banach spaces. Our aim is twofold. On the one hand, we characterize which spreading systems of Banach spaces are unconditional. On the other hand, we provide examples of quasi-Banach spaces equipped with conditional systems with symmetry-related properties to illustrate the connections between symmetry, greedy-like properties, and the Schauder basis property in the absence of local convexity.

papers.title: On sparse universally rigid graphs in $\mathbb{R}$
papers.abstract:
A graph is said to be 1-universally rigid if, for any generic realization of its vertices on the real line, the realization cannot be deformed out of the line in any higher-dimensional Euclidean space while preserving all edge lengths. In this paper, we investigate the sparsity of 1-universally rigid graphs in different manners.
  First, we show that an Erd\H{o}s-R\'enyi random graph $G(n,p)$ is 1-universally rigid with high probability whenever $p \geq C\log n \cdot \log\log n/n$ for some sufficiently large constant $C>0$. These techniques also imply the existence of 1-universally rigid graphs of arbitrarily large girth, which resolves a problem suggested by Dantas e Moura, Jord\'an, and Silverman in a non-constructive manner. We also study how sparse a 1-universally rigid graph can be, proving that there exists an absolute constant $\varepsilon>0$ such that every sufficiently large 1-universally rigid graph on $n$ vertices has at least $(3/2+\varepsilon)n$ edges. This breaks the natural $3/2$ barrier arising from degree-2 extensions and makes progress towards a question of Jord\'an and Nguyen.

papers.title: Decay of space plasma turbulence downstream of bow shocks: MMS magnetosheath unbiased campaign observations
papers.abstract: Turbulence properties in the solar wind change with increasing heliospheric distance. Observations from different missions have shown how spectral indices converge towards a $f^{-5/3}$ spectrum in the inertial range as the solar wind reaches one astronomical unit, and how the cascade rate decays as the plasma moves away from the Sun. We evaluate whether these properties display similar trends in a smaller astrophysical system, that of a planetary magnetosheath. Using data from the 2023 Magnetospheric Multiscale (MMS) unbiased magnetosheath campaign, we determine the evolution of the spectral indices and the cascade rate along 15 inbound magnetosheath crossings. WIND observations permitted to monitor the state of the solar wind during the campaign and allowed to study the impact of the upstream plasma conditions on the evolution of the cascade rate downstream the bow shock. Our results show an increase of the cascade rate between two to three orders of magnitude after the plasma crosses the bow shock into the magnetosheath. Once in the magnetosheath, turbulence develops with increasing distance to the bow shock in a way similar to solar wind observations, despite the smaller size of the system. Incompressible Hall-MHD scaling-law estimates of the cascade rate show a clear power-law decay of the cascade rate in the magnetosheath, particularly for the cases with upstream slow wind. This suggests that the way energy is injected into the system plays a role in the decay of turbulence as the plasma moves away from the bow shock.

papers.intro:
The terrestrial magnetosheath, a region formed past the bow shock due to the deceleration and compression of the solar wind at its encounter with Earth’s magnetosphere, is an ideal environment to study plasma physics. The large magnetic field and plasma density in this region are features that distinguish it from the pristine solar wind in the near-Earth environment. Furthermore, its proximity to Earth makes it more accessible for in-situ observations than other regions of space. In order to monitor the plasma conditions in this environment, measurements have been taken using single and multi-spacecraft missions, such as Cluster [27], THEMIS [7], and the Magnetospheric Multiscale (MMS) mission [16].

In particular, MMS measurements in the magnetosheath have lead to striking new discoveries in plasma physics, like the first observation of an electron velocity distribution being reshaped by a standard (ion) reconnection event [17], or the first measurements of electron-only reconnection jets [86, 59]. MMS observations in the magnetosheath have also been especially relevant in the study of turbulence properties, as they have allowed us to analyze intermittency down to ion and electron scales [22], to show the wave-vector anisotropy of velocity and magnetic fluctuations down to sub-ion scales [65, 39], to determine the properties of fluctuations in an electron-only reconnection interval [76], to determine the topology of magnetic and velocity fluctuations at kinetic scales in incompressible plasmas [87], to observe the anisotropy of the cross-scale energy flux [57] and to measure the pressure-strain contributions to the energy transfer [19, 48].

These results have been possible thanks to the high resolution of the instruments onboard the MMS spacecraft, which have allowed us to explore a broad range of parameters and spatial scales. However, this parameter space is constrained by the limitations in the telemetry of data. The downlink of high-resolution data intervals is manually selected by a member of the MMS scientific community, the scientist in the loop (SITL) based on the observation of events with low-cadence mode measurements. The SITL marks for downlink the data intervals that feature clear examples of known physical phenomena. As a consequence, the MMS high-cadence database can be considered to be biased towards certain plasma conditions, leading to a skewed understanding of the events that take place in the magnetosheath. This limitation of the MMS database motivated the creation of the first observational campaign dedicated to collecting an unbiased sample of high resolution data intervals of Earth’s magnetosheath.

The 2023 MMS unbiased magnetosheath campaign provides a uniform sampling of Earth’s magnetosheath at high cadence, with a 33%33\% coverage for 15 magnetosheath inbound crossings. The data intervals that constitute the campaign dataset were selected without any selection criteria besides that the spacecraft had to be located inside the magnetosheath. In addition to offering an unbiased selection of data, the campaign aims to provide observations to study the evolution of plasma properties across the magnetosheath with each inbound crossing. The data from this campaign has already been used to analyze the magnetosheath plasma properties in the unbiased dataset and their relation to intermittency [55], quantify the occurrence of whistler waves in the magnetosheath [79], and determine the change of electron heat flux at different bow shock distances [78]. In this work, we focus on analyzing the properties of plasma turbulence in this dataset, particularly the spectral indices and the energy cascade rate. Our aim is to present these turbulence properties in the unbiased magnetosheath dataset and determine whether they are affected by the distance to the bow shock.

Turbulence properties present a clear evolution with heliospheric distance in the inner heliosphere. Statistical studies have shown a change of the power spectral density (PSD) of magnetic fluctuations above the ion Larmor radius, the so-called inertial range, from a power-law dependence in frequency of f−3/2f^{-3/2} to a steeper one f−5/3f^{-5/3} [20, 71]. In fast winds and Alfvénic slow winds, low frequencies also display a f−1f^{-1} power law, whose breakpoint with the inertial range recedes to smaller frequencies as the heliospheric distance increases [14, 15]. Below the ion gyroradius, the spectra reaches the so called kinetic or sub-ion scales. There, the spectra present a steeper decay in frequency, with power-law exponents between -2 and -4, and a peak generally about -2.8 for observations made at one astronomical unit (AU) [72, 2, 68]. At electron scales, the power spectral density of magnetic fluctuations displays an even faster decay with frequency [3, 68, 38, 50]. In contrast with its evolution at inertial range scales, the spectra in the sub-ion range become less steep with heliospheric distance [25, 58, 69]. The measurement of spectral indices in the magnetosheath and their location with respect to the bow shock also suggest that turbulence follows a similar evolution in this environment: a steepening towards Kolmogorov’s f−5/3f^{-5/3} at inertial range scales as the plasma moves away from the bow shock and the raise of the kinetic range power law, reaching f−2.8f^{-2.8} close to the magnetopause boundary [37, 43]. The 2023 unbiased magnetosheath campaign allows to verify, down to sub-ion scales, whether this statistical results hold true for and unbiased dataset and for individual magnetosheath crossings.

papers.title: Single-Annotation, Multi-Hypothesis Segmentation with Semantic-Spatial Residual Banks
papers.abstract: Multi-rater segmentation datasets show that a single image can admit several valid masks, yet most training sets expose only one annotation per image. We study single-annotation multi-hypothesis segmentation: each training image exposes one fixed mask, while the model must return a finite bank that covers held-out human annotations at test time. Our experiments reveal a representation tradeoff. Banks learned directly from images recover variations in local boundaries and extent but lose structural hypotheses, whereas frozen semantic features preserve structural grouping but underrepresent spatial variation. We introduce the Semantic-Spatial Residual Bank (SSRB), which freezes a semantic bank trained with balanced assignments and learns a residual from the image for each hypothesis. Across five medical endpoints, SSRB improves coverage of held-out masks at $K=8$ over a Probabilistic U-Net under the same one-mask constraint. On LIDC and LIDC-hard, it also produces substantially more distinct useful masks. On BSDS, it preserves the semantic bank's performance in grouping regions. Its advantage grows as more masks are returned, showing that residuals learned for corresponding heads improve coverage of local annotation variation while preserving how regions are grouped.

papers.intro:
A single image can admit several defensible segmentations. Radiologists may draw different extents of one lung nodule, ophthalmologists may disagree on an optic-cup boundary, and people may parse a natural image into different regions [4, 2, 1, 3]. Collecting several masks for every image is costly, however, and many training sets expose only one. A useful model should still return plausible alternatives for a new image without having seen several labels for any training example.

A finite bank can be sampled from a probabilistic decoder or emitted directly by several heads [17, 5, 12, 19]. Direct prediction is simple, but one representation does not serve every kind of ambiguity equally well. Raw image features retain fine boundaries and local extent changes. Frozen semantic features retain object and region structure. With one annotation per image, our two controlled banks expose the conflict: the raw bank is much stronger on fine medical segmentations, whereas the semantic bank is much stronger on the task of grouping regions more broadly.

We first train an eight-head bank over frozen DINOv3 features [28], assigning images to heads with balanced capacities through a linear assignment [18]. We then freeze that bank and train a small raw-image U-Net [27] to correct each head’s mask and rank logits. Each semantic hypothesis anchors one spatial correction. Adding their logits produces eight masks, using the same rule on every endpoint. papers.title: Grounding Image Composition with Label-Conditioned Visual Evidence
papers.abstract: Image composition labels such as center, diagonal, or rule of thirds describe visual structure rather than object categories. KU-PCP provides image-level labels and class-specific geometric elements, but does not show which visible regions people associate with each of its nine classes. We introduce KU-PCP Elements (KU-PCPE), a label-conditioned region-evidence benchmark for photographic composition. Given an image and a label already judged applicable, the task is to segment the visible regions that explain why the label applies. KU-PCPE contains 4,093 single-annotator training masks and a 1,327-task expert test split with three masks per image-label task. The annotations also include exploratory segment-versus-line ratings that describe whether region or semantic-guideline evidence better explains the label. A held-out expert reaches .867 Dice against the other experts, while the strongest deployable model reaches .664, a proposal oracle .672, and the best vision-language model (VLM) proposal selector .395. KU-PCPE exposes the gap between recognizing a composition label and grounding the human-aligned visual evidence that makes it plausible in a particular image.

papers.intro:
Photographic composition is an inherently visual concept. Labels such as center, diagonal, horizontal, or rule of thirds name recurring spatial organizations, but they do not specify which visible structures make the label applicable in a particular image. Two images may share a label for different reasons, and one image may support several labels through different regions, lines, or partitions. This creates an evidence question that image-level classification cannot answer: given an image and a queried composition label, what visual evidence makes that label plausible?

We introduce KU-PCP Elements (KU-PCPE), a label-conditioned region-evidence grounding benchmark for photographic composition. Each task pairs a photograph with one of its KU-PCP composition labels, and annotators select the visible regions they consider jointly responsible for that composition. A mask may contain one or several disconnected regions and may include objects, object parts, background, or negative space. For labels expressed through a line, axis, or spatial relation, the mask contains the visible elements or partitions that carry the relation. A multi-label photograph therefore yields a distinct grounding task for each of its composition labels.

A limited comparison with KU-PCP’s detected triangles shows shared geometry, while our masks also capture the objects, surfaces, and background that make the composition visible.

papers.title: The JWST/PASSAGE Survey: Metallicity Radial Gradients in Emission-Line Galaxy Pairs at Cosmic Noon with NIRISS
papers.abstract: Using JWST/NIRISS slitless spectroscopy from the PASSAGE program, we analyze 17 spectroscopically confirmed emission-line galaxies in candidate interacting systems at $z \sim 1.7$--$3.2$. These galaxies span stellar masses of $7.3 \lesssim \log(M_*/M_\odot) \lesssim 10.4$ and global gas-phase metallicities of $12+\log(\mathrm{O/H}) \sim 7.6$--$8.7$. From spatially resolved emission-line maps, we measure radial metallicity gradients separately for each galaxy, finding values from approximately $-0.2$ to $+0.45$ dex kpc$^{-1}$. The mean metallicity gradients in bins of stellar mass and redshift are consistent with previous measurements, and their scatter is not significantly different from that of the heterogeneous literature compilation in either the metallicity-gradient--stellar-mass or metallicity-gradient--redshift relation. We find tentative evidence for an anti-correlation between the metallicity gradient and the metallicity offset from the mass--metallicity relation, with a best-fit slope of $-0.30 \pm 0.06$, possibly reflecting interaction-driven variations in star formation and chemical enrichment. Galaxies in pairs with comparable component masses tend to exhibit positive metallicity gradients, whereas galaxies in unequal-mass pairs tend to exhibit negative gradients; neither trend is statistically significant in the present sample. Overall, our results reveal substantial diversity in the metallicity distributions of candidate interacting systems at cosmic noon and provide tentative evidence that galaxy interactions may influence the redistribution of gas and metals.

The epoch known as “cosmic noon” (z∼1z\sim 1–3) marks a peak in the cosmic star formation rate and a heightened frequency of galaxy mergers [65, 67]. This period represents a crucial phase in galaxy evolution, during which gravitational interactions and gas dynamics actively shape the internal structure and chemical composition of galaxies.

This period represents a crucial phase in galaxy evolution, during which gravitational interactions and gas dynamics actively shape the internal structure and chemical composition of galaxies.

Gas-phase metallicity, traced by emission lines from the ionized interstellar medium (ISM), encodes the history of star formation and gas flows such as accretion, feedback-driven outflows, and gas recycling [68, 96, 26], while recent studies further show that the physical conditions of ionized gas, such as electron density, are closely linked to star formation activity [62]. Gas-phase metallicity is commonly expressed as 12+log⁡(O/H)12+\log(\mathrm{O/H}), which represents the logarithmic abundance of oxygen relative to hydrogen, normalized such that the solar value is approximately 8.69 [4]. The spatial distribution of metallicity, which is typically quantified by metallicity gradients, provides further insight into galaxy assembly [48, 117, 116, 8]. In the local Universe, disk galaxies often exhibit negative radial metallicity gradients, interpreted as a consequence of inside-out growth [86, 44, 23]. However, galaxy mergers can dramatically alter these gradients through gravitational torques and large-scale gas redistribution, often flattening or even inverting them [85, 107, 15]. Both observations [55] and simulations [73, 16] support the idea that interactions trigger gas mixing and dynamically reshape a galaxy’s chemical profile.

In the local Universe, disk galaxies often exhibit negative radial metallicity gradients, interpreted as a consequence of inside-out growth [86, 44, 23]. However, galaxy mergers can dramatically alter these gradients through gravitational torques and large-scale gas redistribution, often flattening or even inverting them [85, 107, 15]. Both observations [55] and simulations [73, 16] support the idea that interactions trigger gas mixing and dynamically reshape a galaxy’s chemical profile.

Systematic measurements of metallicity gradients in interacting systems across cosmic time are thus critical for constraining models of gas inflows, star formation regulation, and the role of mergers in galaxy evolution [55]. Until recently, such studies at high redshift have been limited by the sensitivity and resolution of available instruments.

papers.title: Underdamped Stochastic Optimal Transport with Landauer boundary conditions: machine learning and analytical solution
papers.abstract: Finding optimal transport protocols for underdamped stochastic processes is a difficult yet important problem in control theory. In this paper we develop a direct method, based on machine learning, to find the optimal solution of the problem in the presence of non-linear boundary conditions, including those modelling the Landauer bit-erasure problem. The dynamics is steered from a single-peak to a double-peak distribution in position space, by only acting on a controllable external potential. The problem is highly non-linear, and analytical solutions are not available in general. We benchmark our numerical results with a perturbative expansion, which is expected to hold in a suitable overdamped limit.

Over the last two decades, stochastic mass transport has become the focus of strong cross-disciplinary interest for independent but intertwined reasons. In control engineering, see e.g. [59], identifying the cost of stochastic mass transport with the Kullback-Leibler divergence (e.g. [12, § 2.3]) between the realized and a reference process, typically free diffusion, can assess the performance of an actuator accomplishing an assigned task in the presence of noise. The stochastic optimal transport problem of minimizing the Kullback-Leibler divergence is usually referred to as the dynamic Schrödinger bridge [36]. In the overdamped formulation of the dynamic Schrödinger bridge, the optimal control problem is described by a Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman equation that can be greatly simplified using the Cole-Hopf (or logarithmic) transform [21, § VI]. This also is true in the underdamped case for controls that are functions of both position and momentum. Numerical solutions for large classes of boundary data can then be found using proximal algorithms [8] that exploit recent breakthroughs [29] in the theory of gradient flows, see [55, 2] for thorough overviews.

In physics, interest in stochastic mass transport is motivated by advances in nano-system manipulation and the emergence of stochastic (or finite-time) thermodynamics [45]. Motion at nano-scale is inherently affected by Brownian forces, whose effect cannot be avoided even in a near vacuum [32]. A fundamental question is how nano-systems can efficiently harness randomness in order to move between assigned states or perform thermodynamic work on larger scales [7]. Considerable experimental efforts, see, e.g., [5, 34], focus on demonstrating optimal “information ratchets”: control at minimum energy cost of the dynamics of a nano-system by changing the effective kinetic barriers to Brownian motion depending on the position of the system. Optimization of memory bits operations [37, 14, 4], including Landauer bit-erasure [35], belongs to this class of problems. In stochastic systems, thermodynamic state indicators such as work, heat and entropy become fluctuating quantities whose statistics is governed by precise fluctuation relations, reviewed e.g. in [28]. In particular, fluctuation relations express physical measures of dissipation in terms of information-theoretic measures of time-asymmetry, such as the Kullback-Leibler divergence between a process evolving forward-in-time and a backward-in-time counter-part [10]. This Kullback-Leibler divergence, identified as the mean entropy production, specifies a natural cost for stochastic optimal transport in finite-time thermodynamics: it vanishes if and only if the system is at thermal equilibrium. Interestingly, if small-system dynamics is modelled by an overdamped (Langevin-Smoluchowski) stochastic differential equation (see e.g. [43]), stochastic optimal transport admits an exact mapping into classical deterministic optimal mass transport [3].

A second reason for interest for stochastic optimal transport, resulting in explosive growth in the number of publications, comes from generative modelling [57, 25, 58] in machine learning. A deep neural network can learn to generate data from noise by means of a two-step process. First, a forward stochastic process destroys structure in a data distribution by adding noise over a finite time interval. Next, a neural network is trained to revert the process by learning a backward evolution that interpolates between the initial data distribution and the one realized at the end of the forward evolution. Dynamic Schrödinger bridges provide a concrete implementation of this idea [16, 6], which we may also refer to as “stochastic interpolant theory” [1] and has a wide range of important applications, from sampling to image reconstruction [61].

A crucial difference from stochastic interpolant theory is that physically relevant models of nano-system dynamics evolve according to Langevin-Kramers dynamics. The Langevin-Kramers dynamics pose kinematic restrictions, including the coexistence of a conservative and a dissisipative component in the drift, and that control is exerted by varying a mechanical potential. How can computational strategies be adapted, and how can their accuracy be assessed in stochastic thermodynamics?

papers.title: Resonant Amplification of Demographic Noise in Stochastic Common-Pool Resource Dynamics
papers.abstract: Common-pool resources are vulnerable to overexploitation, yet many social-ecological systems exhibit persistent oscillations. We introduce a stochastic eco-evolutionary model in which harvesting strategies and resource availability shape one another. In the infinite population limit the system approaches a stable state through damped oscillations. Demographic noise continually excites these modes, generating instead robust macroscopic quasi-cycles, whose frequencies depend on the noise ratio, the relative timescale between strategy and resource, and the harvesting pressure. The model reproduces the distinct frequency peaks, observed in empirical global fish-landings data for high- and low-income countries, showing that persistent environmental fluctuations can emerge naturally from demographic noise.

papers.title: Addendum to "Optimal Steering of a Linear Stochastic System to a Final Probability Distribution, Part II"
papers.abstract: We hereby fill in a gap in an induction argument used in the proof of a theorem on state-covariance controllability of linear stochastic systems in an earlier paper by the authors. The mathematical statement is true. The missing point in the proof concerns the assertion that, in the canonical single-input case, the control can be assigned arbitrary endpoint values. We amend the argument by proving a slightly stronger induction statement that permits arbitrary finite endpoint jets of the control. An independent approach to homogeneous state-covariance controllability was provided in a paper by Abdelgalil and Georgiou (2025) as a corollary of strong controllability results on $\GLp(n,\mathbb R)$, and shown herein that it extends to the case of additive noise as well.

papers.title: Current-driven transient dynamics of magnetic-octupole domain walls in noncollinear antiferromagnets
papers.abstract: Current-driven magnetic-octupole domain walls in noncollinear antiferromagnets are promising for fast spintronic devices, yet their transient dynamics are not yet fully understood. Here, we investigate spin-orbit-torque-driven domain-wall motion in Mn$_\text{3}$Sn using a multipole micromagnetic framework. The three symmetry-related 60{\deg} walls exhibit equivalent current-driven dynamics, unlike their field-driven motion. For a representative 60{\deg} wall, the post-pulse motion is governed by relaxation of the current-induced rotation of the surrounding octupole domains, with a characteristic time of approximately 33 ps quantitatively captured by a uniform-domain analytic model. By resolving spatially nonuniform texture dynamics beyond this analytic description, the simulations further reveal an additional slow relaxation in a composite 180{\deg} wall associated with the relative motion of its constituent walls. The post-pulse response also varies systematically with the exchange stiffness and magnetic anisotropies. These results identify distinct domain and internal-coordinate relaxation channels and establish the intrinsic time scales governing pulse-controlled positioning of magnetic-octupole domain walls in antiferromagnetic spintronic devices.

Current-driven domain-wall motion underpins proposed spintronic architectures for memory, logic, and unconventional computing [1, 17, 14, 15, 28, 29]. Antiferromagnets are attractive because they offer ultrafast dynamics and weak stray fields [11, 2, 4, 23]. However, their small net magnetization makes electrical detection and manipulation challenging. Noncollinear antiferromagnets provide a distinct opportunity because their spin textures can be represented by cluster magnetic multipoles that govern macroscopic responses such as the anomalous Hall, Nernst, magneto-optical Kerr, and spin Hall effects [25, 16, 9, 3, 20]. In Mn3​Sn\text{Mn}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\smash[t]{\text{3}}}\text{Sn}, the inverse triangular spin structure is described by a cluster magnetic-octupole order parameter, and magnetic domains correspond to different orientations of this octupole moment. Magnetic-octupole domains and domain walls have been detected through Hall and Nernst transport, directly visualized by magneto-optical imaging, and manipulated using magnetic fields and electrical currents [9, 18, 24, 30, 33]. Recent studies have demonstrated experimentally and theoretically that magnetic-octupole domain walls in noncollinear antiferromagnets can exhibit fast current-driven motion, highlighting their potential for electrically controlled antiferromagnetic domain-wall devices [30, 31, 32, 6].

The transient response of a domain wall after a driving force is applied or removed can reveal dynamical memory associated with the relaxation of the wall profile or other coupled degrees of freedom. In conventional ferromagnets, deformation of a moving wall can be described in terms of a Döring-like effective mass, giving rise to finite acceleration and deceleration times [5, 19, 26, 27, 34]; inertial effects have also been predicted to govern switching in antiferromagnets [12]. Using a multipole micromagnetic framework, we recently showed that field-driven magnetic-octupole domain walls in Mn3​Sn\text{Mn}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\smash[t]{\text{3}}}\text{Sn} deform and acquire a Döring-like effective mass [35]. Current-induced spin-orbit torque, however, acts simultaneously on the wall and the surrounding octupole domains. Previous theoretical work has investigated the SOT-driven dynamics of spatially uniform Mn3​Sn\text{Mn}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\smash[t]{\text{3}}}\text{Sn}, including its response to current pulses [21]. How these uniform order-parameter dynamics couple to the translational motion of a spatially nonuniform texture, and how additional internal degrees of freedom modify the transient response of a composite wall, remains unresolved.

We first show that, unlike field-driven motion, spin-orbit torque produces identical steady-state and transient dynamics for the three symmetry-related types of 60∘ walls. papers.title: Expected shortfall estimation and capital coverage under overlapping scenarios
papers.abstract: Expected shortfall (ES) is routinely estimated from a short sample of profit-and-loss (P&L) scenarios built from overlapping multi-day returns, while the non-parametric estimators applied to such data are designed under independent sampling. We study how this mismatch affects estimation accuracy and capital coverage, and how it interacts with serial dependence and heavy tails in the underlying P&L. Working within the coherent risk estimation framework, we compare six order-statistic-based ES estimators on fit, bias, and capital-coverage metrics. Following the Fundamental Review of the Trading Book (FRTB), we use a one-year estimation window and ES at the $2.5\%$ confidence level as a benchmark setup. We combine simulations with market data on twelve risk factors and ninety-nine equity portfolios. We show that overlapping sampling does not merely add noise but shifts ES estimates systematically downward, thereby weakening capital coverage. Serial dependence acts in the same direction, and heavy tails amplify both effects. More conservative weighting mitigates the underestimation but does not remove it. On market data, the confidence level at which the estimated capital covers realized losses roughly doubles in median under overlapping sampling for every estimator, while the $\textrm{ES}_{2.5\%}$-to-$\textrm{VaR}_{1\%}$ ratio, which links the FRTB base market risk capital metric to its pre-FRTB predecessor, changes comparatively little. Overlapping sampling can thus substantially understate ES-based capital. Since many banks apply a small set of standard estimators in their FRTB regulatory or economic capital model in a historical simulation approach, this understatement is likely to be common for many institutions, and combining simulation-based assessment of estimation risk with coverage-based diagnostics offers a practical method to detect it in model validation and monitoring.

papers.intro:
Risk management plays a critical role in safeguarding the solvency of financial institutions and, in aggregate, the stability of the financial system. This role rests on the ability to reliably estimate the capital required to absorb losses arising from realized adverse economic scenarios. For market risk, capital requirements are quantified through risk measures, which are backed by a well-developed mathematical theory. The central goal of this theory is to determine what a ‘good risk measure’ should look like, and how to quantify, represent, and manage risk, see Artzner et al. [1999] for the seminal paper on coherent risk measures, or Föllmer and Schied [2016] for a comprehensive treatment.

This role rests on the ability to reliably estimate the capital required to absorb losses arising from realized adverse economic scenarios. For market risk, capital requirements are quantified through risk measures, which are backed by a well-developed mathematical theory. The central goal of this theory is to determine what a ‘good risk measure’ should look like, and how to quantify, represent, and manage risk, see Artzner et al. [1999] for the seminal paper on coherent risk measures, or Föllmer and Schied [2016] for a comprehensive treatment.

In risk measure theory, one assumes that the true probability law of the underlying profit-and-loss (P&L), cash-flows, or exposure vectors is known, which, practically speaking, can never be satisfied. Hence, the estimation of risk measures has become a central topic in its own right, see McNeil et al. [2015]. The need for efficient estimation methods is reinforced by regulatory frameworks such as the Basel III reforms’ Fundamental Review of the Trading Book (FRTB), under which expected shortfall (ES) at the 2.5%2.5\% confidence level replaced the traditional value-at-risk (VaR) at the 1%1\% confidence level as the main Pillar I market risk metric for banks using internal models, see BCBS [2019]. This regulatory shift reflects the emphasis placed after the 2008 financial crisis on capturing the severity of tail losses rather than relying solely on a single quantile. In practice, market risk is computed, or more precisely estimated, using finite samples, e.g. based on annual stress period data for Pillar I purposes, and thus ES estimation accuracy is not a peripheral statistical concern. In particular, while the underlying risk measure can be coherent and sound, inadequate estimation procedures can lead to systematically biased capital reserves that are fragile to the shape of the P&L distribution, see Danielsson [2008], Kellner and Rösch [2016], Barendse et al. [2023] and references therein.

In this paper we focus on ES estimation risk and the related capital coverage sufficiency. A wide range of ES estimation methodologies have been proposed, from historical simulation and parametric approaches to extreme-value-theory-based and fully stochastic techniques; we refer to the survey of Nadarajah et al. [2014], which catalogs more than 45 estimation methods, and to the more recent treatments in Righi and Ceretta [2015], Chen [2008], and Ruiz and Nieto [2023]. While estimation risk has received considerable attention, see e.g. Cont et al. [2010], Risk and Ludkovski [2018], Francioni and Herzog [2012], Frank [2016], Lauer and Zähle [2017], Bartl and Eckstein [2026], the overwhelming majority of the ES estimation literature studies estimators through a traditional large-sample lens: consistency, rate of convergence, and asymptotic normality, typically under the assumption that the P&L is observed as an independent and identically distributed (i.i.d.) sequence. While this is a standard and mathematically convenient assumption, it sits uneasily with the practical way risk estimators are actually deployed. Namely, risk estimates are not computed in asymptotic large sample size regimes but rather using a specific functional and a fixed sample size, and then recomputed on a periodic basis, see BCBS [2019, MAR 33.6].

A recent strand of the literature takes this practical reality seriously by considering the desired estimator properties directly within finite-sample environments, rather than recovering them asymptotically, see e.g. Bartl and Tangpi [2023], Gaspar [2026], and references therein. In particular, Aichele et al. [2026] introduce the notion of coherent risk estimators (CREs): finite-sample analogues of the monotonicity, cash-additivity, positive homogeneity, and subadditivity axioms of coherent risk measures, imposed directly at the level of the estimator acting on a sample of fixed size nn, together with law-invariance and comonotonicity. They show that the class of comonotonic, law-invariant CREs is exactly the class of LL-estimators with non-negative, decreasing, and normalized weights, i.e. negatives of weighted averages of the ordered P&Ls. Crucially, this characterization is distribution-free, in the sense that a given CRE satisfies these properties for any underlying P&L distribution. This finite-sample, distribution-free perspective is particularly well suited to the market risk regulatory setup, where the sample size is often fixed to the number of observations over one year, for example when a historical simulation approach is calibrated to a period of financial stress, cf. BCBS [2019, MAR 33.6] and EU CRR [2013, Article 325bc], rather than treated as a parameter that can be sent to infinity.
