papers.title: Recycle only when you have to!
papers.abstract: AlphaFold 3-like models (e.g., Boltz, Protenix, etc.) have pushed the frontier of protein binder design. This architecture is used both for the generation of binder candidates (e.g., by hallucination or converting these models into backbone or full atom generative models) as well as for the screening of these candidates for valid binders. In this paper, we start from the observation that AlphaFold 3's confidence metrics (ipSAE, ipTM) as well as structural consistency metrics can be predicted directly from the trunk even at early recycling. Because our proposed predictor is cheap, differentiable, and available at every cycle, it can be used in two distinct ways: as a decision signal to wisely spend the recycling budget for screening and as an objective for hallucination-based design. We show that both applications lead to increased performance at significantly reduced computational cost.

Several methods have recently succeeded in designing de novo minibinders [30, 21, 22, 24] and antibodies for specific epitopes [2, 20, 26, 24]. De novo binder design typically involves a generative as well as a scoring step. The former creates plausible candidate protein binders, while the latter selects promising candidates for experimental validation. Our work improves both steps.

Several methods have recently succeeded in designing de novo minibinders [30, 21, 22, 24] and antibodies for specific epitopes [2, 20, 26, 24]. De novo binder design typically involves a generative as well as a scoring step. The former creates plausible candidate protein binders, while the latter selects promising candidates for experimental validation. Our work improves both steps.

The screening step typically involves scoring the design by refolding its sequence. Designs are rejected if their refolds have low confidence or are structurally incompatible with the generative step. For state-of-the-art design pipelines, such as RFDiffusion and BindCraft, the computational cost is dominated by this refold. This is because the generative step of these pipelines involves an inverse folding that typically samples multiple sequences per design. As a concrete example, BindCraft typically uses 20 sequences per design. All of these sequences need to be refolded. The screening step has been shown to provide a significant boost to the binding rate [26, 22, 2]. Furthermore, recent work suggests that sampling more candidates followed by more stringent screening also improves binding [5]. A significant reduction of the numerical cost at the same refold fidelity is thus highly desirable.

papers.title: Learning Clean Generative Processes from Noisy Measurements
papers.abstract: We study how to learn a generative model of clean images using only noisy observations. Diffusion processes and their generalizations to non-Gaussian noise require posterior predictions at every noise level. We first show that it is possible to learn these predictions from independent noisy views using Noise2Noise regression, but only at or above the noise level of the training data. To learn the predictions below that level, needed to generate clean images, we impose consistency: a prediction should equal its expectation after continuing the sampling process. We derive conditions under which consistency uniquely determines the continuation to the clean image distribution and verify them for Poisson, binomial, Gamma, and negative-binomial measurements. Experiments on CIFAR-10, photon-counting microscopy, and synthetic aperture radar show that the required posterior predictions can be learned from noisy views alone and that the consistency relation repairs the continuation beyond the noise level of the data, which severely deteriorates without consistency.

papers.intro:
Can one learn to generate clean images from a dataset of noisy observations? This question arises naturally in scientific imaging. For example, photon-counting microscopy often allows only short exposures with a few photons per pixel, because more light would damage the sample (Krull et al., 2024). In synthetic aperture radar (SAR), images are corrupted by speckle (Dalsasso et al., 2022; Dalsasso et al., 2021). In cryo-electron tomography the electron beam damages the sample, so the dose is kept low and projections are very noisy (Buchholz et al., 2019; Liu et al., 2022; Kishore et al., 2026). In each case the noise model is known, but clean images are unavailable. This presents a challenge for diffusion models, which are typically trained by regressing onto clean images.

Can one learn to generate clean images from a dataset of noisy observations? This question arises naturally in scientific imaging. For example, photon-counting microscopy often allows only short exposures with a few photons per pixel, because more light would damage the sample (Krull et al., 2024). In synthetic aperture radar (SAR), images are corrupted by speckle (Dalsasso et al., 2022; Dalsasso et al., 2021). In cryo-electron tomography the electron beam damages the sample, so the dose is kept low and projections are very noisy (Buchholz et al., 2019; Liu et al., 2022; Kishore et al., 2026). In each case the noise model is known, but clean images are unavailable. This presents a challenge for diffusion models, which are typically trained by regressing onto clean images.

Lehtinen et al. (2018) showed that denoisers can be trained using only noisy images. Their method, Noise2Noise (N2N), trains a network to predict a second noisy measurement of an image from the first. If the two measurements are independent conditional on the clean image, and averaging the second measurement over its noise gives the clean image, the minimizer of the expected squared error is the posterior mean of the clean image given the first measurement. The network therefore learns a denoiser without ever seeing a clean image. Later work obtained the two noisy views from a single measurement, either by adding further noise (Moran et al., 2020; Pang et al., 2021) or by splitting the measurement into two parts with independent noise. Variants of splitting exist for Gaussian, Poisson, Gamma and negative-binomial measurements (Neufeld et al., 2024; Leiner et al., 2025; Monroy et al., 2025). Since Gaussian diffusion models generate images with denoisers at a sequence of noise levels (Song et al., 2021), N2N allows one to train them from noisy data. Daras et al. (2024) take this route: noisy images at one noise level supervise the denoisers at all noisier levels, and the consistency loss of Daras et al. (2023a) extends them to cleaner levels.

To address this, we build the generative process directly from the specific noise model that produced the data. We index the process by an information level aa that increases as the noise decreases, such as the precision (inverse variance) of a Gaussian measurement or the exposure of a photon count. Its state at level aa is distributed like a measurement at that level, and as aa grows, the normalized state converges to the clean image. papers.title: VitisGP: Multi-Task Benchmark for Genotype to Phenotype Grapevine Prediction
papers.abstract: As climate change reshapes grape-growing conditions, predicting grapevine phenotypes from genomic variation is increasingly important for identifying and breeding cultivars suited to emerging environmental pressures. Existing research on the grapevine genotype-phenotype relationship using machine learning has often focused on individual traits, isolated regions, or a limited set of predictive models. We introduce VitisGP, a multi-phenotype curated dataset, integrating genome-wide SNP data with 26 heterogeneous phenotype prediction tasks spanning sommelier-curated aroma traits (N=11), botanical traits (N=14) and wine color---across 1,197 Vitis vinifera cultivars. We employ VitisGP to benchmark phenotype prediction, comparing machine-learning models with differing inductive biases---L2-regularized logistic regression, Random Forest, XGBoost, CatBoost, GBLUP and Transformer-based models, providing the first systematic comparison of this breadth on harmonized grapevine data. Across the benchmark, CatBoost achieves the strongest overall performance (macro-average AUROC=0.696 across 26 tasks), although model performance varies substantially across phenotype classes, with sensory and color traits showing stronger predictability than agronomic characteristics. VitisGP provides the community with a resource for investigating the genomic basis of phenotypic traits and screening grapevine diversity for climate-relevant characteristics.

papers.intro:
The accelerating pace of climate change poses a growing threat to global agriculture, with grapevine (Vitis vinifera) cultivation being particularly vulnerable. In recent years, unpredictable temperature regimes, water availability, and disease pressure have severely affected grapevine growth and, in extreme cases, compromised entire cultivars Wolkovich et al. (2018); Van Leeuwen et al. (2024). Such environmental pressures directly alter grape physiology with downstream consequences for grape and wine quality van Leeuwen et al. (2019); Van Leeuwen et al. (2024). These challenges, together with the growing need for climate-resilient cultivars, motivate the development of computational approaches linking grapevine genetic variation to agronomic and sensory phenotypes.

Machine learning (ML) has increasingly been applied to agriculture as genomic and chemical measurements from various crops—grapes, wheat, and other produce—become available at larger scales. Recent deep-learning approaches in genomics Avsec et al. (2021); Ji et al. (2021), as well as methods developed specifically for crop genomics such as CropFormer Wang et al. (2025) and GEFormer Yao et al. (2025), have explored convolutional and attention-based architectures to learn representations of genomic variation. In grapevine, a central objective is to characterize the genotype-phenotype relationship, mainly identifying genetic traits/variation associated not only with specific sensory characteristics, but also with traits relevant to resilience under changing environmental conditions.

Current work, however, has largely focused on relatively narrow phenotype definitions or on isolated regions: the study proposed in Gačnik et al. (2017) investigates genomic-botanical associations in wine and table grapes; Khilari et al. (2022) trains classifiers on alcohol and acidity as quality proxies and Tiwari et al. (2022) focuses on a single cultivar. These also include predicting aroma precursors Flutre et al. (2022), and drought-related physiological traits Brault et al. (2021). While these studies demonstrate the feasibility of computational phenotype prediction, they remain limited in task diversity, cultivar set size and model capacity.

More widespread wine review datasets spawn99 (2025), provide valuable free-text descriptions, but tend to pool user data without a common protocol. Often, academic studies also employ inconsistent standards for chemical and sensory characterization Yang and Lee (2020). At the same time, professional wine-tasting frameworks—such as those developed by the Wine & Spirit Education Trust (WSET) Wine & Spirit Education Trust (2017) — provide standardized vocabularies for describing aroma, structure, and other sensory characteristics. Combining information available in existing wine resources with the structured terminology of professional tasting frameworks, offers an opportunity to construct richer representations of grapevine phenotypes. We therefore assemble a dataset of 1,197 Vitis vinifera cultivars with sommelier-profiled olfactory descriptors, structural attributes and botany-level agronomic traits, paired with genome-wide Single Nucleotide Polymorphism (SNP) data. To our knowledge, our dataset is the first to combine high-fidelity, expert-curated sensory phenotypes with grapevine genomics. Using VitisGP, we propose a benchmark to investigate the following question: Across heterogeneous grapevine phenotypes, which class of predictive model—linear, tree-based ensemble, or attention-based—provides the most reliable genotype-to-phenotype prediction, and does the answer vary by phenotype class?

Our contributions are threefold: first, we present a curated grapevine dataset of SNP genotype data from 1,197 V. vinifera cultivars paired with high-fidelity sommelier sensory profiles and agronomic phenotypes. Second, we compare a diverse set of established prediction methods, including L2-regularized logistic regression (L2LR), GBLUP, elastic net, LASSO, Random Forest (RF), XGBoost (XGB), CatBoost (CB), and Transformers. papers.title: Boundary stabilization of a moving interface in a 2 x 2 weakly hyperbolic system of balance laws: application to continuous sedimentation
papers.abstract: We design a boundary feedback for the level of the sediment bed of a continuous settler and prove that it exponentially stabilizes the linearized closed loop under a small-gain condition. The unit is modeled by a 2 x 2 system of balance laws in which the bed surface, the interface, is not a smooth part of the solution but a moving shock between a weakly hyperbolic free-settling zone and a strictly hyperbolic compression zone. We describe it by the Rankine-Hugoniot relations and map the problem onto a fixed domain. Moreover, we prove local well-posedness with a continuation criterion given by a single margin function. Then we linearize the system near an equilibrium. The linearization couples a dissipative distributed layer to one scalar, the interface position, whose equation does not contain the control. We solve this by infinitedimensional forwarding: a Sylvester kernel cancels the interface trace and isolates the interface pole, and a proportional feedback then sets its decay rate. Every hypothesis is verified on an illustrative example, a laboratory-scale continuous settler containing a bed of compact polystyrene beads.

papers.title: Mage-VL-Cowork: A Full Training Recipe to Learn Hybrid Computer Use From Evolved Harnesses
papers.abstract: Effective computer-use agents (CUAs) should seamlessly combine visual GUI interaction with code and terminal execution within a single policy. We present Mage-VL-Cowork, a 4B hybrid CUA trained from a general multimodally aligned checkpoint through an end-to-end, progressive five-stage curriculum across midtraining, SFT, and RL. To power this curriculum at scale, Mage-CUA-Forge replaces per-task agent construction with reusable, skill-conditioned generation workflows and application-specific preparers, synthesizing 293,806 desktop and web tasks across 6,915 skills while reducing recurring per-task expenditure by 82.6%. Rather than directly distilling a default teacher, we evolve the teacher harness and instantiate specialized CUA harnesses to yield high-quality trajectories alongside stage-specific supervision. Mage-VL-Cowork-4B finally climbs to 66.0% on OSWorld-Verified through different training stages with more efficient reasoning cost, achieving state-of-the-art performance at its parameter size and pushing forward the frontier of on-device intelligence.

papers.intro:
Computer-use agents (CUAs) for productivity perceive graphical desktops through screenshots and act through keyboard and mouse commands. This GUI channel is universal, but it is a modeling choice rather than a property of the domain, and an expensive one: a typical screenshot can require thousands of tokens, increasing the cost of processing high-resolution visual input and grounding interface elements. A person fluent with a computer does not confine themselves to the mouse: they open a terminal when a terminal is faster and read a file to confirm what a dialog claims to have saved. Restricting the policy to pixels forces it to re-derive through the GUI what a single command would accomplish, and removes the most reliable channel it has for checking its own work. We therefore train a hybrid CUA that acts through two action channels: the GUI channel, with visual observation and coordinate control, and the terminal channel, a persistent shell environment in which it may run code, invoke command-line utilities, and call application libraries directly.

Hybrid access does not by itself produce hybrid competence, even for frontier teachers. Prior work shows that access to application tools does not ensure their effective use, and that the same tool set can affect different models differently [1, 2]. The policy must learn which channel is appropriate for the current operation and at what level of abstraction to act. Effective hybrid execution routes each operation to the channel where it fits best: coding and terminal execution for structured files (such as updating a spreadsheet with one library call rather than dozens of clicks), and GUI interaction for visual or live application state (such as browser settings that a running browser caches in memory and overwrites on exit). Because even frontier models exhibit suboptimal channel routing under a naive setup, distilling their default rollouts passes those same limits on to the student. The harness is not a neutral container: its tool interfaces, context handling, and guidance directly shape how a fixed teacher model acts. Evolving the harness before large-scale rollout elicits stronger hybrid execution than the teacher achieves by default and carries those improvements across the entire training corpus.

We introduce Mage-VL-Cowork, a hybrid CUA trained on 318,837 teacher trajectories over 293,806 synthesized tasks and environments that cover 6,915 atomic skills in an agent-constructed skill taxonomy. Three design decisions define the pipeline:

1. Learning from an evolved hybrid CUA harness. To collect high-quality demonstrations even when a frontier teacher’s default channel routing is imperfect, we evolve the harness including its scaffold, tool interfaces, prompts, and terminal execution environment, before large-scale rollout. Evolution here is as much pruning as growth: unlike skill libraries that continuously accumulate tools [5, 6, 7], we remove overlapping or ill-suited tools so the teacher produces clean hybrid trajectories that yield much larger gains when distilled into the student (§3.1, §6.7). Moreover, harness evolution produces specialized configurations with different tool sets—including a GUI harness, a terminal harness, and the hybrid CUA harness—allowing us to roll out the same synthesized tasks under multiple harnesses to collect trajectories emphasizing distinct capabilities across our training stages (§4). 2. A single policy that learns the hybrid execution policy. Mage-VL-Cowork observes full-desktop screenshots and emits coordinate mouse and keyboard actions, and in the same episode may execute code and terminal commands on the machine it is operating. The two channels are complementary: pixels are the only channel that reaches spatial, canvas, and rendering-dependent state, while code edits at the abstraction the instruction is written in and lets the agent check its work against ground truth rather than against a screenshot of a dialog. Unlike systems that route between a GUI operator and a coding operator at the orchestrator level [8, 9], the choice is internal to the policy and is therefore something the training data must teach (§3.1). 3. Workflow-first task and environment synthesis. Agent effort is spent once per skill rather than once per task. For each atomic skill, an authoring agent constructs and debugs a reusable generation workflow that combines LLM nodes with application-specific preparers, which materialize input artifacts such as a Calc workbook or a Thunderbird profile with a populated mail store. Combined workflows produce a task package of instruction, environment setup script, and rubric, and gate nodes check its consistency before the task is accepted. Shared workflows and preparers propagate each improvement across all subsequently generated task instances. Task synthesis, including skill-based generation, has also been studied in terminal settings, where the environment is a container filesystem [10, 11]; on a full desktop the environment is application state, which is what the preparer exists to produce (§3.2).

papers.title: Hybrid Computer Use: A Unified Programmatic, Semantic, and Visual Interface for General Agents
papers.abstract: Computer-use agents increasingly tackle tasks ranging from everyday desktop activities to long-horizon professional workflows. Yet interfaces centered on screenshots and mouse-and-keyboard actions can impose a human-interaction prior, requiring repeated screen interpretation while leaving the computer's semantic and programmatic capabilities underexposed. We argue for exposing these capabilities and letting models choose and combine them. We introduce Hybrid Computer Use (HCU), a unified interface for general agents that combines three complementary channels: programmatic interaction through code and command-line tools, semantic interaction through accessibility (AX), and visual interaction through graphical user interfaces (GUI). Our HCU supports efficient AX interaction and guards against stale-state actions during channel switching. A supplementary HCU skill guides agents in selecting and coordinating channels to use the unified interface effectively. Our designed AX tools return compact observations, execute actions in batches, and report their effects as AX diffs, so the model needs fewer round trips. On OSWorld 2.0, HCU achieves the highest Partial and Binary scores among the compared systems. Analyzing agent trajectories, we find that all evaluated models improve with HCU yet allocate work across the channels differently and consistently outperform compared baselines in terms of both efficiency and task success, highlighting the value of unified computer-use interfaces that allow flexible channel selection and combination.

papers.intro:
AI agents are increasingly able to carry out user requests by operating software applications on computers directly. Computer-use research has expanded from everyday desktop tasks in OSWorld 1.0 [1] to long-horizon workflows and specialized professional software in OSWorld 2.0 [2]. As tasks become more involved, agents must sustain progress across many operations, making interaction efficiency important alongside task performance.

Computer-use research has expanded from everyday desktop tasks in OSWorld 1.0 [1] to long-horizon workflows and specialized professional software in OSWorld 2.0 [2]. As tasks become more involved, agents must sustain progress across many operations, making interaction efficiency important alongside task performance.

Most existing computer-use interfaces mirror how humans operate software: inspect the screen, locate a UI control, and use the mouse or keyboard. While this approach offers broad coverage with human-like perception and action, it also imposes a strong human-interaction prior on the action space of a frontier Large Language Model (LLM), overlooking more efficient channels for interacting directly with the system. An agent with existing computer-use interface may spend substantial effort precisely locating a field by screen coordinates even when the application exposes its identity and value through accessibility data, or manipulate data through repeated click-and-drag actions when code could process it directly.

Modern computer systems offer a wide range of interaction tools that fall into three complementary channels: visual interaction through GUIs, structured semantic access through accessibility APIs, and direct programmatic access through code and command-line tools such as Bash. Accessibility (AX), originally developed for assistive technologies and now also used for automation, exposes application UI controls, their properties, and supported operations [3, 4]. Code and command-line tools provide direct access to files, data, and software, while GUI interaction supplies visual evidence and control where structured access is insufficient.

Prior work [5, 6] combines programmatic and visual interaction but makes limited use of the semantic channel provided by AX. UFO2 combines UI Automation with GUI and application-API execution [7], while Tactile exposes semantic actions alongside OCR and visual fallbacks [8]. CUA Driver, an open-source computer-use interface, supports all three channels but favors AX-based interaction in the background to preserve the user’s active desktop [9]. We build on these efforts to organize reference-addressed AX actions, in-call wait steps, and post-action feedback for efficient, sustained interaction, while exposing all three channels within a general agent for model-directed selection and combination.

We introduce Hybrid Computer Use (HCU), a unified interface for general agents that combines three complementary channels: programmatic, semantic, and visual interaction (Figure 1). HCU adds AX and GUI tools to the agent’s own programmatic tools via the Model Context Protocol (MCP), with cross-channel action guards to maintain a consistent view of the current desktop state and an HCU skill to guide the model in selecting and combining the exposed channels. Our designed AX channel lets the model read a compact AX view, act on several targets in one call, and see the resulting changes without a separate observation. Because all three channels act on the same desktop, an action in one can invalidate the evidence held by another; action guards therefore re-check targets and layouts against live state before each input. A supplementary HCU skill explains how to use these tools and when each channel is most effective, helping the model follow the execution and feedback contracts and reduce invocation errors.

On OSWorld 2.0, HCU achieves the highest Partial and Binary scores among compared systems, advancing the performance–efficiency frontier (Figure 1, right). With GPT-6 Astra, it reaches 72.37% Partial, outperforming CUA Driver by 3.55 points. With Claude Opus 5, it improves Partial by 3.75 points and Binary by 3.76 points over the model’s official leaderboard result, reaching 35.19% Binary at 20% lower Cost. papers.title: When Everyone Can Build a Model: Mechanistic Inference in the Age of AI
papers.abstract: Modern deep learning and AI-assisted code generation are lowering the technical barrier to building mathematical models of biological systems that reproduce complex observations. This lets researchers with domain expertise build semi-mechanistic, hybrid models constrained by prior knowledge and augmented with learned structure without extensive training in modelling. However, easier construction does not make interpretation easier: predictive success of such so-called grey-box models does not establish that an inferred mechanism corresponds to the one that generated the data, and the learned component can absorb errors in the mechanistic part. Many biological modelling problems are underdetermined, so several, possibly infinitely many, models may reproduce the same data equally well. This ambiguity enters at two modelling choices: which variables can affect others, and which response function describes the underlying mechanism. For the first choice, causal inference provides a formal framework stating which causal relationships and intervention effects are identifiable from the data and available knowledge. For the second, ensemble analyses quantify the uncertainty and the range of behaviours still allowed by models that fit equally well. Together, they turn a single good fit into an explicit account of what is supported, what remains open, and which experiment would decide.

papers.intro:
Building a mathematical model that reproduces the dynamics of a biological system once required expertise in both biology and mathematical modelling, but this barrier is eroding (Martins dos Santos et al., 2024; Stalidzans et al., 2020). Grey-box models mix structure fixed by prior knowledge with learned structure (Psichogios and Ungar, 1992; Thompson and Kramer, 1994), so they can fit data that a purely mechanistic model cannot. Examples include universal differential equations (UDEs, Rackauckas et al., 2020) and physics- or biology-informed neural networks (Raissi et al., 2019; Lagergren et al., 2020). AI code-generation tools now put such models within reach of domain experts, for whom they are a genuine opportunity. A close fit, however, invites a mechanistic reading of the model’s structure and parameters, and in biomedicine this reading is where the risk lies. The model’s interactions and fitted parameters can be read as a disease mechanism, a drug target, or an explanation for treatment non-response, and a wrong reading points discovery at the wrong target. The problem is not new: expert-built models can also fit well while representing the wrong mechanism. What has changed is that a trained modeller, who would ask whether alternative structures explain the data equally well, may no longer be involved, and the new tooling does not supply that skill.

A good fit is weak evidence for a mechanism (Oreskes et al., 1994), because many biological modelling problems are underdetermined: many models reproduce the same data equally well. A bad fit, by contrast, is strong evidence against it (Popper, 1959), although only together with its auxiliary assumptions (Duhem, 1954; Quine, 1951). A black-box model can legitimately answer this question from observational data, provided new data come from the same distribution as the training data. In mechanistic or grey-box models, ambiguity arises from two choices: which variables can affect which others, and which response functions describe how variables depend on their inputs. The causal route does not aim to recover the full structural causal model. Instead, it identifies the causal effects that are determined by the causal structure and the observational distribution, without requiring the response functions to be known. This distinction matters because the full structural causal model is almost never identifiable from observational data alone (Bareinboim et al., 2022).

papers.title: Strong-Field-Driven Non-Linear Vibronic Coupling in an Asymmetric Donor-Acceptor Oligomer
papers.abstract: Understanding how nuclear motion couples to intramolecular charge transfer beyond the perturbative regime of light--matter interaction remains an open problem. We tackle this problem by investigating the electron-nuclear response of an acceptor-donor-acceptor oligomer with structural asymmetry due to the partial fluorination of an acceptor unit. Adopting real-time time-dependent density functional theory combined with Ehrenfest dynamics, we excite the systems with a resonant pulse of varying intensity, spanning the weak-, intermediate-, and strong-coupling regimes. When nuclei are clamped, field-driven charge preferentially flows from the donor to the fluorinated acceptor, with selectivity reduced upon increasing intensity. With moving ions, the early-time spatial response remains qualitatively unchanged, despite a distinct, spatially asymmetric charge redistribution. In the strong-field regime, nuclear motion preserves the preference for field-driven charge accumulation on the fluorinated acceptor, although the process takes approximately twice the time as in the fixed-nuclei scenario. Mode-resolved kinetic-energy analysis reveals that, with increasing field strength, the laser-induced nuclear response shifts from selected bond stretchings to collective low-frequency modes. These results provide a benchmark for assessing the interplay between vibronic dynamics and strong-field coupling in donor/acceptor oligomers.

papers.title: Roadmap: Image reconstruction in emission tomography for the era of fast Monte Carlo simulation
papers.abstract: Quantitative image reconstruction in positron emission tomography and single photon emission computed tomography depends on how accurately the forward model describes photon emission, transport and detection. Monte Carlo simulation is the most complete model available, yet it is mostly used as an offline reference rather than inside the reconstruction. This roadmap asks what it would take to change that. The main obstacle is not only simulation time. Iterative reconstruction requires the expectation of the measured data and the gradient of the data fidelity, whereas Monte Carlo simulation produces noisy realisations of a complete acquisition. GPU implementations, variance reduction and learned surrogate models have made simulations much faster. At the same time, modern scanners acquire ever larger data sets with larger system models, and further gains in quantitative accuracy require more detailed physics. We discuss how fast Monte Carlo simulation can improve the modelling of the system response, scatter, positron range and the joint estimation of activity and attenuation, how noisy simulations can enter reconstruction algorithms, and which computing hardware makes this feasible. Monte Carlo simulation is most valuable where analytic models fail, and most practical solutions will combine both. The most immediate benefit of fast simulators is the validation and calibration of faster analytic models, together with more accurate, absolutely quantitative scatter estimates. Key open problems are the use of noisy simulations as expectations, in particular for sparse data, the computation of gradients and adjoints, the allocation of a limited simulation budget, and the use of scattered events as a source of information rather than a nuisance. Faster simulators are necessary but not sufficient, and progress requires simulators and reconstruction methods to be developed together.

papers.title: Control-Oriented Modeling of Heat Exchangers with Improved Low-Flow Dynamics
papers.abstract: Existing low-order models of heat exchangers can lose dynamic accuracy at low flow rates, when fluid residence times become significant. This paper proposes two control-oriented models that improve the low-flow performance. The first extends a finite-volume formulation with the first spatial temperature moment, whereas the second uses Chebyshev--Lobatto collocation. Both capture the coupled heat-transfer and transport dynamics and improve the performance when the system behavior is dominated by the inlet-temperature dynamics. At equal state dimension, comparisons with a high-order reference show more accurate delayed outlet-temperature responses while retaining steady-state accuracy.

papers.intro:
Heat exchangers are used in a multitude of applications, ranging from district heating networks and domestic heating [8] to industrial production [6] to automotive applications [3] to conditioning of process media in research and development [15]. The latter typically requires accurate temperature control to maintain prescribed thermal operating conditions [15]. Model-based control is promising for meeting these requirements [6], [12], [11], but it depends on the complexity and quality of the underlying model. Here, a dilemma arises: accurate models are often of high order—e.g. infinite-dimensional—[9], [4], whereas the low-order models are often inaccurate—especially under low-flow conditions—and/or do not permit physical interpretation [3], [12], [10]. To solve this dilemma, the present paper proposes two control-oriented, low-order models of heat exchangers that are more accurate even under low-flow conditions, thus providing a sound basis for model-based estimation and control.

To solve this dilemma, the present paper proposes two control-oriented, low-order models of heat exchangers that are more accurate even under low-flow conditions, thus providing a sound basis for model-based estimation and control.

An ideal control-oriented heat exchanger model describes the dynamics from the inlet to the outlet temperature on both sides, while explicitly accounting for the strong flow rate dependency of these dynamics. Distributed-parameter models, based on physical insight, satisfy this requirement, but their direct use in real-time algorithms is limited by their infinite-dimensional nature [4, 9] and conventional upwind discretization schemes—like the method of lines (MOL)—introduce numerical diffusion [7]. In [10], a distributed-parameter model was discretized using the finite-volume method, with a low number of cells, and the steady-state accuracy was improved by incorporating the stationary solution of the underlying PDE; thus, a low-order model with high steady-state accuracy was obtained. This so-called power-balance approximation was used for model-based control in [11].

The main problem with the power-balance (PB) approximation is that it relies on a small fluid residence time, hence it becomes inaccurate for low flow rates (low-load operation), and even shows unphysical behavior for rapid changes of the inlet temperatures—which may be the case if a 3-way valve is used to bypass the heat exchanger in low-load operation. It is shown in this paper that in the pure-transport case, i.e. no heat transfer, the single-volume power-balance approximation corresponds to a (1/1)\left(1/1\right)-Padé approximation—which shows a step-wise change to −1-1 at the output under a step-wise change of the input to +1+1, and thus a step-wise change of the outlet temperature in the wrong direction!

This paper proposes two finite-dimensional approaches for improving the approximation of convective transport without introducing explicit time-delay operators. The two approaches are similar to the power-balance approximation both in terms of complexity and steady-state accuracy, yet with improved low-flow performance. The first approach extends the power-balance approximation by retaining the first spatial temperature moment in addition to the mean temperature of each finite volume. This additional state captures the leading-order spatial asymmetry of the local temperature field and thereby improves the representation of convective transport when the fluid residence time is significant, yet without requiring a finer finite-volume discretization. The second approach uses Lagrange interpolation at Chebyshev–Lobatto (CL) nodes to approximate the spatial derivative through a differentation matrix acting on the vector of all nodal temperatures. The resulting approximation can achieve high spatial accuracy with comparatively few nodes.

papers.title: The Generalized Twin Image: Understanding Regularized Phase Retrieval
papers.abstract: Image priors can dramatically improve phase retrieval reconstruction, but their effectiveness strongly varies between imaging modalities. We introduce the generalized twin image, which extends the classical twin-image ambiguity from Fourier phase retrieval to any invertible sensing operator, to understand this effectiveness. The ambiguity extends to undersampled and oversampled measurements, remaining exact under undersampling and for oversampled coded Fourier measurements. We show that it provides a simple criterion to assess regularization effectiveness: the image prior should favor the ground truth over its generalized twin image. We propose the total-variation ratio as a simple measure of this preference, and derive closed-form estimates for structured random phase retrieval models. Experiments with a pretrained denoiser demonstrate that the ratio predicts regularized reconstruction performance across different sensing models.
papers.intro:
Phase retrieval is a nonlinear inverse problem that arises in a broad range of applications, including crystallography [1], holography [2] and ptychography [3], whenever one aims to reconstruct the underlying complex-valued signal from real-valued intensity measurements. Fourier phase retrieval (FPR) [4], in which the measurements are the magnitudes of the Fourier transform of the signal, is of central interest and lays the foundation for many other modalities. The reconstruction difficulty given a modality is closely related to its ambiguities, i.e., false solutions that generate the same measurements as the ground truth. Besides the global phase shift ambiguity inherent to phase retrieval, FPR has two extra ambiguities: translation and conjugate reflection, the latter also called the twin image [4, 5]. In consequence, FPR suffers from the well-known twin-image stagnation problem [6], which algorithms impose constraints such as nonnegativity, realness and bounded support [7] to mitigate. Uniqueness up to these ambiguities holds under practical conditions [4], but no known algorithm is guaranteed to reach the solution [5].

Structured random models for phase retrieval have been proposed to combine the efficiency of Fourier-based models and the robustness of random models [9]. They are a cascade of structured random layers, each of which consists of a Fourier transform and a random diagonal matrix. The same reconstruction quality as with dense random models can be achieved once there are two layers [9].

The same reconstruction quality as with dense random models can be achieved once there are two layers [9].

Image priors have greatly enhanced reconstruction quality in inverse problems [10]. In phase retrieval, including regularization for structured random models enables reconstruction with one layer, i.e., one random mask added to FPR, and with very few measurements, well below the weak recovery threshold [11, 12]. A central question remains how the effects of regularization depend on the sensing model, and whether they can be quantified.

In this paper, we extend the twin image of FPR to any invertible sensing operator with optional undersampling and oversampling, as the generalized twin image. It is an exact ambiguity with undersampling, and, for a Fourier transform and an optional random mask, also with oversampling by zero-padding. Feasibility of unregularized reconstruction given sufficient measurements is predicted by whether the generalized twin stays an exact ambiguity. For regularized reconstruction, image priors become more effective if the generalized twin varies more than the ground truth, as they favor low-variation signals. We propose the total-variation (TV) ratio to quantify this property, and derive closed-form estimates for structured random models of different depths. We numerically validate these estimates and perform regularized reconstruction with a pretrained denoiser at different model depths, showing that the TV ratio predicts reconstruction accuracy. The generalized twin provides a scheme to analyze the optimization landscape for other phase retrieval modalities.

papers.title: MoETok: Sparse Expert Routing for 1D Visual Tokenizers
papers.abstract: Modern visual tokenizers aim to preserve fine-grained visual details while learning high-level semantic representations for downstream generation and understanding. Query-based 1D visual tokenizers encode images into flexible latent sequences, yet how individual learnable queries gather and encode image information remains poorly understood. We reveal that these queries spontaneously develop complementary roles under semantic supervision: a small set of Content queries captures high-level semantic information, while a larger set of Detail queries preserves fine-grained visual details for reconstruction. To adapt token processing to these heterogeneous roles, we introduce MoETok, a 1D visual tokenizer that routes tokens through sparsely activated experts. Jointly optimized with reconstruction and semantic objectives, the router learns role-specialized processing paths adapted to each token's representation. Across model scales and token budgets, MoETok consistently improves reconstruction, semantic representation, and autoregressive generation over dense tokenizers under matched supervision and active computation. On ImageNet, it combines strong reconstruction and semantic representation with state-of-the-art class-conditional generation within the 1D tokenizer family. We further validate MoETok at scale in a unified autoregressive model jointly trained for understanding and generation with a next-token cross-entropy objective. The resulting model combines competitive visual understanding with state-of-the-art generation among unified discrete models, matching or surpassing diffusion-based models such as BAGEL and Qwen-Image on benchmarks including DPG-Bench (87.61), GenEval2 (40.04 GM), and WISE (0.49).

papers.title: CalibCause: A Quality-Gated, Interpretable and Calibrated Deep Learning Framework for Diabetic Retinopathy Grading
papers.abstract: Most deep learning systems for diabetic retinopathy (DR) grading are evaluated on a single data source, with limited evidence of cross-site generalisation, uncertainty calibration, and interpretability. We propose CalibCause, a quality-gated mixture-of-experts framework that combines per-expert visual explanations, label-free image-quality conditioning, knowledge distillation, and calibrated confidence with deferral. We evaluated the framework using 51,310 fundus images from EyePACS, DDR, and APTOS 2019, with IDRiD and DeepDRiD for external testing. Evaluation included pooled testing, leave-one-environment-out experiments, paired bootstrap confidence intervals, and local grade-threshold adaptation. On the pooled test split, the label-free distilled student achieved quadratic weighted kappa (QWK) of 0.863 and accuracy of 0.865 with 27.8 million parameters, 52% fewer than its teacher. Across held-out environments, the label-free model achieved mean QWK of 0.741 compared with 0.743 for a plain ConvNeXt-Tiny baseline, while adversarial invariance did not improve cross-site grading accuracy. Refitting grade thresholds using 200 labelled images increased held-out EyePACS QWK from 0.533 to 0.621 for the label-free model. After vector scaling, expected calibration error ranged from 0.025 to 0.036 across CalibCause variants, and deferring the least confident 20% of images increased student accuracy from 0.865 to 0.923 on the remaining images. These findings demonstrate that quality-aware grading, interpretable expert routing, model compression, and calibrated deferral can be integrated without sacrificing cross-site performance relative to a plain baseline, although reliable deployment still requires local validation and adaptation.

Image quality is also tied to disease. QGDR [5] describes this as quality–severity coupling: poorer images tend to belong to patients with more advanced disease. In their data the share of referable DR rose from 17.4% to 27.8% as image quality fell on EyeQ [6], and from 28.6% to 81.9% on DDR. A quality filter therefore discards the images most likely to come from patients who need referral. QGDR instead uses quality as a signal that conditions the grader, in line with earlier quality-aware work [7, 8].

papers.title: Do LLMs Know When They Are Wrong About Molecules? In-Context Property Prediction with Self-Reported Uncertainty
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are used in many domains, but molecular property prediction with them is still little explored. In this work we evaluate the capability of 7 frontier LLMs to predict molecular properties together with a self-reported uncertainty from in-context examples, and compare them with classical baselines trained on the same molecules. We use 4 datasets and screen each for contamination of the training data of the LLMs: three are clean, and the fourth, ESOL, is memorised by most of the models and serves as a comparison. On the clean datasets every LLM improves with the context, at 30 examples the most accurate one beats every baseline. The requested reasoning effort changes accuracy little. The self-reported uncertainty ranks the prediction errors weakly, with Spearman rank correlations of up to 0.46, about the level reached by the uncertainties of the baselines. Combining uncertainty and prediction, on lipophilicity the most certain half of the best LLM is the most accurate at small context sizes; on BACE and antiviral, and on lipophilicity at large context sizes, the best LLMs are on par with the best baseline. On the contaminated ESOL dataset the LLMs show no improvement with the context size, as expected for a memorised dataset, and their stated uncertainty is smaller on the molecules whose value they recall.

Uncertainty matters specifically in two scenarios. The first is active learning, where an uncertainty selects the samples to label. Ideally, the samples with the highest prediction error should be taken, but without label, the prediction error is unknown. The second is selective prediction [14], the use of predictions without measuring them: the most certain predictions are kept, and the error of the kept fraction measures accuracy and ranking together. For both purposes, the uncertainty must rank the actual prediction errors well; whether the magnitude of the stated uncertainty also matches the observed errors, its calibration [32], is a separate property that this study does not assess. For classical molecular models ranking and calibration have been compared for ensembles, sampling and evidential methods [24, 51], and stated confidences of language models have been found over-confident on text and on chemistry questions [60, 41]. An uncertainty benchmark needs data the models cannot recall, because a recalled value is predicted with almost no error and nothing requires the stated uncertainty to register that it was recalled rather than predicted [6, 7].

We evaluate 7 frontier language models on 4 molecular regression datasets: lipophilicity, BACE-1 inhibition, inhibition of the SARS-CoV-2 main protease from a challenge of 2025, and ESOL. The test molecules of the first three occur in none of seven open pre-training corpora, and a zero-shot screen finds only insignificant retrieval of their values by any panel model, whereas ESOL is retrieved by most and serves as the control. Each model predicts 150 test molecules per dataset with a stated standard deviation from nested contexts of 30 to 1,000 training molecules, in three calls per molecule and, at the small context sizes, in three independent context draws; eight classical methods are trained on exactly the same molecules, and six of the models are also run along a ladder of reasoning efforts. We analyze how accurate the models are over context sizes and reasoning levels, which uncertainty ranks the prediction errors best, as needed for active learning, how accurate the most certain predictions are, as needed for selective prediction, and, with the contaminated ESOL dataset as the comparison, how a memorised dataset behaves on the same measures.

papers.title: A Temporal Cellular Sheaf Framework for Multi-Agent Systems with Switching Communication Topologies
papers.abstract: Cellular sheaves serve as a natural modeling framework for encoding heterogeneity in the state and interaction spaces of multi-agent systems. This work examines switching communication graphs with the use of temporal cellular sheaves, which we construct to represent heterogeneous agent state spaces, the maps that relate them, and their respective communication constraints. We then develop sufficient conditions under which a multi-agent system defined on a temporal cellular sheaf can solve the target tracking problem by generalizing the existing concept of joint connectivity. Using a Lyapunov-based stability analysis, we demonstrate that the target tracking error of the network converges to a neighborhood of the origin.

papers.intro:
A central objective in the study of multi-agent systems (MASs) is the design of decentralized or distributed control laws which ensure coordination and system stability, provided the communication topology meets certain constraints [1, 2, 3]. Heterogeneity is commonly represented in these systems through nonidentical agent dynamics, accounting for agents operating in different domains. Agents that operate in different state spaces or contain different sensing modalities offer another form of heterogeneity. Networks of this form are commonly constructed via matrix-weighted approaches which equip graph interactions (edges) with matrix-valued weights, representing varied communication or sensing relationships [4, 5, 6, 7, 8].

Standard graph-based models of MASs are limited in that they do not provide a framework which simultaneously captures heterogeneity in agent dynamics, local-to-global consistency constraints, and compositional structure. Moreover, extending such models to time-varying settings introduces additional difficulties, since both the communication topology and coordination constraints may evolve over time. Cellular sheaves provide a formalism for addressing these challenges [9].

Using a cellular sheaf framework, a communication network can be represented by a graph, and vector spaces can be assigned to both nodes (agents) and edges (interactions). Linear maps encode sensing, communication, or compatibility constraints between agents, allowing users to model both individual and joint state spaces in a unified structure. Matrix-weighted graphs and bearing-based approaches can be recovered as a particular subclass of these representations (e.g., [4, 5, 10, 11]). Cellular sheaves have emerged as a natural modeling framework across a diverse range of applications, including the diffusion of information in social networks [12, 13], neural network inference and training [14], multi-agent coordination [15], leader-following consensus [16], the modeling of hybrid dynamical systems [17], and asynchronous distributed optimization [18]. Cellular sheaves generalize the classical graph Laplacian to accommodate for heterogeneous agent state spaces and linear edge-based restriction maps [16, 15]. In particular, cellular sheaves connect multi-agent coordination problems with tools from computational algebraic topology [19].

Sheaf Laplacians and cohomology offer mechanisms to analyze information propagation and global coordination in distributed systems. For instance, [16] formulates heterogeneous multi-agent coordination over a fixed communication network as a harmonic extension problem, where target states serve as boundary data. The resulting decentralized control law yields exponential convergence to a neighborhood of the unique sheaf-consistent global state. Despite these advances, existing cellular sheaf-based approaches to multi-agent coordination primarily assume a fixed communication topology [12, 16]. In practice, the communication topology of a MAS may vary over time due to sensing constraints, environmental interference, or hardware failure. papers.title: Partial Interval Multicover Is NP-Complete Even for Unit Intervals
papers.abstract:
For a interval family $\calI$, a point set $X\subseteq\mathbb R$, demands $d:X\to\Z_{\ge0}$, and $p\in\Z_{\ge0}$, partial interval multicover asks for a subfamily $S\subseteq\calI$ minimizing $|S|$ subject to $$
  |\{x\in X:\dep_S(x)\ge d(x)\}|\ge p,
  \qquad \dep_S(x)=|\{I\in S:x\in I\}|. $$ We prove that the unweighted decision problem is NP-complete even for unit intervals, answering the open question in~\cite{Li2026}.

We reduce from independent set on cubic planar graphs. In Subsection 2.1, we represent vertex choices by bits and replace graph edges by grid paths. For any fixed choice of the original bits, choosing the new bits optimally adds the same constant to the original reward. Subsection 2.2 represents each grid bit by selected positions in a sequence. A block of consecutive positions earns a reward when it contains a specified number of selected positions. Large rewards ensure that every optimal selection of BB positions represents the grid bits correctly; this part of the reward is the same for every choice of the grid bits. Subsection 2.3 represents positions by equal-length intervals and blocks by points, so that the selected count in each block equals the coverage depth at its point. Subsection 2.4 turns the exact-count rewards into coverage demands by adding a linear term. Equal interval lengths ensure that this term contributes the same total whenever exactly BB intervals are selected, so it does not change which selection is best. Finally, Subsection 2.5 proves that the two decision instances have the same answer and that the construction has polynomial size.

papers.title: From WSIs to Bulk, Spatial and Single-Cell Transcriptomics via Multi-Scale Graph Neural Networks
papers.abstract: Understanding the spatial distribution of gene expression is key to studying complex diseases like cancer. While Spatial Transcriptomics (ST) and Single-Cell Transcriptomics (scT) provide high-resolution insights, they remain expensive and scarce. In contrast, standard histopathology Whole-Slide Images (WSIs) paired with bulk RNA sequencing are widely available. This work introduces a Multi-Scale Graph Neural Network (GNN) capable of simultaneously predicting bulk, spatial, and single-cell transcriptomics directly from WSIs. By extracting morphological features using a Pathology Foundation Model (PFM) (UNI2-h) and constructing spatial graphs at both patch and cell levels, the model learns the hierarchical relationships within the tissue. The network is trained on a combined dataset of The Cancer Genome Atlas Program (TCGA), Visium, and Xenium samples across lung, kidney, and breast tissues. A hybrid training strategy is employed, leveraging direct supervision alongside weakly supervised consistency losses to ensure predictions align across biological scales. Results show the model accurately predicts gene expression at the slide level and moderately at the patch level (strongest on Xenium), and achieves moderate correlation at the challenging single-cell level. Furthermore, downstream tasks explore the clinical relevance of these predictions, demonstrating their utility in survival analysis, spatial hazard mapping, and tumor classification via molecular signatures.

papers.intro:
Understanding genes is key to grasping how our body works and evolves, as well as making sense of complex diseases such as cancer. That is why ST and scT may provide critical insights for understanding and effectively treating tumors. The rapid evolution of ST and scT has transformed our understanding of tissue biology by enabling the systematic measurement of expression levels for all or most genes throughout tissue space [1]. Despite their revolutionary potential, these methods remain constrained by high experimental costs (thousands of dollars per slide), and are not yet routine in most hospitals. On the other hand, histopathology is already a common practice in cancer diagnosis, producing hematoxylin and eosin-stained WSIs. WSIs are high-resolution digital representations of histopathology slides that capture the complete morphological context of the tissue. They preserve cellular structures, tissue architecture and spatial organization of cells.

Although ST provides a good understanding of the spatial distribution of genes, it does not offer the finest granularity available. In one patch there are often dozens to hundreds of cells, so the expression of each spot is actually the mixture of the gene expressions of each cell within each patch. scT achieves the finest granularity available, providing the gene expression for each detected cell in a WSI. Additionally, WSIs are often used as a conclusive diagnostic tool because many diseases, including cancer, are characterized by abnormal spatial organization within tissues [2]. By mapping mRNA within tissues, we improve our ability to visualize and interpret biological processes, since abnormal mRNA expression is frequently associated with human tumor initiation, development, progression and metastasis [3].

The relationship between tissue morphology and gene expression arises from the fact that tissue architecture and histological appearance are a direct manifestation of underlying genes at play. Differences in cell type, microenvironmental context and the presence of a tumor can result in characteristic morphological signatures. These morphological features can share a high amount of information with gene expression [4]. Therefore, using WSIs to predict ST and scT represents the next logical step, that not only assists doctors in diagnosing tumor slides but also enables a wide range of downstream tasks such as biomarker discovery and survival prediction.

ST and scT have advanced rapidly in both experimental and computational methods, yet there remains a critical limitation in accurately predicting transcriptomic profiles. Moreover, current deep learning models can infer partial gene expression patterns from histopathology slides. However, their predictions often show limited gene coverage, weak generalization across different tissues, and low accuracy in reconstructing the full transcriptome. While the acquisition of spatial data is expensive and time-consuming, bulk gene expression data, which provides the average gene expression across the whole tissue, is far more accessible and abundant. However, the translation from bulk-level to spatial gene expression profiles remains under-explored.

To bridge this gap, this work leverages three types of data: (1) WSIs paired with bulk gene expression; (2) WSIs paired with ST; and (3) WSIs paired with scT. WSIs are typically divided into smaller, fixed-size patches to enable efficient processing by deep learning models. ST requires that patches align with the spots where mRNA was sequenced (arranged across the WSI in a predefined grid pattern to enable spatially resolved transcriptomic profiling). In addition, in cases where scT data is available, each detected cell has an associated gene expression profile, although these profiles can be very sparse, since each cell may have counts for only a few of the genes in the panel. On the other hand, if only bulk gene expression is available, the spatial information is lost and the gene expression corresponds to the mixture of the whole tissue. This poses a challenge, as the bulk gene expression does not correspond exactly to the WSI and the spatial relationship between the WSI and the genomic data is unknown [5]. Despite this, the bulk gene expression can be reasonably approximated as representative of the average gene expression across the WSI, given that the WSI and the sampled tissue originate from the same primary tumor.

Most existing models that have the capability of predicting at the single-cell level employ the same training strategy: treating each spot as a bag of cells and using Multiple Instance Learning (MIL) to predict the spot’s gene expression. This way, the model learns how the aggregation of the cell’s gene expression should look like through weakly supervised learning. This strategy was employed in a state of the art model, DeepSpot2Cell [10], which leverages a PFM and spatial multi-level context to predict scT using spot-level supervision. papers.title: First Light with the Dark100 Array of PANOSETI Telescopes at Palomar Observatory
papers.abstract: Dark100 is the first phase of an extensive array of Panoramic SETI (PANOSETI) telescopes at Palomar Observatory, California. PANOSETI telescopes are small, 0.5-m Fresnel lens telescopes instrumented with 1024-pixel silicon photomultiplier (SiPM) cameras. The telescopes were originally designed to search for ultra-fast optical transients, but they also function as cost-effective imaging atmospheric Cherenkov telescopes (IACTs). Dark100 will use seven of these widely separated IACTs to map the ultra-high-energy (UHE) gamma-ray sources on the Galactic Plane at high resolution. Dark100 will also leverage the IACT technique to search for evidence of ultra-heavy dark matter in a mass range that extends beyond 100 TeV. Deployment of the first four telescopes and enclosures was completed in December 2025, and commissioning of the next three is scheduled to finish by the end of 2026. The array has so far collected more than 100 hours of 3-telescope data on sources including the Crab Nebula and Markarian 421. Here we present the current status of Dark100.

papers.intro:
In recent years, the Large High Altitude Air Shower Observatory (LHAASO) has detected dozens of gamma-ray sources at ultra-high energies (UHE; E>100E>100 TeV), many with no sign of a spectral cutoff [4]. Gamma rays at these energies require parent particles with energies of order 1 PeV, for which candidate sources have been dubbed "PeVatrons." However, the angular resolution of particle detector arrays like LHAASO is limited, and many UHE sources are extended or have multiple plausible counterparts, so the origin of the emission often remains unclear. Gamma-ray data are especially critical for the handful of objects that are not detected at any other frequencies.

Gamma rays at these energies require parent particles with energies of order 1 PeV, for which candidate sources have been dubbed "PeVatrons." However, the angular resolution of particle detector arrays like LHAASO is limited, and many UHE sources are extended or have multiple plausible counterparts, so the origin of the emission often remains unclear. Gamma-ray data are especially critical for the handful of objects that are not detected at any other frequencies.

Imaging atmospheric Cherenkov telescopes (IACTs) offer much finer angular resolution, but UHE observations pose two challenges for them. First, the gamma-ray flux falls steeply with energy, so large effective areas and long exposures are required. Second, UHE air showers are so extended that their images are often truncated by the edge of the camera’s field of view (FoV), or they land far outside a compact array where reconstruction becomes difficult. Dark100 is a new array of IACTs that tackles both of these challenges by using cost-effective telescopes from the Panoramic SETI (PANOSETI) experiment.

The name "Dark100" refers to another goal of the array: the search for ultra-heavy dark matter (particle masses above 100 TeV). For this purpose, Dark100 will use the same gamma-ray detection method, with photons as a tracer for potential dark matter interactions.

papers.title: PersonaChatBench: Evaluating Chat Assistants with Diverse Simulated Users
papers.abstract: Conversational assistants are expected to help people with diverse backgrounds, preferences, and communication styles. Yet evaluations centered on a single cooperative user provide limited insight into how reliably an assistant serves users with different personas. We introduce PersonaChatBench, a framework for evaluating task competence and responsiveness to diverse user needs. PersonaChatBench pairs the same underlying task with multiple simulated users, each guided by a private persona card that specifies distinct needs, preferences, and interaction behaviors. By holding the task fixed while varying the user, the framework examines how assistant performance changes across user conditions. We evaluate 20 language models across six domains, separately assessing native task outcomes, fulfillment of expressed persona needs, and simulator fidelity. Our results show that task performance and need fulfillment vary across personas and domains. Strong task performance does not necessarily translate into satisfying individual needs, and models' relative strengths in meeting those needs are not consistent across domains. PersonaChatBench makes these differences measurable, revealing gaps obscured by aggregate scores and helping identify which users an assistant serves well and where adaptation is needed. It provides a basis for evaluating consistency across users and guiding the development of assistants that better accommodate diverse needs in everyday applications.

People who bring the same request to a conversational assistant may need different kinds of help. A patient unfamiliar with medical terminology may need accessible explanations, whereas an informed patient may want the reasoning behind each question. A traveler may prefer detailed comparisons, a clear recommendation, or reassurance before making a decision. These differences affect what users disclose, how they respond, and what constitutes a satisfactory outcome. Evaluating an assistant therefore requires understanding both whether it accomplishes the task and how effectively it serves the person participating in the conversation.

papers.title: Magnetic Johnson noise from arbitrarily shaped conductors: experimental validation of the fluctuation-dissipation finite-element method
papers.abstract: Magnetic Johnson noise--magnetic noise caused by thermal current fluctuations in conducting materials--can interfere with measurements and limit their sensitivity. As the sensitivity of experiments increases, it becomes increasingly important to accurately estimate the magnetic Johnson noise from experimental components with complex shapes during both the design and analysis phases. A particularly powerful approach is to combine the fluctuation-dissipation theorem with finite-element calculations. This versatile approach can be used to calculate the magnetic Johnson noise from conductors of arbitrary geometry for a wide range of frequencies and for magnetic field detectors with general geometries, such as a finite-sized loop or a gradiometer. Using a SQUID gradiometer array, we measured the magnetic Johnson noise from conductors with complex geometries and compared the results with calculations performed using this method. The calculations reproduce both the measured noise amplitude and its frequency dependence, providing an experimental validation of this method. We also performed a detailed analysis of how the geometry and material parameters affect the frequency dependence of magnetic Johnson noise.

Thermal current fluctuations in conducting materials generate fluctuating magnetic fields that can limit the sensitivity of precision measurements. This magnetic Johnson noise has been investigated in a variety of experimental settings, including biomagnetic measurements based on superconducting quantum interference device (SQUID) sensors,[32, 20] applications involving trapped atoms,[10] searches for permanent electric dipole moments (EDMs) of atoms and neutrons,[17, 19, 18, 6, 7] and high-frequency magnetic measurements using conductive radio-frequency shields.[27]

Estimates of magnetic Johnson noise are typically performed using one of two methods: the direct method or the reciprocal method. In the direct method, the fluctuating current density is given by the conductivity of the material through the Johnson-Nyquist theorem,[12, 22] and the resulting fluctuating magnetic field is calculated either by solving Maxwell’s equations[32, 20] or by applying the Biot-Savart law.[17, 26, 24] The reciprocal method, on the other hand, makes use of the fluctuation-dissipation (F-D) theorem,[8, 16] of which the Johnson-Nyquist theorem is a special case. With this method, the magnetic Johnson noise (fluctuation) is determined from the power dissipated in the conductor body (dissipation) when it is driven by an oscillating magnetic field.

papers.title: Hydrodynamic regimes of the edge-tone in a simplified recorder mouthpiece
papers.abstract: The acoustic mechanism of flue instruments originates in the interaction of an air jet with a sharp edge, the labium. Previous studies have examined isolated edge-tones or full instruments in which acoustic resonance obscures the underlying hydrodynamics, and a systematic understanding of how geometric parameters govern jet stability is lacking. We present a large-scale parametric study of the jet-labium interaction in a simplified recorder mouthpiece without a resonator, using more than 200 two-dimensional direct numerical simulations with an immersed boundary method. We vary the mouth distance, the labium angle, the vertical offset of the labium, and the Reynolds number (Re), and characterize the dynamics through spectra of the transverse force on the labium. The baseline configuration oscillates as a predominantly periodic Stage I edge-tone with Strouhal number St ~ 0.07, nearly constant for Re >= 330 and for all labium angles at the baseline mouth distance, so the frequency is set by the geometry rather than by viscosity. The mouth distance has the strongest influence: it is the only parameter that introduces a second oscillation stage, and the Stage I frequency is inversely proportional to it. The second stage is weakly present at five and six windway heights, established from six and a half, and dominant from eight, where it strongly modulates the amplitude. The vertical offset mainly affects the strength of the oscillation, and the labium angle does not change the instability mechanism. A baseline configuration is identified for future aeroacoustic coupling studies.

papers.intro:
The acoustic mechanism of flue instruments has long remained a challenging problem in musical acoustics [1], and despite decades of investigation, many aspects of the underlying flow physics are still not fully understood. The sound in these instruments originates from an aerodynamic process in which a thin air jet emerging from a narrow windway interacts with a sharp edge known as the labium [2]. The oscillatory deflection of this jet produces pressure fluctuations that couple with the resonant air column to sustain tonal sound production. Because the stability of the oscillation and the characteristics of the emitted sound depend strongly on the jet behavior near the mouth, understanding the fluid dynamics of this region in isolation from the downstream resonator is essential. This is the aim of the present study.

The fundamental aerodynamic configuration underlying sound generation in flue instruments is the edge-tone : a planar free jet impinging on a wedge-shaped edge that, under certain conditions, develops self-sustained oscillations without the presence of any resonating cavity. It belongs to the wider class of self-sustained oscillations of impinging free shear layers [3]. This configuration has been studied for nearly two centuries, since Sondhauss first noted in 1854 [4] that audible tones could be produced by blowing a jet against an edge without a resonating column. The edge-tone represents the canonical aeroacoustic building block of flue instrument acoustics, and a thorough understanding of its behavior is a prerequisite for understanding the more complex dynamics of complete instruments.

The first systematic experimental investigations of the edge-tone established its most characteristic features. Brown [5] conducted careful quantitative experiments on a jet issuing from a narrow slit and impinging on a wedge, documenting four distinct oscillation stages11 1 The phenomenon described by Brown and many other subsequent studies as “stages” is in some recent publications referred to as “modes,” or “hydrodynamic modes.” In this work we choose to keep the term “stages.”, the hysteresis between them, and the coexistence of multiple frequencies. He found that the oscillation frequency varies systematically with jet velocity and edge-to-nozzle distance, and proposed a semi-empirical formula capturing these dependencies. It was also noted that the whole edge-tone phenomenon occurs within the sound-sensitive range of the jet, and that at low speeds the feedback is predominantly hydrodynamic while acoustic effects become significant at higher speeds [6]. Powell [7] later related sound production to the unsteady motion of vortices within the jet, emphasizing vortex shedding as a primary driver of self-sustained oscillations, attributed the sound to the dipole associated with the fluctuating force on the edge, formulated a gain criterion for the oscillation, and developed a feedback-loop model in which a dipole sound source at the edge re-excites the jet at the nozzle exit.

Nyborg [10] presented a dynamic theory that described the shape of the oscillating jet centerline and predicted frequency ratios between stages. Crighton [11] later derived a linear theory for the frequencies of the operating stages of the jet edge-tone feedback cycle, and Kaykayoglu and Rockwell [12] measured the instantaneous pressure fields during unstable jet–edge interaction.
