More recently, Vaik, Varga and Paál [13, 14] carried out a detailed parametric study of the edge-tone by both computational and experimental means, covering a wide range of Reynolds numbers and dimensionless nozzle-to-edge distances for both top-hat and parabolic exit velocity profiles. Their work confirmed the exponent of 11 in the frequency scaling law, clarified the Reynolds number dependence of each oscillation stage, and showed that the convection velocity of the jet disturbance is not constant between the nozzle and the edge, contradicting a common assumption in theoretical models [9]. They also demonstrated that two-dimensional simulations of the incompressible Navier–Stokes equations reliably reproduce experimental results, validating the use of this framework for systematic parametric studies. These findings built upon earlier incompressible simulations by Paál and Vaik [15], who reproduced three distinct oscillation stages numerically for the first time and documented the dependence of stage selection on Reynolds number and nozzle-to-edge distance. The rich nonlinear dynamics associated with stage transitions, including spontaneous jumps between stages at fixed flow conditions and the simultaneous coexistence of multiple stages, were further characterized by Vaik and Paál [16] through combined experimental and numerical investigations. Bamberger et al. [17] similarly combined experiment and two-dimensional numerical simulation for a parabolic edge-tone configuration, verifying the linear frequency-distance scaling law and achieving agreement between experimental and computational Strouhal numbers within 13–15%. Nagy, Szabó and Paál [18] later proposed a feedback model for the edge-tone using linear adjoint stability theory, calculating the open-loop gain of the oscillation without empirical constants and showing that a purely hydrodynamic potential vortex at the edge tip is a physically consistent and energetically sufficient feedback agent at low Mach numbers.

papers.title: Meshless Latent Dynamics Models for Model Order Reduction of time-dependent Partial Differential Equations
papers.abstract:
Latent dynamics learning has emerged as a prominent approach for Model Order Reduction (MOR) of time-dependent, parameterized Partial Differential Equations (PDEs). Traditional autoencoder-based approaches are intrinsically tied to fixed spatial discretizations during both training and inference, motivating the development of meshless methodologies. In this context, conditioning provides a natural mechanism for representing temporal evolution through spatially continuous functions, enabling mesh-agnostic Latent Dynamics Models (LDMs).
  In this work, we introduce a unified mathematical framework for mesh-agnostic LDMs based on conditioning in Neural Fields (NeFs). Leveraging a taxonomy of conditioning mechanisms (weak, strong, and pure), we formulate meshless LDMs as NeFs conditioned on a latent state. We establish a Universal Approximation Theorem (UAT) for this class of models and analyze their stability by deriving Lipschitz bounds for different conditioning mechanisms. Our analysis reveals an expressivity--stability trade-off, providing insight into why more expressive conditioning, despite its higher representational capacity, can potentially degrade performance during temporal extrapolation. Finally, we provide a comprehensive comparison of meshless and mesh-based architectures in the continuous limit of the spatial discretization, showing that meshless models guarantee grid-independent Lipschitz bounds, unlike mesh-based counterparts.
  Our experiments across Burgers' equation, Navier--Stokes flow past a cylinder, and linear advection show that meshless LDMs can achieve predictive accuracy comparable to or better than their mesh-based counterparts while using only 2% of the trainable parameters and exhibiting nearly constant error across spatial discretizations.

papers.intro:
The numerical approximation of Partial Differential Equations (PDEs) underpins a wide range of applications, including engineering [58], medicine [31], and computational physics [75]. Nevertheless, a detailed investigation of parameterized systems using full-order models, e.g. Finite Element (FE) and Finite Volume (FV) methods [79], is often infeasible due to the prohibitive computational burden of repeated simulations, which is further exacerbated for time-dependent problems [70]. Model Order Reduction (MOR) addresses this limitation by designing surrogate models that enable reliable many-query and real-time system investigation at a reduced computational cost [7, 77].

Nevertheless, a detailed investigation of parameterized systems using full-order models, e.g. Finite Element (FE) and Finite Volume (FV) methods [79], is often infeasible due to the prohibitive computational burden of repeated simulations, which is further exacerbated for time-dependent problems [70]. Model Order Reduction (MOR) addresses this limitation by designing surrogate models that enable reliable many-query and real-time system investigation at a reduced computational cost [7, 77].

While classical linear strategies such as the Reduced Basis (RB) approach [45, 84] are well-established and enable efficient online evaluation with certified error bounds, they frequently display significant limitations when applied to complex systems characterized by a slow-decaying Kolmogorov nn-width [67]. Recent advances in deep learning have considerably broadened the scope of MOR by replacing the linear ansatz with nonlinear latent representations learned directly from data, frequently using Autoencoders (AEs) [55, 34, 73]. In the setting of time-dependent systems, a prominent instance of this paradigm is latent dynamics modeling [91, 62], which aims at capturing the system’s temporal evolution within a low-dimensional latent space, while a separate mapping reconstructs the corresponding high-dimensional physical state. This decoupling substantially reduces the computational complexity of time integration in Latent Dynamics Models (LDMs) by exploiting the intrinsic low-dimensional structure of the solution manifold [59]. Importantly, the empirical success of these reduced architectures is now increasingly supported by rigorous theoretical guarantees, such as Universal Approximation Theorems (UATs) [30, 96].

This limits their applicability across varying spatial resolutions and prevents evaluating the solution at arbitrary, off-grid locations. Furthermore, it ties the model’s parameter count to the specific discretization employed during training and evaluation. As a result, changing the spatial resolution may require the use of interpolation, which introduces numerical errors, or training a new model, which incurs additional computational costs. A promising alternative is provided by Neural Fields (NeFs), which represent physical fields as continuous functions of the spatial coordinates [103]. By directly learning maps from these low-dimensional coordinates to physical quantities, NeFs naturally yield resolution-independent representations, decoupled from the underlying (typically high-dimensional) discretization of the domain [17]. However, time-dependent or parameterized systems require the field representation to account for changes in the system state without retraining. To address this, the temporal evolution captured in the latent space is directly incorporated into the continuous field through conditioning, a procedure by which the latent variables modulate the network’s weights and biases. The resulting Conditional Neural Fields (CNeFs) allow a single architecture to describe an entire family of spatial fields corresponding to different physical parameters and times. Building upon this idea, recent methodologies combine low-dimensional latent dynamics with meshless decoders [87, 105, 82], resulting in mesh-agnostic architectures for parameterized, time-dependent systems.

Nonetheless, the integration of CNeFs into dynamics modeling currently lacks a unified theoretical framework, leaving the design of latent conditioning mechanisms largely empirical. This raises fundamental questions regarding the trade-offs among different conditioning schemes, particularly with respect to error accumulation over time. In this work, we address these gaps by introducing a unified framework for meshless LDMs based on CNeFs, in which the decoder’s dependence on the latent variables is interpreted as a conditioning mechanism. Within this framework, we show that the conditioning strategy determines the sensitivity of the decoded solution to latent perturbations, revealing an expressivity–stability trade-off: highly expressive decoders can amplify temporal integration errors, whereas weak conditioning yields tighter bounds on this amplification. We further establish a UAT for weakly conditioned meshless LDMs (which naturally extends to stronger forms of conditioning), showing that weak conditioning retains sufficient expressivity while offering greater robustness to latent perturbations. Moreover, we compare meshless and mesh-based LDMs by investigating their Lipschitz constants in the continuous limit of mesh refinement, further quantifying how these bounds influence the magnitude of the learned latent trajectories. Finally, we numerically validate our theoretical findings on three computational mechanics benchmarks: the Burgers’ equation, the Navier–Stokes equations, and a linear advection problem.

papers.title: Backpropagation-free Deep Learning for Time-Series Classification
papers.abstract: Deep neural networks for time series classification (TSC) are trained almost exclusively by error backpropagation, which imposes update locking and the weight-transport problem. Backpropagation-free learning rules such as Direct Feedback Alignment (DFA), Direct Random Target Projection (DRTP), and the diffusion-inspired NoProp relax these constraints but have been evaluated almost exclusively on 2D image benchmarks. We adapt these three learners to univariate TSC with 1D convolutional architectures and present the first systematic study of them across 112 datasets from the UCR time series archive, with one hyperparameter-optimized configuration per method. The optimized learners reach mean F1 scores of 0.76 to 0.79, below ROCKET (0.83) and InceptionTime (0.84). We propose an analysis framework that relates the per-dataset gap to InceptionTime to dataset properties and tests convolutional feature learning by replacing the flatten readout with global average pooling, measured as a difference-in-differences (DD) against a backpropagation control on the identical architecture. Intra-class temporal variability is the dataset property most consistently associated with the gap for all three learners (partial Spearman $\rho$ from $0.28$ to $0.40$). Pooling harms DFA and DRTP more than backpropagation (DD $-0.025$ and $-0.055$), consistent with near-random convolutional features, whereas NoProp tolerates pooling as backpropagation does (DD $+0.013$). Relative to backpropagation on the same architectures, DRTP reduces training floating-point operations (FLOPs) by 33% and trains faster only on series longer than about 700 time steps, DFA yields no computational reduction, and NoProp reduces peak memory by 38% at the cost of 48% longer training.

papers.intro:
Time series classification (TSC) is a foundational machine learning task, extensively studied and benchmarked [1]. Historically, state-of-the-art accuracy has been achieved by non-neural ensembles such as HIVE-COTE 2.0 [2]. However, achieving this performance requires significant computational complexity, often making it impractical since training takes hundreds of hours. Consequently, deep learning models, particularly Fully Convolutional Networks (FCN) [3] and InceptionTime [4], have become the dominant paradigm. These neural methods are highly competitive in accuracy while training orders of magnitude faster, primarily because they learn powerful, task-specific feature representations through end-to-end training.

Historically, state-of-the-art accuracy has been achieved by non-neural ensembles such as HIVE-COTE 2.0 [2]. However, achieving this performance requires significant computational complexity, often making it impractical since training takes hundreds of hours. Consequently, deep learning models, particularly Fully Convolutional Networks (FCN) [3] and InceptionTime [4], have become the dominant paradigm. These neural methods are highly competitive in accuracy while training orders of magnitude faster, primarily because they learn powerful, task-specific feature representations through end-to-end training.

Despite their representational power, deep neural networks rely heavily on error backpropagation (BP) to learn these features. Backpropagation enforces strict constraints as it requires storing intermediate activations for the backward pass and mandates sequential layer-by-layer weight updates. This creates two fundamental limitations: update locking, which renders the learning process inherently sequential and highly memory-intensive, and the weight transport problem, which requires physically and biologically implausible symmetric forward-backward weight matrices [5].

Backpropagation enforces strict constraints as it requires storing intermediate activations for the backward pass and mandates sequential layer-by-layer weight updates. This creates two fundamental limitations: update locking, which renders the learning process inherently sequential and highly memory-intensive, and the weight transport problem, which requires physically and biologically implausible symmetric forward-backward weight matrices [5].

To bypass these computational overheads, non-neural methods like ROCKET [6] achieve high computational efficiency by applying a large number of entirely fixed, random convolutional kernels. However, this presents a fundamental trade-off: fixed random features sacrifice the ability to adapt representations to specific datasets or downstream tasks. To bridge this gap, backpropagation-free (BP-free) neural methods, such as Direct Feedback Alignment (DFA) [7], Direct Random Target Projection (DRTP) [5], and the diffusion-inspired NoProp [8], have been proposed. These methods decouple layer-wise dependencies, eliminating the need for sequential backward propagation while retaining the ability to learn. However, these methods have been primarily evaluated on 2D image classification benchmarks, such as MNIST and CIFAR-10 [8, 5]. Their effectiveness, stability, and computational dynamics on 1D time-series data remain entirely unexplored.

These methods decouple layer-wise dependencies, eliminating the need for sequential backward propagation while retaining the ability to learn. However, these methods have been primarily evaluated on 2D image classification benchmarks, such as MNIST and CIFAR-10 [8, 5]. Their effectiveness, stability, and computational dynamics on 1D time-series data remain entirely unexplored.

In this paper, we ask whether any of these learners capture task-specific temporal features on 1D data, or whether they instead rely on fixed random features as ROCKET does. We adapt three BP-free paradigms, DFA, DRTP, and NoProp, to univariate sequences and evaluate them against standard backpropagation across 112 datasets from the UCR archive, each with per-method hyperparameter optimization. To test for feature learning directly, we intervene on the readout, replacing the position-sensitive flatten with global average pooling and measuring a difference-in-differences against a backpropagation control on the identical architecture, which cancels the effects of architecture and dataset difficulty. Our findings separate the three methods into two regimes. DFA and DRTP depend more than backpropagation on the flatten readout, whereas NoProp tolerates pooling as backpropagation does.

papers.title: Nexus-VLA: Bridging Human and Robot Experiences via a Shared Hierarchical Semantic Latent Space
papers.abstract: Large-scale egocentric human videos provide rich and scalable manipulation experience for robot policy learning, yet substantial embodiment gaps in visual appearance, kinematic structure, and action spaces hinder effective knowledge transfer. Existing methods often decouple cross-embodiment knowledge alignment from robot policy learning, making it difficult for human manipulation knowledge to directly and fully contribute to robot action learning. To address this issue, we propose Nexus-VLA, a hybrid policy learning framework that enables cross-embodiment knowledge transfer through end-to-end human-robot joint training, allowing human manipulation experience to directly contribute to robot policy learning. We first introduce a hierarchical cross-embodiment semantic alignment paradigm that progressively establishes shared manipulation semantics from task intent to fine-grained interactions, enabling more complete use of the manipulation knowledge contained in human videos. Building on this hierarchy, we design a shared manipulation latent representation that jointly encodes multi-level shared knowledge into an internal representation directly used for continuous action generation, improving policy learning efficiency while effectively leveraging human knowledge. Across RoboCasa-GR1, OOD settings, and real-world robot experiments, Nexus-VLA achieves an 80.5% task success rate on RoboCasa-GR1 and demonstrates strong advantages in human-data utilization, learning efficiency, and cross-scenario generalization.

Despite these differences, humans and robots share similar manipulation semantics and interaction structures when performing the same task. Therefore, a central challenge in learning robot policies from human videos is to identify such shared representations and transform them into a unified representation that effectively supports robot action generation.

papers.title: Dark Halos, Intermediate-Mass BH and Nuclear Stellar Clusters in Dwarf Spheroidals
papers.abstract: We exploit the halo densities of three dwarf spheroidals recently obtained to investigate their dark matter distribution. We address the well-known DM halo core-cusp issue by finding that the NFW $\Lambda$CDM halo profile is in strong disagreement with these inferred halo densities, which instead result very well-reproduced by the Burkert halo cored profile with the central density $\rho_0$ and the core radius $r_0$. These structural parameters result connected among themselves and with the length scale of the stellar matter component in a way similar to that present in disk systems. By analyzing the properties of dark halo densities in their innermost regions, we find no trace of a central intermediate-mass black hole or of a nuclear stellar cluster.

The dSph kinematics consist of an ensemble of independent measures, each of them coming from a single star. Until recently, the advantage that dSphs do not require the complex dark-luminous mass decomposition needed in disk systems has been paired with the fact that, in these systems, the 3D kinematics and distribution of the tracers of the gravitational field are not fully known. As a matter of fact, to mass model these galaxies, one has to resort to the complex Jeans Equations, rather than to the much simpler Poisson Equation used in disk systems. In addition, until recently, dSphs had a limited number of stars whose motions were measured (Battaglia et al., 2013). All this triggers large statistical errors and large systematic uncertainties, making it difficult to probe the distribution of DM in these systems (see the Introduction of (Yang et al., 2025) and references therein).

papers.title: How to feed your dragon: the role of turbulence in AGN activity
papers.abstract: Active galactic nuclei (AGN) are thought to be important drivers of galaxy evolution. However, the way AGN jets couple their energy to the interstellar medium (ISM) remains poorly understood. Recent observations have revealed $\sim$kpc-scale jets in galaxies of different morphological types. Here, we use idealized turbulent box simulations with accreting black holes to investigate how jet-ISM interactions and feedback shape the evolution of jets. We show that a turbulent ISM is a key ingredient in both jet launching and jet propagation. Without turbulence, jet feedback initially shuts off the cold gas supply to the black hole and the system enters a steady state with jet power $\leq 10^{39}\,\mathrm{erg\,s^{-1}}$ for a $10^{6}\,\mathrm{M}_\odot$ black hole. In a turbulent medium, jets fill voids with hot diffuse material which the turbulence then carries away, replenishing the black hole's fuel supply. However, above a critical jet efficiency factor, the jet begins to significantly deplete its fuel supply and enters a self-limiting accretion regime. This critical factor depends on the ISM Mach number, with lower turbulence yielding a lower threshold. Moreover, while the jet power depends on the ambient gas density in the vicinity of the black hole, we find that, at fixed turbulent structure, the morphology and extent of jet propagation are largely insensitive to the average background density; turbulence in the ISM dominates over mean density in setting how far jets propagate, although denser media experience higher total energy injection and stronger heating.

AGN jets can be launched by spinning SMBHs, powered by the extraction of black hole spin energy through magnetic fields that are supplied by the accreting gas [14]. Assuming the accretion disk is magnetically arrested, accretion onto the SMBH sets the energy available for this feedback. Yet the feeding of the black hole itself can be strongly influenced both by the surrounding gas conditions and by the feedback itself.

The interplay between the ISM and AGN is complex, and the conditions of the ambient ISM strongly influence how gas is transported to the SMBH. In particular, the level of turbulence on kpc scales can by itself regulate the black hole’s feeding [8, 9, 23, 22]. Supernova (SN) feedback, one of the sources of this turbulence, can affect BH growth in different ways [1, and references therein]. On the one hand, stellar feedback can limit accretion onto the black hole by heating and expelling gas [30, 40, 2, 65], and dense star-forming regions can divert gas from the nucleus [37, 80]. On the other hand, stellar feedback can drive winds that funnel gas toward the BH and enhance the accretion rate [42, 64], and stellar ionizing radiation can further boost the inflow [65]. In the maintenance mode as well, different strengths of turbulence in the medium on kpc scale can affect gas transport to the SMBH [23, 22].

The interplay between the ISM and AGN is complex, and the conditions of the ambient ISM strongly influence how gas is transported to the SMBH. In particular, the level of turbulence on kpc scales can by itself regulate the black hole’s feeding [8, 9, 23, 22]. Supernova (SN) feedback, one of the sources of this turbulence, can affect BH growth in different ways [1, and references therein]. On the one hand, stellar feedback can limit accretion onto the black hole by heating and expelling gas [30, 40, 2, 65], and dense star-forming regions can divert gas from the nucleus [37, 80]. On the other hand, stellar feedback can drive winds that funnel gas toward the BH and enhance the accretion rate [42, 64], and stellar ionizing radiation can further boost the inflow [65]. In the maintenance mode as well, different strengths of turbulence in the medium on kpc scale can affect gas transport to the SMBH [23, 22].

Conversely, SMBHs can significantly affect the ISM. AGN feedback can heat, expel, or redistribute gas, thereby cutting off the supply of material for both star formation and further accretion onto the BH. As a result, jet outflows can regulate their own power [85, 73], leading to a self-regulated duty cycle. Intermittent jet activity has been investigated in several studies and has been attributed to, for instance, magnetic instabilities and jet-induced turbulence [66, 52].

Observations provide strong evidence for interactions between the ISM and AGN [41, 34, 46, 45, 32]. For example, low-power jets, such as FR0 sources [4, 5, 7], are stalled on kiloparsec scales for millions of years, allowing ample time for jet energy to influence ISM properties. When resolved, these jets exhibit complex morphologies with asymmetric structures [36] which can be linked to the jet-ISM interaction [75, 57, 58, 78, 18]; also see Mukherjee [59] for a recent review. Furthermore, Murthy et al. [60] showed that even low-luminosity AGN can expel most of the cold gas out to ∼\sim500 pc, potentially starving the black hole.

[62], Yuan and Narayan [87] showed that hot accretion onto a non-spinning black hole can still launch collimated, quasi-relativistic jets via the disk-driven Blandford–Payne mechanism [13] together with wide-angle winds. These winds reach much lower velocities than the jet but carry a higher mass and energy flux [86]. For spinning black holes the outflow can also include both relativistic jets and broader winds [55, 61]. Beyond GRMHD, hydrodynamical simulations that prescribe non-collimated outflows on larger scales have also been used to study how wide-angle jets and winds couple to the ambient medium [38, 81, 28, e.g.].

SMBH feeding and feedback are in constant interplay, which is why they must be studied jointly [35]. However, connecting AGN jet launching to its galaxy-scale feedback effects is challenging because no single method spans the full range of scales. Conventional GRMHD simulations cannot reach the Bondi radius for realistic gas temperatures [61], and even multi-zone GRMHD models [25, 39] do not extend to kiloparsec scales. Galaxy-scale simulations, conversely, capture the overall impact of AGN feedback but rarely resolve Bondi-scale accretion without becoming prohibitively expensive. Targeted and super-Lagrangian refinement is beginning to bridge this gap, resolving the Bondi radius in idealized simulations of galaxies [26, 47], in galaxy clusters and groups [19, 8, 9, 23, 22], and in some cosmological runs [3]. To date, however, these either omit AGN feedback or lack a well-resolved, multiphase turbulent ISM, which remains prohibitively expensive in full cosmological volumes. A complementary route is to model the unresolved physics: Su et al. [74] applied the Cho et al. [25] multi-zone GRMHD solution as a sub-grid accretion-and-feedback prescription in galaxy-scale simulations, but found that this alone does not reproduce realistic black hole growth.

papers.title: FOCUS: First-Order Control Using Optimal Transport Supervision for Imitation from Observations
papers.abstract: Imitation learning from observations must recover behavior from state-only demonstrations without known temporal correspondence. Differentiable simulators provide pathwise policy gradients, but differentiating through long, contact-rich trajectories can make optimization unstable. We introduce FOCUS, which combines local optimal-transport alignment with short-horizon differentiable actor-critic learning. FOCUS matches agent rollout windows to multiple sampled expert segments using a soft best-of-$K$ objective that emphasizes locally compatible matches. The resulting transport-based costs provide differentiable imitation rewards, while a learned critic bootstraps value beyond the rollout horizon. FOCUS requires neither temporally aligned trajectories nor expert-aligned initialization or teacher forcing. Across contact-rich locomotion tasks in DFlex, including a musculoskeletal humanoid controlled by 152 muscle activations, FOCUS improves sample efficiency and training stability over adversarial imitation-from-observation methods and prior differentiable imitation baselines.

papers.intro:
Imitation learning from observations (ILfO) must recover control from state-only demonstrations, without access to expert actions or known temporal correspondence between learner and expert trajectories. This makes supervision fundamentally ambiguous: the learner must determine both what behavior to imitate and where its current behavior corresponds to the demonstration.

This makes supervision fundamentally ambiguous: the learner must determine both what behavior to imitate and where its current behavior corresponds to the demonstration.

Optimal-transport (OT) methods are well suited to the alignment problem because they can compare trajectories or state distributions without requiring point-wise temporal correspondence [12, 39, 9, 15, 23, 7]. In practice, however, these methods typically convert transport costs into surrogate rewards and optimize the policy with zeroth-order RL, inheriting the sample inefficiency and high-variance updates of black-box policy optimization [36]. Adversarial ILfO methods similarly learn from state-only demonstrations through discriminator-derived rewards [52, 60, 6], but can be sensitive to reward modeling, discriminator stability, and tuning.

Differentiable physics simulators provide a complementary route by exposing path-wise policy gradients through the environment dynamics. Simulators such as Brax [16], Warp [35], and DFlex [56] have made this setting practical, while first-order control methods such as SHAC [56], AHAC [19], and SAPO [55] stabilize differentiable control through short-horizon rollouts and critic bootstrapping. These methods, however, assume access to an environment reward. Differentiable imitation already addresses some alignment challenges: GDTW-IL [10] matches observed trajectories through known dynamics, and ILD [8] combines unsynchronized state matching with truncated gradients, using behavior-cloning pretraining. DiffMimic [45] uses expert-aligned initialization and teacher forcing.

papers.title: Personalised 3D Mnemonics for Vocabulary Learning in Context
papers.abstract: Augmented reality (AR) can support vocabulary learning by placing mnemonic cues in the physical contexts where new words are encountered. Prior work has augmented real objects with bilingual labels, audio, keywords, and 3D visualisations of those keywords interacting with the objects, but these cues are typically predefined by system designers. This limits scalability and reduces learners' ability to construct personal mnemonic links. By grounding mnemonics in objects that learners already recognise, use, and associate with prior experiences, a system could connect new vocabulary to existing mental models rather than requiring learners to adopt designer-defined associations. We outline a proof of concept and a storyboard of a generative AR approach in which learners create personalised 3D mnemonics by transforming familiar objects in their surroundings into situated mnemonic anchors. We position this concept within a timeline of related work and argue that recent advances in generative 3D asset creation enable a new design point: personalised 3D mnemonics that do not merely place content in the physical learning environment, but modify familiar real-world objects so that they become part of the mnemonic itself.

papers.title: Two-coloring the points of a projective plane
papers.abstract: Let us color the points of a projective plane of odd order $n$ with two colors, say red and blue. Erd\H{o}s asked the question of determining the maximum number of balanced lines (that have the same number of red and blue points). The answer is $n^2$, and in the corresponding trivial coloring the unbalanced lines go through a point. In this paper, we consider the Galois plane $\mathrm{PG}(2,q)$ and determine the number of unbalanced lines for a non-trivial coloring. The problem can also be generalized to $(r,b)$-colored lines (see Definition 1.1) and in many cases we extend the results to the generalized problem. Our strongest result for Galois planes of prime order $p$ describes all 2-colorings with at most $\max\{3p+1,4p-22\}$ not $(r,b)$-colored lines (see Theorem 5.13). Finally, in case of the generalized problem, we allow even more not $(r,b)$-colored lines if $r$ is small and the order is prime (for more details, see Theorem 5.18).

papers.intro:
Determining the chromatic number of a projective plane of order nn is an easy exercise. It is 33 for the Fano plane and 22 for n≥3n\geq 3. In spite of this, there are several interesting problems for colorings of projective planes. For example, one can impose extra conditions on color classes (one may require that they are arcs, or blocking sets, see Csima, Füredi [9], or [6]), or can consider other variants of the chromatic number (such variants were introduced by Voloshin [19], and for projective planes the upper chromatic number was considered first by Bacsó and Tuza [4], then in [5]). One may also consider balanced colorings in which the size of color classes differs by at most one (the balanced upper chromatic number was introduced by Araujo-Pardo, Kiss, Montejano [2], and considered later in [7]). There are probably many other interesting problems for coloring; for example, Alon and Füredi [3] consider colorings in which the distribution of colors is unique for the lines.

papers.title: On nowhere-zero ${3}$-flows in Cayley graphs on groups of order ${p^2n}$
papers.abstract: We consider Tutte's $3$-flow conjecture in the class of Cayley graphs on groups $G$ of order $p^2n$, where $p$ is a prime and $n$ is square-free and coprime to $p$. The conjecture has been proved by J. Zhang and Z. Zhang in the case where $n$ is a prime (Discrete Mathematics, 2023); and by the authors in the case where $p=2$ (arXiv:2603.24175). In this paper, we prove the conjecture in the case where $p > 2$ and either a Sylow $p$-subgroup or a Hall $n$-subgroup of $G$ is a cyclic group.

An orientation of Γ\Gamma is a digraph DD obtained from Γ\Gamma by assigning one of the two possible directions to each edge of Γ\Gamma. Note that parallel edges may be assigned opposite directions. For an edge e∈E⁡(Γ)e\in\mathrm{E}(\Gamma), we denote by D⁡(e)D(e) the associated arc of DD. papers.title: Exponential stability of port-Hamiltonian systems with unstructured, measurable Hamiltonian densities
papers.abstract: For first-order port-Hamiltonian systems in the dissipative setting considered here, we characterise exponential stability without any further regularity or block-structure assumption on the Hamiltonian density, thus closing a gap persisting in the literature. The proof requires revisiting the computation of the adjoint generator of the port-Hamiltonian semigroup. Finally, we provide both examples and non-examples showcasing the inconclusiveness of known conditions on the Hamiltonian densities necessary for the application of characterisation results in the literature.

papers.intro:
In recent years, stability properties for example systems have shown growing interest. In particular, due to the possibility of invoking arguments from linear algebra, a particular focus was given to a class of 11-D hyperbolic partial differential equations often referred to as port-Hamiltonian systems -- or sometimes called distributed port-Hamiltonian systems11 1 One of the mathematical sources for these systems is [8], where these systems were called ‘port-Hamiltonian systems’. Hence, we shall employ the same custom here; see also the discussion in [12].. We refer to [13, 14, 8, 10] for some classical and more recent sources on port-Hamiltonian systems. In the literature, one can now find a characterisation of strong stability for these systems ([17]) and a characterisation of exponential stability ([11]); quantified strong stability results are available in [2]. Whereas the former criterion invokes only the invertibility of a family of matrices, the latter two require the matrix norm of the inverses to satisfy certain bounds across the entire family.

In the literature, one can now find a characterisation of strong stability for these systems ([17]) and a characterisation of exponential stability ([11]); quantified strong stability results are available in [2]. Whereas the former criterion invokes only the invertibility of a family of matrices, the latter two require the matrix norm of the inverses to satisfy certain bounds across the entire family.

The characterisation from [17] applies to all port-Hamiltonian systems in the setting considered here. In contrast, the ones in [11, 2] ask for a regularity condition satisfied by the port-Hamiltonian system in question. More precisely, the asked-for property is the boundedness of an associated family of fundamental solutions, which holds, for instance, if the Hamiltonian density is of bounded variation or leaves the relevant spectral subspaces invariant. In any case, the regularity condition has been subject to an open problem in [11, Problem 1.6], which asks as to whether this condition is needed to obtain exponential stability results in the first place. We will answer this question in the negative. In fact, more profoundly, the present article resolves the issue of the characterisation of exponential stability for port-Hamiltonian systems irrespective of the regularity property. Hence, we provide the full picture of the characterisation of exponential stability, closing the gap in the literature. It remains to analyse the quantified strongly stable decay of systems violating the regularity condition.

papers.title: Completeness and dynamical stability in exoplanet occurrence rates
papers.abstract: Exoplanet population studies are often quantified through the "occurrence rate" of certain types of planet. This value can be calculated from a survey of a sample of stars by taking the "detection rate" and correcting with a completeness factor. This completeness is calculated via detection limits on each individual star, and can be calculated either individually for each detected planet or averaged in a certain area of parameter space. We test whether either the average completeness or individual completeness performs better than the other. We also test whether including dynamical stability constraints in the detection limits improves the occurrence rate results. We use synthetic sets of exoplanetary systems and calculate occurrence rates for each and compare to what the value would be with perfect information. We compare how close each method is to the ground truth to assess which is most suitable. Overall, in our synthetic sets, the average completeness is more reliable though it can be a problem if there is a sharp change in the underlying population within the area of parameter-space considered. We find that using dynamical stability conditions causes a bias in the occurrence rate and do not recommend using these.

With the number of exoplanets ever-growing (Christiansen et al., 2025), studies of the exoplanet population statistics, which began in the 2010s (Howard et al., 2010; Gould et al., 2010; Johnson et al., 2010; Mayor et al., 2011, e.g.), are becoming more numerous. This is expected to increase further with large samples of exoplanets expecting to be detected by future space missions such as PLATO (Rauer et al., 2025), Earth 2.0 (ET) (Ge et al., 2022), and the Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope (Spergel et al., 2015; Penny et al., 2019), as well as the upcoming data releases of Gaia (Gaia Collaboration et al., 2016; Lammers and Winn, 2026).

One main value calculated in exoplanet population statistics is the planetary “occurrence rate" or “planet frequency", a measure of how common planets with certain parameters are. This can be calculated as a value with uncertainties in a region of interest or as a parameterised function of, for example, orbital period (Fulton et al., 2021, see e.g.). The occurrence rate can also be calculated as the number of planets per star (Mayor et al., 2011, sometimes referred to as the planet frequency;) or as the fraction of stars with at least one planet in the required range (Montet et al., 2014, e.g.). In this work we calculate the value of occurrence rates in discrete regions of parameter-space (planet mass-period) using the number of planets per star. We expect the results to be relevant to the other cases as well.

To calculate the occurrence rate in a given region of parameter space, the number of planets detected (in that region) per star sampled is measured. This then needs to be corrected for the planets that have likely been missed, called the completeness correction. Completeness refers to the completeness of the survey; if the survey is sensitive to a set of planet parameters in 40% of stars, its completeness is 40%. This completeness can be calculated in different ways, either averaged across the region of interest (Pinamonti et al., 2022; Bryant et al., 2023, e.g.), or only calculated for each detected planet that is included in the occurrence rate sum (Howard et al., 2010; Mayor et al., 2011, e.g.).

Completeness of a survey is usually calculated based on “detection limits", these are a measure of in what region of parameter space a planet would have been detected should it exist. Detection limits are traditionally calculated through series of injection-recovery tests (Wittenmyer et al., 2011; Fulton et al., 2021), however other methods, such as sampling the parameter space consistent with noise in the data, exist (Standing et al., 2022, e.g.). Completeness, at a location in parameter space, is then the fraction of stars in the sample for which the data is sensitive to planetary signals.

Completeness, at a location in parameter space, is then the fraction of stars in the sample for which the data is sensitive to planetary signals.

Detection limits classically use information from the data only. After subtracting the best-fit model, injection-recovery tests are performed on the residual radial velocity (RV) timeseries, exploring a range of RV semi-amplitudes KK and orbital periods PP. Populating the (PP,KK) space with many injection-recovery tests, it is possible to construct a robust limit curve above which a certain percentage of signals is detected (e.g. the 95%\% detection limits). However, additional constraints besides the data can be provided. As such, the recent code ARDENT (Stalport et al., 2025) verifies the dynamical plausibility of the injected planets 11 1 https://github.com/manustalport/ardent. Based on a combination of analytical criteria and, if needed, N-body simulations coupled with a chaos indicator, ARDENT explores orbital stability in the period-mass space supposing an additional injected planet into the system. As a consequence of this stability check, entire ranges of orbital period can be excluded due to their dynamical instability, pushing down the detection limits to zero. It is important to note that as working hypothesis, ARDENT supposes the stability of the nominal system (i.e. composed of the detected planets only).

ARDENT computes detection limits both without and with the stability constraints. The former, based on the data only, are called “data-driven" detection limits. The latter are referred to as “dynamical" detection limits, due to their supplementary dynamical information (Stalport et al., 2025). We created a synthetic system to illustrate the use of ARDENT. We supposed a 1-planet system composed of an eccentric giant planet (ee=0.4, PP=200d, MM=1MJM_{J}), and created a residual RV timeseries composed of Gaussian white noise. We use a standard deviation of 2 m/s, and quote uncertainties as would originate from photon noise of 0.8 m/s. For this example, we generated 100 RVs spread over 300 days. We first derived the data-driven detection limits based on 5000 injection-recovery tests, as illustrated by the brown curve in Fig. 1. Then, we computed the dynamical detection limits (in red-yellow). ARDENT scans the period-mass space below the data-driven detection limits, and further rejects the dynamically unstable regions. In this example, the eccentric giant prevents the existence of any additional planet down to 90 days. If there are no detected planets, then a dynamical detection limit and a data-driven one are identical.

The two methods represent different philosophies of what the detection limit is testing. Using data-driven limits is asking the question “what planets would have been detected in the dataset we are using?" whereas the dynamical limits are asking “what planets can we say do not exist in the systems we are observing?". It is unclear if one of these is better than the other; perhaps the dynamical limits are better since more information is being used. However, the use of detection limits with information from dynamical stability to calculate occurrence rates has not been tested.

papers.title: Morse theory and topological degree for resonant mean field equations on Riemann surfaces with boundary
papers.abstract: In this paper, we establish Morse theory for the Neumann mean field equation on a compact Riemann surface at $\rho=4\pi m$, $m\in\mathbb N$. To address the loss of compactness associated with bubbling, we use Bahri's theory of critical points at infinity. Assume that the reduced functionals are Morse and that the leading scale coefficient does not vanish at their critical points. We classify the critical points at infinity arising from interior, boundary, and mixed concentration, compute their Morse indices and local relative homology, and establish deformation lemmas at resonance. We prove that, for $m\geq 2$, every sufficiently negative sublevel is homotopy equivalent to the boundary-weighted barycenter space of order $m-1$. The Euler--Poincar\'e identity gives the Leray--Schauder degree at resonance without assuming nondegeneracy of the solutions. If all solutions are nondegenerate, we further obtain strong Morse inequalities with explicit Betti numbers over $\mathbb Z_2$. As a consequence, we obtain existence and multiplicity results, as well as criteria for solutions with prescribed Morse index.

papers.title: GRB 241113B: the first SVOM and EP gamma-ray burst A soft GRB likely seen on-axis, from soft X-rays to gamma-rays
papers.abstract: In 2024, two new missions were launched to detect high-energy transients. EP and SVOM aim to observe soft transients from X-ray rich gamma-ray bursts (XRR), X-ray flashes (XRF), to fast X-ray transients (FXT). GRB 241113B, the first soft gamma-ray burst (GRB) jointly detected by EP and SVOM from soft X-rays to gamma-rays (0.5--1000~keV). GRB 241113B has an $E^{obs}_{peak} \approx 35$ keV and a redshift (z) likely between 0.5 and 3.5, with $T_{90,\gamma} \approx 42$~s (4--30~keV). This burst can be classified as either an XRR or XRF, depending on the fluence ratio used. The afterglow is achromatic and featureless with a normal decay ($\alpha \approx -1.40$). The prompt emission does not satisfy the shock-breakout relation, and thus a geometry comprised of a jet is preferred. However, the afterglow fitting favors a jet viewed on-axis dominated by synchrotron emission due to electrons in a slow cooling regime, interacting with a wind medium. The bulk Lorentz factor ($\Gamma$) indicates that the motion of the jet is ultrarelativistic ($\Gamma_{0}>100$), which discards the dirty fireball model. Hence, the jet baryon loading should be compatible with that of classical GRBs (C-GRBs). The prompt spectral properties of GRB 241113B ($\alpha$, $E^{\mathrm{obs}}_{\mathrm{peak}}$, $E_{\gamma,iso}$) are comparable to those of XRFs/XRRs and are in the continuity of the C-GRB distributions, setting it apart from the extragalatic FXT population solely detected by EP. Hence, the SVOM mission, with the benefit brought by the instrument ECLAIRs with its high sensitivity and low energy threshold (at 4keV), is able to detect the potential $\gamma$-ray counterpart of soft transients also observed by EP and help to differentiate them from FXTs. The latter show the interest of the joint operation of both missions to better study the landscape of soft transients.

Gamma-ray bursts (GRBs) consist of gamma-ray prompt emission that lasts from a few milliseconds up to thousands of seconds with an extragalactic origin (Metzger et al., 1997). The GRB prompt emission arises mainly from internal shocks within a high relativistic jet (Rees and Meszaros, 1992; Sari and Piran, 1997; Piran, 1999; Kumar and Zhang, 2015). This jet can then interact with the circumburst medium (CSM) and produce external shocks from which accelerated electrons will cool by radiating broadband X-ray to radio synchrotron emission called the afterglow (Mészáros and Rees, 1997; Sari et al., 1998; Zhang et al., 2006).

papers.title: Spherical law for optimal layouts of random graphs
papers.abstract: Can the nodes of a random graph be placed in an auxiliary space $\mathbb{R}^{M}$ so that its connectivity becomes local? The spring electric layout is a standard algorithm to try to find such local graph layouts; we study it as a statistical-physics problem by considering the Gibbs ensemble of spring-electric layouts. For graphs with independent edges we solve the model exactly at large number of nodes $N$ and fixed embedding dimension $M$. The node positions obey a spherical law: they are uniformly distributed in an $M$-dimensional ball; for $M=2$ this is closely related to Girko's circular law. Crucially, the ground state energy is flat across all layouts with that density: an optimal layout for one graph is asymptotically optimal for any other. Optimal layouts of i.i.d. graphs are therefore frustrated liquids, macroscopically constrained but microscopically unoptimizable. We discuss relations to graph-partitioning, Laplacian eigenmaps, and dimensionality reduction, and outline how this harsh result breaks down for correlated graphs.

papers.intro:
Graphs have no intrinsic notion of space. Yet, embedding the nodes of a graph such that connected nodes are close by can give insight into the structure of activity such as traveling waves (as in [1]). Usually, such graph layouts or embeddings are used to visualize networks (e.g., in [2]) and data (e.g., in [3]). Additionally, graph layouts are used to investigate connectomes [4, 5, 6, 7] under the paradigm of wiring-length minimization. For large random graphs, the most widespread class of graph-layout algorithms is the force-directed layout, e.g., pioneered in [8, 9]; here, attracting forces pulling together connected nodes compete with repelling forces keeping all pairs at distance. A prominent member of this class is the spring-electric layout, the name pointing to the choice of forces. For more classes of graph layout algorithms see [10, 11, 12]. It is barely possible to visualize random graphs of O⁡(1000)O(1000) nodes well and force-directed layouts are typically used for smaller graphs [13]. As such it appears that theory has focused on the complexity of computing force-directed layouts or improving their efficiency [14] rather than on the properties of the resulting layouts. For our purpose, to understand whether a network admits some locality once its nodes are tidied up, it is irrelevant whether layouts are visually pleasing.

Energies in equilibrated force-directed layouts can be related to modularity of the graph [15]. Taking an inverse perspective, the forces can be chosen such that the layout algorithm maximizes the likelihood of the layout as a latent-space model of the node connection probabilities or other graph characteristics [16]. Graph embeddings are closely related to graph partitioning, i.e., the separation of nodes into partitions such as to minimize edges across the partitions. The statistical physics of graph partitioning (see e.g. [17, 18, 19]) shows similarities in the approach and in the results with the setting studied here.

The details of the model and the main result are presented in Sec. 2 and Sec. 3, respectively: Specifically, we argue that for independent edges, optimal layouts are asymptotically frustrated liquids: They fail to find a good balance between the disordered attraction and the homogeneous repulsion and the single nodes are free to move without changing the energy/ cost. Derivations of the results are shown in Sec. 4. In Sec. 5, we briefly point to different layout algorithms, correlated edges and other possible extensions.

papers.title: Electron-electron interactions mediated by overdamped vibrations: Implications for chirality-induced spin selectivity
papers.abstract: Motivated by chirality-induced spin selectivity (CISS), we investigate spin polarization during molecular electron transfer through a correlated bridge in the presence of a rapidly relaxing Peierls mode. By modulating both electronic hopping and spin--orbit coupling, the mode mediates two-body spin-spin interactions, including isotropic, anisotropic, and Dzyaloshinskii-Moriya exchange. We derive these interactions using an exact Lang-Firsov transformation for a four-site chiral bridge. We then include fast vibrational relaxation in the joint electron--vibration master equation and derive the reduced electronic dynamics to second order in the vibronic coupling, retaining both coherent and dissipative contributions and the finite-time buildup of the vibrational response. We test our derivation by numerical simulations, finding spin polarization accumulated at the acceptor after unpolarized injection, with nonmonotonic dependence on damping and bridge filling. Within the postulated local-loss model, our results show that rapid vibrational relaxation does not preclude spin polarization through a correlated bridge and provide a framework for assessing vibration-mediated interactions and dissipative dynamics as ingredients of CISS in molecular electron transfer.

papers.intro:
Chirality-induced spin selectivity (CISS) refers to the correlation between molecular handedness and electron spin, whereby charge motion through chiral systems can generate spin polarization [1, 2, 3]. Since its first observation, CISS has been reported in a broad range of molecular and supramolecular systems, including DNA and biomolecular assemblies, motivating interest in both its microscopic origin and its potential applications in molecular spintronics and quantum technologies [4, 5, 6]. More recently, time-resolved magnetic-resonance experiments on donor–chiral-bridge–acceptor molecules have probed the spin states of radical pairs generated by photoinduced electron transfer (PET) [7, 8, 6, 9]. These experiments provide a molecular setting for investigating the intrinsic origin of CISS [9, 10], without the need to include external components such as substrates, interfaces or electrodes.

This motivated theoretical efforts to understand CISS in isolated molecules [11, 12, 13], highlighting the crucial role of spin-spin interactions between the transferred electron and the one remaining on the donor during the charge separation dynamics. In particular, we have recently shown [13] that simultaneous modulation of hopping and spin-orbit coupling (SOC) by torsional modes typical of these molecules [14] mediates a Dzyaloshinskii–Moriya interaction (DMI). This interaction mixes singlet and triplet states, giving rise to a substantial spin polarization in the spin-correlated radical pair. Moreover, the triplet component predicted by this model and its non-trivial magnetic field dependence are consistent with experimental observations of CISS by time-resolved electron paramagnetic resonance [13].

Mechanisms involving electron–vibration scattering, polaron formation, and correlated vibronic dynamics have consequently been proposed in the context of CISS [18, 20, 21, 22, 23, 24]. Recent work has shown that Peierls coupling enables spin-dependent interference in chiral tight-binding models even when the purely electronic system does not support spin polarization [25]. These results motivate treating vibrations not only as a source of decoherence, but also as mediators of effective electronic interactions. An important question is how these vibration-mediated processes are modified when the molecular mode relaxes rapidly into its environment. Using electronic Green functions with vibronic self-energies incorporating a finite vibrational lifetime, Fransson showed that vibration-induced exchange splitting can produce sizable spin selectivity in molecular junctions [18]. His subsequent work identified vibrational dissipation as essential for establishing a stationary spin polarization and spin-polarized currents [17].

Recent work has shown that Peierls coupling enables spin-dependent interference in chiral tight-binding models even when the purely electronic system does not support spin polarization [25]. These results motivate treating vibrations not only as a source of decoherence, but also as mediators of effective electronic interactions. An important question is how these vibration-mediated processes are modified when the molecular mode relaxes rapidly into its environment. Using electronic Green functions with vibronic self-energies incorporating a finite vibrational lifetime, Fransson showed that vibration-induced exchange splitting can produce sizable spin selectivity in molecular junctions [18]. His subsequent work identified vibrational dissipation as essential for establishing a stationary spin polarization and spin-polarized currents [17].

Here we provide a systematic derivation of both the effective electronic Hamiltonian and the dissipative contributions that remain after eliminating the rapidly relaxing vibrational mode. To this end, we investigate a correlated four-site bridge coupled to a Peierls mode that modulates both spin-independent hopping and SOC. We first perform an exact Lang–Firsov transformation of the electron–vibration Hamiltonian to identify the induced one-body corrections and two-body interactions, including isotropic, anisotropic, and Dzyaloshinskii–Moriya exchange. This transformation retains the vibrational degree of freedom. Starting from a postulated local-loss Lindblad equation for the joint electron–vibration system, we then eliminate the rapidly relaxing mode to second order in the vibronic coupling, retaining the mixed electron–vibration correlations that generate both coherent and dissipative contributions to the reduced electronic dynamics.

papers.title: A General-Purpose Adaptable Foundation Model for Total-Body PET Kinetic Modelling
papers.abstract: Voxel-level kinetic modeling in total-body dynamic positron emission tomography (TB-PET) enables precise physiological quantification but complicates parameter uncertainty estimation. While generative consistency models (CMs) can rapidly estimate Bayesian posterior distributions, they are constrained by type of tracers, kinetic models, and protocols. Training them from scratch whenever a new tracer, model or protocol is used can be computationally intensive. To address this, we introduce LoRACM, a parameter-efficient framework utilizing low-rank adaptation (LoRA) to transfer a pretrained foundation CM to novel TB-PET scenarios. We evaluated three adaptation scenarios using simulated and human data: scanner and protocol transfer for FDG two-tissue compartment modeling; FP-CIT simplified reference tissue modeling; and high-temporal-resolution FDG blood flow imaging via the adiabatic approximation to tissue homogeneity model. Each adaptation was trained in less than 3 hours on a single NVIDIA A100 GPU using 50,000 simulated pairs. In simulations, LoRACM showed strong agreement with results from Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC, which we use as reference posterior distributions), yielding median Kullback-Leibler divergences of 0.05-0.11 and median absolute percentage errors below 1.2% for each kinetic parameter of interest. In human data, LoRACM generated total-body K_i maps comparable to the ones made by non-negative nonlinear least squares (NNLS) fitting and a consistency model trained from scratch. Striatal dopamine binding potential estimates predicted by LoRACM correlated with NNLS estimates (r = 0.968-0.988). LoRACM produced total-body blood flow imaging with FDG matching the one made by NNLS. These underscore the potential of adapting a pretrained CM with LoRA for fast and reliable posterior parameter inference for kinetic models across distinct TB-PET applications.

papers.intro:
Dynamic positron emission tomography (PET) enables physiological quantification through kinetic modelling of radiotracer delivery, exchange, and retention, supporting measurements such as glucose metabolism and receptor binding beyond static uptake [1, 2, 3, 4]. Total-body and long-axial-field-of-view systems provide increased sensitivity and simultaneous multi-organ coverage [5, 6, 7], enabling concurrent acquisition of tissue time activity curves (TACs) and image-derived input functions [8]. Translating this acquisition capability into physiological measurements requires parameter estimation methods that accommodate both large image volumes and diverse kinetic behaviour.

Dynamic positron emission tomography (PET) enables physiological quantification through kinetic modelling of radiotracer delivery, exchange, and retention, supporting measurements such as glucose metabolism and receptor binding beyond static uptake [1, 2, 3, 4]. Total-body and long-axial-field-of-view systems provide increased sensitivity and simultaneous multi-organ coverage [5, 6, 7], enabling concurrent acquisition of tissue time activity curves (TACs) and image-derived input functions [8]. Translating this acquisition capability into physiological measurements requires parameter estimation methods that accommodate both large image volumes and diverse kinetic behaviour.

Established approaches for PET kinetic parameter estimation in dynamic and total-body PET include standard compartmental modelling typically fitted via non-negative nonlinear least squares (NNLS) [1, 4], alongside graphical and linearized methods such as Patlak and Logan analyses [9, 10], generalized Patlak modelling [11], spectral analysis, and basis-function reference-tissue methods [12, 13]. Direct parametric reconstruction further integrates kinetic modelling with the PET measurement model to improve statistical efficiency [14, 8]. However, these approaches primarily provide point estimates of kinetics rather than full kinetic parameter posterior distributions [15]. While Bayesian inference enables full characterization of posterior distributions, sampling via Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) demands repeated model evaluations and convergence assessments for each TAC [16], imposing a substantial computational burden on total-body imaging due to the large number of voxels. Likelihood-free alternatives such as vPET-ABC require careful calibration of the accepting threshold [17].

Deep learning methods accelerate PET kinetic modelling via supervised [18] and self-supervised approaches, such as those by De Benetti et al. [19] and Tehlan and Wendler [20]. However, these methods primarily yield parameter point estimates without uncertainty quantification. Generative methods were introduced to facilitate posterior estimation in dynamic PET. Liu et al. demonstrated conditional variational autoencoders for kinetic model parameter estimations [21]. Following developments in denoising diffusion probabilistic models [22, 23], Djebra et al. applied an improved diffusion model to brain PET for kinetic posterior estimation, reporting more than 230-fold faster computation than MCMC [24]. Recently, consistency models [25] have emerged and adapted for fast simulation-based inference [26]. Our previous work introduced a consistency model (CM) for voxel-wise PET kinetic posterior estimation and total-body parametric imaging [27], achieving MCMC-level accuracy while being over five orders of magnitude faster.

However, diffusion models are locked to specific protocols, tracers, and kinetic models. Training them from scratch for new scenarios is computationally intensive, especially in clinical settings. Parameter-efficient transfer learning offers a solution to this bottleneck [28]. Low-rank adaptation (LoRA) retains pretrained weights while learning updates through low-rank matrices [29]. This study introduces LoRA for CM (LoRACM) by adapting the pretrained CM to different scenarios using LoRA. We evaluated LoRACM across three adaptation tasks: 1) a new protocol for F18{}^{18}\mathrm{F}-fluorodeoxyglucose (FDG) two-tissue compartment modeling (2TCM) [1], 2) F18{}^{18}\mathrm{F}-FP-CIT simplified reference tissue modeling (SRTM) [2], 3) and high-temporal-resolution FDG with the adiabatic approximation to tissue homogeneity (AATH) modeling [30]. These results demonstrate that LoRACM can transfer pretrained consistency models across distinct PET kinetic modeling applications, lowering the barrier to deploying kinetic posterior estimation for new tracers and protocols. LoRACM is integrated into our open-source PET-TRACER toolbox (https://github.com/yundumbledore/PET-TRACER), featuring a graphical user interface to support accessible deployment across the PET community.

papers.title: Optimal climate policy in incomplete electricity markets
papers.abstract: Incomplete long-term contracting in electricity markets can expose investors and consumers to inefficient levels of risk. This paper investigates how incompleteness impacts the optimal choice of climate policy. We develop a game-theoretic model of optimal policy-making in anticipation of how electricity market agents react to a given policy when gas prices and demand are uncertain and contracting is incomplete. In illustrative experiments, we observe that renewable subsidies and carbon prices induce an insurance co-benefit when markets are incomplete. This is because, relative to a complete market benchmark, incompleteness shifts investment from renewables toward gas and exposes consumers to uninsured risk from inter-annual volatility in electricity prices. By incentivizing investment in renewables, subsidies and carbon prices indirectly counteract these distortions. Consequently, incompleteness increases the optimal subsidy and carbon price levels in our experiments. Renewable subsidies exhibit a stronger insurance effect than carbon pricing, as the latter leads to more investment in gas with carbon capture and storage and more volatile electricity prices. While carbon pricing is more economically efficient than subsidies in complete markets, incompleteness shrinks its efficiency advantage and even leads to cases where subsidies are more economically efficient.

papers.title: Digital sovereignty in professional translation workflows: a case study of migrating from Windows to Linux
papers.abstract: This study examines digital sovereignty in professional translation through a screening of computer-assisted translation tools and translation management systems, and a case study of migrating a translator's workstation from Windows to Linux. The framework combines three principles - Control, Continuity and Exit - with three practical requirements: native Linux operation, independence from mandatory external services, and independent access to essential data and resources. Drawing on documentary evidence and the limited number of responses received from providers, the ecosystem screening distinguishes Linux accessibility from operational independence: browser-based platforms may remain dependent on provider-controlled infrastructure. The migration case demonstrates the feasibility of reconstructing one professional workflow around a locally operable Linux core, using LoopCAT, LibreOffice and locally run TranslateGemma, alongside tools for optical character recognition, communication, credential management and backup. Selected cloud services remained available where needed. The findings suggest that digital sovereignty depends on how workflow dependencies are organized, rather than on individual applications or operating systems. It does not require technological isolation, but meaningful control over essential components, continuity of work and practical exit options. The framework is tailored to the case examined here and may require adaptation to other professional workflows.

papers.title: Nonlinear visco-elasto-plastic model for the stress-strain and stress-relaxation in metallic glass
papers.abstract: We develop a nonlinear visco-elasto-plastic (VEP) model for the stress-strain response of metallic glasses by connecting the deformation dynamics with the material relaxation time obtained from independent stress-relaxation measurements. The material is modeled as a Maxwell-type element, with a nonlinear elastic spring and a stretched-exponential dashpot whose behavior is determined from the separate stress-relaxation data. The model captures the effects of temperature and strain rate on the initial elastic response, stress overshoot, post-yield softening, and steady flow. We independently determine the reference material-time function $X_0(\varepsilon)$ from the stress-relaxation response and the nonlinear material-time variable $X(\varepsilon)$ from the elastic-viscoplastic strain decomposition based on the stress-strain response. We introduce an Eyring-type function or material-time ratio $\phi(\varepsilon)=X(\varepsilon)/X_0(\varepsilon)$ which quantifies the change of relaxation dynamics during nonlinear deformation. Our model provides a simple connection between structural relaxation and yielding in metallic glasses.

Mechanical response of liquids and amorphous materials can be understood from the classical picture introduced by Frenkel, where the response is controlled by the competition between elastic deformation and structural relaxation [15, 49]. At times shorter than the structural relaxation time τ\tau, the material behaves more like an elastic solid, whereas at longer times structural rearrangements become possible and the response becomes viscous [58]. In the Maxwell-Frenkel picture, the relaxation time is related to the viscosity and the high-frequency shear modulus through τ=η/G∞\tau=\eta/G_{\infty} [49, 9], where η\eta is the viscosity and G∞G_{\infty} is the infinite-frequency shear modulus. Thus, the relaxation time gives the natural time scale that separates solid-like and liquid-like mechanical behaviors [41, 54].

In supercooled liquids and metallic glasses, the disordered atomic structure gives rise to a complex mechanical response that strongly depends on temperature and deformation rate [42, 19]. Deformation generally starts with an elastic regime, followed by nonaffine strain-softening, yielding, stress overshoot, eventually reaching a Newtonian-like steady plastic or viscous-flow regime [27, 2, 55]. These features depend strongly on temperature, strain rate, and the structural state of the glass. One of the most important signatures of the nonlinear response is the stress overshoot observed during constant-strain-rate deformation [27]. The stress first increases, reaches a maximum, and then decreases toward a steady-flow value [27]. The magnitude of the overshoot changes strongly with temperature and strain rate, indicating a competition between the imposed deformation time scale and the intrinsic structural-relaxation time of the material [27, 31].

papers.title: Approximate Bayesian Fusion
papers.abstract: Distributed inference plays an important role in modern computational statistics and machine learning. In the frequentist setting, methods can often aggregate results by simply averaging estimators computed on data subsets. However, distributed Bayesian inference is more challenging, as it requires reconstructing the full posterior by combining subposterior distributions computed on different machines. Bayesian Fusion performs distributed Bayesian inference exactly, but at a sizeable computational cost. We propose a method that uses numerical approximations to reduce the cost of the most computationally expensive steps of Bayesian Fusion, and expands its domain of applicability. We bound the numerical error as a function of the step size of the approximation. Under regularity conditions, our approach can approximate the target posterior distribution to an arbitrary degree of accuracy, and is a practical and efficient alternative for large-scale distributed Bayesian inference. In numerical experiments on a logistic regression with more than $300{,}000$ observations, our method reaches the accuracy reported for Divide-and-Conquer Bayesian Fusion about two orders of magnitude faster. On a proportional hazards model with non-Gaussian posteriors, which lacks the lower bounds that Bayesian Fusion requires, our method reproduces funnel features of the posterior that simpler methods like Consensus Monte Carlo miss.

This may arise from computational constraints, the scale of the dataset, or restrictions on data sharing. Distributed inference addresses this by analysing data subsets, or shards, separately and then combining the results. In Bayesian inference, this is challenging because independent shard analyses produce subposteriors that must be recombined to recover the full posterior, which is a non-trivial task.

A wide range of methods has been proposed for this problem. In this work we do not consider methods based primarily on subsampling the full dataset (Welling & Teh 2011, Nemeth & Fearnhead 2021, Bierkens et al. 2019), but we focus on approaches that initially perform inference independently on each shard and subsequently combine the resulting distributions or samples. These approaches range from fast approximations to exact but computationally expensive methods.

A wide range of methods has been proposed for this problem. In this work we do not consider methods based primarily on subsampling the full dataset (Welling & Teh 2011, Nemeth & Fearnhead 2021, Bierkens et al. 2019), but we focus on approaches that initially perform inference independently on each shard and subsequently combine the resulting distributions or samples. These approaches range from fast approximations to exact but computationally expensive methods.

At one end of the spectrum, approximate methods simplify either the subposteriors or their combination. Consensus Monte Carlo (CMC) (Scott et al. 2016) combines subposterior draws by weighted averaging. It is exact when the subposteriors are Gaussian, but its error can be arbitrarily large when they are not. Density-based approaches instead estimate or smooth individual subposteriors before combining them, with kernel density estimates (Neiswanger et al. 2014) or the Weierstrass transform (Wang & Dunson 2014), but density estimation becomes increasingly difficult as the dimension grows. More flexible approximations have also been developed using diffusion-based models of shard-level subposteriors (Trojan et al. 2024).

Consensus Monte Carlo (CMC) (Scott et al. 2016) combines subposterior draws by weighted averaging. It is exact when the subposteriors are Gaussian, but its error can be arbitrarily large when they are not. Density-based approaches instead estimate or smooth individual subposteriors before combining them, with kernel density estimates (Neiswanger et al. 2014) or the Weierstrass transform (Wang & Dunson 2014), but density estimation becomes increasingly difficult as the dimension grows. More flexible approximations have also been developed using diffusion-based models of shard-level subposteriors (Trojan et al. 2024).

At the other end of the spectrum, exact methods target the full posterior itself. Monte Carlo Fusion (MCF) (Dai et al. 2019) uses a rejection-sampling construction to simulate from the exact posterior distribution given samples from each of the subposteriors. However, this approach is computationally expensive, particularly as the dimension or the number of subposteriors increases. Bayesian Fusion (BF) (Dai et al. 2023) improves computational performance over MCF by embedding fusion within a sequential Monte Carlo framework. Furthermore, Divide-and-Conquer Bayesian Fusion (Chan et al. 2023) recursively combines subposteriors through a tree-structured scheme, which improves efficiency further. These methods are exact, or consistent when implemented with SMC, but they remain expensive, scale poorly, and require model-specific bounds that make them hard to apply.

In this work, we develop and analyse Approximate Bayesian Fusion (ABF). ABF retains the sequential Monte Carlo structure of BF, but replaces the unbiased estimates of its importance weights with a simple numerical approximation. The contributions of this article are: 1. papers.title: The lattice of antichains of intervals: Dyck paths, level sets, and sweep dimension
papers.abstract: The Clarke-Cormack-Burkowski lattice $\mathcal{E}_n$ is the lattice of antichains of intervals of the chain $\{0,1,\dots,n-1\}$, the algebraic structure underlying minimal-interval semantics, a query semantics used in information retrieval. We give an explicit, elementary anti-isomorphism between $\mathcal{E}_n$ minus its top element and the Stanley lattice of Dyck words of semilength $n+1$ (an anti-isomorphism whose existence is implicit in work of Ferrari and Munarini), under which the rank of an antichain is $\binom{n+1}{2}$ minus the area of the associated Dyck word. Hence the rank generating function of $\mathcal{E}_n\setminus\{\top\}$ is the reverse of the Carlitz-Riordan $q$-Catalan polynomial. Using a local limit theorem for the area of random-walk excursions, we confirm unconditionally an asymptotic formula of Tak\'acs: the size $\lambda_n$ of the largest level set of $\mathcal{E}_n$ satisfies $\lambda_n\sim\kappa\,4^{n+1}/(n+1)^3$, where $\kappa\approx1.0807$. Finally, for the antichains of intervals of an arbitrary finite poset $P$ we study the sweep dimension, the minimum number of linear orders needed to separate every interval from every element outside it. It equals the Dushnik-Miller dimension of the lattice of convex subsets of $P$, it is the least $k$ for which $P$ maps into $\mathbb{R}^k$ so that every interval is the preimage of an upper orthant, and it lies between $\max(2,w)$ and $2w$, where $w$ is the width of $P$, both bounds being tight. Antichains of intervals embed, preserving joins, into $k$-dimensional staircase regions.

papers.intro:
In modern information-retrieval systems, such as web search engines, the fact that a document (seen as a sequence of words) satisfies a query is not enough to determine its relevance. In fact, the user is often interested in the regions of the document that satisfy the query, and in particular in the minimal regions that satisfy it. For instance, if a user searches for “(A AND B) OR (C AND D)”, it is not enough to know that a document contains both AA and BB (or both CC and DD): the user wants to know where these terms occur, and in particular whether they occur close to each other.

This idea is formally captured by minimal-interval semantics Clarke et al. Each interval in the text of a document is a witness of the satisfiability of the query, that is, it represents a region of the document that satisfies the query; only minimal witnesses are kept, since they are the most informative ones.
