papers.title: Connectivity-Aware Client Selection in Decentralized Federated Learning
papers.abstract: Decentralized federated learning (DFL) has emerged as a scalable alternative to centralized federated learning, removing the single point of failure and communication bottleneck at the server. However, most existing decentralized approaches rely on full-neighborhood broadcasting, where each client transmits its model update to all of its neighbors in each communication round. While effective, this results in significant communication overhead and high energy consumption. This paper applies spectral graph tools as lightweight client selection methods that leverage the graph topology by analyzing the spectral properties of the graph Laplacian over a fixed communication graph. Specifically, we exploit eigenvector embeddings and heat/diffusion kernel similarities to guide each client in selecting only a subset of structurally relevant neighbors, i.e., those that are most beneficial for the convergence of the federation process. This topology aware randomization matches or outperforms uniform neighborhood subsampling and approaches the accuracy of full broadcasting. The largest gains, about $3$ percentage points, emerge under strong data heterogeneity on larger, structurally rich graphs, while the total number of transmitted messages is reduced by $50\%$ compared to naive broadcasting.

papers.intro:
Federated Learning (FL) is a distributed paradigm that enables collaborative training of a global model across decentralized edge devices without sharing raw data [1]. Unlike centralized training, where data are aggregated on a single server, FL performs on-device training and transmits only model updates. This preserves privacy, reduces communication costs, and makes FL a promising solution for diverse applications [2, 3]. While FL provides significant privacy benefits, its reliance on a central server for model aggregation introduces a single point of failure. The entire training process is susceptible to server-side issues, including hardware failures, network outages, or malicious attacks, which can halt the process and compromise the global model’s integrity [4, 5]. To overcome this vulnerability, a paradigm known as Decentralized Federated Learning (DFL) has emerged. DFL eliminates the central server, instead leveraging a peer-to-peer network where devices communicate directly with their neighbors to share and aggregate model updates. This distributed architecture not only removes the single point of failure but also improves scalability and resilience, as the system can continue to operate even if some devices fail or become disconnected [6, 7, 8].

Most DFL studies assume a complete communication graph, where each client transmits its updates to all others [9, 2, 10, 11]. This all-to-all scheme simplifies convergence analysis but incurs high communication overhead, often prohibitive in bandwidth- or energy-constrained systems [10]. To overcome this, more practical approaches design sparse topologies or intelligent client selection [12, 13], typically constructing the graph by (i) thresholding a similarity measure over a complete graph [14], (ii) selecting neighbors by model or gradient similarity [15], or (iii) accounting for divergences in local data distributions [16]. However, these methods ignore the fixed communication topology, which restricts connections between certain pairs of nodes.

This letter proposes a connectivity-aware neighbor selection mechanism that mitigates the communication and energy inefficiencies of naive neighborhood broadcasting in DFL. Each client selects a subset of its neighbors according to Laplacian-based similarity measures computed from the client adjacency graph. Our decentralized client selection framework relies exclusively on the communication topology and does not require access to local data distributions or model parameter dynamics, making it more energy- and communication-efficient than full broadcasting. Within this unified framework, we investigate two alternative ways of deriving topology-aware similarities from the graph Laplacian, which are then used to guide the same neighbor selection process: • Spectral Embedding: clients are represented in a low-dimensional space induced by selected Laplacian eigenvectors, and neighbors are chosen based on proximity in this spectral embedding. • Heat Kernel Similarity: client similarity is defined through diffusion dynamics over the graph, where neighbors with stronger heat kernel interactions are preferentially selected. The paper is organized as follows. We review related work in Section II, discuss the methodology behind the topology-aware client selection in Section III. Section IV presents experimental results that validate our approach, and we summarize our findings in Section V.

papers.title: Critical fluctuations in the edge--triangle exponential random graph models
papers.abstract: We prove quantitative limit theorems for the edge density $Q$ in the dense edge--triangle exponential random graph model at criticality and under parameter perturbations of order $n^{-1}$. At the fixed critical parameters $(\alpha_c,h_c),$ the centered fluctuations satisfy $n^{2/3}(Q-\mathbb{E} Q)\Rightarrow \mathcal{N}(0,\sigma_0^2)$, with explicit variance $\sigma_0^2>0$. This disproves the quartic fluctuation conjecture of Bianchi, Collet and Magnanini (2024). Gaussian limits also hold $(\alpha_c+ \lambda/n,h_c + \gamma/n)$, except when the coefficients satisfy $-\frac{11}{16}+\frac{2}{9}(\gamma+\frac49\lambda)=0$. Under this linearity condition, the limiting laws of $\sqrt n(Q-2/3)$ have densities proportional to $\exp\{-81z^4/64+9\theta z^2/8\}$, where $\theta=-57/16+8\lambda/27$. We obtain a sharp $n^{-1/3}$ rate in $1$-Wasserstein distance for the Gaussian limits and an $O(n^{-1/2})$ bound for the quartic limits. The proofs combine Stein's method for exchangeable pairs with conditional row estimates and a local Dobrushin contraction.

Exponential random graph models (ERGMs) assign probabilities to graphs through an exponential family whose sufficient statistics are some specific subgraph counts. They allow dependence between edges through local interactions that affect global graph structure; see, for example, Holland and Leinhardt (1981); Frank and Strauss (1986); Park and Newman (2004). In this paper, we focus on the dense edge–triangle ERGM, in which the sufficient statistics are the numbers of edges and triangles.

papers.title: Lane-Emden equation for the superposition of a local and nonlocal operator with the "wrong sign"
papers.abstract: We consider the Lane-Emden equation associated with the operator $-\Delta - \gamma \, (-\Delta)^s$ (for positive $\gamma$). First we consider the equation in the entire space and we prove that no Serrin-type critical exponent arises in the $H^1(\mathbb R^n)$ framework. Secondly we consider the problem settled in an open, bounded and connected set and we prove the existence of a positive solution for sufficiently small $s$.

papers.title: Optimal Average Distortion for Non-Expansive Embeddings of Euclidean Metrics into the Line: With applications to cut-matching games and vertex expansion
papers.abstract:
We show that any $n$-point Euclidean metric admits a non-expansive embedding into the line with average distortion at most $O\left(\sqrt{\frac{\log n}{\log\log n}}\right)$, matching a known lower bound.
  We also present two applications of this result. First, we give a cut-player strategy with an optimal spectral guarantee for the undirected cut-matching game. Second, we give an improved spectral approximation for vertex expansion in high-degree graphs.

papers.title: Comparison of melanin subtypes using pump-probe microscopy
papers.abstract: Pump-probe microscopy (PPM) is used to probe excited state dynamics of endogenous chromophores to generate contrast that is unavailable in traditional forms of microscopy. Here we apply PPM to characterize melanin, a pigment central to photoprotection, skin and eye pigmentation, and melanoma pathogenesis. Melanin is notoriously difficult to analyze due to its structural and chemical complexity. We imaged melanin from six different lesion categories: cutaneous nevi, lentigo, cutaneous malignant melanoma, conjunctival melanocytic lesions, vulvar melanocytic lesions, and a murine melanoma model, across 21 independent biological samples and 109 regions of interest. Using model fitting, adapted phasor analysis, and support vector machine classification, we characterize and quantify excited-state dynamics as a surrogate for chemical and structural heterogeneity. Heterogeneity of melanin separates cutaneous from non-cutaneous lesions, but is not correlated with malignancy. Benign lentigo is the most heterogeneous population in the dataset, exceeding cutaneous malignant melanoma, while conjunctival lesions are the most homogeneous despite receiving direct solar exposure. Classification on full transient absorption curves separates most subtypes well above the six-class chance level. These findings demonstrate the ability of PPM to reveal subtle differences in melanin photophysics across diverse tissue environments, with implications for optical tissue classification and the understanding of melanoma pathogenesis.

papers.intro:
Melanin is a natural pigment that is responsible for coloration of skin, hair, and eyes, photoprotection from ultraviolet radiation, and binding of heavy metals[1, 2, 3, 4]. Most melanin is synthesized through the oxidation and polymerization of tyrosine and phenol derivatives in a process known as melanogenesis within specialized cells called melanocytes [1]. In humans, melanin occurs primarily as two chemically distinct pigments: eumelanin, a black-to-brown pigment derived from the oxidative polymerization of L-dopa, and pheomelanin, a yellow-to-reddish brown pigment derived from oxidation of cysteinyl-dopa precursors. During eumelanogenesis, dopachrome is a key intermediate that undergoes decarboxylation to form 5,6-dihydroxyindole (DHI) or tautomerization to form 5,6-dihydroxyindole-2-carboxylic acid (DHICA)[5]. DHI and DHICA oxidatively couple into small oligomers, which oxidize further into nearly planar sheets[6]. Four to five of these sheets, each containing four to eight indole units, stack with a graphite-like interlayer spacing of 3.4 Å to form protomolecules approximately 15 Å in size [7]. Melanocytes package melanin into melanosomes, small organelles of approximately 11 μ\mum size, and deliver them to neighboring epithelial cells, including keratinocytes in cutaneous and vulvar tissue and non-keratinized conjunctival epithelial cells in conjunctival tissue [8, 9].

Four to five of these sheets, each containing four to eight indole units, stack with a graphite-like interlayer spacing of 3.4 Å to form protomolecules approximately 15 Å in size [7]. Melanocytes package melanin into melanosomes, small organelles of approximately 11 μ\mum size, and deliver them to neighboring epithelial cells, including keratinocytes in cutaneous and vulvar tissue and non-keratinized conjunctival epithelial cells in conjunctival tissue [8, 9].

Melanocytes share a common neural crest origin, yet their differentiation is also shaped by anatomical location and local microenvironment, giving rise to biologically distinct melanocytic populations [1]. In the skin, ultraviolet radiation (UVR) exposure drives increased melanin production as part of the photoprotective response, but it also introduces heterogeneity in both pigment distribution and the underlying molecular structure of melanin [2]. Conjunctival melanocytes lie at the conjunctival surface, and transfer melanosomes to the overlying non-keratinized epithelium. Unlike uveal and retinal pigments, they receive direct solar exposure [10]. However, conjunctival melanomas display a unique tissue architecture not found in the skin. The conjunctiva consists of a stratified non-keratinized epithelium lacking rete ridges where the concepts of papillary and reticular stromal organization are not applicable [9]. Although UVR has been implicated indirectly in the pathogenesis of vulvar melanoma, potentially affecting local immune responses, its contribution is far less significant than in cutaneous melanoma because vulvar tissues are generally not exposed to UVR [11, 12, 13]. Prior pump–probe studies have shown that the pump-probe signatures, interpreted as differences in melanin composition and aggregation, differ between melanomas that metastasize and those that do not, underscoring the biological relevance of melanin heterogeneity [14, 6, 15].

Prior pump–probe studies have shown that the pump-probe signatures, interpreted as differences in melanin composition and aggregation, differ between melanomas that metastasize and those that do not, underscoring the biological relevance of melanin heterogeneity [14, 6, 15].

Due to the broad and featureless absorption spectrum of melanin, most conventional imaging techniques are not well suited to study melanin, particularly its spatial heterogeneity. Linear techniques such as reflectance confocal microscopy and optical coherence tomography lack chemical specificity [16]. Multiphoton fluorescence lifetime imaging and Raman spectroscopy have been used to analyze cellular and biochemical changes in melanin exposed to UVR [17, 18, 19]. Fluorescence lifetime imaging microscopy, harmonic generation, and coherent Raman scattering have been successfully applied to melanocytic samples [20, 21, 22, 23, 24], but analysis of the chemical heterogeneity across different melanin populations has not yet been reported, to the best of our knowledge. A comprehensive review about melanin characterization was recently published by Ito and Wakamatsu [25]. Pump-probe microscopy (PPM) has been used to distinguish melanomas that metastasize from melanomas that do not [14, 26, 6], to investigate the chemical structure and building blocks of melanin [27, 28, 29, 15], and to image melanin in specific lesions such as conjunctival and vulvar melanoma [30, 31]. These studies addressed either diagnosis within a single lesion type or synthetic melanin standards, leaving the broader comparison of biologically distinct melanin populations unexplored. In this manuscript, we use PPM to systematically characterize melanin’s chemical heterogeneity across a diverse set of melanocytic lesions, including conjunctival melanocytic lesions, vulvar melanoma, nevi, cutaneous malignant melanoma, lentigo, and a mouse melanoma model. These specimens represent biologically and anatomically distinct melanin populations.

papers.title: The Berger conjecture for three dimensional manifolds
papers.abstract: A conjecture of Berger says that on a simply connected manifold all of whose geodesics are closed, all unit speed geodesics have the same shortest period. In this paper we will show that the S^1-action induced by the geodesic flow is free. We use symplectic geometry to investigate the topology of the quotient of the unit tangent bundle T^1M/S^1 by the S^1 action that comes from the geodesic flow. We show that this quotient admits the structure of a smooth symplectic manifold and that this symplectic manifold is symplectomorphic to S^2 \times S^2 equipped with a split form. This will enable a computation involving the Euler class of the orbibundle T^1M\rightarrow T^1M/S^1 which will lead to a solution of Berger's conjecture for three-dimensional manifolds.

Riemannian manifolds all of whose geodesics are closed have long been objects of particular interest, especially since Zoll and Tannery discovered metrics on the sphere with this property that are different from the round metric. The most familiar examples are the compact symmetric spaces of rank 11, the so-called CROSSes: spheres equipped with the round metric, real, complex, and quaternionic projective spaces equipped with their Fubini–Study metrics, and the Cayley plane. papers.title: Basis statistics for phylogenetic tree shape: tree balance formulas beyond expectations
papers.abstract: Summary statistics that measure the shapes of phylogenetic trees contributed to quantitatively understanding evolutionary processes. Among phylogenetic summary statistics, the tree balance indices have been designed to capture intuitive notions of balance or imbalance in trees. Here, we characterize the tree balance indices in terms of basis statistics, mapping the exponentially large space of rooted, binary, unlabeled trees to lower-dimensional spaces. We observe that many tree balance indices can be represented in terms of linear functions of these low-dimensional spaces, enabling us to compute exact formulas for the means, variances, and covariances of many balance indices under the Yule--Harding model. The new framework recapitulates existing formulas for the expectations of 8 indices: Sackin index, average leaf depth, total cophenetic index, $\hat{s}$-shape statistic, Colless index, corrected Colless index, quadratic Colless index, and rooted quartet index for binary trees. It produces new formulas for the expectations of 9 additional indices: equal weights Colless index, total $I$ index, total $I'$ index, Rogers $J$ index, total internal path length, total path length, average vertex depth, stairs1 index, and stairs2 index. Moreover, the framework also allows us to calculate the exact variance of all 17 indices that are represented by the bases as well as the covariance and correlation for all $\binom{17}{2} = 136$ pairs among the 17 indices.

The Yule-Harding model or equal-rates Markov model (henceforth termed the Yule model), first studied in the context of phylogenetic trees by Harding [38], serves as a useful null model of evolution [60]. In the Yule model, a branching process begins with one lineage. At a set of discrete future times, a lineage randomly chosen among extant lineages splits into two, and all lineages have an equal probability of being the next to split. This process forms a rooted, binary phylogenetic tree, as each lineage can be traced back to the starting lineage through a unique path of splits. papers.title: RTPolicy: Real-Time (32.9 Hz) Multi-View Visuomotor Policy for Robotic Manipulation on Edge Devices
papers.abstract: Low inference latency is critical for closed-loop robotic manipulation, especially under asynchronous inference, where action chunks must be updated promptly to correct accumulated deviations. However, existing visuomotor policies rely on computationally expensive visual backbones, resulting in high inference latency and deployment overhead. In this paper, we propose RTPolicy, a multi-view visuomotor policy that attains accurate manipulation with high inference efficiency. Its core design combines view-aware feature fusion with visual compression to aggregate complementary information across camera views into a compact token representation. The representation conditions a flow-matching action generator with the robot state and flow time, reducing the cost of action generation. Extensive experiments demonstrate that this design reduces the computational cost of visual representation and action generation while preserving visual information required for manipulation. On the RoboTwin~2.0 single-task clean evaluation across 50 tasks, RTPolicy attains a mean success rate of 52.26\%, outperforming the strongest leaderboard baseline $\pi_0$ (46.4\%). We further evaluate RTPolicy under asynchronous streaming inference on a real bimanual platform, where RTPolicy attains a mean success rate of 72.0\% and sustains real-time inference at 30.35 ms (32.9 Hz) on the RDK S600 and 149.72 ms (6.7 Hz) on the RDK S100, both in INT16. papers.intro:
Precise manipulation requires policies that learn from demonstrations while maintaining temporal coherence and responding to new visual observations, especially under asynchronous inference. Visuomotor policies therefore predict short action trajectories and execute them in a receding horizon, as in action chunking [1]. Closed-loop correction [2, 3] keeps the executed plan consistent with the current observation. Inference latency therefore directly determines how quickly fresh observations can affect the executed trajectory.

Existing methods address individual sources of inference cost. Consistency and flow-based policies [6, 7, 8] reduce the number of action generation steps, but generally leave the visual encoder and multi-view conditioning path unchanged. Diffusion Policy (DP) [9] offers low latency, but its mean success rate is 29.3% and its single-view setup does not address the cost of multi-view conditioning (Fig. 1). Achieving low latency and high manipulation accuracy with multi-view inputs remains a challenge for deployment on edge devices.

Hence, we propose RTPolicy, a visuomotor framework that jointly reduces the costs of visual encoding, multi-view conditioning, and iterative action generation. It uses a frozen DINOv3 ConvNeXt encoder [10] to obtain visual features from multi-view images. VGGT [11] and VO-DP [4] have demonstrated the value of geometric visual representations for perception and manipulation. To preserve spatial information across views, our view-aware feature fusion module assigns a learnable embedding to each view and exchanges information within and across views. A visual compression module then compresses the fused representation into a compact visual condition before it feeds a flow-based Diffusion Transformer. This framework reduces visual conditioning cost while retaining spatial information for precise manipulation (Fig. 1). In simulation and on a real bimanual platform, RTPolicy attains the highest mean success rate among the compared methods while supporting real-time deployment across the tested devices (Fig. 1). papers.title: Hyperbolic embedding of higher-order simplicial networks
papers.abstract: Many biological interactions involve groups rather than pairs, as when several proteins assemble into a multi-protein complex. Simplicial complexes naturally capture these collective interactions. Existing hyperbolic embeddings represent network hierarchy and similarity through a few interpretable coordinates, but rely only on pairwise links: they cannot distinguish three units engaged in a common interaction from three units connected only in pairs. We introduce here the hyperbolic higher-order (HHO) embedding, which embeds a simplicial complex into the Poincar\'e disk, while incorporating its group interactions. The hyperbolic area of the triangle spanned by three interacting nodes then measures how compactly their interaction is represented. Testson synthetic and real-world networks, including a co-authorship network and the protein interaction network of \textit{Escherichia coli}, show that HHO reduces the hyperbolic area of triangles representing simplices relative to those obtained from pairwise network embeddings. HHO also recovers node groups more accurately than pairwise embeddings and a weighted-clique alternative, with performance competitive with Euclidean embeddings, while providing a low-dimensional representation that can be analyzed with the tools of network geometry.

papers.intro:
Complex networks provide a powerful framework to describe the structure of a wide range of real systems, from technological infrastructures to social, biological, and brain networks [1, 2]. A central question, both from theoretical and applied perspectives, concerns the latent geometry that underlies the observed connectivity patterns. In this context, hyperbolic geometry has emerged as a particularly fruitful paradigm for modeling real complex networks, mainly because of its ability to simultaneously represent hierarchies, degree heterogeneity, and community structures [3, 4, 5, 6].

A central question, both from theoretical and applied perspectives, concerns the latent geometry that underlies the observed connectivity patterns. In this context, hyperbolic geometry has emerged as a particularly fruitful paradigm for modeling real complex networks, mainly because of its ability to simultaneously represent hierarchies, degree heterogeneity, and community structures [3, 4, 5, 6].

In parallel, the study of collective phenomena in complex systems has progressively moved beyond the framework of purely pairwise interactions to incorporate higher-order interactions, modeled by hypergraphs or simplicial complexes [7, 8]. This growing recognition of the importance of higher-order interactions in complex systems highlights the need for novel analytical tools that jointly capture latent geometry and higher-order connectivity, and that can be applied across diverse domains, from synthetic networks to real interconnected systems. The present work contributes to this direction by introducing a general method to embed simplicial complexes in hyperbolic space through a multilayer representation.

This growing recognition of the importance of higher-order interactions in complex systems highlights the need for novel analytical tools that jointly capture latent geometry and higher-order connectivity, and that can be applied across diverse domains, from synthetic networks to real interconnected systems. The present work contributes to this direction by introducing a general method to embed simplicial complexes in hyperbolic space through a multilayer representation.

The seminal work of Krioukov and collaborators showed that many complex networks can be understood as realizations of geometric graphs in hyperbolic space [3]: nodes have latent coordinates in a negatively curved space, and the probability of a link depends on a combination of popularity, encoded by the radial coordinate, and similarity, encoded by the angular coordinate [9]. This framework reproduces heavy-tailed degree distributions, strong clustering and hierarchical organization within a single geometric model [3, 5], and the map of the Internet inferred from it accounts simultaneously for its topology and its routing properties [4]. Network geometry has since been formalized as a general framework relating topology to latent geometry [5], and hyperbolic coordinates can be inferred from real network data, either by maximum likelihood, as in Mercator [6], or by manifold learning, as in coalescent embeddings [10]. Hyperbolic geometry has attracted considerable interest in machine learning as a framework for representing hierarchical and relational data. Notable examples include Poincaré embeddings [11] and hyperbolic graph neural networks [12]. Its suitability for hierarchical representations is supported by the fact that trees can be embedded in hyperbolic space with arbitrarily low distortion, even in low dimensions [13].

In many complex systems, interactions occur among groups of entities rather than exclusively between pairs: several authors co-sign a scientific article, multiple species compete for shared resources, and proteins interact collectively within molecular complexes, naturally giving rise to higher-order (HO) network representations based on hypergraphs and simplicial complexes. Hypergraphs and simplicial complexes provide the natural language to describe such higher-order interactions [7, 8, 14]. In a simplicial complex, every subset of a group is itself a group, which makes the tools of algebraic topology available [15]. Group interactions qualitatively change collective dynamics. In simplicial contagion models, in which transmission requires the joint presence of several neighbors, the transition to an endemic state becomes discontinuous, a behavior that pairwise models do not reproduce [16]; higher-order Kuramoto dynamics on simplicial complexes can make synchronization explosive [17]; and in models of ecological competition, interactions among more than two species stabilize the coexistence of large communities [18]. Group interactions also have a structural signature. In co-authorship and many other datasets, new group interactions preferentially form among nodes that are already linked, a process of simplicial closure that makes higher-order structure partly predictable [19], and persistent homology characterizes the higher-order organization of scientific collaborations across disciplines [20]. In neuroscience, for instance, cliques and cavities reveal aspects of the higher-order organization of brain networks that are invisible at the level of simple pairwise interactions [21, 22, 23, 24]. In all these cases, the group interactions carry information that their pairwise representation does not.

Cellular networks offer a particularly natural setting in which latent geometry and higher-order structure coexist. Many biological processes involve more than two partners, such as a protein complex assembled from several subunits or a metabolic reaction involving multiple substrates and products, and are therefore not faithfully represented by pairwise edges[25]. At the same time, the metabolic networks of E. coli and human cells have been shown to be congruent with an underlying hidden geometry in which proximity encodes structural similarity[26]. Protein interaction networks, in which experimentally characterized complexes define higher-order groups on top of pairwise interactions, therefore constitute a natural testbed for geometric and higher-order methods.

Despite these parallel advances, the two lines of research (hyperbolic geometry and HO representations) have remained largely disconnected. Existing hyperbolic embedding methods for network data, whether based on maximum likelihood [4, 6], on manifold learning [10, 27], or on gradient-based optimization [11], take as input a graph of pairwise connections. Applying them to a simplicial complex therefore requires first reducing it to its 1-skeleton, the graph of its edges. This reduction is lossy: a filled triangle, which represents a genuine three-body interaction, and an empty triangle, formed by three independent pairwise links, have the same 1-skeleton and are thus embedded identically. More generally, higher-order interactions are often represented by projecting each group onto a clique in a pairwise network. However, this projection discards information about group membership and introduces pairwise links that may not correspond to actual dyadic interactions, thereby artificially increasing network density [28].

papers.title: The Unusual X-ray Spectrum of R Mon
papers.abstract: The optically obscured young star R Mon illuminates Hubble's Variable Nebula and has historically been classified as an intermediate mass pre-main sequence Herbig Be star. We present Chandra observations of R Mon revealing a hard X-ray source viewed through high absorption from circumstellar gas known to be present from previous CO observations. The X-ray spectrum is characterized by line emission from the He-like Fe K complex (6.7 keV) tracing very hot plasma and fluorescent Fe emission (6.4 keV) from cold gas near the star that is irradiated by hard X-rays. Low-level variability on a timescale of less than one day is detected, but no large impulsive flares. The hot plasma and variability cannot be explained by shock models and magnetically confined plasma is inferred. The hard X-ray spectrum of R Mon does not resemble the soft spectra of prototypical Herbig stars but is remarkably similar to some class I protostars such as NGC 2071-IRS 1. As judged by its X-ray and infrared properties, we conclude that R Mon is a class I protostar and thus provides a rare snapshot of an emergent intermediate mass star enveloped in X-ray irradiated gas and dust.

The massive young star R Mon illuminates Hubble’s Variable Nebula (NGC 2261). R Mon has historically been classified as a pre-main sequence Herbig Be star with a peculiar and variable spectrum (G.H. Herbig & K.R. Bell 1988; L.A. Hillenbrand et al. 1992). The central star is obscured by dust and visible only in scattered light in the optical. The extinction toward R Mon is wavelength dependent. The infrared observations of L.M. Close et al. (1997) give AV = 13.8±\pm1.2 mag but optical measurements yield lower values due to the increased effects of scattered light. The distance to R Mon is estimated to be ∼\sim800 pc based on the assumption that it is associated with the nearby young cluster NGC 2264 (M.F. Walker 1956; B.F. Jones & G.H. Herbig 1982). This is in reasonably good agreement with the distance of 760 pc estimated by L.M. Close et al. (1997). A second fainter IR source (R Mon B) is present at an offset 0.67′′-0.71′′ from R Mon along P.A. ≈\approx 291.5∘ - 293.6∘ and is classified as an accreting classical T Tauri star (cTTS) (L.M. Close et al. 1997; G. Weigelt et al. 2002; S.J. Thomas et al. 2023).

Herbig (1982) who also concluded that R Mon has a latitude-dependent wind (predominantly polar). Additional evidence for ionized mass loss was provided by extended centimeter radio continuum emission detected in high resolution VLA observations (S.L. Skinner, A. Brown, & R.T. Stewart 1993).

A short 10 ks pointed Chandra X-ray Observatory (CXO) observation in 2018 (Table 1) obtained with the Advanced CCD Imaging Spectrometer (ACIS-S) detected a faint X-ray source near the R Mon 2MASS near-IR position with a hard X-ray spectrum and high median event energy E50 = 5.06 keV. There were no detected events with energies E << 3.89 keV. The hard spectrum shows a fluorescent Fe Kα\alpha line (6.4 keV) and bears no resemblace to soft-spectrum Herbig Ae/Be stars like AB Aur (A. Telleschi et al. 2007), HD 163296 (D.A. Swartz et al. 2005), and HD 100546 (S.L. Skinner & M. Güdel 2020). This motivated us to obtain a deeper Chandra observation of R Mon with the objective of acquiring a better quality spectrum suitable for more detailed analysis and to confirm the presence of the fluorescent Fe line. The new Chandra observations discussed herein show that R Mon is a variable X-ray source and confirm the hard spectrum and fluorescent Fe emission. We discuss possible origins of the X-ray emission in the context of what is known about other young stars and protostars.

papers.title: Andreev-Enhanced Conductance in a Bilayer Graphene Quantum Point Contact
papers.abstract: Quantum point contacts provide a platform for probing mode-dependent Andreev reflection. Here, we demonstrate Andreev-enhanced conductance in a gate-defined bilayer graphene quantum point contact coupled to a superconducting aluminum electrode. Electrostatic gating enables sequential mode occupation, verified by normal-state conductance quantization. In the superconducting state, the conductance is enhanced within the conductance plateaus, while the enhancement decreases between plateaus, consistent with the nonlinear transmission dependence of Andreev reflection. The enhancement yields effective transmission probabilities up to 0.9, and extends over a bias window of approximately 140 $\mu$V, which we associate with a proximity-induced superconducting gap, close to the gap of the aluminum film. For in-plane fields, the enhancement persists up to the critical field, and the bias window follows the spectral gap predicted by Abrikosov-Gor'kov theory. In contrast, perpendicular fields suppress the enhancement approximately linearly from zero field, deviating from homogeneous pair breaking and indicative of flux penetration.

papers.title: SecPO: Principled Adversarial Training for Prompt Injection Security
papers.abstract: Recognized as a top threat to AI agents, prompt injection allows instructions from untrusted data (email, documents, websites) to manipulate the agent's operation. The existing best-defended LLM, Meta-SecAlign, is trained with the DPO loss but still suffers from attack success rates (ASRs) approaching 100% under adaptive prompt injections. One reason is that DPO anchors the model around the undefended reference model, which is insecure. We show an idealized reference model---an injection-invariant, utility-preserving oracle---can nevertheless be approximated, as its output distribution in training is interestingly accessible. This new observation motivates a theoretically principled SecPO loss. Another Meta-SecAlign shortcoming is that it trains on weak simulated attacks. We implement an efficient adversarial training (AT) pipeline that synthesizes strong injected inputs (best@240), and train the model on them. Our AT reduces ASRs by 1.5-14.5$\times$ across three SoTA adaptive attacks, compared with Meta-SecAlign; the SecPO loss reduces them by a further 2.4-4.6$\times$ compared with using DPO loss. In agentic workflows, our SecPO + AT Qwen3.6-27B is much more secure than Meta-SecAlign: 8.8% vs. 78.8% AgentDojo ASR@800 under the AttackerMovesSecond attack. Moreover, our defended model shows no noticeable reduction in benign utility in nine benchmarks covering agentic tool calling, instruction following, science, and math. We release our $\href{//github.com/Sizhe-Chen/SecPO}{\text{code}}$, $\href{//huggingface.co/datasets/Sizhe-Chen/Qwen3.6-27B-Instruct-SecPO-trainset}{\text{training data}}$ (with optimized injections from AT), and $\href{//huggingface.co/Sizhe-Chen/Qwen3.6-27B-Instruct-SecPO}{\text{model}}$.

Rapid progress in large language models (LLMs) unlocks exciting agentic applications: a software engineering agent can work autonomously for seven hours on a complex task in a codebase containing 12.5 million lines of code, with only occasional human guidance [4]. A running agent interacts frequently with the real-world environment (e.g., code repositories, websites, documents) that may not be trusted. An attacker can post malicious content to hijack an agent’s execution. In an actual incident, the attacker created a GitHub issue with a specially crafted title; a coding agent read the malicious title and was hijacked into executing attacker-controlled code [19]. This prompt injection attack is listed as the top threat to AI agents [69]. Vulnerabilities to prompt injection allow external attackers to control the agent through simple actions, such as creating a GitHub issue [19], sending an email [80], or writing a sentence (“disregard all prior instructions and …”) in a file [29]. AI agent deployment has been held back due to uncontrollable security risks from prompt injections [92].

papers.title: Approximate Polynomial Satisfiability and Integral Closure Membership in the Counting Hierarchy
papers.abstract:
Andrews, Garg, and Schost recently, in a breakthrough result, placed Hilbert's Nullstellensatz (HN) in the Counting Hierarchy ($\CH$) using constant-depth circuits for multivariate resultants. While HN deals with exact polynomial satisfiability, Guo, Saxena, and Sinhababu (CCC~2018; Theory of Computing~2019) introduced approximate polynomial satisfiability (APS) as a natural approximative analogue of polynomial system satisfiability. They proved its $\mathsf{NP}$-hardness and a $\PSPACE$ upper bound, and used APS to construct hitting sets for $\overline{\mathsf{VP}}$ in polynomial space, substantially narrowing the GCT chasm in geometric complexity theory.
  We place APS in the Counting Hierarchy for rational polynomials given by arithmetic circuits. Our proof combines Noether normalization with a geometric restriction on how points in the image of a polynomial map approach the origin, reducing APS to a test on multivariate resultants which allows solvability in $\CH$. It complements the independent and concurrent proofs of Balaji, Shirmohammadi, Tavenas, and Worrell, and Andrews, Garg, Oliveira, and Schost. Moreover, we also place integral closure membership testing in the Counting Hierarchy. Here, the question is whether a given polynomial $f$ is integral over $\C[f_1,\ldots,f_m]$. Our approach uses a global annihilator criterion and an effective degree bound to reduce non-integrality to APS in polynomial time.

papers.title: Faster #PPM from faster #3SAT
papers.abstract:
The counting variant (#PPM) of the permutation pattern matching (PPM) problem asks for the number of occurrences of a permutation pattern in a host permutation of length $n$. The problem admits faster algorithms than the trivial $O^*(2^n)$ time enumeration; the best known running time, for both PPM and #PPM, is $O(1.415^n)$ (Gawrychowski and Rzepecki). It is also known that PPM is ETH-hard: an algorithm with running time $2^{o(n/\log{n})}$ would imply a subexponential algorithm for 3SAT (Jel\'{i}nek, Opler, and Pek\'{a}rek).
  We give a reduction in the opposite direction, showing that an algorithm for counting satisfying assignments of a 3-CNF formula (#3SAT) in time $2^{O({n}/{f(n)})}$, where $n$ is the number of variables, yields an algorithm for #PPM with running time $2^{O({n \sqrt{\log{f(n)}/{f(n)}}})}$. In particular, the recently claimed refutation of ETH by OpenAI implies a #3SAT algorithm with an improvement factor $f(n) \in \Omega(\sqrt{\log{n}}/\log\log{n})$ in the exponent; this yields, through our reduction, a subexponential algorithm for #PPM.

papers.title: Only the immortal can (almost) flock while turning: Two-dimensional chiral immortal flocks, time crystals and non-universal sub-logarithmic roughness
papers.abstract: We study two-dimensional chiral ``dry'' (non-momentum conserving) ``immortal'' (number conserving) ``flocks'' (polar ordered active fluids). Noise driven fluctuations about the noise-free ``time crystal'' state, in which the velocity rotates uniformly in time, obey coupled Kardar-Parisi-Zhang-like equations for the local velocity orientation and a conserved concentration field; the latter field stabilizes order. Orientational fluctuations grow only sub-logarithmically, and number fluctuations are suppressed (``hyperuniform''); both exhibit nonuniversal scaling exponents. There are three different universality classes of disordering transitions.

papers.title: Quantitative Ultrasound Characterizes Perfusion Trajectories in Healthy and Inflamed Gingival Wound Healing
papers.abstract:
Rationale and Objectives: Visual examination of extraction-site healing provides limited insight into underlying vascular recovery. We developed a quantitative ultrasound framework to assess gingival perfusion and persistent inflammation.
  Materials and Methods: Patients (n = 51) undergoing extraction and socket preservation were imaged longitudinally using color-flow ultrasound and laser speckle contrast analysis (LASCA) from 2 weeks to 3 months after extraction. Pre-scan-converted Total Recall Imaging (TRI) data with phase information were processed using scan conversion, bilateral filtering, and power estimation to derive velocity-weighted color pixel density (CPDvel). Gingival regions of interest were automatically segmented using deep learning and assessed with Dice and Bland-Altman analyses. CPDvel was compared between healthy and inflamed visits in early (<35 days) and recovery (>35 days) periods and with LASCA.
  Results: Segmentation achieved a mean Dice score of 0.98 and median of 0.99 (IQR, 0.98-0.99), with minimal area bias (-0.005%; 95% limits of agreement, -1.68% to 1.67%). Median CPDvel decreased by 81% between early and recovery periods in healthy visits (p = 0.01), compared with a nonsignificant 26% reduction in inflamed visits (p = 0.31). During recovery, CPDvel was higher in inflamed than healthy visits (0.12 vs 0.03 cm/s; p = 0.04). LASCA showed smaller reductions (13% and 9%, respectively). CPDvel was positively correlated with LASCA in healthy (one-sided p = 0.03) and inflamed visits (one-sided p = 0.13).
  Conclusions: TRI-based quantitative ultrasound enabled automated perfusion assessment with reduced dependence on scanner display settings. Distinct perfusion patterns and more pronounced temporal changes than LASCA support its potential for noninvasive monitoring of oral wound healing and persistent inflammation.

papers.title: Dirichlet form approach to stochastic thin-film equations
papers.abstract:
The thin-film equation describes the evolution of a thin liquid film driven by capillarity and limited by viscosity. For sufficiently small film heights, thermal fluctuations may not be neglected. Since the thin-film equation as an overdamped evolution equation has a gradient flow structure, the informal implementation of the fluctuation-dissipation principle is straightforward. In this paper, we work out that the concept of Dirichlet forms and the related construction of Markov processes are tailor-made for this type of overdamped continuum evolution with thermal noise. However, the concept of Dirichlet forms relies on the availability of a Gibbsian equilibrium measure, which, in case of the thin-film equation, limits the treatment to the $(1+1)$-dimensional case.
  By means of Dirichlet form theory, we obtain the existence and uniqueness of the evolution of laws on configuration space. We show that the regularity of the realizations of this Markov process matches the heuristics. In a simplified situation with a Gaussian reference measure and a non-degenerate mobility function, we characterize it as what is called an energy solution. The latter provides a pathwise decomposition of the driving forces into a deterministic and a thermal one, which was the starting point.
  Applying the same techniques in the spatially discretized setting proposed in [Math. Comp. 92 (2023), 1931--1976], we obtain the same results uniformly in the discretization parameter. In particular, Galerkin as well as spectral approximations of the stochastic thin-film equation are shown to be uniformly tight in optimal topologies. In the simplified setting, we also prove Mosco convergence of the associated Dirichlet forms and thereby obtain convergence of these approximations.

papers.title: RecIS: Unifying Sparse and Dense Computation for Efficient Recommendation Training
papers.abstract:
Modern recommender models scale sparse representations and dense computation together. They process thousands of heterogeneous feature fields, long user-behavior sequences, and trillion-scale Embedding parameters, while their dense networks increasingly use large Transformer architectures. The resulting execution mismatch creates fine-grained operations within stages, load imbalance and synchronization delays across devices, and GPU resource bubbles between stages. As models grow, these costs become a primary limit to scalable recommender training. Although existing systems improve Embedding caching and data prefetching, these inefficiencies still coexist in the GPU-centric workloads we study and jointly limit end-to-end throughput.
  We present RecIS, a unified framework for GPU-centric recommender training. RecIS treats the complete path from input features to dense computation as one optimization target and coordinates three complementary mechanisms. First, adaptive fusion combines fragmented feature transformations with vectorized memory access. Second, a GPU Embedding engine uses hash-based sharding and hierarchical communication to balance request placement and eliminate redundant transfers; it also specializes aggregation for forward and backward index structures. Third, a multistage pipeline overlaps input preparation for future iterations with dense computation in the current iteration. Together, these mechanisms reorganize a fragmented sparse front end into a dataflow that continuously feeds dense computation.
  We evaluate RecIS on representative industrial recommender models across distributed training platforms. Compared with PICASSO and TorchRec, RecIS reaches up to $2.62\times$ and $1.15\times$ their throughput, respectively, while reducing step latency by up to 61.5\% and 12.9\%. RecIS provides an efficient and scalable training system for large recommender models.

papers.title: A four-dimensional residue calculus for quaternionic slice regular functions
papers.abstract: We develop a 4-dimensional residue calculus for quaternionic slice semiregular functions. Its local singularities are isolated real poles and 2-dimensional spheres. For the latter, we introduce a spherical residue and characterize it as a spherical Laurent coefficient, as the sum of two classical residues on any full complex slice, and by a finite differential procedure involving alternating spherical and slice derivatives. The residue theorem expresses a weighted boundary flux on a circular domain as the sum of the real and spherical residues it contains. Beyond this formula, polynomially weighted flux moments recover every coefficient of every finite principal part, including the companion coefficient at a spherical pole, invisible to ordinary residue summation. Once the polar components and order bounds are fixed, the quotient of the real polynomial ring by the global pole polynomial is the finite-dimensional algebra of weights. We prove that the residue pairing is well defined and nondegenerate, and identifies formal principal parts with the full quaternion-valued real dual of this algebra. Hermite interpolation and the Chinese remainder theorem provide global weights selecting each local coefficient. We separate the regularity domain of the function from the geometry of integration: for a smooth noncircular integration domain compactly contained in a circular ambient domain, away from the reals and with boundary disjoint from the polar set, we establish an exact residue formula with an explicit volume correction governed by the Cauchy-Fueter operator. The theory includes higher-order poles, exceptional points, product domains, and zero divisors. Applications give formulas for rational and oscillatory integrals on the imaginary hyperplane and characterize the rational data on the 3-dimensional imaginary subspace of the quaternions admitting a canonical slice regular extension.

papers.title: From Training Exposure to Membership Evidence: A Controlled Study of OLMo 2
papers.abstract: Whether a language model was trained on a document matters for copyright, privacy, and benchmark contamination. Yet most membership-inference (MI) evaluations on language models collect members and non-members after the fact, so success may reflect distribution shift and failure is inconclusive. We re-ran OLMo 2 1B's official 50-billion-token mid-training stage, replacing selected training chunks with documents from 7,814 pairs matched on domain and difficulty. For each pair, a coin flip determined which document was inserted and which was held out. The run released by the Allen Institute for AI (AI2) from the same seed saw identical data everywhere else and serves as the counterfactual. One exposure raises a previously unseen document's likelihood on average but rarely identifies it. Using the counterfactual as reference, the reference ratio has an area under the ROC curve (AUC) of 0.767 but, with one threshold across domains, catches 3.8% of members at a 1% false-positive rate (FPR). In contrast, 13 matched pairs give a paired test 80% power at the 5% level to detect training on a collection, given same-domain non-members and a close reference. A reference trained with another seed recovers 92% of the counterfactual's AUC advantage over chance, whereas reference-free attacks stay within 0.07 of chance when pooled over domains. The full official post-training recipe, re-run on both models, leaves 89% of the average effect. Even with a closely matched reference, substantial document-level variability limits individual membership inference. We will release the checkpoints, per-token log-probabilities, and the evaluation documents; the code is available at https://github.com/ali-bana/OLMo-Twin.

papers.title: Patch-Based Deep Kernel Learning for Data Assimilation and Bias Correction with Extremely Sparse Observations
papers.abstract: Data Assimilation (DA) reconstructs the state of a spatio-temporal system by combining sensor observations with the output of a numerical model. Since model states are high-dimensional while observations cover only a small fraction of the domain, DA is a challenging large-scale estimation problem, central to weather forecasting and oceanography. Classical variational methods such as 3D-Var rely on a hand-crafted background error covariance that assumes unbiased errors, and therefore cannot capture state-dependent correlations or systematic model biases. Moreover, their cost grows with the size of the domain. Deep learning (DL) methods can perform DA and bias correction (BC) non-linearly, but typically offer limited interpretability and no calibrated uncertainty estimates. We propose a hybrid framework that couples a convolutional neural network (CNN) with a learnable-kernel Gaussian Process (GP) to jointly perform DA and BC from extremely sparse observations. The model is trained end-to-end by maximizing the marginal log-likelihood, learns a data-driven covariance over the whole grid, and provides both the Maximum A Posteriori analysis and its uncertainty by design. A patch-based strategy reduces the $O(N^3)$ training cost of exact GPs over $N$ grid points to $O(N)$ for a fixed patch size. Inference remains exact and only requires solving a linear system whose $O(m^3)$ cost depends on the number of observations $m \ll N$, not on the domain. The learned covariance can also replace the hand-crafted one in 3D-Var, improving its accuracy without changing the variational formulation. Experiments on sea surface temperature and salinity, with both synthetic and real, extremely sparse in-situ observations, show that the framework outperforms 3D-Var, a classical GP and a competing DL model, while reducing inference time by more than 98% with respect to 3D-Var.

papers.title: Multiple Swap Local Search Approximations for Uniform-Cost Capacitated Facility Location with Extensions to Outliers
papers.abstract:
We study metric facility location with customer incompatibilities, where the clients assigned to each facility must satisfy prescribed independence constraints. We first consider the setting of facility-opening costs and where there is a single matroid $\mathcal M$ over the clients and the set of clients assigned to an open facility must be an independent set in $\mathcal M$. We develop a polynomial-time \((1+\sqrt{2}+\epsilon)\)-approximation algorithm for this setting. We further obtain a polynomial-time \((15+\epsilon)\)-approximation algorithm for the case of non-uniform facility-opening costs when $\mathcal M$ is a partition matroid that only permits $b_g$ clients to be assigned to a facility for each group $g$ in the partition. Both settings are substantial generalizations of Capacitated Facility Location with uniform capacities.
  Our algorithms are based on local search using add, delete, and single-swap operations. As with CFL, bounding the connection cost is reasonably straightforward using supermodularity of the minimum connection-cost function. However, bounding the facility opening costs requires novel arguments in both cases. We use a ``compression'' argument based on matroid exchange principles to identify a subset of the locally opened facilities whose size is no larger than that of an optimal facility set. The opening costs of facilities outside this subset can be bounded using supermodularity, while bounding the costs of the remaining facilities requires different arguments.
  It is natural to consider a variant where each possible facility $i$ has its own matroid $\mathcal M_i$ defining the subsets of clients it can feasibly serve. We also show problem is at least as hard to approximate as Set Cover even if all $\mathcal M_i$ are partition matroids that have the same partition of clients, just different group bounds $b_g$.

papers.title: Hyperelliptic curves on $(1,d)$ abelian surfaces for $d\leq 15$
papers.abstract: Bryan, Oberdieck, Pandharipande and Yin predicted the number of hyperelliptic curves on general abelian surfaces under a transversality condition. Some of the numbers have already been confirmed. In this paper we construct singular hyperelliptic curves on $(1,d)$ polarised abelian surfaces for $d\leq 15$ confirming a few predicted numbers, namely of (geometric) genus $g=d$ and of geometric genus $k+3$ on $(1,2k)$ and $(1,2k+1)$ polarised surfaces. Moreover, we have found that all genus 7 hyperelliptic curves on general $(1,8)$ polarised surfaces are double coverings of curves locally embedded into $(1,4)$ polarised surfaces. More interestingly, there is a unique genus 9 hyperelliptic curve (up to translation) locally embedded into a general $(1,12)$ polarised surface and it is a Klein covering of a curve locally embedded into a $(1,3)$ polarised surface.
